About this work

Sermones et Exhortationes ad Monachos — "Sermons and Exhortations to Monks" — gathers Trithemius's addresses to his community as a reforming Benedictine abbot, pressing for stricter observance of the Rule against the lax monasticism of his day. They sit with his other reform texts — De Triplici Regione Claustralium, De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis — and together they form the pastoral engine of his Sponheim programme: the sermons are where the reform treatises are preached.

This is the 1516 Strasbourg edition (BSB scan) — the second of two witnesses of the Sermones et Exhortationes in this corpus (the other is prdl-24393), a separate Strasbourg printing of the same year. The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No published English translation is known;

    Sermons and Exhortations to Monks

    Sermons and Exhortations to Monks, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, afterward of Wuerzburg. Of these sermons there are two books: the first is called the book of Homilies, the second the book of Sermons.

    The Decastich of Ottomar Luscinius of Strasbourg on the homilies of Johannes Trithemius to monks

    If it is not enough for anyone to follow your gentle laws, O Christ, laws of equity, unless he recalls the monks: Serapion, Paulius, and Antony, who once set foot upon the path that bristles with countless rough places; who strives to show that the body is tormented by a rough cloak, and does not allow a feather-bed on the couch; that fasts may drive away the swollen pride of the mind; that brief rest may cherish the half-sleeping limbs: these things they taught silently by their deeds. But Trithemius is more apt than they, for he has power both with tongue and hand.

    With the grace and privilege of the Imperial Majesty.

    Maximilian, by the favor of divine clemency elected Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, and King of Germany, Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, etc.; Archduke of Austria; Duke of Burgundy, Brabant, etc.; Count Palatine, etc.: to the honorable and devout John Trithemius, beloved by us, Abbot of Saint James the Greater at Wurzburg, imperial grace and every good thing.

    Since you have humbly set forth to us that you have composed various editions of both ancient and modern authors, collected not without great labor, vigils, and diligence, which you desired with your whole mind to be brought forth into the light; and since, for a matter of this kind, our beloved subject and that of the Holy Roman Empire, Master Johannes Haselberg of Constance, offered himself with a most ready spirit to be the agent, and therefore procured at great expense the forms by which he may be able to print the aforesaid works: we, therefore, desiring that provision be made for the indemnity of the aforesaid Master Johannes and for the ornament of your honor, lest your works, composed by you with great labors and vigils, should lie hidden as though covered with rust, but rather should shine forth more and more each day, have given and granted to the aforesaid Master Johannes Haselberg of Constance full faculty and authority in every respect, as by the tenor of these presents we give and grant it.

    We decree that he may print, sell when printed, and dispose wherever he wishes of whatever, among treatises and little works, has been edited by you, the aforesaid Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James the Greater at Wurzburg, and has been reviewed and approved by the honorable Conrad Peutinger, doctor and our faithful beloved councillor. We forbid all and singular chalcographers and printers of books, of whatever condition, under the penalty written below, commanding more strictly that they shall not dare or presume to print or publish such works, or similar ones, for ten years after they have been published by the said Master Johannes, nor to publish, buy, or sell them when printed by others, throughout the whole Roman Empire and in our hereditary lands.

    We command all and singular our beloved faithful subjects and those of the Holy Roman Empire, of whatever estate, condition, dignity, or office, whether ecclesiastical or secular, under penalty of our indignation and that of the Holy Roman Empire most grievously, and of ten marks of pure gold, to be applied, one half to our treasury and the other half to the aforesaid Master Johannes Haselberg, as often as anything shall have been done to the contrary, that they assist the same Master Johannes of Constance with their favor and aid in their places and lands, and by no means permit the said works and treatises to be printed, or those printed elsewhere to be sold. Rather, let them immediately declare in our name that all who presume to do anything against this our grace and prohibition have incurred the sentence of this our indignation and that of the Holy Roman Empire, executing in this matter our expressed will.

    In testimony whereof, these letters have been authenticated with our seal impressed on the back. Given in our town of Innsbruck, on the tenth day of the month of November, in the year of the Lord 1513, in the twenty-ninth year of our Roman reign, and the twenty-fifth of Hungary.

    Letter

    Johannes Trithemius, called the Sponheimite, to his reverend father and teacher, lord Johannes of Colenhausen, abbot of the monastery of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter in Seligenstadt, but formerly my predecessor at Sponheim: reverence and honor.

    I do not know, my ever-venerable teacher, under what unlucky star that monastery of Sponheim was built, since an abbot rarely dies in it, but almost all of them, overcome by weariness, as I find from the annals, have for nearly seventy years now resigned of their own free will. We are not wholly ignorant why you too, following the example of those before you, deserted us poor men before the time; we rightly blame both our poverty and the rebellious rashness of certain persons. I now experience, alas, the cause that moved your mind to leave the Sponheim abbacy, wholly barren and unfruitful, over which you presided for thirteen years from the reform, not without continual anxiety of mind and infinite labors. I pass over the wrongs of very many of the brothers which you endured; all these are indeed daily doubled upon me.

    You ordered me to send to your fatherliness the book of my exhortations to the brothers, which I recently composed by lamplight amid the raging occupations of worldly affairs. Although it is unworthy of your reading, nevertheless I have been unwilling to resist a parent's command. Therefore I beg your gentleness graciously to apply the file of correction: if anything is lacking, add it; cut away what is superfluous; and either commit what is inept to the flames or certainly set it in order. Farewell, sweetest father, and remember me. From Sponheim, the sixth day of the month of August, in the year of the Christians 1386.

    Homily I. Folio III.

    In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here begins the first book of exhortations to monks, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim and later of Würzburg. On the spiritual warfare of monks.

    It befits Christian warfare, brothers, and especially that of monks, to be subject to the various calamities of this world, and, like gold in the furnace, to be continually exercised and tested by tribulations. For it belongs to monks to surpass, by a higher manner of living, the common rule of Christian warfare, and to obey not only the Lord's commandments but also his counsels. It belongs to monks, for love of God, utterly to despise riches, honors, and all the profane pleasures of the world, and, once fleshly desires have been overcome, to be constantly free for God alone. For a monk is so called as being solitary, from unity, so that by the very designation of his name he may be admonished to contempt of the world.

    Accordingly the office of a monk is to stand with himself in solitude, clean and purified from vices, and sweetly to love Christ above all things. For Christ is the goal of monks, toward which regular discipline is directed; whoever refuses to imitate him is indeed neither a monk nor a Christian. Therefore, my brothers, we must know that not everyone who says to me, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he shall enter into the kingdom of heaven. And what the will of God is, the holy Apostle disclosed, saying: This is the will of God, your sanctification. But since the necessary consummation of this commanded sanctification requires from us great endurance of evils in all things, and humility, because no one is holy by his own powers, we must, my brothers, keep continual consideration of our vocation before ourselves, lest, growing sluggish in most destructive idleness, we be overcome in the military contest by the enemy, who, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking some incautious person, and one languishing in soul, to devour as he perishes.

    For we are soldiers of God, fighting against a threefold adversary, namely the flesh, the world, and the devil. It is a two-sided war and an exceedingly hard contest: to suffer as enemy the one whom nature has given as familiar. Let us therefore arm ourselves, dearest brothers, with the ornaments of the virtues, because whoever is adorned with the splendor of good works is not easily overcome by the adversary. First, let us fortify ourselves with the most constant faith of the holy and undivided Trinity; its devout and sincere confession by mind and mouth drives far away all the wicked devices and deceits of demons, and, overcoming the greatest enemy, casts him down and utterly enfeebles him. Then let us take up for ourselves a most fervent charity toward God and neighbor, which is fearful to demons above all things, especially if it has been rooted in true Christian humility. Let us not give confidence to our soul, since he is called blessed who is always fearful; but he who is of hard mind will fall into evil. Let us follow Christ our light, who said in the Gospel: I am the way, the truth, and the life, because no one comes to the Father except through me. Now therefore, brothers, attend to those things which are read in the holy Scriptures concerning our Savior, because he who says that he remains in Christ, that is, in the way of truth, should strive to walk just as he walked.

    But it was necessary for him first to undergo the reproach of the cross and so to enter into his glory, by which we too, his soldiers, however unworthy, are admonished that we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations. For this reason the Lord himself, king of all things, admonished us in the Gospel, saying: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. Behold, Christ is set before us as the way to eternal life; though he was Lord of heavenly and worldly things, for our sake he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, in which, voluntarily and not compelled, he bore our weaknesses, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death, even the death of the cross. And so, if it was necessary for the Lord of the whole universe first to suffer, it certainly cannot be that we too, his imitators, wicked and most vile sinners, should not have to suffer many things:

    On spiritual warfare.

    It certainly cannot be that we too, his imitators, wicked and most vile sinners, should not have to suffer many things, we who justly endure all that we suffer by our own demerit. For no one comes to the glory of the city above unless he has first been justified here from sin; but since the afflictions of the righteous are many, he will by no means be able to be righteous who has refused to endure adversities for righteousness in this world.

    Therefore, my dearest brothers, let us imitate in much patience and humility our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who, made man for us, voluntarily endured the greatest things, and in this world was never without the bitterness of persecution. For from the hour of his most holy nativity until the departure of his spirit from his body, he existed for us most patiently, always in the bitterness of this present life; and the bitterness of his future Passion, foreknown, never withdrew from his foreknowledge. For although he was almighty God, made man for us, he knew all things, understood all things, foresaw all things; nor could anything of those things which he was to suffer be hidden from him, who, that he might suffer, was made passible in the world, while remaining the impassible God that he was.

    But born of the Virgin Mary without [unclear] commerce, [unclear], and soon on the eighth day he is circumcised; and he who had no sin is wounded for our offenses. By night, as a child, he is led into Egypt before the face of his persecutor; and he who was Lord of all, poor and needy, unknown in the midst of the nations, is exiled for seven years. Finally, through all the days of his life in this world he most patiently endured continual labors, and never refused to undergo any adversities for the glory of the Father. For the righteous and innocent one willingly suffered all hard and bitter things for us most unworthy ones; by the most bitter death of the cross he redeemed us from the destruction of perpetual damnation, and in his own blood mercifully reconciled us to the Father.

    Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, as the prince of the apostles forewarned, let us, my brothers, be armed with the same thought, so that in compassion we may diligently recall to memory those things which he, innocent, endured for us. For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him, gloriously triumphant. Behold, Christ calls us to the glory to which he has gone before; he gives the weapons with which he himself first overcame the prince of the world; he prescribed the form by which the soldier ought to follow the king to the crown. To the palace of heaven Christ calls his soldiers, whom [unclear] lead, endowed with the gifts of virtues; and the victors receive rewards, to reign forever.

    Therefore, my dearest brothers, always pursuing our warfare most zealously, let us continually declare war on vices and desires, so that, just as the flesh wars against the spirit, so we may fight continually, watching in prayer and fasting against the kindler of vices. As long as we live in this world we are pilgrims away from the Lord, and like gymnosophists we contend in the arena, carrying out the necessary course of life in continual struggle. But we fight not by our own strength, but supported by the mercy of our King, who said to his imitators in the holy Gospel: Without me you can do nothing. And lest we flee the battle of warfare set before us as impossible, he said elsewhere: In the world you will have distress; but take confidence: I have overcome the world. And so that we might know that the Lord Jesus is always present in this world with his servants, he promises us thus in the apostles: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age.

    Having received this promise of security, O soldiers of Christ, my dearest brothers, why do we hesitate? Why do we not stand bravely against all the insolences of this world? Let us always have our King and protector present as we fight; and do we wretches fear to engage against a weak enemy, who overcomes no one except the willing? Gird yourselves, I pray, for the unconquerable warfare of Christ, which you have professed under a twofold condition: one when, in the sacred font of baptism, renouncing Satan, you swore the words of Christian instruction; the other when you solemnly put on this garment of monastic religion. A great necessity of making progress constrains you, if you weigh your profession with due consideration, since the duty of the Christian name commands that you must observe the evangelical commandments, and the vow which you voluntarily made requires that you keep the precepts of monastic institution. It is no longer enough for us unto salvation to fulfill those precepts which are set down to be observed by Christians in common, but also [unclear] most diligently.

    that you keep the monastic ordinances which you promised. “Vow,” says Scripture, “and pay.” Again another Scripture says: “If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it. For an unfaithful and foolish promise is displeasing to him, and it is much better not to vow than, after a vow, not to pay what was promised.” And Saint Augustine admonishes us how necessary it is to pay to God what has been promised, saying: “There are certain things which we owe to the Lord even without vowing them; and there are certain things which we do not owe unless we have vowed them. But after we promise them to the Lord, we are bound of necessity to pay them.”

    But now, my brothers, I ask you carefully to weigh what you have vowed to the Lord your God, and diligently to consider under what necessity of paying what you promised you have been placed. For you have vowed to your God, not to a man, obedience and the conversion of your morals according to the Rule of our most holy lawgiver Benedict, and perpetual stability in this religious order. But the obedience which you have promised to God you owe to his vicar, a man, whom you have learned from the Rule that you profess to bear the place of Christ in the monastery. And what the conversion of morals ought to be according to the Rule you plainly see in the fourth chapter, entitled “On the Instruments of Good Works,” in which you find the whole sum of monastic perfection comprehended in a few words.

    Indeed, you have all heard what our divine father commanded to be done concerning novices, and you know that it was done in the case of each one of you at the beginning of his profession. For he says thus: “The one to be received shall promise in the oratory before all concerning his stability, and the conversion of his morals, and obedience, before God and his saints, so that if ever he should act otherwise, he may know that he is to be condemned by God, whom he mocks.” Consider now, therefore, brothers, under how great a necessity you have been placed for regular observance, since unless you fulfill in deed what you promised when you received the monastic habit, you will be judged before the almighty Lord not as servants of God, not as friends, not as monks, but as mockers.

    Therefore always remember the Rule according to which you promised to establish your morals, and labor like true soldiers of Jesus Christ, continually watchful in the fear of the Lord, since, as Scripture says, unless you hold yourselves steadfastly in fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown. Attend to your calling, because the Lord has called you not to idleness, not to the pleasures of this world, nor to pursuing the desires of the flesh, but rather to continual labor, to abstinence from all delights, and to the constant mortification of the flesh under the image of the Crucified, so that you may bear his stigmata in your hearts.

    You have now certainly put your hands to the plough of holy heavenly agriculture, in which you are commanded to sweat continually with labor, and never to look back even [unclear], but, always advancing from virtue to virtue, to pant toward the highest summit of perfection. For to live as a monk is nothing other than to shun the company of men and, in solitude, by the desire of most fervent love, actively to please God alone. Hence Scripture says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth; he will sit solitary and be silent, because he will lift himself above himself.”

    Therefore, if you wish to be perfect, you who are bound by the regular institution to love perfection, begin from the way of life that Christ taught; and you who already, for love of him, despise all things, do not neglect humbly to conquer, overcome, and despise even yourselves. But the servant of Christ has nothing except Christ, loves nothing, seeks nothing except Christ, so that he may be perfect and please him whose service he has voluntarily professed. But the monk who has anything besides Christ cannot be perfect, since true love is not divided, nor is the mind truly united to diverse and contrary things. For this reason the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me.”

    You indeed, most beloved brothers, have already, as I trust, left the world and whatever you had in the world; and you have laid aside not only all the things of the world that you possessed and could have possessed, but also every desire to have possessions; and you have come to this monastery of the divine prelate Martin, in which the poverty of temporal things is great, and this alone has been given to us in place of riches: not to find occasions for avarice. But just as punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause does, so want does not make a poor man blessed, but voluntary [unclear] for the love of Christ

    On the Advancement of Spiritual Warfare.

    patience in poverty itself. For the Lord in the Gospel did not proclaim just any poor persons blessed and destined to be given the kingdom of heaven; rather, as you know, he declared that only the poor in spirit are to be blessed. For contempt of riches is not sufficient for salvation, unless the renouncer of gold also strives with all his strength, through patience and humility, constantly to imitate the Savior. For it is easier to despise the world than to spurn and deny oneself. Yet whoever wishes to imitate the Son of God and attain evangelical perfection must become a despiser not only of the world and temporal things, but also of his very self. For the Savior says in the holy Gospel: Unless someone has renounced all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple. And lest we should think this sufficient for perfection, he again testifies more openly concerning contempt of oneself, saying: If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake and the Gospel’s will save it. Christ became obedient to the Father even unto death; if, as you have promised, you wish to imitate him, brothers, it is necessary that you deny yourselves to yourselves. For he will not be able to be a monk who has not first wholly renounced his own will. You who before God and all his saints have promised to live according to the monastic rule may not thereafter appropriate your own will, since what has once been consecrated to God must no longer be recalled to human uses. For you are ruled not by yourselves but by Christ; hence you retain in your power neither willing nor refusing. For you are dead, as holy Christophilus says, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. If you desire to rejoice without end with him, you must now in this time fight vigorously for love of him.

    For no one will be crowned with Christ except the one who, striving lawfully, has persevered to the end, since he who does not know how to persevere cannot conquer.

    On the Advancement of Spiritual Warfare: Second Homily

    [unclear]

    As often, dearest brothers, as remembrance comes to my mind of that moment when, though I cried out against it and resisted, you appointed me, unworthy as I am, as abbot over you, so often I am wholly shaken within myself by the bitterness of my heart, and I am compelled, even unwillingly and unknowingly, to shed tears. For I know that by my own merits I have not been placed over you; but whether this was done by yours, I do not know. May almighty God grant that this appointment of me was not made by reason of my demerits or yours. Why did you wish it so, brothers? You raised up as leader a young man, unlearned and by no means fit for the warfare that we profess, so that it is now altogether necessary for me both to teach and to learn, when neither perfection of life commends my teaching, nor consideration of age yet obtains for the shepherd the necessary authority. In these three years already I have sufficiently experienced with how many miseries I am entangled, while I alone am compelled to bear the weaknesses of you all, and I, unhappy man, am supported by no one. Who will deliver me from the vanities of this world, into which I have been recalled, I who entered the monastery in order to escape every care and solicitude of the present life? But since it is truly necessary to bear the burden placed upon my shoulders, I ask you, brothers, earnestly extend to me the helping hands of your prayers, so that in your midst, by the Lord’s granting, I may deserve to conduct myself in such a way that I do not transgress the condition of spiritual warfare which the rule prescribes for us. For we are professors of the same warfare, nor does the vow distinguish the office by which solemn profession, at the beginning of this life, made me bound as shepherd together with the sheep. Hence, when I speak to you of the spiritual warfare which, by God’s mercy, we have professed, my intention is, insofar as the Lord Jesus will deign to grant, to shake myself also from the feathers of sloth and tepidity toward the fervor of holy newness

    Homily II. Fol. V.

    [unclear]: and to summon all of you, as far as I am able, to the keeping of the military order. For we are frail and weak, and we do not remain long steadfast in a holy purpose unless by daily exercises we continually renew the fervor of the spirit. For by reason of my office I am bound to set before you publicly those things which can conduce to your salvation; it belongs to you to listen patiently in all things to me as I speak, as the pastor of your souls. For although, being young, I am not fit to teach so great a multitude of elders, nevertheless, since you have appointed me pastor over you, I am compelled, under necessity of salvation, to govern the flock which I have undertaken.

    What is in me I willingly do according to my powers, and although I have scarcely lived long in this anxiety of pastoral care, I, a young man, will teach you elders, and I will show without interruption how you ought to serve as soldiers for him under whose arms you have sworn. For the dreadful warning of our lawgiver does not escape me, when he says: Let the abbot know that whatever the father of the household may find less useful in the sheep lies as the fault of the shepherd. And what follows concerns you, my brothers, if, when I preach and admonish, contempt for the word of God should arise. Again, he says: Only then will he be free, if all diligence has been applied by the shepherd to a restless or disobedient flock, and every care has been shown for their diseased acts; their shepherd, absolved in the judgment of the Lord, may say with the prophet to the Lord: I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have spoken your truth and your salvation; but they, despising, have spurned me. And then for the disobedient sheep entrusted to his care, death itself becomes for them a prevailing penalty.

    Here no covering of excuse is left; no place for evasion is granted, but the danger of both parties is publicly described. For I, holding the place of abbot, if I have not announced to you the justice of God, if I have not corrected you when you sin according to the Rule, have denied my office; and whatever holiness is found lacking in you will be imputed wholly to me. For it is mine, by reason of the pastoral office, to say what is expedient for the salvation of your souls; but yours is humbly to hear those things which I shall pronounce in the name of the Savior, and faithfully to fulfill them from a great heart, so far as each one is able. You have heard the danger along with me if you despise me when I preach to you the word of God.

    But that, by the Savior’s mercy, we may all escape secure, let each one of us diligently pursue what is commanded him in this spiritual warfare, taking the greatest care lest, having become deaf hearers of the truth, we lie to the Lord. Let us diligently remember the vow which we have made, and let us preserve inviolate until death the holy order which we profess. Let us hear our king saying in the Gospel to his soldiers: If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also my servant will be.

    We priests and Levites, all cloistered monks, are servants of the eternal king, and are bound by a twofold reason to great holiness, since we have at once received the order of clerics and profess the rule of monastic purity. Therefore let us follow our teacher, for whom we serve as soldiers, along the path of the severity of all virtues; and when his [unclear] begins to burn in the soldier’s heart, he fears no adversities. For charity, as Saint Gregory says, is never idle, but does great things if it is true; but if it refuses to work, it was not perfect charity.

    Therefore, cloistered soldiers, you who have pledged that you will serve the eternal king forever, cast away now the works of darkness and put on charity toward God and neighbor, which is the strongest armor of salvation for all. If anyone has been clothed with it, he fears no labors, however hard, no adversities of this world, no intimidation by men: not thirst, not persecutions of men, not reproaches, not mockeries, not prisons, not chains, not any harsh and adverse things whatever; but everyone who has once perfectly tasted the charity of God

    On the progress of spiritual warfare.

    Whatever raging things of the world [there may be], he will remain. The true lover of God rejoices in tribulations, is glad in adversities, exults in persecutions for the sake of justice. He follows his king, seated in heaven; there he dwells in mind and in the desire of his soul, where he does not doubt that his savior reigns.

    Whatever pleasure and delights are seen anywhere in the world produce, for the servant of Christ who burns with true charity, a stench and horror as of the vilest dung, because he loves nothing earthly, nothing transitory, nothing perishable, but him alone to whom he has devoted himself, with the whole intention of his mind.

    For the true soldier of Christ thinks nothing of the things of the world; he cares not for the flesh but for the mind, as one who is not ignorant of what is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has approved himself.” Indeed, all who serve an earthly emperor always obey his commands in everything, and immediately, without contradiction, go wherever he has ordered. All follow him as one, and whatever he has commanded in the name of the king, no one in the whole army contradicts.

    You also, soldiers of the king of ages, who have appointed me as your leader and instructor in his place, hear through my mouth the command of your emperor Jesus Christ, and do what he commands us in the holy Gospel. Hear what he orders, and consider how you ought to serve as soldiers in the observance of regular discipline. “He who ministers to me,” he says, “let him follow me.”

    Listen, monk, bearing the cloistered campaigns: the heavenly emperor, whom you serve at the altar, speaks to you. If you wish to be my minister, you must follow the virtue of patience and humility which you have learned from me. For I have given you an example, O my soldiers, so that as I have done, you also should do likewise. Charity, O monk, compelled me to be born in the world as man from a virgin; let that same charity preserve you always pure and humble in the cloister for love of me. The Father also enjoined upon me the work of human salvation; for your sake I strove always, with unceasing meditation, to bring it to completion; and you, if you love me, take care to preserve inviolate until death the holy purpose of monastic life which you have undertaken for your sins.

    I was always voluntarily subject and obedient to my heavenly Father in all things, even to the most bitter death of the cross; you also, if you wish to come to me, humbly obey your abbot, established in my place, always in all things according to the rule. I have never transgressed in anything the commandment which my Father gave me; and unless you preserve inviolate until death the three principal vows of monastic institution, you are by no means to be numbered among my ministers and soldiers.

    Though I was rich, for your salvation I became poor and needy; but unless you, for love of me, have despised and relinquished all things, you will not be able to be my disciple. Poverty, hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and continual labors in the world I endured for your sake; unless in these things, according to your rule and to the best of your strength, you have followed me patiently and voluntarily, you will certainly be neither my minister nor my soldier nor my monk. For in your patience you will possess your soul.

    I desired nothing in this world, possessed nothing, loved nothing earthly, but, walking poor, humble, and meek, I always in all things subjected myself most perfectly to my Father’s will, ready to receive injuries and blows. But you, O cloistered monk, who profess the monastic rule under an abbot or prior: if from now on you follow the desires of your flesh; if you possess private property or ownership in the monastery; if you love anything besides me; if you despise the commands of your superior; if you do not serve me perseveringly in humility, know for certain that I shall not have you as a soldier, nor count you as monk, minister, or disciple, but, judging you a fugitive, apostate, faithless man, liar, mocker, perjurer, and unbeliever, I shall condemn you eternally without mercy, as you have deserved, with my betrayer Judas and the fallen angels.

    What your lips vowed to me is no longer yours but mine; but if you usurp for yourself what is mine, you do not wish to be my monk and faithful servant, but a thief and wicked robber, impious and unjust; and do not doubt that, when I come, I shall judge you such. But if you have persevered faithfully in the holy purpose until death; if you have kept inviolate, under the power of my vicar whom I appointed shepherd over you, the will which you solemnly consecrated to me; if obedience, poverty, and

    All things. II. Fol. VI.

    ...if you shall have kept chastity with humility, for love of my name, unto the end; if you shall always have striven to please me alone in all your actions; if you shall have taken care to follow me without interruption along the steep road of the virtues: knowing this without doubt, know most certainly that, as a servant made my very dear friend, I shall have you as a soldier to be crowned with me in my kingdom; I shall love you, I shall cherish you, I shall establish you glorious forever in the midst of my saints.

    Hear me now, my servant, you who, for reverence and honor of my name, have enrolled yourself in the warfare of monks; and with a great and perfect heart follow the footsteps of my feet, as that teacher of yours, the blessed friend, once taught you and with all his efforts imitated. Let not the enticements of the flesh deceive you, O strenuous soldier; let not the vain and destructive dealings of this world seduce your soul, dedicated to me. Never yield to the exceedingly deceitful suggestions of the unclean spirit, who rages wholly for your destruction; but remember that your sojourn in this age is very brief, and that death stands before the doors, which no one of mortals has ever been able to escape.

    Let those last things which you must necessarily undergo always stand in your memory; and from the very swift passing-away of the pleasures of the flesh which have gone by, take up for yourself a necessary dread and contempt of the future things of this sojourn. Just as labor for my sake, considered brief in the world and borne with patience and charity, prepares eternal happiness for my soldiers, so the desires and pleasures of the flesh, which suddenly pass away, plunge the soul of a sinful man down to hell, to be tormented without end.

    Therefore direct all your desires to me, monk who minister to me and who follow me by the steep road of regular observance. Offer me your heart if you desire happiness; seek me alone if you love your own life and salvation. When you have loved God, you are tranquil and holy; when you have followed him, you are blessed and glorious without end.

    What, brothers, would you do if it happened to you to hear these words which we have spoken from the mouth of our Savior and King as he spoke? What, I say, would you do? I certainly believe that there would be great compunction in your hearts if you heard Christ speaking in person. But we, holding the place of Christ in the monastery, speak the words which he has given, and you do not attend. We set before you the necessary arena of salvation, and you show no signs of compunction.

    Why it was fitting that I say these things, if you do not know, I pray you, understand. I see some of you shrinking from sacred readings, given over to vanities, and caring for nothing less than the perfection of the spiritual warfare; their god is the belly, and their glory is in confusion. Do you think, most worthless knaves, who have no taste for anything spiritual, that Christ is to come again from heaven to speak to you those things which he committed to his preachers to be spoken? Have you not heard Paul saying: “Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death shall have no further dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God.”

    Once Christ was seen on earth; once he appeared visible among mortals; once he preached the way of eternal salvation; he will not add a second time. He appointed pastors and vicars over his household to teach the ignorant; wishing to make manifest their authority, he said in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me.” Therefore hear those whom Christ has set over you as rulers, to whom he entrusted the distribution of spiritual wheat, as he said in the holy Gospel: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the lord has set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season? Blessed is that servant whom, when the lord comes, he shall find doing thus.”

    We therefore exhort you, brothers, in the Lord Jesus, and with what diligence we can we beg you, do not consume your days in vanity, but consider the exceeding brevity of this life, and bring forth worthy fruits of repentance while it is granted to you at the proper time, lest, if you neglect to repent, the time be cut off. For you know what the divine Scripture says to us: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.” Cease, I pray, to put off the good, because no one of you knows when he is to die; rather, attend to that true saying of the wanton poet Naso, who thus admonishes: “But make haste, and do not defer yourself to the coming hours: he who is not ready today will be less fit tomorrow.” No one [unclear] life for himself

    On the progress of spiritual warfare.

    Let [no one?], brothers, promise himself a long [life]; rather let each one think that death is near at hand, and therefore let him live so prepared as though he were to depart from the body tomorrow. For the hope of a longer life has deceived many, and, by holding them back from the fervor of a holy purpose, has suddenly plunged them into the lower world. Therefore perfect your warfare, which of necessity will end not long from now, so that you may not fear to appear before your king when he comes. Always remember that you do not have here an abiding city, nor can you remain long in this mortal life, but death will come quickly and compel you to depart.

    For whoever is a true monk and desires to be a faithful soldier of Christ despises all the delights of this world, always thinks of his Lord as present to him, and, casting away from himself all impediments and little burdens, cares above all things how he may be able to please him greatly. He ought not to be anxious in seeking the necessities of life, since the providence of the pastor disposes all these things for those subject to him. Let the whole care of the monk be to keep himself unstained from this world, so that, free and released from all things, he may seek nothing except God, think of nothing except Jesus crucified for us.

    O happy soldier of Christ, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised, if he shall remain faithful, prudent, and watchful in the love of God even to the end. Certainly nothing is happier than a good monk, to whom the Son of God promises himself as reward; nothing also is more laborious, since, placed in the arena of combat, he is daily in peril concerning his salvation; and nothing is stronger than the monk who conquers the world together with the devil, nor anything weaker than he who is overcome by his own flesh.

    Therefore you, O monk, must always keep watch against the hidden enemy of your salvation, who is never more easily conquered than if he is kept far from the entrance of the mind. Hence, if you desire to come away victorious against him, do not allow the engines of his deceit and fraud to be brought nearer to you. Guard first of all your senses, lest death enter through the windows; and then especially beware the ambushes of the enemy, when for a time he has allowed you to be secure in your devotion. Never forget the admonition of the wise man, who says: If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house, that is, your conscience, will quickly be overthrown. Therefore Solomon said in Proverbs: Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil. For as soon as a monk has presumed upon security, already without doubt he tends toward destruction.

    Therefore it is fitting that the soldier of Christ always be prepared against his adversaries, so that, as long as he lives in this mortal body, he may not trust that he has perfectly overcome them. For the flesh always desires against the spirit, and, lest the soul ever be overcome, as long as one happens to live, it is necessary to fight. As often as you have conquered your invisible enemy, rising again he always engages you with greater savagery, so that he who cannot obtain victory by strength may at least by persistence bring on despair. But you, most valiant soldier of Christ, take care that you do not fail in the arena of this very brief contest; take care that you do not lay down the arms of necessary defense before the battle is completed at the end. For the Savior says: He who has persevered to the end will be saved.

    Do not give rest to your soul as long as it has been granted you to remain in this miserable pilgrimage, but always do some good, lest the devil ever find you idle. Always remember the admonition of Scripture, saying: Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly, because neither work nor reason nor wisdom nor knowledge will be among the dead, where you are hastening. For there is no one who lives forever, but we all die, and we fall down like waters into the earth, which will no more return to their former state. Then there will no longer be time for working, nor for earning eternal happiness, but whatever a man has sown here now in time, then he will receive as reward.

    Therefore, again, labor in holy things like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. But no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has approved himself. For of those too who contend in the arena, no one will be crowned unless he has contended lawfully. Moreover everyone who contends in the arena abstains from all things. In another place also the same lover of Christ says: I wish you to be without anxiety. You therefore, soldier of Christ, who contend in the arena of daily combat so that at last you may appear glorious forever before your God, [ought?] to imitate the corruptible gymnosophist, who, contending in the arena for a corruptible indeed

    Homily III.

    VII

    ... lest the crown be overcome, he abstains from everything, so that naked and free he may run the more swiftly. Therefore, if you desire to walk the way of God in true purity, if you are concerned to conquer the enemy in the contest of struggle, put off the garments of earthly cares and all the hairs of fleshly pleasures. For whoever has learned to run naked, with hair and clothing cast away from himself, carries around nothing by which he can be held by the adversary except the unencumbered body. For he who runs naked has stripped himself of every anxiety over things that clamor around him, and thinks of nothing other than victory; nor does he care what meanwhile is happening with wife or children. Nothing present recalls him from his course; the swiftness of his companions does not frighten him; among many he competes as though alone; he hastens breathless toward the prize as though certain. Imitate him, soldier of Christ, in the spiritual contest; contemplate the naked Savior hanging naked on the cross, so that you may be able to overthrow the adversary so much the more easily, the less he sees you to possess of the vanity of the world. Therefore fight naked, light, and unencumbered on every side; naked and released from all things, fly into heaven. Naked you came into this world; naked you are to return to the earth. Considering these things earnestly, my brothers, so run that you may lay hold of eternal life with all the saints. Amen. The homily ends.

    ... and take up the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, praying at every time in the Spirit with every prayer and supplication, and in it keeping watch with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints. To the Thessalonians likewise he says: But we, who are of the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and charity, and for a helmet the hope of salvation. These are the arms, brothers, with which the soldiers of Christ, clothed, war against the fierce adversary; these should be the badges of the virtues of monks, without which no one obtains victory over vices. The equipment of human warfare, which most mortals pursue far too zealously, consists of helmet, shield, breastplate, dagger, cuirass, belt, lance, and many other things of that kind, with which men about to go out to war arm themselves most carefully; and unless they have been most diligently defended over the whole body, they judge that they are not certainly fit for battle. But the arms of our spiritual warfare are faith, hope, charity, patience, humility, obedience, chastity, together with the holy virtues of the soul enumerated by our holy teacher Benedict in the Rule, under the fourth chapter, where he makes fine mention of the instruments of good works. But would, my brothers, that we were as careful and diligent for these spiritual arms of our warfare as we see worldly men to be solicitous for their corruptible armor. But now, what I say with too much grief, since we shamefully cast away the arms of salvation with which we ought to have been armed, what else remains except that we succumb to our enemy in the contest? But perhaps you will say: If the Christian faith, as the apostle bears witness, belongs to the armor of spiritual warfare, we certainly have never cast it away. For we firmly believe whatever holy mother Church has set before us to be believed, and in that profession of faith we intend steadfastly to remain until death. But so be it. What, however, does Saint James say in the epistle? What will it profit, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him? Just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. Therefore, whenever Scripture speaks of faith, [unclear] not common and [unclear] ... feet in preparation for the gospel of peace. In all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one.

    What the armor of spiritual warfare is.

    As James says in his epistle. But works of piety must be joined to the Christian faith. You believe in one almighty God, creator of heaven and earth: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. You do well. The demons also believe and tremble. What then? Where are the works by which your faith may be shown to have been formed in Christ? Idle and dead is the faith that is not commended by holy and necessary works. We believe in Christ: it is well, if we follow Christ's examples. For if we do not follow Christ in works of piety, in vain do we flatter ourselves about faith alone. You, I say, believe, and the demons believe. With love faith belongs to a Christian; without love faith belongs to the devil. You believe rightly if you love God with all your heart according to your powers. But if you do not truly love God, you have an idle and dead faith. The proof of love, as Saint Gregory testifies, is the performance of work. For thus the Lord speaks in the Gospel: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. This, therefore, is true faith: ordered according to Christ's teaching by good and holy works. If with faith and work together you believe in the Lord Jesus, surely you hold the shield of salvation in your hands, in which, by the Lord himself granting it, you will easily overcome all adversaries.

    Of this armor it is written: By faith the saints conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained the promise. John also says: Everything that is born of God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. And the prince of the apostles, Peter, thus admonishes us, saying: Brothers, be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith. True faith and trust in our Lord Jesus Christ is an unconquerable and most powerful armor, against which no adversary has ever been able to stand, as is written in the book of Chronicles. King Jehoshaphat said to his army: Believe in the Lord your God and you will be secure. In Ecclesiasticus also we read thus: You who fear the Lord, believe him, and your reward will not be made void. And again: In your work believe from the faith of your soul, for this is the practice of the commandments. He who believes God attends to the commandments; and he who trusts in him will not be diminished.

    Take care now, therefore, dearest brothers, and always strive with the highest zeal to carry in your hands this shield of faith, formed by holy works, against all attacks of your enemies, because he who is fortified by this unconquerable shield is never conquered by the adversary. Confirming this, Saint Augustine says on the words of the Lord: No riches are greater, no treasures, no honors, no substance of this world is greater than the Catholic faith, which saves sinners, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores the penitent, increases the righteous, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins and widows and married persons in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, and places believers in the eternal inheritance with the holy angels. Just as in the root of a tree absolutely no appearance of beauty is visible, and yet whatever beauty or comeliness is in the tree proceeds from it, so from faith [unclear] is; since without faith it is impossible to please God. For one who comes to God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.

    But the more anyone loves, the more he advances in faith. For faith without charity is like a useless shield thrown away and without a strap. O faith, treasure richer than all things, when formed in the mind of a human being, you make the mortal equal to the immortals, conquer demons and kingdoms, and bravely overcome all hard and adverse things. Faith is the foundation of all virtues; without it no spiritual building stands. Faith is the enlightener of minds and the chief instrument of spiritual warfare. For without the shield of faith the devil is not conquered, nor is the attack of wanton flesh overcome. Let us consider, therefore, brothers, how necessary for salvation faith formed by charity is for us, without which, as we fight in this warfare, neither victory is granted to us nor confidence reserved. For faith is the shield in which we most easily conquer the enemy of our salvation, if we attach the handle of divine love. For blessed Pope Gregory says: Then are we truly faithful to him, if what we promise in words we fulfill in works. Since in this armor faith is the foundation of all good works, all our operations

    Homily III. VIII

    rightly ought to precede, so that the mind may be able to arrive at love. For unless faith is first held, spiritual love is by no means reached. For charity does not precede faith, but faith precedes charity, because no one can love or hope for the good which he refuses to believe.

    But since you now faithfully believe also what he commands, and have set the foundation of the spiritual building upon a firm rock, now you must also without delay do the remaining things that are left for perfection. Therefore love peace and truth, so that in the faith of Christ, as true soldiers, you may be able at all times to remain stable and most firm. For, as Scripture bears witness, truth is great and stronger than all things, and there is nothing unjust with it. He who loves truth is a true disciple of Christ, and loves Christ himself, who says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” All the ways of the Lord likewise are mercy and truth; from this [unclear] fell through pride, because he did not remain in eternal truth.

    Therefore holy [Christophilus?] Paul commands the soldiers of the Lord to gird themselves in truth; in this he wished to show the state of perfection toward which cloistered persons especially ought to aspire. For what else is it to love truth than to be the person one is commanded to be, and to live according to the rule of justice, true and solid, such as holy perfection by grace requires of nature? Hence Firmianus Lactantius says: “He who is zealous for truth should cast away pleasures hostile to it and troubling, which bind the soul to themselves and do not allow it to be free. But let him always prefer true things to false, eternal things to brief ones, useful things to pleasant ones. Let nothing be pleasing to the sight except what can be done justly, piously, religiously; nothing sweet to the hearing except what makes the soul better.”

    Thus soldiers have their loins girded in truth when, out of love for God, despising the enticements of the flesh and the vanities of the world, they strive according to their powers so to conduct themselves and live that they may be able in all things to please the highest Truth, which is God. After this the soldier of Christ is commanded to put on the breastplate of justice, without which no one will be able to serve the Lord rightly and fruitfully. Justice is to preserve and distribute to each one what is owed to him according to law or nature. And this is the most excellent of all virtues; without it there can be no piety, no religion, no holiness, and no discernment of goods and evils. For it is light and great splendor, from which the force and dominion of every good arises among mortals. Justice is the mother of innocence, the nurse of concord, the parent of friendship, the begetter of piety, and the guardian of religion. Justice, as Scripture bears witness, is perpetual and immortal; injustice, however, is the acquisition of death.

    By what means the Christian soldier ought to put on this breastplate of justice, our Savior himself declares in the holy Gospel, saying: “All things whatsoever you wish that men should do to you, do you also do likewise to them.” Therefore, my brothers, keep this manner of living in our [unclear]: that each one do to his fellow-soldier in all things just as, according to the right judgment of reason, he desires at all times that it be done to him by others. For this is the first duty of justice, that one harm no one; then that in common uses [unclear] to his brother what conduces to salvation by just reason as his own. O what great peace mortals would enjoy if they followed the exhortations of the Apostle, by which each is commanded to bear the burdens of the other. Everyone, says Scripture, who does justice is now born of God.

    This, brothers, is the breastplate of justice: to keep the commandments of God, to love one’s neighbor, and to love God most ardently above all things. This is the strongest garment of our warfare: to show worship and piety to God, holiness to ourselves, and brotherly charity to our neighbor. Whoever has not been under justice shows that he belongs not to Christ’s soldiery but rather to the company of demons. For justice is the greatest virtue, which distributes to each one what is his; unless you keep it most diligently, you lose the name both of monk and soldier. Therefore render worship and piety to God; obedience to your [unclear] or rector, together with reverence, of which one belongs to the heart, the other to action. Nor is it enough to obey superiors outwardly, unless from the inward affection of the heart we likewise think rightly about them. And the true justice of monks, brothers, is this: that each one conducts himself without offense according to the prescribed rule of the law, granting to each his own proper dignity: reverence to his superior, concord to his equal, discipline to the lesser, worship and obedience to God.

    What the armor of spiritual warfare is.

    to oneself holiness; to an enemy patience; to a poor man mercy; to all men brotherly charity in the Lord. Therefore holy Christophilus says: “We are debtors, brothers, not to the flesh, that we should live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” Therefore he serves God rightly who gives to each what is his.

    Then we are commanded to have our feet shod in preparation for the gospel of peace, so that the good which we ourselves have come to know by the Lord’s generosity we may also cheerfully share with others. For our law, brothers, according to which we are commanded to serve the Lord, is the gospel of Jesus Christ, to which all rules and constitutions of cloistered persons are ordered. For monastic constitutions were not made on account of the gospel, but the statutes of monks were made on account of the gospel. For a Christian who is not a monk can be saved, but a monk cannot be saved unless he has been a Christian. Let certain excessively superstitious and foolish cloistered persons be ashamed, who value their rule and statutes more than the gospel of Christ; who keep the traditions of men, customs leading to prisons and chains, but pay no heed to the constitutions of God and the law of the universal Church. The words of our Savior, speaking to the Jews according to Matthew, rightly apply to them: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?” For evangelical doctrine must be preferred by far to all the constitutions of the whole world. But after the gospel the statutes of the universal Church hold the first place of authority, and no constitutions or rules of monks are comparable to them in dignity. Let us take care to live according to evangelical purity, and we shall be perfect in the monastic way of life of the fathers.

    Let our feet always be shod in preparation for the gospel of peace, so that we may put to death in ourselves the desires of the flesh, and through love of God and neighbor have peace with all. For without peace and the concord of brotherhood, mortification of the flesh is of no benefit, as Saint Jerome says: “Whoever afflicts the body but abandons concord does indeed praise God with timbrels, but he does not praise him in the choir.” Hence peaceful Solomon, praising the man, says in Proverbs: “Better is a dry morsel with joy than a house full of victims with strife.” And again

    Homily III Fol. IX

    he restrains anger, treads down the proud, loves the humble, calms the discordant, reconciles enemies; with all he is gentle, burdensome to none, troublesome to none, oppressive to none; he does not know how to be exalted, he does not know how to [unclear]. And let him who receives it hold it fast; let him who loses it seek it again; let him who has cast it away inquire after it, because whoever is not found in that same peace will be disowned by the Father, disinherited by the Son, and nevertheless made a stranger to the Holy Spirit. He cannot now approach the inheritance of the Lord who has refused to observe the testament of peace. The place of God is in peace, but the dwelling of the devil is in anger and disturbance. Therefore every man who does not have this threefold peace in his heart, who does not offer it with his mouth, nor show it in his works, is to be called neither a monk nor a Christian.

    Now the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” If those who make peace are called sons of God, without doubt those who confound peace are sons of Satan. Therefore, my dearest brothers, have among yourselves that peace which the world cannot give, which is the peace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, of which Isaiah the prophet says: “And the work of justice shall be peace, and the service of justice silence and security forever.” For God is the Lord of peace and love; therefore whoever violates peace and brotherly love is made manifest as not being a true lover of God. If the true peace of Christ is in your hearts, you will fear no adversities of this world. Among you also let there be true peace, not feigned, because Christ desires peace not from the mouth but from the heart, and wishes one’s neighbor to be greeted with affection rather than with lips. Therefore if any one of you has saddened his brother in anything, let him make satisfaction to him as soon as possible before sunset; and take care, all of you, that the sun not set upon your anger, because inveterate anger generates hatred and strips the soul of every adornment of virtues. Therefore, monk, if you have sinned against your brother, quickly do penance before him, and falling at his knees beg pardon.

    “And,” he says, “the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, through every prayer and supplication”: we soldiers of Christ should always hold it in our hands. The word of God, which is contained in the holy Scriptures, is a victorious defense against all assaults of demons, as we are admonished by the example of our Savior, who, when tempted by the devil, with calm hand

    On the reading and study of the divine Scriptures

    by us. For everyone who sins mortally opens the door of his heart to the devil; he closes it to God; nor can he trust in the help of the Most High so long as he has remained lying in crime without repentance.

    Here ends Homily 2.

    On the reading and study of the divine Scriptures: Homily Four.

    Since every Scripture, divinely inspired, as the holy apostle of Christ says, is useful for teaching, or for arguing, for correcting, for training in justice, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work, we ought gladly to devote ourselves to the reading of the divine Scriptures, and to direct all the zeal of secular literature in which we once labored toward the point of this contemplation. For in the divine Scriptures whatever saving knowledge requires is found most abundantly expressed, so that what you do not find there is in no way necessary for salvation. For the majesty of the divine Scriptures far surpasses all the knowledge and teaching of the whole world: the Holy Spirit poured it into the men of God so that it might be written, and, so that it may be understood by studious readers, bestows the grace of his illumination.

    Turn this Scripture over diligently, my brothers, with purity of mind and the fervor of twofold charity, because whoever truly loves God spends in sacred readings all the time he can find for leisure. Let there be for you, I pray, incentives toward the wholesome study of the Scriptures in the frenzied deeds, so to speak, of carnal lovers: when they receive the letters and gifts of their mistresses, they do not cease to read them, and often read them again and kiss them; and, what is a greater sign of love, they hang them either from the neck or at the breast, so that the dear memory of her whom they desire may never depart from the mind. Consider, brothers, the madness of carnal people in love, and blush at your own lukewarmness toward the love of God. Which of you is affected toward the holy Scriptures of God with such love of heart as a blind lover is inflamed with desire toward the filthy, utterly vain, and most mad love-letters of one little prostitute? He, because of love for the absent woman whom he desires, follows her letters and little gifts with repeated kisses; examining each stroke because of excessive love, he searches it out with repeated looks; in everything he does he always thinks of the absent woman; anxiously he hastens to come into her sight.

    O if we who are called Christian monks, who serve the supreme and immortal king Christ Jesus, who are commanded to love our God above all things, and are ordered to love nothing in this world except him: if, I say, we pursued our creator with as great a love as carnally minded men observe and love their corruptible and mortal girlfriends. Holy Scripture, read every day, brings God to our minds; it makes his will manifest to us; it instructs us what we ought to do, and lays open what we should beware. Through it the Almighty speaks with us, and, forming us by an invisible instruction, consoles us, as the holy apostle says: For whatever things have been written were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope.

    Therefore the true soldier of Christ, and especially the cloistered one, who loves God in his whole heart and desires to please him alone, embraces the divine Scriptures, and most of all the holy Gospel, with affection, and is constantly occupied in reading it with meditation. But whoever neglects the reading of the divine Scriptures plainly shows that he is not a true lover of God. But what does Scripture itself say? He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be detestable. Blessed indeed are those who search the testimonies of the Lord; with their whole heart they seek him. Therefore you, my brothers, if you truly love the Lord Jesus in your whole heart, if as true soldiers you desire to please him above all things, if finally you desire to advance toward the perfection of the monastic life, ought always to occupy yourselves in the reading of the divine Scriptures with fervent affection.

    How useful the reading of the Scriptures is, blessed Jerome indicates, saying: Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. For after God nothing in this life is taken up more sweetly, nothing is felt more pleasantly, nothing more powerfully separates the mind from love of this world, nothing so strengthens the soldier of Christ against all the temptations of adversaries, nothing disposes and confirms the monk so greatly for every good work, as frequent reading and ardent study of the Scriptures. Indeed, if the benefits of the Almighty which

    Homily IV. Fol. X.

    ...bestowed upon the human race, when by reading through the whole wide extent of Scripture we call it back to memory with zealous devotion, they will furnish us the greatest matter and occasion by which, burning more deeply in the love of God, we may advance. For what else does the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures contain than a certain ordered fabric of good things which God has either already bestowed on human beings, or has promised that he will also give? Or what is there that can so strengthen us for the endurance of evils and render us willingly patient as if we read in the Gospel that the Son of God suffered innocently for us, and after him the victories of the holy martyrs?

    For sacred Scripture contains the things that are necessary for us unto saving knowledge, and it warns us what, as soldiers in this pilgrimage, we ought profitably to seek, and what also to avoid. Hence again Saint Jerome says: "Our riches are to meditate on the law of God day and night." Let us therefore prepare strength for ourselves; let us take up perfect might, so that amid the darkness of errors and the confusion of night the light of Christ's knowledge may appear, and days and nights may have a protecting light, so that with Scripture as guide we may be able to come to the holy land.

    For what is better than this instruction? What sweeter than this discipline? What more delightful than our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true salvation and sweetness of faithful souls? Let Christ be our banquet; let sacred reading be our food and drink. For what can the life of a monk or priest be without knowledge of the Scriptures? We know Christ not by sight, not by hearing, not by touch, but by the reading of the Scriptures; and the more we advance by reading toward true knowledge, the more we take delight in the holy Scriptures.

    For what is sweeter than to know the will of God and not to be ignorant of the prizes of his promises? For as Jerome says, the field of the divine word is exceedingly rich, having in itself every delight, and whatever you wish is born from it, just as they report of the manna in the desert, that when it was eaten it tasted in the mouth of the eater according to his will and desire.

    Therefore, my brothers, read the divine Scriptures more often, through which you can plainly know the will of God and arm yourselves most strongly against the snares of the devil. For if, according to the Apostle Paul, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, he who does not know the Scriptures does not know the power and wisdom of God; and how will he know Christ? For ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ, and he who does not know Christ will not belong to his fellowship, as holy Christophilus says, because if anyone is ignorant, surely he will also be ignored.

    Moreover, the more constant anyone has been in the study of the divine Scriptures, the greater understanding and sweetness he receives from their reading. But it especially befits you, brothers, to turn over the divine Scriptures daily by reading and learning, since to you both abundant time free from occupations is granted and a place sufficiently suitable because of the rarity of those who come by is offered. Therefore I exhort and admonish you, if you love your salvation, always to have divine readings in your hands, so that all the time which, after the worship of prayer, is allowed you without labor may be spent on the study of sacred Scripture.

    Let no day pass, my brothers, on which the monk serving as Christ's soldier does not read something from the sacred volumes that may make him better in his holy purpose. Rather let him follow the counsel of Saint Jerome, who says: "Let the divine Scriptures always be in your hands and be continually turned over in the mind; nor should you think it enough to store the commandments of God in memory, unless you strive also to fulfill them in works."

    For God requires two things of us, my brothers. First, he wishes us to know his most holy will; second, that we do what we have come to know. But we cannot know his commandments if we are ignorant of the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Nor does he do the will of God who is ignorant of it; nor will he know it who has not learned it. Learn, therefore, what is the pleasing will of God, so that you may do it; do what is known, so that you may understand more fully. For no one understands the will of God better than he who, once he has known it, does it out of love.

    And so, if you desire to become a most learned interpreter of the divine Scriptures, learn to begin the study of knowledge not from words but in holy works. For then you will grasp the rich knowledge of sacred reading, if you have kept your heart clean from every sin and, fervent in the love of God, have continually turned over the holy Scriptures with compunction. For the knowledge of the divine Scriptures is the high mountain on which Moses speaks with the Lord, to which the [unclear] of vices...

    On the reading and study of the divine Scriptures

    A man polluted with filth is forbidden. For thus it is read in Exodus: “Take care that you do not go up onto the mountain, nor touch its borders. Everyone who touches the mountain shall surely die. Whether it be beast or man, it shall not live.” A man indeed touches the mountain and dies whenever someone, puffed up with secular literature, takes offense at the simplicity of the divine Scriptures. But a beast touches the mountain and is overwhelmed with stones whenever a man, sunk in the fury of carnal passions, advances to the study of sacred Scripture without a purified mind.

    If, therefore, you wish profitably to turn over the readings of the divine Scriptures, if by reading you desire to arrive at true knowledge, take care first of all to put away every swelling of pride and every rashness of unbelief, and then to cleanse the chamber of your heart from all uncleanness of carnal pleasures. For God, as canonical Scripture says, resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. No proud, inflated, arrogant, and rash man, no man of carnal mind, luxurious or restless, is held fit for the study of sacred Scripture, but only the humble, gentle, mild, modest, chaste man, tranquil in body and mind.

    [Dine prosper?] says in an epigram: “A mind that is not quiet cannot search the commandments of God. Therefore, that religious study may be exercised, the quarrels of the wicked must be cast aside. Hearts free from the tumult of the world may search the law in whatever quiet they can. Therefore, that the mind may be found intent upon pious studies, let divine love conquer fleshly battles. For the temple of the Lord grows through sacred threads, and silently the house that will not fall is built.”

    Therefore proceed to the study of the Scriptures with devoted minds and with a heart pierced in the love of God and humbled in true contrition, because the Lord will not enlighten you unless he has first made you cleansed from every iniquity. For, as Scripture itself says, perverse thoughts separate from God; but proven virtue corrects the foolish, since wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins; for the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding. Therefore we must pray more often to the Lord with holy David: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts.” For no one understands the holy Scriptures of God usefully who does not turn himself to the Lord with his whole heart through [unclear].

    Therefore, if you wish to understand the divine utterances both rightly and profitably, take care first of all with the utmost zeal to keep yourselves, as far as you can, clean from every pollution of sin. I beg you, do not let the mad folly of certain monks seduce you, who try to excuse their ignorance with a worn-out proverb, saying: “What need have we of knowledge of the Scriptures, we who have no office of preaching? We embrace the counsel of the wise man, who says in the book of Proverbs: ‘He who walks simply walks confidently.’ It is enough for us to live simply, since the servant who knew his lord’s will and did not do it will be beaten with many blows; but he who did not know it, and committed things worthy of blows, will be beaten with few.”

    O foolish and utterly ruined [unclear], who despise saving knowledge and love ignorance of the divine Scriptures rather than understanding. Will deliberately sought ignorance make you liable to fewer blows? Or will you therefore be guiltless before God when you sin, because you are voluntarily ignorant of God’s commandments? You will be tormented with a twofold punishment: one because you have despised knowing the way of God’s commandments, the other because you do not keep his words. What you allege is not simplicity, but rather a double impiety. For if, according to the prophet, blessed are they who search the testimonies of the Lord, who could doubt that those are accursed who neither seek God nor attend to his Scriptures, but rather despise them with hardened mind?

    Hear what Solomon says to you in Proverbs: “Where there is no knowledge of the soul, there is no good, and the folly of a man supplants his steps.” Of you also, O most foolish men of darkness, that saying of Saint Jerome is understood: that there ignorance is no longer excusable, where it is known what it is that is being ignored. But you must beware still more lest at last you be counted with those who said to God: “Depart from us; we do not want the way of your sciences.”

    You understand Solomon’s word wrongly, who think it was said simply about ignorance. “He who walks simply,” without any deception of his neighbor, “walks confidently” in keeping God’s commandments; but he who corrupts his ways cannot lie hidden, but will be made manifest. [Dine?] again says: “The lips of the righteous instruct many—

    All Things, IV. Folio XI.

    [unclear]: but those who are unlearned will die in poverty of heart. What is more pitiable than an unlearned priest, who, even if he does not have the office of preaching, is nevertheless, by reason of the order he has received, bound to knowledge of the Scriptures?

    For God wills that everyone fulfill his holy will, which no one who is ignorant of it is able to do. Therefore the Lord first commands that you learn what is pleasing to him; secondly, that you do it. How then will you think ignorance of the law excusable, through which you have first become transgressors of the will of God?

    Why do you think almighty God handed over to human beings the volumes of his Scriptures? Was it so that they should read them, and that they should be understood by them, or so that, unread, they should be despised? Certainly the Scriptures of God’s commandments were given to mortals so that they should read them, and thereafter so that they should fulfill them in deed. But you, who with deliberate mind wish to be ignorant of God’s writings: how [unclear] God’s pleasure handed over the volumes of Scripture to all his own? Or will you be able to be useful, who were not hearers before?

    For it can happen that one who knows the will of God either observes it or neglects it; but it cannot happen that one who is ignorant of it fulfills it. Indeed, someone will more easily fail to do the good that he knows than fulfill in deed what he does not know. No one does the good that he does not know.
