Saint Augustine says in a certain place concerning the ignorant: Not everyone who is ignorant is free from fault. For that ignorant person can be excused from punishment who did not find what he might learn. But it will not be possible to pardon those who, having persons from whom they might learn, did not give their effort to instruction.

    Hence also Saint Leo the pope says: If ignorance seems intolerable in laypeople, how much more in those who are in authority; nor is it worthy of excuse or pardon. Therefore, brothers, ignorance of the divine Scriptures does not make you excused before God, but doubly guilty, you who desire to be utterly ignorant of what it is fitting for you to do concerning the will of God. For a man ought not to be ignorant of the divine will [unclear]; it is necessary for the salvation of every mortal, which [unclear] he will find without knowledge of Scripture.

    Indeed, just as from knowledge [unclear] the fear of God comes into human beings, and from its knowledge love is born, so from ignorance there comes [unclear] you will think excusable, through which you have first become transgressors of the will of God. The Scriptures of God’s commandments were given; thereafter, that they should be fulfilled in deed.

    But you, who [unclear] disciples, shamefully ignorant in mind, unruly and wandering, to whom we impute ignorance all the more because they are less inclined to discipline. It is shameful indeed not to know what you are ordered to know; more shameful not to learn it; but most shameful of all to despise it. And there are some among you who do not know saving knowledge [unclear], if I should add that there are also others who utterly despise the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Certainly I do not lie: you know that what I say is true.

    For some of you have opposed my studies gravely, even to the point of envy, seeking, at their urging, to bring me into denial of the Scriptures, so that they might make me a tiller of fields and a keeper of pigs rather than of souls. But they strive in vain to hinder the divine oracle; under its impulse I have resolved, as long as I live, to set all the honors and riches of the world beneath the study of the Scriptures.

    I am your abbot as long as he who called me shall will it. If one of the two is necessary, I prefer to give up the abbacy rather than renounce the holy study of the Scriptures. For I know truly that nothing more salutary can befall a cloistered man in this life than if he has begun truly to love the divine Scriptures.

    Whoever among you wishes to follow my instruction will have me as leader of the journey and likewise as companion. But whoever has scorned to follow me as I learn will nevertheless be compelled to hear me as I teach, even unwillingly. These things have been said against those who, savoring earthly and passing things, cast away from themselves the fear of the Lord; who, ignorant of almost everything, despise learning.

    I know the face of my flock, and I believe that I am not wholly ignorant of the inclinations of each of your hearts. Therefore I shall not cease to exhort you to the holy studies of the Scriptures, knowing that a lover of sacred reading cannot be a doer of fleshly vices. For the more

    On the daily renewal of resolve.

    ... the more zealous a monk has been in learning the Scriptures, the less is he inflamed by the fires of carnal pleasures. For although, according to the opinion of Saint Jerome, the monk seems to have the office not of one who teaches, but rather of one who laments, nevertheless, because he professes the warfare of Christ, it is fitting, indeed necessary, that he know the well-pleasing will of almighty God, to whose words and arms he has sworn. But just as a soldier cannot know the will of his lord when he is far absent except through messengers and letters, so the monk will not understand the commands of the eternal King except through sacred readings and sermons, the evangelical Scriptures.

    The reading of the Scriptures opens the gate of salvation to those who do not know; it leads the studious reader by a straight path to the knowledge of God; it makes the lover of it despise all worldly things and love nothing other than true wisdom. But nothing is more shameful than for a monk in the spiritual life to be unwilling to make progress, and knowingly to wish to be ignorant of the will of God. Let no one flatter himself on account of his weakness or ignorance, since he who is ignorant will be ignored, and he who hates saving knowledge is deservedly condemned. When the Lord was about to send the preacher into all the earth, he forewarned him, saying: Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves, lest either you be tripped up by someone through ignorance, or you contrive injury against someone through deceit. For there is little difference in fault between being able to deceive and being deceived. I ask you therefore, dearest brothers, that you be willing to attend to the Rule of our lord father Benedict, which admonishes you in many places to toil very frequently in readings of the divine Scriptures. For in the Scriptures we are taught, instructed unto all piety, how we ought to live in this very brief pilgrimage of our sojourn, so that we may be able to please the Lord our God above all things. For it belongs to monks to despise the world and all the pleasures of the present life for the love of God; manfully to restrain the unlawful motions of the flesh; to devote themselves also to prayer, reading, and meditation on the Scriptures; and continually to raise the mind from earthly things to heavenly. Blessed is that monk who has not gone away in the counsel of the impious, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the chair of pestilential men, but meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, learning here in the Scriptures the wisdom of God, whose fruit, after the end of this pilgrimage, he is to receive: eternal life.

    On the daily renewal of holy resolve: [unclear] the fifth:

    You have heard, dearest brothers, the reading recited to us from the book of holy Job, in which he laments the misery of the human race, and the calamity of this life, together with its unstable brevity. “Man,” he says, “born of woman, living for a brief time, is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state.” “Behold,” he says, “the brief years pass by, and I walk a path by which I shall not return.” “All flesh will fail together, and man will return to ashes.” What, brothers, do you observe among these things, or what do you think? Is there any man among us who does not know himself to be mortal, who could truthfully say, “I shall not be moved forever”? Alas, my brothers, how blind we are, though we hold our eyes open; how forgetful and sluggish we are as travelers, we who know most certainly that we are going to die, and yet trust in the vanity of the present life as if we were not mortal. But who is the man who will live and not see death, who will rescue his soul from the hand of hell? Behold, Scripture says, all die, and like water we flow away upon the earth. Therefore remember, my brothers, that death does not delay, and all that has passed will be counted brief; because, as the holy lover of Christ Paul says, it is appointed for men to die once, and no one will be able to escape this common law of necessity. O if now we were daily to set before the gaze of the mind the hour of coming death, which each one of us must necessarily undergo shortly, and if we were so to order our life and conduct that we might always be found prepared, how happy and secure our departure could become. Did not the King of the living and the dead, Christ himself our Lord, wishing us always to be prepared for death, forewarn us in the holy Gospel, saying: Therefore you also must be ready, because at the hour when you do not think it, the Son of Man will come. But how much it profits to...

    For purity of mind, frequent meditation on death: the Wise Man in Ecclesiasticus warned us, saying: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Thought of future death brings in fear; fear, however, necessarily shakes the mind, and, like a nail driven by a hammer, fastens all the movements of the flesh and of pride to the wood of the cross. In consideration of this opinion, many of the gentile philosophers used to say that the whole life of a wise man is a certain continual meditation on death.

    Hence Saint Jerome also says: Nothing will profit you so much toward temperance in all things as frequent meditation on this brief and uncertain life, which passes away like a leaf carried off by the wind, and, when it is not feared, falls into death. Therefore remember your death, which you can escape by no counsel, and you will easily be able to overcome all movements of the flesh. For he who daily thinks that he is going to die despises present things, and, unless he is utterly foolish, will prepare himself for the things to come.

    For I know, and I confess that I have in part experienced it, that the will of the human mind cannot long remain uniform in the holy fervor of the spiritual life; and therefore it has seemed good to call the memory of death often back before your eyes, so that, while the mind is shaken by fear of future things, the fervor of the holy purpose may be renewed daily. For the human spirit, bound to the body for the exercise of itself, is exceedingly fluid and unstable: now it is snatched toward this, now it is moved toward that. Therefore the Wisdom of God says in Proverbs through Solomon: “My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes keep my ways.” As though he were saying: Unless you have enslaved the whole love of your heart to divine wisdom, you will never be stable and confirmed in keeping the commandments of the Lord.

    For just as the heart is the first principle of motion in a human being, so there is the greater need to guard it for the preservation of life, since, if it is struck by an uncertain disease, the whole life of the body is already in danger. Hence it is written: “With all watchfulness keep your heart, because life proceeds from it.” By the name of the heart, however, we understand the affection by which someone is drawn aside toward love of some thing, clinging to it so much that it involves the whole will. Hence the psalmist says: “If riches abound, do not set your heart on them,” that is, do not love them from the desire of the will.

    Nothing is more changeable than the human heart, which is altered by almost every thought and can with difficulty remain in the same purpose unless it restrains itself by a certain violent intention. Saint David, not ignorant of this, said to the Lord: “But I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever. Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled.”

    Therefore, my most beloved brothers, if any one of you desires to serve our Lord and Savior in true purity of heart, if anyone wishes to be a monk both in deed and in name, let him learn first not to trust in himself but in God, and let him take care to renew the good purpose of holy conduct always by fresh instruction, not only daily but, as far as he is able, even at each hour and moment. For the fervor of spiritual conduct, to whose practical operation the whole institution of cloistered life is recognized to be ordered, cannot long remain at the same point, since, if it does not always advance toward what lies ahead, it necessarily runs back toward lower things and, what is worse, weaker things.

    In the arena of spiritual exercises there is no lingering permanence of station, because it is the property of the human heart by its natural motion always either to advance toward better things or to fall back into that which is evil. Hence, if you do not make progress in spiritual conduct, you necessarily fail; if you do not go forward toward holier things, you certainly retreat. Since experience has made this clear to us, I do not cease to admonish your charity that you always stretch your desire in good conduct toward what lies further ahead, lest you fall into the destructive danger of failing in the very place where you have not renewed the appetite for making progress.

    The fervor of a spiritual purpose directs one toward the love of God, and it is preserved in no other way than in him. Now the love of God is not absurdly to be compared to fire, because, just as fire, when the fuel of wood has been withdrawn, is necessarily extinguished, so the love of God, if the continual exercises of good works are lacking, is in danger of dying and vanishing away. Hence there is that saying of the Savior in the Gospel: “I have come to send fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” O monks, happy is that conscience in whose breast nothing burns except the love of Christ, which loves God above all things, which despises all pursuits of vanity. Now, brothers, consider your consciences most diligently and examine them exactly, whether you love God above all things

    On the daily renewal of holy purpose.

    If the fire of divine love now burns in you, apply the necessary fuel, lest through your lukewarmness you should at some time feel the little flame of holy fervor utterly extinguished. Believe me, brothers, for my own experience has taught me: you will preserve the fire of divine fervor burning in you with easier exercise than you will kindle it again once it has been extinguished.

    Whoever, therefore, has already experienced in himself the love of God, whoever has received heavenly charity in his heart, let him take the greatest care not to fall back into the negligences of his former life. Let him apply the necessary fuel of spiritual exercises, so that he may be able to preserve in himself the fervor of God as it advances. Let him beware not only of great sins, but also of small negligences, and, as far as he can, of the very least; for he who despises the least things gradually falls, and he who does not always fear danger to spiritual fervor and holy purpose will quickly feel the loss.

    For Scripture says: “If you do not steadfastly keep yourself in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown.” Blessed, therefore, is the man who is always fearful, who does not presume upon the virtues he has received, who judges with certainty that he is failing whenever he has not found himself advancing at every moment toward higher things.

    But truly, brothers, I judge very strongly, unless the assessment of certain works deceives me, that in some of you the fire of holy fervor is not yet present, since they seem to love the true pursuits of monks but little. That this is manifest from their conduct none of you will be able to ignore. I have indeed not considered it wholly superfluous to admonish those who so far seem to have made little progress, since the hand of the Lord has not been shortened so that it cannot save the penitent.

    For I trust in the mercy of the living God, who, because of his very great charity toward them and because of the exercises of piety of those who walk among you according to the purity of the rule, will grant them at some time [to conquer themselves?], to love the pursuits of holy fervor more ardently.

    What is this, brothers, that you do not live monastically in the monastery, and, having professed the life of the spirit, walk according to the flesh? Do you not know how perilous it is for a monk to live in worldly fashion in a cenobium, and by lukewarm conduct to violate the vows of holy purity which all of us once made?

    Know, I pray, that the last things of all cloistered persons are very near the end, so that, as good and zealous monks who love your own salvation, not of common things but rather

    Homily V. Fol. XIII.

    storms: for just as meat set to the fire and often removed is never properly cooked, so the soul, often fallen back into sloth, is by no means truly enlightened by the divine Spirit. For Scripture says to the Lord: “Those who withdraw far from you will perish; and you have destroyed all who work iniquity.” For if the mind, through sloth, has withdrawn farther from the fervor of divine love, it stands very near to hell and despair; more rarely and with greater difficulty does it recover to true repentance.

    Whoever therefore among you, my brothers, desires to flee from the midst of Babylon, whoever longs to come to the inward fervor of the spirit, let him with the utmost and continual effort strive to drive from himself the torpor of mind and sloth, and daily to renew the purpose of divine love. It is a hard thing, I admit, to resist the evil habit of the flesh, and, in an old [unclear], to think new thoughts against custom. Certainly, brothers, no one with a lukewarm will can afterwards rise again from the depths of hell; nor will anyone be able to overcome an evil habit without great violence and a long contrary habit. For no one becomes holy by his own powers, but it is God who works all things in all; nevertheless it is plainly established for us that the kingdom of God suffers violence, and whoever neglects to do violence to the motions of his flesh will not attain to the fellowship of the saints of the Lord.

    Hear now, monk, whoever you are who are lukewarm toward the love of God and slothful; hear, whoever you are, and take thought: unless you rise continually from the torpor of an evil habit of life, unless you bring violence upon yourself by a habit contrary to [it], unless you prepare your heart to resist in the fervor of divine love, [unclear] you will see the face of God in glory. Sloth is the root of despair; and not only the root, but also its nurse and mother. If once it has oppressed the mind of a man dedicated to God, it at once closes off every way to salvation. For the kingdom of heaven has not been promised to those who sleep; eternal blessedness has not been prepared for those who grow drowsy in leisure and idleness. Rather, the crown is laid up for those who manfully command the motions of the flesh, and the happiness of glory is given to those who follow the spirit, not the flesh.

    No virtue is acquired without labor; no enemy is overcome without an encounter. If you desire to be crowned, if you desire to conquer, you must fight bravely and perseveringly. Wherefore also Solomon cries out to you, lazy sluggard: “When will you rise from your sleep?” If you are lazy, your harvest will come like a spring [unclear], and poverty and want will flee from you [unclear]. For he who gathers in harvest is a wise son, and he who sleeps in summer is a son of confusion. For he who works his own field will be filled with bread; but he who delights in idleness will be filled with poverty.

    This, brothers, is the good season for working; this is the opportunity for meriting the eternal blessedness granted to us by the Lord God, which is suddenly taken away in death. For Scripture says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, work earnestly; for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge will be among the dead, to whom you are hastening.” If the eternal good of blessedness that is promised delights you, the labors of the struggle that are set before you must not frighten your minds. For no one will be crowned by the Lord unless he has striven lawfully; no one attains the summit of eternal blessedness except those who, by fervor of spirit, have overcome the illicit movements of the flesh.

    We must always fight, brothers, against the threefold battle-line of the devil so long as we live in this pilgrimage; for no one here is seen to become unsurpassable who is not gradually overcome by tepidity [unclear]. Saint Augustine proclaims: “No one ought to be secure in this life, which is wholly called temptation; for he who could have become better from worse may not become worse from better.” Hence Solomon says in the Book of Proverbs: “Desires kill the lazy man.” Just as constancy bestows perfection on every good work, so sloth, the stepmother of all religion and perfection, destroys the spiritual mind. Saint Jerome says: “Nothing in a holy purpose is worse than leisure; for not only is no new good acquired, but even what has been acquired is shamefully made worse.” The principle of a holy spiritual life advances by continual progress, and the joy grows and increases; but through cessation it becomes torpid and fails.

    Therefore, brothers, the mind must be renewed by daily and fresh increases of the virtues, and those things to be avoided must be measured not by what has passed, but by what remains. Idleness, which is the mother and nurse of evils, and foremost of the enemies of the virtues, must be fled; but sloth is to be overcome not by fleeing, but by resisting. For Scripture says: “Idleness has taught much evil.” For every idle man is in desires vain and pernicious [unclear]. Therefore the monk who desires to be a soldier of Christ and of true purity of mind must always be occupied in some exercise, so that idleness may not beget vice.

    On the daily renewal of holy purpose.

    pernicious thoughts may find a place by which they are strengthened. Just as rust consumes iron, and a garment is gnawed by worms, so idleness enervates the mind; and virtue of the soul, long neglected, gradually ebbs away and is utterly rooted out. Therefore flee idleness, and overcome sloth.

    But since we cannot remain firmly and without alteration of mind in one state of divine love, it is necessary for us, lest we fall away entirely, to renew our holy purpose every day, so that as often as, through the negligence of human weakness, we begin, however slightly, to grow sluggish from spiritual fervor, so often, examining ourselves by the memory of future things and by contemplation of the Lord’s Passion, we may at once bring our conscience back to its former purpose of making progress.

    But this must be most carefully guarded against by us: that we not put off this holy effort to make progress until tomorrow, since it has often been harmful to have deferred to a future time a good thing that could have been done sooner. Therefore the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not delay to be converted to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” Augustine also says: “Why do you defer the good until tomorrow, saying: life will still be long? For who knows whether it will be long? But if it is not good, what does it profit that it will be long?”

    Without a good life, the conduct of a monk should be called death rather than life. The remedies of a more corrected life, therefore, must not be deferred by any delays, lest the time for conversion perish through tardiness, when now no delay is granted for repenting. For he who promised pardon to the penitent did not promise tomorrow. No one who fears God delays turning to repentance, nor prolongs today’s salvation until tomorrow. But every man who knows himself to be established in lukewarmness of mind, and who defers amendment of life from day to day, is deceived by the hope of a longer life; for if he knew that he would die tomorrow, today without doubt he would change his purpose. The hope of a longer life has wretchedly deceived many, who, while they daily defer the amendment of their manner of life, suddenly fall into the abyss of death.

    Who among you, brothers, does not resolve in his mind to take up the purpose of a more corrected life before he dies? For I believe that each one of you intends still to practice greater piety toward God before he falls into the danger of death. And why do you wait so long? Why do you defer from day to day? Behold, you who now live healthy and do not devote yourselves to the spiritual exercises of divine love when you can, while the Lord waits patiently: the last day will come for each of you, and it is already hastening, on which, when the angel of death presses urgently, the power whose exercise you have delayed so long will be taken away from you.

    Therefore again and again I ask you, brothers, and with whatever diligence I can I admonish you: turn to the Lord our God with your whole heart while you live safe and sound, and do not delay your will any longer, lest you also lose the power granted to you. Think, and think again often, that we are not citizens of this world, but strangers and pilgrims; nor do we have here a lasting city, but we seek the one to come, and day by day we are hastening toward death, even though we do not know it.

    On the love of quiet and solitude.

    The sixth homily.

    There are two intellects created from the beginning, which I know is hidden from none of you, dearly beloved brothers: namely, the angelic and the human. But when the angelic intellect was created, Holy Scripture does not plainly disclose; yet the opinion of the Fathers counted the creation of the angels as a work of God and reckoned it among the works of the six days. There are, however, some who write that the angels were created long before this visible world; and just as we cannot prove this by the testimony of the divine Scriptures, so neither should we rashly attack it. For there are several grave and holy men who have placed the creation of the angels long before the beginning of the world.

    Now the angelic intellect was made from the very beginning in the actuality of all knowable things, and it knew all that it could know, and afterward admitted nothing toward its own perfection. For it was created by the Lord in the natural perfection that it could have, and required no manner of increase by which it might understand more. For [unclear], joined to God, was made a pure intellect by nature, and does not, in our fashion, need exercise in order to understand; its being admits no corruption. And so, adhering to its object through the affection of love, God, whom it understands to be the center of its blessedness, immediately and

    Homily VI.

    ... contemplates and loves immutably; he is blessed and fears no alteration of himself. But the human intellect, which our teachers have called the soul, was indeed created at the beginning in all ignorance, and knows none of those things which the angelic intellect understands by nature. These two intellects differ as act and potency; light and darkness; knowledge and ignorance; habit and privation; beginning and end; simple and composite; substance and accident; nature and art; truth and likeness. For all things, as divine Scripture testifies, which are present in the angelic intellect by nature and from the beginning, the human intellect will attain through arts at the end, as the Lord Jesus says in the holy Gospel: “In the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they will be like the angels of God in heaven.”

    For in order that the mind may be trained toward understanding through many labors, as if through arts, it has been placed for a short time in the workshop of the body. If there, turned toward God, it has duly completed its craft through love, then at last, going forth from here, it becomes equal to an angel. But if, consenting to the motions of the flesh, it has not kept its proper order, then, disturbed and wretched, like the apostate spirits who fell, it will depart from the body to be tormented eternally. For since our mind, or soul, was created in ignorance and privation of all things, it must necessarily come to knowledge of things by continual action, motion, and art. For the end makes the human intellect equal to the angelic, changing its potency into act; and it will make from privation a habit, from the empty the full, from the imperfect the perfect, from the deprived one who possesses, from the dark the luminous, from the nocturnal the diurnal, from the lunar the solar, and from the earthly the heavenly. This end, my dearest brothers, is the beginning of eternal salvation; no one can happily come to it who does not strive with all his strength toward the summit of perfection.

    But since it is difficult in the midst of crowds always to keep unbroken this necessary effort of advancement, where a thousand occasions of sinning are presented, the holy fathers, founders of the monastic order, taught us by word and example to flee the world, and to avoid company not only in mind but also in body. Of those who were stronger in spirit, many hastened to the desert, so that in mind they might become nearer to the Lord in proportion as in body they had withdrawn farther from the world. Of them we read the saying of the prophet Isaiah: “The wilderness will rejoice and will blossom like the lily; sprouting it will sprout, and it will rejoice, glad and praising.” Others, wishing to benefit many, established cenobia, in which they placed a multitude of monks, whose way of life would be separated from peoples and nevertheless social among themselves mutually. For it does not suit everyone to sit in the desert; for some it is more fitting to serve the Lord in the midst of brothers. For our monasteries too have their own solitude, so that whoever wishes to be solitary can do so in the midst of brothers, provided he has maintained the privacy of the cell in which he dwells.

    For a monk, according to the interpretation of his name, is called solitary, because in mind and body he is separated from the tumult of this world. Therefore, as I am about to make today’s sermon, [unclear] your progress in spiritual conduct. I ask you, I say, and exhort you in the bowels of brotherly charity, to love the quiet of the cell as the workshop of your salvation, in which there is much peace for those who love God, and great advantage for perfecting the intellect toward the knowledge of the highest truth. For the prophet Isaiah says: “In silence and hope will be your strength.” He who does not love the solitude of the cell and the quiet of silence by no means loves purity of mind, but, wandering in body, always drinks in new vanities in his soul.

    Hence blessed Jerome says: “Why do we desire the crowds of cities, we who are reckoned from singularity? For to me a town is a prison, solitude a paradise.” If the desert and solitude delighted us, brothers, this place would offer great advantage for our purpose, where, apart from poor peasants, a guest is rarely met; no one disturbs our quiet, no one troubles us, no one brings in spectacles or rumors of momentary novelty. But I see few lovers of inward quiet among you, and I grieve exceedingly, because I know very well that a monk cannot advance in spiritual conduct if it is clear that he does not love the quiet of the cell. But he who knows how much good the secrecy of solitude confers upon the soul loves his cell and does not easily go outside, always fearing in the tumult

    On the love of quiet and solitude.

    ...to lose what he had gathered with great labor in secret. For, as Saint Augustine says, he is less stirred by pleasures who is not where there is a crowd of pleasures; and he suffers less the troubles of avarice who, placed far from men, does not see riches. Therefore, since the holy Spirit of God loves the secrecy of the mind but shudders at public exposure, it belongs to you, brothers, to love the solitude of cells as the workshop of all virtues, and never to withdraw yourselves from its dwelling-place without reasonable cause. For the monk who loves secrecy, not idleness, who has learned to remain steadfastly in his cell, sometimes enjoys many holy consolations, of which the wandering and restless man is necessarily deprived. Just as a fish dies if it is kept too long out of water, so the devotion of a monk perishes if he wanders too often outside his cell. Let us imitate John the Baptist, whom Chrysostom says is the chief of monks: he, a monk, lived in the desert as soon as he was born, was nourished in the desert, and as a monk awaited Christ in solitude. For just as it is difficult for a tree placed beside a road to preserve its fruits until maturity, so it is difficult for a monk who often wanders outside his cell and is occupied in the affairs of the world to preserve the fruits of righteousness unspotted to the end [unclear]. For a mind that is run together with the cares and anxieties of the world is rarely truly rooted in the love of God. Indeed, movement of the body often alters the state of the mind, and a man who is always submerged in external things is never illumined by the fervor of the divine Spirit. For the quiet of the mind [unclear] from the solidity of monastic [unclear]; let him learn to be quiet in his cell, not idle; tranquil, not sleepy; always devoted to spiritual exercise, not dissolved by sluggishness of spirit.

    The instruments of spiritual exercises in the cell are four: to read, to write, to pray, and to meditate. But a fifth is granted to few: those who, after true purity of heart, are raised to the mountain of contemplation of the Lord. Finally, these four exercises of monks who remain in the solitude of the cell are to be so moderated that they generate neither weariness nor sluggishness of mind, but that a fitting time be assigned to each activity, so that, while variety lightens the mind, the little body may not be burdened beyond its strength. Therefore let the reading of the divine Scriptures have its own suitable hour for study; and when it perceives that the desire of devotion is present, let it at once be changed into fervent prayer. Manual labor, however, which is enjoined upon the monk dwelling in the tranquility of solitude, is very useful, lest a harmful lukewarmness arise in the mind. For the reading of the holy Scriptures stirs the monk to the love of God; meditation on the Lord’s passion and on the benefits of God inflames the mind to the fervor of most ardent love; prayer strengthens the weak spirit; and manual labor, temperately continued, preserves him from sluggishness and weariness. When we pray earnestly and devoutly, we speak with our God, who is present everywhere; but when we read in the holy Scriptures, we are taught by the Lord himself what is to be sought by us or avoided. If prayer is ardent in the love of God, it purifies the mind from sins and vices; reading, however, instructs and forms it, as Saint Isidore says: "By prayers," he says, "we are cleansed; by reading we are instructed. Therefore both are good, if both are possible; if both are not possible, it is better to pray than to read." Therefore the monk who desires to spend his time in the cell usefully and fruitfully should strive continually, by turns, to occupy mind and body in these exercises, since the spirit that keeps watch amid such labors offers no entrance to perverse thoughts. Hence the divine Jerome, admonishing a monk, says: "Always do some good thing, so that the devil may find you occupied." For he is less assailed by the enticements of the flesh who, always usefully occupied, admits no weariness of mind. But when any monk, a cautious guardian of his soul, is carried by alternation from the exercise of one good work to another with the desire of holy fervor, his effort is strengthened toward constancy in all virtues, and he falls into weariness so much the less

    Homily VI.

    ...how much more study is wont to be varied, and to use alternations against weariness. Hence again Jerome says: Prayer should frequently interrupt reading, and with a pleasing alternation of holy prayer should approach the soul that is constantly attached to it. The monk who does not love the secrecy of the cell is not a true soldier of Christ, since he bears the name and habit of a monk without the works; and he who ought to have been solitary for the love of God, having returned in mind to the world, loves the pursuit of vanity. Hence the holy pope Gregory says: He who lives bodily removed from human beings, but plunges himself in thought into the tumults of human intercourse and into desire for earthly things, is not solitary, although he dwells in solitude. But if someone is bodily pressed by the crowds of the people, and yet suffers no tumults of secular cares in his heart, he is not in the city, even if he moves in the midst of human beings. And this is what Saint Jerome says against Jovinian: The wise man, he says, can never be alone. For he has with him all who are and who have been good; and he has a free mind, and brings forth whatever he wishes, and transfers himself wherever he wishes. For what he cannot do in body he embraces in mind; and if there is a lack of human beings, he speaks with God. Therefore a good man will never be alone. And so, remaining in your cell, always beware idleness, since nothing so enervates all the powers of the mind as idleness, after it has produced sloth from itself. If you have ardently loved God, you will never be idle, because the true love of Christ does not allow torpor to arise in the soul; it always drives one toward the will of the beloved friend. And just as a certain carnally wise man truly said, “Let him who does not wish to become listless love,” so experience has taught us in spiritual love that it does not permit the mind which it has begun to inhabit to grow torpid through idleness and laziness. For divine love always drives one toward better things; and the more it has advanced by burning, the greater increase it takes of itself. But the workshop of this love is a clean conscience; if a monk desires to have and preserve it clean, it is necessary first of all that he despise the vanities of the world and the affairs of temporal things. For it is not possible that a twin love should reside in one breast; nor can a man love Christ who does not wish to despise the world. For since God, in the Trinity of persons, is one in the essence of substance, either he alone is loved by us, or he is not loved with a partner. Therefore, so that the conscience may remain clean in all purity, and so that the mind may be able to love God above all things, let the monk love the secrecy of the cell, and never withdraw from the exercise of inward sweetness. For in the cell of a good and wise monk there is the highest tranquillity; and if anywhere there is an earthly paradise, it is in the monastery of those who live according to the purity of the cenobitic institution. There is peace, piety, goodness, light, virtue, honor; there is joy, purity, sweetness, and great tranquillity of life, where the devoted praying monk speaks with the Lord, and the future sweetness of the heavenly kingdom is tasted beforehand by the contemplative soldier. O cell, paradise of monks truly serving God: you surely are a little garden of most honorable delight, in which the mind is joined to God through love, and is sweetly raised up through desire. The monk who loves, venerates, and cultivates you is a true soldier of Christ, and serves the Lord in the fullness of virtues. But he who abhors and deserts the secrecy of the cell despises the workshop of his own salvation. Therefore I beseech you, my dearest brothers, begin to inhabit the secrecy of the cell with the desire of the mind; without love for it no one will be able to attain perfection of the virtues in the monastery.

    On the manual labor of monks: Homily VII.

    “The labors of your hands, because you shall eat,” says the prophet of the Lord; “blessed are you, and it shall be well with you.” If all who live from the labor of their own hands are judged blessed, certainly no idle man eats bread without guilt and crime. For almighty God imposed this punishment on the first-formed man for the transgression of the original commandment, declaring to him that in the sweat of his face he would work food from the earth with his hands. But since in Adam we have all sinned, we are necessarily subject to the same punishments to which it is agreed that he was subjected. He labored with his hands for the food by which he might live, nor did he eat bread idle. Hence the holy father

    On the manual labor of monks.

    Father Benedict, detesting the idleness of monks, says in the Rule which he handed down to us: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul; and therefore at fixed times monks ought to be occupied in the labor of their hands, and again at fixed hours in divine reading. For then they are truly monks, if they live by the labor of their own hands, as our fathers and the apostles also did.” Hence also the holy Christ-loving Paul says in the epistle: “He who does not work shall not eat.”

    In the beginning of the monastic state this was the custom of monks: that they admitted no one into their fellowship without labor, not so much on account of the necessities of food as on account of the salvation of the soul, lest through idleness an occasion be given for harmful thoughts. At that time monks had no fixed revenues, no tithes, no rents, no annual proceeds at all; but all, living together in common, procured food and clothing for themselves with their hands, burdening no one by the exaction of debt.

    The holy apostles of our Savior also, though they had the power to live from the preaching of the Gospel, preferred to labor with their hands, lest they should seem to have burdened any of the faithful, and so that they might have not only the means by which they themselves could live, but also something with which they might supply necessities to the needy. But afterward, when monks began to have revenues and rents, the former pursuits of simplicity soon failed; and pride gradually increased along with the riches of temporal things, to such an extent that in time monks refused all labor of the hands. As long as the monks were poor and humble in birth, they worshiped God in truth; but afterward, when they began to abound in riches, duplicity drove out simplicity, and the arrogance of nobles uprooted the humility of monks. For the integrity of regular observance gave birth to an abundance of temporal goods; but little by little the riches of monks utterly extinguished the purity of the order. And when the integrity of regular observance had been removed, soon, in many monasteries, the riches of temporal goods also failed by the just judgment of God.

    From their number was the present monastery of Sponheim, neither the last, my brothers, nor the first, which for many years remained miserably desolate in both conditions, to such a degree that the five monks only who were living in it, leading a dissolute life, did not have the means from which to obtain the necessities of life for themselves. Hence, when the mercy of God at last provided, Frederick, duke of Transylvania, having called upon the counsel of the fathers of the reformed order, in the year of the Christians 1469, expelled the monks deformed in life, deposed the abbot, by name Otto of Cologne, and placed in this monastery four others of the observance of Bursfelde, summoned from the monastery called Montis Speciosi. Over them he set as abbot Johannes, from the noble family of Budischbach, which they commonly call de Carbonaria Domo, a man such as you have seen and heard, worthy of eternal memory; he found this place in extreme poverty, and, presiding for almost fourteen years with great patience, renewed it into the state in which we now live.

    Therefore, since want of temporal goods still presses hard upon us, there would be need of continual labor, by which we might nourish ourselves with necessary food and free the house of God in which we dwell from debt. But what are your labors, or how much can they contribute to us for such great needs? We are few in number, and, being unsuited to rustic labors, the institution of the priestly order does not permit us to spend the whole day in the field turning stones with our hands and to neglect the divine service. We are wretched and weighed down by excessive poverty and by lack of all necessities; and if we have labored much, we profit little from it, and if we have worked little, we shall certainly fail all the more in spirit. For man, as Scripture bears witness, is born to labor just as [unclear] to flying. Therefore, lest you eat your bread idle, you will have to be bound to some honest and useful labor, by which the mind may be relieved from weariness of regular observance, and severe want may be repaired at least in some small measure.

    In the summer season for hay, and in the days of autumn for the vintage, we have been accustomed to employ you only outside the monastery, namely when labor is very necessary and the scarcity of hired workers increases the price and wage of servants. At other times we have resolved to keep you in the monastery, because your labors, in comparison with the expenses of the monastery, contribute little to its needs, and very few of you, as it seems to us, willingly come forward of your own accord for rustic pursuits. There is also another consideration which stirs my mind, lest you, by external

    that I should readily occupy every hand without reasonable cause and manifest necessity; for I find that labors of this sort do not accord in you with regular observance, but rather destroy than promote the integrity of monastic discipline among you. I blush to say it, and nevertheless I am compelled to utter it: your labors outside the monastery and the cell bring more destruction than salvation to the purity of souls. For what do you labor at, and what are your pursuits in your labors? Is it not to wander about, to run to and fro, to indulge in feasts and cups, and to occupy the rest of the time with vain and useless conversations?

    You do not have in yourselves that holy fervor of the Spirit of God by which we read that the ancient monks of our institution were once inflamed: for the common necessity, with such desire, such zeal, and such effort, all and each labored with their own hands that you would have thought the whole business of the monastery was placed in the providence of each one. For they labored with their own hands as though each individually had to sustain the whole congregation. Yet amid these things they discharged the service of divine worship by day and night with such cheerfulness as if they had not been occupied at all in labors of the hands.

    Who among you, brothers, is an imitator of such men, so that he regards the poverty of our whole community as his own, or strives according to his strength to relieve it by laboring in the sweat of his face? They, laboring with their hands, besought God with unceasing hearts; but you, intent on tales, satisfy neither your duty with your hands nor, as monks, with your minds. Also in the time of regular fasting, they either diligently kept the measure of abstinence appointed for them, or, if because of the greatness of their labors they could not, they ate for this reason, that they might be rendered fit and suitable for the labors. But you do not eat in order to labor; rather, you labor in order to eat, when according to the Rule you ought to have fasted. You take occasion from labor to break the fast.

    Moreover, how filthily and most vilely some of you treat their garments, what zealous lover of regular discipline can bear with equanimity? Whose, pray, are the things, my brothers, that you wastefully consume? Everything that belongs to the monasteries of the servants of God is the patrimony of Christ, and the whole is dedicated to God; nor is it lawful for anyone to misuse the things of Christ, or for them to be turned to another use. Do you not know what our holy lawgiver Benedict says to you in the Rule? “If anyone treats the things of the monastery filthily or negligently, let him be corrected. If he does not amend, let him be subject to regular discipline.” And in the chapter on the cellarer of the monastery he says: “Let him regard all the vessels of the monastery and all its substance as if they were the consecrated vessels of the altar.”

    Finally, I cannot and ought not keep silent about how filthily and negligently most of you treat everything, as though either they were not seen by God, or the sloth of none of them caused loss to the goods of the monastery. Know, brothers, that in warning you beforehand I announce to you that for all these things, as also for your other sins, you are going to render account to the Lord God. I reduced your labors outside the monastery for this reason, lest by working badly you should sin more gravely; and I enjoined upon you manual work: to copy books, to bind them, and similar tasks, which you can perform within the enclosure of the monastery with tranquility of mind and body.

    Would that you did even these works of your hands with diligence for the love of God, lest you eat bread altogether idle. There is no manual work which in my judgment befits a monk more than to copy books of sacred reading, and to prepare what is necessary for others who are copying. For this holy labor may often be interrupted by prayer, and one may keep watch for the food of the mind no less than of the body. Necessity also urges us to devote ourselves with diligence to copying books, if we desire to have at hand that with which we can profitably occupy ourselves in turn in spiritual study.

    For you see that the whole library of this monastery, which once was distinguished and great, was by the disordered monks before us so thoroughly dispersed, sold, and alienated [unclear] that no more than fourteen volumes were found here by us. The industry of the art of printing, recently invented in our days at Mainz, indeed brings many volumes to light every day; but it is by no means possible for us to acquire them all, since we are still oppressed by the greatest poverty. Therefore I warn and exhort you, who do not come very willingly to external labors of the hands, that for the honor of God you labor with diligence in copying volumes; for just as idleness is the enemy of the soul, so moderate labor is the spiritual preserver of life. For a monk, because he is a soldier of the eternal King, ought never to be idle. Idleness begets acedia, and that brings upon the soul the want of destructive death. But the labors of monks are to be so moderated that

    On the Manual Labor of Monks

    [unclear] for divine colloquies; but amid the works of the hands, let meditation on the Scriptures burn in the heart; and after it has brought the mind into the ardor of the spirit, let it at once be changed into most devout prayer. Therefore let the monk, Christ’s soldier, be like a clean animal of God, which chews the cud, always having in the mouth of his heart the nourishment of the holy Scriptures, lest the mind lie open to vain and pernicious thoughts, or a foul or idle word break forth from the mouth of the speaker.

    Let him always be mindful while working of the Scripture that says: Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. For everyone who loves the Lord Jesus in truth renews in his heart every day, with tears and prayers, both his teaching and his passion. For he is not a true lover of God who forgets his commandments even for a moment. Indeed, as Scripture says: Those who love the Lord seek the things that are well pleasing to him; and those who fear his holy name will be filled with his law. Hence one of the saints said to the Lord: In my heart I have hidden your words, that I may not sin against you.

    Therefore the soul must always be stirred up, and renewed daily with spiritual goads, lest it grow lukewarm through sloth or languish in the idleness of inertia. The exercise of labor in monastic discipline, zeal for reading and prayer, and diligent keeping of vigils are true incitements to the virtues. But nothing is more destructive to the holy purpose of a monk than idleness, since it both excites the flesh to lust and weakens every virtue of the mind and extinguishes the fervor of the spirit. For idleness in the cloister is the fuel and nourishment of evils. Therefore wherever you may be, whether in the field or in the cloister, always avoid despisers of their own [unclear]. For he who touches pitch will be defiled by it; and he who makes himself a companion of sinners will not be immune from crime. Consider your words carefully, so that you detract from no one at all, nor listen to another detracting; for the detractor and the willing listener alike both serve the demon, the one by speaking, the other by listening.

    Labor like a good soldier of Christ Jesus, and diligently work with your hands at whatever is enjoined on you by obedience; nor let it seem hard to you to obey another’s command, for in return for it a crown of eternal happiness is prepared in heaven for your spirit. Hence no labor, no length of time, no observance ought to seem burdensome to a monk, by which the glory of eternal blessedness is acquired.

    Consider, my brothers, the brevity of this life, and do good while it is permitted; for he who now sows sparingly will also reap sparingly after death, and each person will receive a fitting reward for his own work, not for another’s. The time for laboring is very short, but the reward that is owed to good works is everlasting. Consider, my brothers, how strong men entangled in the world and all lovers of this age are in earthly and perishable matters, but how weak and infirm in heavenly matters, so that you should take care to please God as much as they labor continually to appear rich and glorious to the world. For for temporal glory many do not refuse to be defiled even unto death, but for the hope of future happiness they disdain either to do or to endure even a little. For earthly gains they endure any injuries whatever with the greatest patience, and for a heavenly reward they refuse to endure even the insult of the slightest word. They can stand all day with strength before an earthly king, prince, or judge; but in prayer before the almighty Lord they cannot endure for the space of one hour. They willingly endure many adversities to acquire perishable riches, but they neglect heavenly goods all the more, the more delightfully they are occupied in love of transitory things.

    Let the conduct of these men admonish you, dearest brothers, to flee all cares of this world so much the more, since it is now permitted to you to handle the business of earthly things less. Always devote all your solicitude and care to the acquisition of heavenly goods, and labor most diligently at all times for the reward of future blessedness. For, as Scripture testifies, your life upon earth is a warfare, and whatever a man has sown, this also he will reap. Know that death hastens on, and at every moment a part of life, never to return again, is extinguished. Watch, therefore, my dearest brothers, watch, because you do not know when the Lord our God will come to each one for the judgment of death, [unclear]

    [unclear] whatever is enjoined on you by obedience; nor let it seem hard to you to obey another’s command, for in return for it a crown of eternal happiness is prepared in heaven for your spirit. Hence no labor, no length of time, no observance ought to seem burdensome to a monk, by which the glory of eternal blessedness is acquired. Let him always be mindful while working of the Scripture that says: Therefore the soul must always be stirred up, and renewed daily with spiritual goads, lest it grow lukewarm through sloth or languish in the idleness of inertia. The exercise of labor in monastic discipline, zeal for reading and prayer, and diligent keeping of vigils are true incitements to the virtues. But nothing is more destructive to the holy purpose of a monk than idleness, since it both excites the flesh to lust and weakens every virtue of the mind and extinguishes the fervor of the spirit. For idleness in the cloister is hunger and nourishment [unclear]. Therefore wherever you may be, whether in the field or in the cloister, always avoid despisers of their own [unclear]. For he who touches pitch will be defiled by it; and he who makes himself a companion of sinners will not be immune from crime. Consider your words carefully, so that you detract from no one at all, nor listen to another detracting; for the detractor and the willing listener alike both serve the demon, the one by speaking, the other by listening. Labor like a good

    Homily VIII.

    Whether at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning, lest when he comes suddenly he find you sleeping. Watch, therefore, at every time, praying that you may be deemed worthy to escape all the evils that are to come, and to stand with confidence before the sight of the Son of God who judges all things. For, as the divine [apostle of Christ?] bears witness, we shall all stand before the judgment-seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body according as he has done, whether good or evil.

    Blessed is that monk whom the Lord shall find watching in good works, who has prepared himself for the wedding feast of the heavenly Lamb in true purity of heart, who will not fear to meet the Judge. Let that memorable saying of Saint Jerome on the Gospel according to Matthew always be in your hearts: “Whether I eat or drink, or do anything else, that voice always seems to sound in my ears: Rise, dead, and come to judgment.” As often as I think of that day of future examination, so often I tremble in heart and body. Therefore, my brothers, if there is any joy in the present life, it must be conducted in such a way that the bitterness of that dreadful judgment never recedes from memory.

    O that day, great, terrible, exceedingly fearful, and very bitter, on which the sun and moon will be darkened, not by diminution of light but by comparison with majesty; where every argument of excuse will cease; where all things will be manifest, and nothing will be able to lie hidden from the Judge. For he who knows the hidden thoughts of minds will then judge openly; he is neither forestalled by favor, nor bent by mercy; he is not corrupted by gifts and presents; he will not be softened by prayers; nor thereafter will any satisfaction appease him.

    Placed in this life, therefore, brothers, let each of you do as much as he can for his soul, because repentance for sins made here alone is useful and fruitful, while there is still a place for pardon and the sentence of justice is still deferred. He who delays doing good and doing penance until the [hour?] of death is [near?] to damnation, because the good that he neglects while healthy and unharmed he will rarely restore when sick and already about to die. For Saint Pope Gregory says: Whoever does not fear to defer the fruits of repentance until the hour of death is himself witness against himself that truly repenting was never in his mind. Now therefore turn yourselves to our Lord with your whole heart, doing penance before him, and so live, I beg you, that when it is time to depart from here, you may not fear to appear before his face.

    That One Must Pray Without Intermission, Homily VII.

    Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, brothers, in the Gospel according to Luke, wishing us to be constant in prayers, warned us thus, saying: It is necessary always to pray and never to fail. This counsel of the Lord befits monks above all mortals, and all cloistered persons in whatever religious order, whose every action and whole life, indeed whatever they do, should at least be in conformity with prayer.

    For all who profess the monastic warfare are called spiritual not without reason, insofar as by that very name they are admonished to despise the pleasures of the flesh for the love of God, and through true charity to walk in fervor of spirit. For the holy apostle of Christ says: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God, because if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live. But we know that without persistence in prayer the fervor of the spirit cannot long subsist in us. Again, to the Thessalonians he says: Rejoice always; pray without intermission; give thanks in all things, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you.

    But what the manner of praying is, the Savior taught us in the Gospel, saying: But you, when you pray, enter into your chamber, and with the door closed, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. And in another place he said to the Samaritan woman: Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such as will worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

    That prayer is of the heart rather than a lengthy discourse of the mouth is plainly established from Christ’s teaching, because, since God is spirit, he must be worshiped in no other way than with inward fervor of spirit. For great is the power of prayer of the heart in the fervor of spirit; of the multiplying of words without attention of mind

    That one must pray without ceasing.

    ... no usefulness at all. Hence Jerome also says: God is to be prayed to not in words only, but with the heart. Therefore the chanting of fifty psalms with purity of heart, serenity, and spiritual gladness is better than the recitation of the whole Psalter with anxiety of heart and sadness. And the blessed pope Gregory says: True petition is not in the sounds of the mouth, but in the voices of the heart, that is, in holy thoughts. For it is not words but desires that make the stronger voices in the ears of God.

    Except, therefore, for those prayers which we are bound to say either by decree of the Church or by the institution of the monastic order, abundance and multiplication of words in the rest contributes nothing, or little, to true inward devotion of mind; for where there is no fervent desire in the love of God, a lengthening of discourse is brought in to support it. For holy Augustine says: Let much speaking be absent from prayer, but let fervent intention persevere; for to speak much in praying is to conduct a necessary matter with superfluous words. For prayer comprehends many things in few words, so that the simplicity of faith might quickly learn the sufficiency of its salvation, or prudent reflection might stand amazed at the profundity of the mysteries.

    But for those to whom, because of hardness of the inner heart, the compunction of fervor is lacking, when they prostrate themselves for prayer there is need of more extended speech, crying, and tears, so that long practice of the mind may at last strike out the burning fire of divine love in [unclear], until in the affection of holy prayer they are lifted up in the Spirit of God. But afterward, when the fervor of divine love and compunction has penetrated the mind, thereafter there is no longer need for the exercise of words; rather, the continuation of spiritual kindling is required, lest the fire of spiritual fervor be extinguished. To this end our holy father wished the prayers in the community to be shortened, so that if anyone wished to pray by himself in spirit, he could do so.

    But there are some who are so wandering, so hard of heart, and find little or no spiritual compunction while praying; for them liberty is ruinous, and solitude often gives rise to despair. Pay attention, I ask you, dearest brothers, to these things which I say to you, and consider how greatly you are obliged to pray without ceasing. It is not enough for a monk, striving toward perfection in the school of Christ the eternal king, to discharge the canonical prayers; nor is it sufficient for a man solemnly dedicated to God by vow

    Homily VIII.

    [unclear], since it has two wings and neither strays nor grows sluggish. Let us therefore pray in the highest fervor of spirit, and let us live with as much purity of conscience as we can, since that man's prayer is perfect and pleasing to God whose cause and tongue both cry out, whose deed and speech agree with his supplication, whose life and thought lend support to his prayers for protection. For without the righteousness of truth every prayer will be fruitless, since we know that God does not hear sinners, and that salvation is far from sinners, as Scripture says: He who turns his ears away so that he does not hear the law, his prayer will be abominable. The holy prophet also says in the psalm: If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me. For just as no medicine helps in a wound unless the iron is first drawn out, so the prayer of that man profits nothing if deceit still remains in his mind or hatred in his breast.

    But in order that God may hear your prayer, first of all the conscience must be cleansed from every stain of mortal sin, and the mind must take up a true purpose of amendment. To pray to God and at the same time offend in many things: what else is this than to mock God? For in two ways prayer is intercepted so that it is not heard by the Lord: one, when the one praying still commits evil by sinning; the other, if for God's sake he does not forgive his debtor the debt. You, therefore, who desire to have the fruit of your prayers, who wish to come with the penitent to the mercy of God, take care that you do nothing evil against the will of God, and take diligent care that you truly forgive from the heart all things committed against you by men. For you know that the Lord said: Forgive, and you shall be forgiven.

    But after you have cleansed your conscience from evil and forgiven every offense to your neighbor, then you will be fit for prayer if, in the fervor of holy purpose, you have been rightly ordered toward God. Now approach confidently to pray to the Lord; prostrate yourself humbly in his sight, and pray with purity of heart and fervor of spirit. Do not cease from prayer as long as you live in the flesh. Let your prayer be pure, simple, clear, and manifest; let it be full of gravity and weight, and adorned with the beauty of true humility. Do not ask in prayer for anything contrary to the salvation of the soul, nor pray too importunately for a temporal thing, since it is shamelessness to ask God for riches, which provide the greatest occasion for pride and frequently stain Christian purity.

    Folio XVIII.

    It is not shameless if you ask for daily bread, since it is one thing to seek material from which you may become proud, and another to ask for the necessary food by which you may live. Do not justify yourself while praying, lest you depart condemned like the Pharisee; nor ask anything from the Lord as though it were owed because of your merits. Rather, humble yourself in all things, so that you may be worthy to receive grace. Remember the humility of the publican, and pray with such humility that you may find with him forgiveness of sins and justification of the soul. For the grace of God is more abundant than the prayer of the suppliant, and when we pray he grants us more than we ask.

    You should not pray with a cry of the voice to him who knows the hidden things of the heart, but in fervor of spirit and with the inward cry of the mind, strike the ears of divine majesty. Nor should you draw out a length of words before him who is spirit, because God will be appeased not by much speaking but by the pure mind of the one praying. At the time of prayer cast away from yourself all malice and disquiet of heart, and, as we often say, forgive if you have anything against your neighbor. For unless you have forgiven your neighbor every debt for love of the Savior, you will obtain nothing from the Lord by your prayers.

    It is said that there is a certain kind of serpent which, when it wishes to go into the water to drink, first vomits out all its poison. You too, monk, imitate this serpent in this respect, and vomit out every poison of anger and bitterness, forgiving your brother the hundred denarii, so that the Lord may forgive you ten thousand talents. As you desire the Lord to be toward you, so you too should show yourself toward your fellow servant. Call upon the Lord with your whole heart and you will find him. Let your prayer be ardent and very pure, so that your mind may be joined to his most holy love.

    Strive for this throughout your whole life: to offer pure prayer to the Lord God at all times. Never cease in prayer, and do not despair of the mercy of the Lord. What God is going to grant, even if he delays it, he does not take away. He does not act with fickleness, nor is his judgment easily moved; what he has promised is fixed. If you pray earnestly, you will see a miracle. Remember that you stand beneath the eyes of God, who understands all the secrets of hearts and knows the hidden things of the mind. Therefore stand watchfully in the sight of him who has known all things, and pray with as much fervor of spirit as you can, so that

    That one must pray without interruption.

    that you may deserve to obtain mercy. For by holy prayer the conscience of the penitent is cleansed; and whoever raises his heart to the Lord in true purity, his prayer does not return empty. O, dearest brothers, if you knew how pleasing to God are the prayers of a pure mind, and how much benefit they confer upon the soul, you would allow no time to pass without prayers. For if our prayer is pure and burning in fervor of spirit, it is a most faithful messenger to God: it speaks to God on our behalf, and obtains all things necessary for our salvation while it prays.

    For this reason I admonish you and exhort you in true charity to pray without interruption, and never to cease from the fervor of the Holy Spirit. Let no time be empty for you, or idle in sluggishness of mind. In the fear of the Lord, I ask you, always be watchful and solicitous, so that you may be able bravely to conquer and overcome the temptations that threaten. As soon as foul thoughts begin to knock at the mind, hasten back to the practice of prayer, and they will by no means be able to prevail over you. For prayer is a great fortification of the soul; in its presence all the contrivances of the opposing side fail. For through most pure prayers all useful things are granted us by God, and all adversities are driven far away. The mind is powerfully kindled in the love of God by pure prayers; and whatever slighter stain may arise is cleansed by praying.

    By holy and continual prayers the [world?] is conquered; the plagues of the soul are healed by devout prayers; by tears and weeping the devil is overcome; and he for whom a thousand cohorts are not enough for battle is weakened by the prayer of one poor man. Just as wax, melting before the face of fire, is dissolved, so at the fervor of pure prayer all the power of demons is crushed and weakened. If a foul thought has been sent into your mind by demons, immediately make the sign of the cross upon your forehead and say: Save me, Jesus Christ, mediator of God and men, and drive away from me all the wickedness of the ancient enemy, through your most innocent passion. What can be shorter than this prayer, or what more powerful? For as soon as it has been uttered with fervor of mind against either the presence or the suggestion of demons, every contrivance of iniquity withdraws.

    For the power of pure prayer is very great, since it both penetrates heaven and by its constancy defeats the powers of the air. Prayer illuminates the mind, purifies the affection, obtains pardon for sins, and strengthens the spirit in the love of God against all adversaries. Nothing so raises the mind from earthly things to the love of heavenly things; nothing so quickly and powerfully destroys the pleasures of the flesh; nothing so illuminates the understanding; nothing also so greatly confounds the adversary of truth as pure prayer, which is poured out to God with fervor of divine love and is adorned by the testimony of a good conscience.

    If you desire to be terrible to demons, if you wish to be a friend of God, keep your conscience pure, and never interrupt spiritual prayer. For devout prayer can do all things, if it is adorned with uprightness of faith and purity of life. Prayer puts demons to flight, weakens the power of malignant spirits, heals the soul languishing in tepidity, and strengthens the weak and feeble spirit in the fear of God. Pure prayer makes one near to God; and the one whom it had received as a servant it makes to be a friend of God. Pure prayer, fervent in the love of God, penetrates heaven and wonderfully illuminates the understanding of the one praying. It closes hell, opens paradise, and brings in the souls of the faithful.

    For the Truth does not lie, who promises in the holy Gospel, saying: Ask, and it shall be given to you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and he who seeks finds; and to the one knocking it shall be opened. Which of you has ever turned to the Lord with his whole heart and prayed, and was not heard? Or who has called upon the Lord, and he has withdrawn himself from him? For Scripture says: Know that the Lord will hear your prayers, if you remain and persevere in fasts and prayers in the sight of the Lord.

    Be mindful of Moses, the servant of the Lord, who cast down Amalek, confident in his own strength, not by fighting with iron, but by praying with holy prayers. For the continual supplication of the just man avails much, and the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the clouds. Elijah was a man subject to suffering like us; and he prayed with prayer that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and heaven gave rain, and the earth gave its fruit. By prayer and tears King Hezekiah obtained fifteen years of longer life, and by prayers changed the sentence of the prophet. By prayers holy men became renowned for miracles, and, supplicating the Lord, called the dead back to life. To the purity of prayer even all things are subject, and there is nothing in us so difficult that devout and fervent prayer

    Homily VIII.

    ... but to obtain. Then, when we pray, we receive the confidence of obtaining what we ask from the Lord, when no perversity of life contradicts our prayers. For the Lord is the hearer of righteous prayer, namely when integrity of life commends the prayer, and no guilt of conscience makes the one praying hesitate. Friendship will not stand between those who are unlike, and between God and a sinner there can be no communion. If you wish to be heard when you pray, take care first of all that you do not disagree with the will of God. Live in spirit very like God, and you will suffer no repulse in prayer.

    Indeed, purity of conscience, in the fervor of divine love, makes a person like God in understanding. Likeness causes love; love, in turn, introduces familiarity; familiarity introduces confidence; and confidence in petition easily obtains what it asks. For just as there is no union among unlike things, so between God and an evil person prayer is of no avail.

    Therefore whoever among you desires to obtain the effect of his prayers must first cleanse the dwelling of his heart from every sin through true repentance; then he must strive to inflame himself by the exercise of holy compunction; afterward he must continually feed his mind in the pursuit of God’s love, so that he may never afterward cease from the good that he begins. But afterward, when, with the desire of divine love always increasing in him, he has brought the exercise of holy purity by long practice into habit, and the mind has begun to have the necessary firmness in a good purpose, then for the first time the likeness of divine communion is gradually introduced, and prayer is formed to its proper state. For the more the mind, stirred up in the love of God, has advanced, the more quickly prayer will obtain from the Lord what it asks. For the love of God alone makes prayer powerful; and the more fervently the mind burns in it, the more easily it will obtain the effect of its petitions. For if you love much, you can do much. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him. But in the one in whom God remains, nothing is stronger than he, except God himself alone.

    There are among you some weak and feeble in spirit who already think themselves strong and perfect in the way of the Lord; their devotion is rare and momentary. Without the wedding garment they boast that they have drawn near to the kingdom of heaven, although they still lie far below. To these I say again what I have often said: because no one becomes the highest suddenly, and unless a monk has subdued all his animal passions through the mortification of the flesh, he does not reach the loftiest mountain of divine contemplation.

    Folio XIX.

    For whoever, being placed in a monastery under authority and obedience, follows his own will against monastic institution, is not worthy to be heard by the Lord in his prayers. But those of whom we are speaking are great and wise in their own eyes: loving their own will, they murmur at everything, and whatever they themselves have not ordered they think badly done. They examine the actions of their brothers with curious inquiry, but they scorn to discern their own negligences. In manners they are lax and disorderly; in words frivolous and loud; unwilling for obedience; and always slow in good works and full of sloth. They neglect all the exercises of the order and devote themselves to private ones according to their own will. And as long as they remain in their rashness, they do not rise up to the true love of God.

    Let lovers of their own will hear what the Lord says: “I have not come to do my own will, but that of the Father who sent me.” Now, brothers, attend to the teacher; unless you live in imitation of him, you will pray without fruit. For the Lord freely hears the prayer of the one who keeps his commandments in truth. But the one who transgresses God’s commandment, who follows with desire the pleasures of the flesh and the consolations of the world, his prayer is not heard.

    For God, just and upright, is believed to hear your prayer gladly when mind and good life together make supplication. But if someone’s manner of life displeases God, how will his prayer please him? For God is spirit, and the person who walks not in the spirit but in the flesh certainly draws very little near to God. You, therefore, monk, who do not walk according to the purity of the Gospel and of the Rule, who love your own will and not God’s, know that you will not feel the efficacy of your prayers unless you first amend your life. For unless the manner of your life agrees with your prayer, you will not obtain what you pray for. Then you cry to the Lord with a great voice, when even with the tongue silent you cry out by good works. For good prayers and an evil manner of life deserve nothing good. Therefore do what a certain wise man advised: and if you have sinned, do not add to it again, but also pray concerning the former sins, so that

    That one must pray without intermission.

    …may be forgiven you. Before [your] prayers, prepare your soul, and be not as a man who tempts God.
