Let the mind be pure and ardent in the love of the Lord; let the conscience be clean and strengthened in the purpose of a holy way of life; and the prayer will be pleasing to the divine ears. If you pray otherwise, you will obtain nothing. He prays well who lives well; and he easily obtains who prays with holy works. Finally, prayer is rendered much effective and pleasing in the sight of God, if it be at all times consonant with the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. For Christ is God and man, the mediator between God and us, through whom we have safe access to the Father, as he himself testifies in the holy Gospel: "No one," he says, "comes to the Father but through me." Whence let no day pass on which you do not at least once give thanks to Christ by praying—who by the pain of his wounds healed the languors of your soul, who shed his blood for you, and by his most innocent death redeemed you, wretched, from the destruction of perpetual death. Truly a man is most ungrateful, and unworthy of the Christian name, who is so far forgetful of Christ's so great benefits that he does not daily, or at least once, render thanksgivings to him. But let the monk—who, dead to the world, is bidden to live for God alone—carry continually in his breast the memory of the Lord's passion, always giving thanks to his Redeemer, always blessing, always adoring; and daily—nay, as much as can be done, in every single moment—let him with tears, compassionating, turn over [in his mind] the bitterness of Christ's wounds. Every day, after the several regular prayers which the Greeks call canonical, with knees bent and mind raised to heaven let him say: "I give thanks to you, and blessing [you] I adore you, O mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus, most sweet God and man, for your most holy incarnation, for your nativity from the Virgin, for [your] circumcision, for the flight into Egypt and the seven years in exile which you endured for us. I adore you, Lord Savior Jesus Christ, for your labors, for [your] hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness; for your journeys, for your teaching and preaching, for your miracles, for the calling of the nations, and for the justification of sinners. I give you thanks, Lord, Son of the living God, for the pain of your wounds; I bless you for the shedding of your most holy blood; I adore you for your death which you most innocently endured; and I beseech you, by your whole passion, [your] piety and clemency, have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death." This most brief prayer the devout monk will recite at least seven times a day, so that as often as he passes before the image of the Crucified, in like manner, with fervor of mind, he may adore Christ. He who is a true lover of Christ always thinks of Christ, speaks of and venerates Christ, [and] does not doubt that Christ is everywhere present to him. The passion of Christ is never absent from his memory; and through the greatness of love he forgets himself, and in Christ is wholly occupied in mind and desire. Whoever is fervent in soul in the love of Christ despises earthly things, conquers the flesh, [and] desires only heavenly things. Waking, he ever thinks of Christ with desire; sleeping, he dreams of Christ; and, continually sighing, with the divine Ignatius he cries: "My love is crucified." He joins sighs to sighs, and Jesus—whom he loves with his whole heart—he discerns present, not with his eyes but with his spirit. With the desire of love urging [him], as often as he gazes on the Crucified, he soon dissolves into tears, and, glowing with the fire of charity, cries out: "O love stronger than all strengths! How sweetly he burns who is inflamed with the desire of Christ!" Rightly did he speak who said: "Love is strong as death." For what can be stronger than the love of Christ, by whose ardor the holy martyrs, despising so many thousand kinds of death, overcame [them]? O my crucified love, have mercy on me; grant me to feel that sweetness of your love of which I speak, that I may always carry about in my heart your most bitter passion. I know, my brothers, I know that there is no more effective mode of praying, nor more useful to us who are still weak, than to be in the memory and power of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Whence, since it is manifest that without a mediator there is no ascent of the mind to God, every good work must be begun in the name of Christ; for then we usefully pour out prayers to God, when with purified conscience we pray through his only-begotten Son.

    Of the custody and origin of thoughts: Homily Nine.

    Solomon, that once most wise king, in the book which he entitled "of the Proverbs," [addresses his] son

    Homily IX.

    ... urged him to true wisdom. Among other things he said: “My son, attend to my wisdom, and incline your ear to my prudence, that you may keep thoughts, and that your lips may preserve discipline.” For it is no small part of wisdom, dearly beloved brothers, if a monk knows how prudently to discern his thoughts and carefully to guard their movements at all times. It is a great thing to think nothing evil; but it is a mark of no less prudence to be able to repel evil thoughts from their very beginning. For the profound judgment of the human heart is always mobile, changing, manifold, and unstable; and to observe its beginnings and restrain its movements is the highest prudence and a great sign of wisdom. If I have said that the heart of man is a mill driven by perpetual motion, I have not departed from the truth, especially if one should wish to weigh its restlessness exactly. For what else is the human heart than a certain mill, always in motion, grinding something? The human heart is never idle; it never rests without motion, but is always doing something; and just as a mill, empty, consumes itself by its own motion, so the heart of man shamefully wastes away of itself when thought of good does not bind it fast. It is always moved toward some object with the desire of its own love; it always grinds, always acts, always is occupied about something delightful, whether it be good or evil. As the body is not moved without the soul, so the mind of man does not remain fixed in good unless it has continually been restrained by holy exercises. Therefore the wise man said in Ecclesiasticus: “Gladness of heart, this is the life of man, and a treasure without defect of holiness; and the exultation of a man is length of life. Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God, and contain yourself; and gather your heart in his holiness, and drive sadness far from you.” What is the gathering of the heart, if not the diligent guarding of thought? For he gathers his heart in the holiness of the Lord who continually observes, in the fear of God, the movements of his thoughts. And therefore Scripture says: “With all watchfulness keep your heart, because life proceeds from it.” Thoughts take the beginnings of their movements from those things which are offered by the senses; and they wander the more dangerously, the less they are considered from the beginning by the judgment of reason. Therefore whoever desires to be watchful over his thoughts, whoever wishes to gather his heart in the holiness of the Lord, should first most diligently guard his exterior senses and set the bridle of prudence upon each one. Concerning hearing and sight, Scripture thus commands: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue; and make doors for your mouth, and bars for your ears.” “Blessed is the man who stops his ears, lest he hear bloodshed, and shuts his eyes, lest he see evil.” In holy Job also we read thus: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think of a virgin.” But against those who through the ministry of the senses have fallen into the pit of sins, the Lord thus bears witness through the prophet Jeremiah: “Because death has climbed in through your windows, it has entered your houses, to destroy the little children outside and the young men from the streets.” Death enters through our windows whenever an iniquitous thought is admitted to the mind through the ministry of sight or hearing. For the house is the conscience, of which Scripture says: “Unless you hold yourself constantly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overturned,” that is, your conscience. This house is very fragile and is quickly overturned unless it is fortified by the continual exercise of the fear of the Lord. “For unless the Lord has guarded the house, he who guards it keeps watch in vain.” Therefore the house of conscience must be fortified by love of the Lord; the senses also must be restrained most diligently, because it is not enough for one to guard his thoughts if he does not turn his ears and eyes away from the occasion of evil. And so, if you wish to be a prudent guardian of your thoughts and a true gatherer of the heart in the holiness of the Lord, hedge your ears with the thorns of compunction and of the fear of God, lest they hear evil, and turn your eyes away, lest through sight they introduce sin. What it is not lawful for you to covet, do not see with desire; and what it is not expedient to have, do not think about. Many have perished through the ministry of the senses; and those who incautiously proceed to look at external things have shamefully lost the inner goods of their enclosure. He who does not fear danger is certainly already near destruction; and he who presumes on his own virtue hastens swiftly toward the ruin of sin. He who fixes his eye on the flashing of lightning will be blinded for the moment; and he who looks upon the beauty of a woman will not be free from danger. I praise the prudence of that monk who in the midst of crowds is alone, and appoints a censor over his senses, lest it admit anything evil to the lady. He has stationed guards beside the gate, who with sword and club repel those who rush in disorderly. Fear

    On the keeping and origin of thoughts

    The holy [fear?] of the Lord never deserts the mind of a wise man, but, like a strong and watchful fighter always standing at the side of his prince, so it guards the [dwelling?] of the heart. It turns its ears away from all buffoonery of words, and closes its eyes lest they see evil. It always walks according to the twelfth degree of humility, with its gaze fixed on the ground, praying with the prophet to the Lord: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; in your way give me life, Lord.”

    Thus I admonish you, brothers: direct your senses in the fear of the Lord, so that you may always be able to keep the dwelling-place of the heart clean and inviolate. Remember the scripture saying: “Be clean, you who bear the vessels of the Lord.” Consider, I beg you, with how great cleanliness and purity of mind you must shine, you who not only by reason of the priestly order bear the vessels of the Lord, but, what is more, are yourselves also vessels of the Lord. For the holy Christ-loving Paul says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” And again he says: “Or do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own?” And elsewhere: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are.” And concerning this same Paul in the Acts of the Apostles the Lord said to Ananias: “Go, because this man is a vessel of election for me.”

    The monk who exercises the priestly order in the church of God is bound by a twofold reason to the observance of most holy purity. For Christ’s soldier must, because of the vow that he made to God, be pure, holy, and constantly unwearied in good works; and by reason of the priestly ministry, circumspect and most diligently watchful. For it is written: “Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently.” You are ministers of almighty God, who daily at the altar offer up his Son, whose work is entrusted to your hands; and therefore great purity of mind and body is required in your manner of life.

    Therefore, so that chaste purity of mind may remain, it is necessary that the instability of thought be restrained. The senses must be guarded at every time, through which the integrity of the mind is corrupted. For you are dead to the world and have now begun to live for Christ. It is not permitted to you to think anything except what is holy; nor is it fitting for you, ministers of God, to love anything earthly. For he whom you serve, O monks, is God; he to whom you minister, my brothers, is almighty. Live pure, holy, and innocent, because it is not fitting for you to be occupied with the business of the world, you who have been called to the soldiery of God. Let the love of God and purity of heart grow in you with time, so that the longer you live in this world, the holier you may become.

    Always turn your sight away from every evil, so that you may be able to remain without failure in good thoughts. Always raise the eyes of your mind to heaven, and do not occupy the sight of the flesh with perishable things. Also always close your hearing against every useless, vain, and foolish speech, and always think with fear on the future judgment of God. Do not pollute your hands with illicit and shameful contact of any things, so that you may be able to offer up the Son of God with a clean body and a pure conscience.

    In food and drink it is not for monks to discern flavors, nor is it fitting for Christ’s soldiers to love bodily delights. Nature requires few things, and rustic foods by which it may be nourished; but appetite, unless it is restrained by the command of reason, is carried off to illicit things, through which the simplicity of nature is violated. Flee excess in all things, and observe regular temperance in your manner of living.

    Let none of you patiently listen to someone disparaging his brother or speaking ill of his neighbor. Let each one of you restrain his tongue from useless speech, and let a good monk blush to speak ill of Christian people. Let that threat of the Lord in the holy Gospel never depart from your memory, when he says: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. A good man brings forth good things from a good treasure, and an evil man brings forth evil things from an evil treasure. But I say to you that every idle word that men have spoken, they shall render an account of it on the day of judgment.”

    O sentence greatly to be feared! If an account is demanded for idle speech, what do detraction, buffoonery, and foul speech deserve? Or if a useless word is judged liable to the reason of strict examination, what will he answer who so easily speaks what is evil and pernicious? An idle word is every speech of men that has been uttered without just usefulness, lacking the reason of lawful necessity. Therefore, brothers, consider your words, and let no one speak a word not pertaining to the matter either of just usefulness or of necessary rea-

    Homily IX. Fol. XXI.

    [unclear]. You have heard, then, the fearful sentence of the Lord, and you are not ignorant of the precept of our holy lawgiver, who says in the Rule: "Buffooneries, idle words, and words that provoke laughter we condemn everywhere to perpetual enclosure, and for such speech we do not permit a disciple to open his mouth." Here the holy father Benedict forbade three kinds of words to monks, and condemned them everywhere to perpetual enclosure: namely buffooneries, idle words, and words that provoke laughter.

    But what buffoonery is, interpretation by the grammarian and by us has made clear. For the vice of buffoonery is opposed to urbanity and modesty, and is a kind of wanton jesting, immoderately provoking the laughter of hearers without shame or honesty, by words and gestures that do not accord with reason, do not befit a good man, and are not suitable to a wise man. It is called buffoonery from the buffoon, who follows the houses of the rich, provoking hearers to laughter with wanton and dishonest words and gestures for the sake of reward or alms. And this kind of words the holy father Benedict forbade to monks and utterly condemned, since those who serve God are rightly judged bound always to abstain in his sight from foul and dishonest words.

    Between buffoonery and excessive speech this seems to be the difference: the former exceeds reason by reason of dishonesty, the latter by reason of superfluity. The former is foul and dishonest, and superfluous without virtue. Foolish talk is rightly joined to these, since it is forbidden not only to monks but also to all Christians. Hence the holy apostle of Christ says: "But fornication and all uncleanness or covetousness, let it not even be named among you, as befits saints of God; nor filthiness, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery, which is not to the purpose, but rather thanksgiving." Idle speech is likewise forbidden to all monks, since, as you have heard, it is prohibited by the Lord in the holy Gospel. Words that provoke laughter do not befit Christian men, and much less are they suitable for cloistered men. For the monk, who is dead to the world, is commanded always to think on his last things; but laughter and every insolence of the present life he is ordered everywhere to contemn for the love of God. Laughter is a confused sound declaring the inward joy of the soul with immoderate mirth. Nothing, however, [unclear]

    On the Guarding and Origin of Thoughts

    [unclear] humility, reverence, and subjection are required, lest anyone seem to speak more than is expedient. From his words a man will be known; he who multiplies utterances in his mouth is foolish in heart. A man's speech is the witness of his conscience: he who loves chastity and innocence of heart, his speeches ought to be chaste and without vanity. For you are ministers of God, brothers of mine; let no vain, useless, or idle speech go out from your mouth, but only that which is good for the edification of hearers, so that it may increase charity in their minds for the illumination of the heart in the knowledge and love of the highest truth. Precious is the tongue of the monk that says nothing at all except holy things; worthy of blessing is the mouth from which nothing is brought forth except what is divine.

    Therefore let each one guard his heart from every wicked thought, since he who is good in heart does not speak an evil word; he who truly loves God does not utter an idle speech. Apply every care and consideration to your thoughts, because there evil must be watched with chief attention, where it takes the beginning of its own processes, so that as soon as it begins to arise it may be cut off at the root. For there is no evil thought so weak that it does not grow with time, if it is nourished by the consent of the thinker. Therefore evil must be conquered at the beginning, while it is still weak, because when delay is interposed, evil gains strength, however small it may seem at first in the heart. A great fire often springs from a small spark; so from a tiny thought a great sin sometimes arises. When a thought gives birth to delight, it is accustomed soon to break out into consent, and consequently even into deed, if it can cast itself headlong.

    But when the will has granted consent through delight to an evil thought for the deed, even if what the soul desires is not brought to completion, nevertheless the sin has already been consummated before God. But what does Scripture say? "Sin, when it has been consummated, begets death." For almighty God looks upon the will of man, whether he wills good or evil. Therefore in the holy Gospel he says: "Whoever has looked at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." God is accustomed to reckon the will as the deed, when a man cannot bring into effect what he wished. Therefore again

    Homily IX. Folio XXII.

    ... the necessity of sinning is generated. Call it the most harsh dominion of death: here is the uttermost depth of evils. Whoever has once entered this abyss of sins rarely, indeed not easily, rises again to purity of heart without the special grace of God and the very great labor of repentance. By his own will the sinner has fallen into this pit of death; but without God's mercy he will not be able to rise again. Most harsh is the yoke of evil habit; if anyone has once submitted his neck to it, he rarely grows strong again for the former freedom of the spirit.

    All these things perverse thought brings about when it is admitted into the mind and, through delight, is changed into consent and deed. For no thought is so small that it does not grow little by little if it is not driven from the mind. Blessed, therefore, is that monk who casts every thought of his upon the Lord; who always and everywhere refuses a place to wicked thoughts; who despises all the perishable riches of the world; who contemns all comforts of the body. He prepares cleanness of heart for his Lord; he loves nothing in this world except the Lord; he orders all his thoughts to the glory of the Savior; and he observes his commandments most diligently.

    What is happier than that monk who presents himself to the world not as a citizen but as a pilgrim? He lives in the world as though he were not in the world; indeed he is greater than the world, for his whole way of life is in heaven. Consider now, therefore, dearest brothers, the brevity of this time, and always remember that you are mortal and soon to pass away. For we have here no abiding city, but we seek the one to come; and since we know that so many thousands of human beings have preceded us through death, let us think how soon we too must necessarily die.

    A time, now indeed brief, but very acceptable, is granted to us, in which we may work the fruits of eternal life. For now is the time for laboring; now is the hour for sowing what is good, because after death each one will receive the reward of his labors, when no further opportunity for laboring is granted. Therefore, my brothers, anticipate this hour of death with holy works, and do not now fail in the sowing of labor, so that in eternal recompense you may be able to rejoice without end. Let no day pass in which each one of you has not become better and has not added something new to the good works he has already sent ahead. Always think upon the value of the future harvest, and no greatness of labor will terrify you.

    On the Daily Struggle of Temptation: Homily Ten.

    In yesterday's sermon, dearest brothers, I admonished your Charity to resist the beginnings of evil thoughts, and to prepare yourselves with all your strength, by good and holy works, for the prize of future reward. But since, as Scripture bears witness, the life of man upon earth is a temptation, I have considered it necessary to discourse in your hearing, as much as the Lord shall grant, on this very matter, so that, forewarned, you may be able to fight more strongly against the invisible adversary.

    You are not ignorant of the words of the wise man, who says in Ecclesiasticus: “Son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.” Let no one think himself free from temptation, brothers, as long as we walk in this mortal way of life; but the more each one has advanced in the fear of God, the more cautiously he should know that he must live. For holy Pope Gregory says: “The more our enemy sees that he is being rebelled against, the more fully he strives to attack.”

    You, O men, the more fully you advance in the spiritual way of life, the more attentively must you keep watch against the adversary of your salvation. For, as Saint John Chrysostom says, our adversary never sleeps, but always keeps watch for the destruction of the human race; none of us can resist him except one who has learned at all times to keep watch in the fear of the Lord. And Saint Leo of the city of Rome says in a certain sermon: “The ancient enemy does not cease everywhere to set out the snares of temptations, so that in whatever way he may be able, by corrupting, to blacken the faith of believers. For he knows into whom to cast the enticements of the flesh, into whom to pour the poison of envy, to whom to apply the incitements of lust. He knows whom to disturb with sorrow, whom to deceive with joy, whom to oppress with fear, whom to sedu[unclear]”

    On the Daily Struggle of Temptation.

    [unclear]. He examines the conduct of all; he searches out the affections of all. There he seeks grounds for doing harm, wherever he has seen anyone more diligently occupied. There are no works of virtue without the trial of temptations; no faith without disturbances; no struggle without an enemy; no victory without an encounter. Hence Saint James the Apostle says in his epistle: Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him. Hence again Scripture says: The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the temptation of tribulation tests just men. But lest anyone should think that the devil is permitted to tempt human beings as much as he wishes, Saint [Christophilus?] cries out: But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make a way out, so that you may be able to endure it. And Saint Augustine says: The devil is permitted to tempt only so much as is profitable for you, so that you may be exercised, so that you may be proved, so that you, who did not know yourself, may be discovered by yourself. For the devil can, with God’s permission, stir up the impulse of temptation; but it lies in your own most free power whether you wish to give or deny consent to the tempter. Hence, when he tempted the Son of God in the desert, he did not drive him on, did not touch him, did not compel him, but only said: Cast yourself down, so that you may understand that he cannot conquer except one who is willing. Therefore the divine [Christian?] chief apostle said: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. For the devil can suggest evil; he cannot compel, nor overcome unless you consent. Our life, as Saint Augustine bears witness, in this pilgrimage cannot be without sin and temptation, because our progress is increased through temptations; nor does anyone become known to himself unless he is tempted; nor can he be crowned unless he has conquered; nor can he conquer unless he has struggled; nor can he struggle unless he has had an enemy and temptations. For Scripture says: He who has not been tempted, what does he know? For no one will be crowned except one who has struggled lawfully.

    Therefore, coming to the service of God, dearest brothers, stand in justice and fear; and as long as you can be conquered by the adversary and subjected to him, do not glory in security. Always keep watch, always be afraid, because the enemy with whom you are engaged in struggle never sleeps, does not rest, does not cease from persecution, always lying in wait for you, and is never wearied. But if at some time he has been overcome, he at once rises up to a new struggle, nor does he desist from attacking the good until, defeated, he utterly succumbs, or else surely conquers those who struggle against him by troublesome perseverance. Hence Saint Pope Gregory also says: When the ancient enemy sees that he is succumbing in the first struggle, he renews other wars of temptations. The crafty adversary of the human race observes the conduct of each and every person, and those things to which they are nearer by vice he places before the face of the heart, and he uses great force to overthrow the state of the mind.

    Stand firmly rooted in the fear of the Lord; you will easily overcome all the temptations of the enemy. For it is written in the book of Proverbs: In the fear of the Lord is confidence of strength. And again: By mercy and faith sins are purged; but through the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil. In Ecclesiasticus, moreover, the wise man said: The fear of the Lord drives out sin. For one who is without fear will not be able to be justified; for the wrath of his animosity overturns him. Therefore, by Solomon’s testimony, that man is called blessed who is always fearful; but he who is hard of heart will fall into evil. Prepare your souls also, through zeal for holy conduct, for temptation, so that when it comes you may be able to resist and stand the stronger for it. For you will easily overcome the devil if, thus prepared, you always approach to do battle. Behold, your adversary, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; and you must resist him in the faith of our Lord Jesus if you desire to obtain victory. Here no place for flight is granted; no brief respite of security is allowed to those who fight; rather, it is necessary that you engage in combat. [unclear] by this condition we human beings have been made, that, having overcome the allurements of the flesh, we ought to become equal to the holy angels. Struggles are never lacking for monks, because as long as we live in the flesh, we are necessarily exposed to temptations. For Scripture says: Many are the tribulations of the just, and from all these the Lord will deliver them. But in all our temptations [remember] that saying of Isaiah the prophet

    let us diligently call to mind the one who says: “You who have been weaned from milk, who have been drawn away from the breast, expect tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope; yet a little while, because of the wickedness of lips, because of a malignant tongue.” Those weaned and drawn away from the breast are men advanced in age, whose part it is to undergo tribulation upon tribulation for God’s sake, so that they may deserve to carry back hope upon hope, as sacred Scripture says: “But we also glory in our tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience, and patience proof, and proof hope. And hope does not confound, because the charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” For through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. Indeed, through temptations we become known to ourselves, and we discover whether we truly fear God. Hence the Lord speaks through Moses to the people, saying: “The Lord your God tests you, that he may know whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul.”

    This world, dearest brothers, is to be compared to a furnace, in which the fire of temptation and adversity continually burns, through which we must necessarily pass. In this furnace of tribulation, straw is burned up, but gold and silver are cleansed from every stain. Straw is turned into ash; gold is reserved for the ornament and adornment of the royal palace. The furnace, I say, is the world; the fire is temptation or tribulation; the gold is righteous men; the straw is the unrighteous and sinners; the craftsman who purifies the gold is almighty God himself, who favors our progress and cooperates by grace toward the merit of virtue. Therefore let us do what God wills; what he imposes, let us patiently bear for love of him, since, as holy [Christophilus?] says, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which shall be revealed in us.” Hence Saint Jerome says: “Who would not wish to be troubled? Who would not desire to be cursed, so as to gain praise by the voice of Christ and to be rewarded with an abundant heavenly recompense? Would that, for the name and righteousness of my Lord, the whole crowd of unbelievers would persecute and trouble me. Would that this whole world would rise up to my reproach, if only I might deserve to be praised by Christ and to hasten to the reward of his promise.” And the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men.”

    Therefore, whoever among you, my brothers, desires to reach the kingdom of heaven, whoever takes care above all things to please God, let him learn gladly to undergo, for love of him, the tribulations of temptations, and joyfully to endure whatever adversity may occur. For there is none of us who does not need daily cleansing; none who does not offend almost at every moment. If, therefore, we love our own salvation, if we demand that our offenses be forgiven us and that we be cleansed from every stain of the heart, let us patiently endure whatever adversity befalls us, since the evils of tribulation, which the soul patiently tolerates for love of God, purify it more than the good works that it performs of its own accord here in this world.

    A great occasion for suffering has been left to us in this place, where want heavily oppresses us, poverty weighs us down, and the debt of another’s [unclear] also constrains us. What adversity do we not experience in this monastery? What storms and tempests do we not suffer, brothers? By what inconveniences are we not harassed? How desolate all the goods of this monastery were when, fifteen years ago, regular observance was introduced, none of you can fail to know. But the tribulation of common want rages more heavily against me, since I must provide you with the necessities of life, and often I do not well know from what source I may pay. Yet your patience consoles my spirit, and the hope that you humble ones have conceived in the Lord Savior, so that I do not doubt that his mercy will come in time; and I hear him saying to me through Isaiah the prophet: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.” Gladly, then, I shall have patience in the poverty that, God thus ordaining, we now suffer, so that after death we may deserve to come to the riches of eternity. For the more in this pilgrimage of ours we have been afflicted by persecutions, poverty, want, labors, and tribulations, the greater rewards we shall obtain, the Lord granting them, in the future recompense of the righteous. It is fitting, therefore, my brothers, to tolerate patiently whatever almighty God has foreordained for [unclear], since, as the divine pope Gregory says, confidence in almighty God is then certain

    On the Daily Contest of Temptation.

    [unclear]: when adversity is added to a good work, and in this world the scourge of God is received with joy, so that a fairer reward may be kept in the future recompense of the saints.

    Again he also says: From the hope of an everlasting inheritance they take joy, whom the adversity of temporal life humbles; for if divine dispensation did not perceive that they were to be saved forever, it would not thus restrain them, to be instructed, under the rule of discipline. When afflicted we lose earthly things; but, humbly enduring affliction, we multiply heavenly goods for ourselves. For the present life is a road, by which we hasten toward our fatherland; and therefore we are often touched in it by disturbances, lest we think this is our fatherland.

    Let the monk therefore rejoice in his adversity; let him be glad when tempted, he to whom the world has been crucified. Let him trust that he belongs to the fellowship of God, who with a pure conscience always works good and receives the contrary in tribulation. For it is the truest sign of divine mercy if a Christian person is struck in this world by various adversities, while serving God with a pure conscience and living in true humility without offense. For the merciful God often strikes in various ways in this world those whom he loves, for whom he has prepared eternal rewards in heaven. But some, knowing that they are able to sin greatly, he forestalls with bodily weakness lest they sin, and in mercy scourges them for their salvation, perceiving that it is more useful for their souls [unclear] the riches of the world and [unclear]; and the unexpected enemy struck him the more heavily because long use of quiet had found him negligent.

    Whence holy Pope Gregory again says: Their own prosperity has laid many low more badly; long-lasting peace had rendered many conquered. By a certain moderation of heavenly dispensation they rejoice that they are exercised even by temptations, because they guard the received glory of virtues so much the more robustly as, shaken by the assault of temptation, they more humbly recognize their own weakness. The way of tribulation is a short road to Christ, and he is found more quickly than in tranquillity in the heart.

    For Saint Ambrose says: There are many who seek Christ in leisure and do not find him; and there are those who seek him in persecutions and quickly find him. In the dangers of his faithful he is present, as he speaks in the psalm concerning the just man, saying: I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him. Let purity of conscience be guarded in adversity; let the unviolated integrity of life always be preserved, and whatever adversities there may be will undoubtedly be for us unto the merit of salvation. The ancient enemy can overthrow no one by fighting, unless he has first found him to have fallen away from himself. He seeks out the soldier who is sluggish in leisure and careless, and most easily lays low the one whom he has found stripped of arms.

    Therefore, my brothers, always keep watch in holy prayers; always persist in good works, so that whenever the tempter approaches, he may never find you idle. Remember the words of our Savior Jesus Christ, saying in the holy Gospel: Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands; and you be like men awaiting their lord, when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once. He keeps watch who, standing firm in the fear of the Lord, never sleeps through sluggishness of mind. He keeps watch who preserves his soul, by the indefatigable constancy of a holy purpose, against any adversities whatever of this world. He keeps watch, whoever does not cease to make daily progress in the love of the Lord. He carries a lamp in his hands, whoever adorns the purpose of holiness with fitting works. He also holds a lamp in his hands, whoever, purified in mind and body, shines for his neighbor by works of holy devotion.

    Hence the holy lover of Christ, Paul, says in the epistle: I beseech you, dearest ones, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God. He who chastises his body through the pursuits of holy abstinence and reduces it to servitude to the spirit has consecrated a living sacrifice to the Lord. Whoever, moreover, has now learned to preserve his body clean and pure from every pollution of sin has undoubtedly sacrificed a holy victim to the Lord. But whoever perseveres in the purpose of holiness unto the end has without doubt offered a pleasing sacrifice.

    Homily X

    But we gird these about ourselves when we keep ourselves pure and unspotted from every form of lust, in body and in mind. The virtue of holy chastity is of great merit before God, and, because of the greatness of the struggle, is to be granted with a special reward in the recompense of the just, as the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Those who keep my sabbaths, and choose the things that I have willed, and hold fast my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name, which shall not perish.” And concerning these the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “For there are eunuchs who were so born from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs who were made so by men; and there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it.”

    But why did he say, “He who is able to receive it, let him receive it”? I think that this statement about eunuchs who castrate themselves for love of the kingdom of heaven is not to be referred to the cutting off of the genital members, as many, thinking so, have strayed from the truth of the Gospel, but rather to the rule of the mind, by which chastity, conceived from love of Christ, is preserved whole. For those castrate themselves for the kingdom of God who, for love of God, keep true chastity of mind and body inviolate. And just as no one is easily castrated in the body without the torment of great pain, so no one can attain to the perfection of chastity without the greatest zeal for labor. And certainly no one is chaste by his own strength, no one modest by his own merits. It is God who gives the good will; it is he also who joins virtue to the will, so that it may have power. But because it does not belong to many to live chastely, he leaves each person to his own judgment, saying: “He who is able to receive it, let him receive it.”

    The cutting off of members does not make the mind chaste, since the root of lust is within and cannot be removed by the amputation of the private parts. But if the mind is chaste and whole, it will easily restrain the insolence of the members. For nothing is stronger than the mind of a human being who, with a pure heart, sweetly loves God above all things. Consider now, dearest brothers, the future rewards of beauty, and the labor of chastity will not weigh upon you. For the great rewards of high estate are reached by the strenuous perseverance of labor. Therefore whoever flees the labor of the contest will never arrive at the renown of honor. Brief now is the time in which we labor, resisting the devil; but very soon the eternal time will come, in which, reigning without end, we shall rejoice with Christ.

    Let the body be chastened by discreet abstinence, lest it kick back against the rule of the mind; let the concupiscence of the flesh be broken by holy exercises, so that it may always obey the counsels of reason. If at any time it begins to strike the mind with wanton impulses, let it also be restrained with blows, because it is better that the back be humbled by the bruise of stripes than that the wantonness of the flesh should cast the soul down into hell. For Scripture says: “He who delicately nourishes his servant from childhood will afterward feel him to be rebellious.” The flesh is the servant of the mind, and it ought always to obey the rule of reason. But if the flesh has been nourished too licentiously, having now grown accustomed to pleasures, it will refuse to bear the rule of the spirit. For a servant is made rebellious against his master whenever, through habit, he is delicately nourished by him. It is difficult, however, to bring a rebellious and defiant servant back to humble obedience after he has long been accustomed to kick back. For it is written: “A servant cannot be instructed by words, because he understands what you say and disdains to answer.” Therefore the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “Fodder and rod and burden for the ass; bread and discipline and work for the servant. He works under discipline and seeks to rest; loosen your hand for him and he seeks freedom. Yoke and thong bend a hard neck, and continual labors bow down a servant.”

    If we begin to borrow these testimonies of the Scriptures from the literal sense for the moral sense, we shall find that all the things said about the servant and the ass fit very rightly with the sluggish and delicate flesh. For truly the flesh is the servant of the soul, and it is always raised up against its mistress unless it is wearied every day by discipline and work. For he who at all times treats it delicately in idleness and pleasures will necessarily find it rebellious against spiritual things, because when the flesh is lifted up in pride, the spirit, languishing in idleness and lukewarm, is weakened. Therefore unless, O brother monk, you continually humble this servant of yours, namely the flesh, through work and abstinence; unless, against its unlawful motions,

    …[unless?] you have imposed upon it the [bridle?] of continence and sobriety, with it going before you will go wholly into the abyss. For we know, as the holy Apostle says, that the flesh lusts against the spirit, and unless by the spirit we have mortified the works of the flesh, we shall die in its corruption. Nothing hurls the soul more deeply into the pit of sin than the insolence of the flesh, which, when it is permitted to live by its own will, struggles against its lord like a rebellious servant. Unhappy flesh, you who by the desire of vanity hurl down the soul: it will not pass unpunished for you if, at your prompting, it commits any evil, since God will judge both. Woe to you when it has sinned with you, because when Adam, as a transgressor of the commandments, is expelled from paradise, Eve, the instigator of evils, necessarily accompanies the wretched man.

    Be in agreement with the spirit, O flesh, because the Apostle says: “Those who are Christ’s have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” And you, O men and brothers, who profess the warfare of Christ, who have voluntarily sworn yourselves to the law of monastic life, who have promised to imitate the footsteps of the Savior: attend to your calling, so that you may walk cautiously, not as the unwise who are driven by every wind, but as true lovers of Jesus Christ, who by the spirit have mortified the deeds of the flesh. You, I say, my most beloved fellow-soldiers, be always watchful in good works, mortifying for the love of Christ our bodies which are upon the earth, constant in fasts and prayers, and continually occupied in meditation on the divine Scriptures. Always stretch yourselves toward the things ahead; daily renew the fervor of your holy purpose with fresh zeal. Flee idleness and all sloth, and [unclear] diligently how brief the time of this life is; and the devil, however fiercely he may rage, is overcome as soon as you have invoked Christ.

    Remember the words of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, saying in the holy Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.” And what is our cross, my brothers, if not a life full of temptations and adversities, and the burden of regular discipline under which we are wearied day and night? But let us gather our hearts, dearest brothers, and gladly endure for the love of God whatever he has wished us to endure, so that at his judgment we may deserve to say: “We have passed through fire and water, and you have brought us into refreshment.” O how glorious a reward is laid up in the kingdom of heaven for the servants of God, who, contending now in this brief racecourse, are wearied for love of him. Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, the immensity of that good which almighty God has prepared in eternal happiness for those who love him, to remain without end forever. The highest happiness of this good is acquired by humility; it is possessed by purity of heart and by the fervor of divine love.

    Let us hasten there, dearest brothers; let us run there with as great devotion of mind as we can, where the spirit is joined to its creator through the enjoyment of sweetness, where the intellect will be perfected in the knowledge of the highest good, which is God. There is the joy of everlasting happiness, which is not diminished; there is gladness which is not brought to an end; there is the perpetual rest from all labors; there is the glorious reward for tribulations and injuries suffered for Christ. Whatever good we now do, there without doubt we shall find laid up; whatever adversity we have patiently endured for the love of Christ, there we shall receive it repaid with a most abundant reward.

    O monk, monk, you who spend fruitlessly the time mercifully granted to you by the Lord God for doing good: what will you reap, or what reward will you receive in that terrible hour, you who are now so sluggish and unwilling to sow? Have you not read what is written about the labors of the saints? “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.” Now is the time to work the field of your heart, O monk; now is the hour to sow good seed with the blessing of cheerfulness, because he who now sows sparingly will also reap sparingly in that repayment of future reward. Now one must labor and never cease from good work, since whatever we have done here now, there without doubt we shall receive. Therefore, if there is any faithful monk among you, if anyone is a zealous lover of his own salvation, let him always think upon the hour of future reward, which no one can escape; let him always prepare himself to render the account of his stewardship. Let no day ever pass on which he has not done some particular good work which he may send ahead for future recompense.

    Homily XI. Fol. XXV.

    Let him consider that he has spent uselessly the day on which he has not sent ahead a good work for which he may expect reward. Let the good monk at all times strive to cultivate the field of his heart, and utterly to root out, as far as he can, all thorns and thistles of evil affections. Let him learn to keep the Lord Jesus above all things with a pure mind and the greatest diligence. Let him sow in the tears of devotion and constancy what he may reap with all the saints in exultation. Let the continual difficulty of laboring not deter the mind; let the hard struggle of the flesh not break the spirit, since he who labors little gathers little fruit at harvest, and he who now sows much in tears for the love of Christ brings back most abundant fruit on that day. For [this?], brothers, is the destination of our journey which we undertake in the present pilgrimage: that, purified by continual exercise of labors and adversities, we may depart from here clean and pure to our homeland.

    On Avoiding the Company of the Wicked: The Eleventh Homily.

    The company of the wicked has drawn many back from the way of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Therefore, my most beloved brothers, we do not cease to admonish you to walk in the way of the Lord with the good and holy, by whose instruction and example you may daily become better. For, as the holy apostle of Christ says, imitating the iambic verse of a certain Greek, Menander: evil conversations corrupt good morals. He does not truly desire to be good whom the conduct of the wicked delights. For no one speaks wicked things unless he is first found corrupted and depraved in his own heart against the purity of the evangelical tradition. As each person is, and as are the things he turns over and performs in the secrecy of his heart by ruminating and thinking, such speech more frequently proceeds from his mouth. For the speech of the speaker is the truest witness of the heart, as our Lord and Savior says in the holy Gospel: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. For a good man brings forth good things from the treasure of his heart, and an evil man likewise brings forth evil things. Since, therefore, he who speaks evil is not good, we must beware of all who use depraved, scurrilous, and pernicious words; in their speech certain shameful things often resound, while words of holiness are heard either never or very rarely. Shameful speech is the sign of an immodest heart, even if deeds do not follow.

    You, therefore, my dearest brothers, who promised according to the rule and the ecclesiastical statutes of the holy fathers to preserve until death, not only in deed, chastity and every kind of purity by a profession both implicit and express, but who ought also to be far removed from every unclean thought: flee the company of wicked men. And he who has fellowship with the proud will put on pride. Hence Saint Pope Gregory says: the weak ought to avoid the society of the wicked, lest they delight to imitate the evils that they frequently behold and cannot correct. And Saint John the bishop says: if a good man is joined to an evil man, either they are made equals, or they are soon separated from each other. For friendships either seek equals or make them. For the nature of things is such that whenever a good man is joined to an evil man, the evil man is not made better by the good, but the good man is contaminated by the evil. For diversity of things can never have concord, and wicked society tempts many.

    There are among you certain brothers, I say it groaning, men professed to regular discipline but very forgetful of it: to them the cell is a prison, the choir a siege, prayer nausea, silence a punishment, the reading of the Scriptures disgust. The love of God either never or rarely raises upward the hearts of those whose whole way of life consists in lower things. Whenever I happen to be absent, they immediately come together among themselves; not about Christ, nor about the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, nor about the integrity of regular observance, but a long discourse is brought forth about the vain and useless affairs of this world; and concerning things about which it is not lawful for a monk to think, they involve themselves in conversation with tales and the wars of kings. But whatever I speak to these men, whatever I say, whatever penance I impose, nothing

    On Fleeing the Company of the Wicked.

    ...makes progress: those whom evil custom corrupted from the beginning of their training. Nothing, moreover, is worse than evil custom. For the monk who is negligent as a novice and young man passes all the days of his life in sluggishness and idleness. For Scripture says: “A young man walking according to his own way, even when he has grown old, will not depart from it.”

    Therefore I say to you, venerable elders; I beg you, I admonish you, and by the mercy of God I ask you with all the insistence I can: so live from now on, so conduct yourselves, so walk, that your habits may accord with the years of old age, and that you who have already advanced far into old age may provide the younger men with an example of holiness for imitation. Without doubt there is ascribed to you whatever is found lacking in the habits of the younger men. For you ought to go before the younger men in all holiness, in word and in deed; you are commanded to show them an example of all perfection, so that, when they behold in you the perfect works of all virtues, stirred as if by a certain impulse of shame, they may be roused to imitation of your holiness. For the habits of elders provide the younger with an example of living, as is said in the proverb: what the old men have sung, this the young have learned.

    But you younger men, show reverence with humility to the elders, considering their grey hair; and those whom you know to be more fervent in the observance of regular discipline, rejoice to have them as instructors by their company. Beware of those who either walk restlessly or observe the purity of regular discipline rather negligently. Not all who are called elders are worthy of the imitation of the younger; nor do years make a monk venerable, but habits established in the love of God with prudence make him worthy of reverence.

    Therefore, whoever among you, dearest brothers, desires to be a true lover of God, whoever desires to make progress in the holy monastic way of life which he professes, let him always flee the company of undisciplined brothers, and let him seek comrades in arms who consent with his own purpose toward the good. For the prophet says in the psalm: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverted.” For evil fellowship has harmed many, and he who delights to dwell with the reprobate will not be free from the contagion of sin.

    Indeed everyone who keeps company with evil and reprobate men must necessarily have his integrity somewhat spoiled by their perversity. For either he will love them and, made like them, will become evil; or he will hate them and will be the enemy of many, and for that reason necessarily restless. But if, overcome by the multitude of the wicked, he has once begun to delight in their company, then he too has already been corrupted, and little by little he will be corrupted still more. But if he has detested the works of the evil, he will labor under a grave distress of mind; and his desire for progressing to what is better will be so much slower in him, the more he is disturbed by the company of the perverse.

    Yet I give thanks to almighty God for you, because, even if not all of you are fervent in charity as I would wish, nevertheless, as I trust, you all live far removed from great sins and from the rashness of pride. And the exhortations and fatherly admonitions which I give you, as I am bound to do daily, you receive gladly, although you do not yet all display them perfectly in practice. But I hope in the Lord Jesus that he will perfect in you the good which he has begun, so that my joy may be fulfilled, and I may see you all, with one zeal, one purpose, and one flame of holy fervor burning, delighting and exercising yourselves in the workshop of divine love.

    But because some of you defer this desire of mine, not yet taking up the spirit of fuller amendment which I desire, I am compelled by just necessity to admonish those who are making progress, that, rising up with a manly spirit, they flee the private and harmful associations of the lukewarm. For as yet the fire of divine love is small in their hearts; as yet the newly kindled and weak flame of holy fervor burns, and unless it is fostered by daily increases it will easily suffer loss. For that reason again and again I admonish you: if you find any opposed, by deed or speech, to the beginnings of inward love, avoid them as a pestilential poison. For just as water extinguishes the fire on which it is poured, so the holy purpose of novices is violated by the examples of the lukewarm. Beware of taking part in the conversations of those whom you see to be negligent in the observance of the commandments of God and of monastic purity, because, since they are driven by passions

    Homily XI.

    ...with the carnal: out of the abundance of the heart they speak nothing but vain and carnal things. For the wicked conversations of old men corrupt the good morals of the young. All their pursuits are vain, and their speeches useless, indeed pestilential, since, being carnally minded, they have not known the exercises of divine love. Indeed, just as one sick sheep gradually corrupts the whole sheepfold, so one slothful and perverse monk in a congregation often becomes the cause of many transgressions. As Saint [Christophilus?] bears witness, a little leaven corrupts with its odor the whole mass of flour with which it is mixed; so young monks, and [unclear], who associate with lukewarm and slothful elders, are imbued with their depraved habits and thereafter are never restored to the integrity of holy fervor. Therefore I say to you elders: be, by good works and chaste and always modest speech, a model of life for the young, so that whenever they are corrected for their offenses, they may not defend themselves by the examples of the elders. For it is most shameful that elders should be guilty in those things for which the younger are deservedly reproved. Live, I pray, old men, in such a way that in your presence the younger may presume neither to say nor to do anything that seems blameworthy.

    Let them fear you as judges of evils, not as acting the part of patrons, since as many as sin by your example are reckoned to have perished by your teaching. Let no one among you become lukewarm or negligent, since desires kill the lazy man, and the vanity of all things destroys the idle monk. Let there be among you no talkative man, no wandering monk, no roving idler, murmuring and restless, since whoever delights in such pursuits both ruins himself by evil conduct and kills his brother by his examples. Let there be among you no mocker of the simple, no despiser of the humble, nor any rash censurer, since he who is quick to mock will be consumed in his foolishness and will not be glorious. He opens his mouth against the humble, is always seeking quarrels, and rejoices that he is talkative about the deeds of others.

    He will not prosper in his counsel; and if he is raised to some honor, he will quickly fall into the depth. His pride is hateful to God, since, although he is stupid and foolish, he boasts that he is learned and wise. Soon his foolishness will be laid bare, and a grievous destruction will seize him.

    Folio XXVI.

    His heart meditates folly, and there is no peace around him. He will be hateful to those near him and to his neighbors, and no faithful friend will accompany him. He leads his life in hypocrisy, having assumed a pretense of dissimulation, and by his foolishness he will draw many into aversion. He hates peace and loves discord; he will be caught in the sloth of his mind, and there will be no one to grieve with him. He will be crushed by a double affliction, because he did not permit peace to those who had it. The devil has made a nest in his tongue, and Satan has fixed his dwelling in his mind. Therefore there is no love of the brethren in his heart, since he sows discord between the shepherd and the sheep. He boasts that he is a friend of God and accepts no one as his equal in regular observance, but he does not understand humility, the greatest ornament of a monk.

    He does not open his mouth for words of spiritual edification, and from his heart nothing but vanity proceeds. All day long, dissolved in mind and wandering in body, he runs about in the monastery; he gives himself to useless and utterly idle speech; he thinks nothing of the salvation of his soul; he cares for his belly as God. Guard your mind from his speech, and do not set your foot in the way of his words.

    Whoever desires to show himself a monk and minister of God, whoever truly loves the Lord Jesus with his whole heart, be cautious and watchful in all your works, and always flee the companionship of those in whose life nothing of heavenly doctrine is seen. Be the companion of humble monks seeking perfection and [unclear], who yields, shaken, to every wind; but strengthen your soul in a good purpose [unclear] to love, or be deceived by the counsel of the depraved. For it is best that the heart be established by grace; and the one who instructs by example toward the good, love and venerate as a father. Have no commerce of familiarity with a restless brother, lest at some time, strengthened by his depraved example, you fall into the rebellion of the proud. Let no angry and murmuring monk full of [unclear] be at your side; and with him who

    On fleeing the company of transgressors.

    ...kicks against his superiors, never consider him a friend. Whomever you see violating the canon of fasting without the blessing of an elder, flee as an enemy of salvation; likewise the man who by talkativeness, or for a [unclear] reason, overturns peace and stirs up quarrels. As from the face of a snake, flee the monk who is rebellious and disobedient to his elders, since he seethes full of the poison of malice and, in the pride of his mind, has lost his soul. He who does not obey the command of an elder is perverse; he who, corrupted, [unclear] is an apostate. Let not the man who speaks slanderously against his brother be in conversation with you, because [unclear] is far off and [unclear].

    Whomever you find wholly solicitous in every zeal to live in regular observance, love and venerate as a father and a most beloved teacher. With confidence enjoy the familiarity of him whose friendship always makes you better in the love of God. With all zeal imitate good men, and follow the conduct of those who live in conformity with monastic perfection. Have as a friend the brother of good will; but turn your ears away from him who is of hard heart. Let the man who is soft in spirit and dissolute in conduct be to you like a man who breaks down hedges in a field. Do not be the companion of him who despises the rule and silence, who distinguishes neither places nor times, who without the prior’s blessing everywhere [unclear] and multiplies [unclear]. The monk who, given to wine and drinking, rather often exceeds the common canon of the monastery is the fuel of lust and the spring [unclear] of all vices.

    The monk who relies on the counsel of his own head against the [unclear] command is close to perdition, and walks festively in danger of his soul. Do not share in the works of an obstinate monk, nor have friendship with the man who, laughing at the deserved deeds of his superior, speaks against them. Be continually in the midst of disciplined men, and let your soul gladly walk with the humble. For he who is joined to good men shares in their virtue, and he who walks with the wicked will fall into a pit. But a monk of perverse will leads very many astray; and he who despises obedience will never be exalted. He who lifts up his voice and cries out with loud shouting cannot hide the foolishness of his heart, and glories in his vanity.

    The friendship of good men is firm salvation for friends, and in the company of transgressors simple innocence is corrupted. The company of those men is best in whom the fear of God has confirmed examples of good works. Nothing is more precious than a friend who fears God, and nothing more dangerous than a companion who is of perverse will. A brother who fears God with all his heart will be a wall of strength for his friend; and the man joined to such a one in holiness of mind is sanctified at all times by the blessing of the Spirit of God. He who rejoices in the midst of those who fear God is sustained, lest he fail, as if by a very strong wall around him.

    From his words the servant of the Most High is known, and works of holiness reveal the good monk. No foul or scurrilous word comes quickly from the mouth of one who fears the Lord; and he who is a true lover of Jesus does nothing that offends goodness. In the mouth of monks who love [God], Christ always resounds; and he who is a true worshipper of God demonstrates the discourse of righteousness both in his mouth and in his work. He who fears God is the best counsellor; and he who walks according to the canon is a prudent judge of thoughts. An elder who fears God and has long been proved and experienced in regular observance is a director of the young; and he who has no stain in his garment should be a good instructor for novices. He who is an understanding teacher and expounder of the divine scriptures, guarding his soul in humility: receive all his words gladly without [unclear], since he has the sinews and solidity of future eternal happiness.

    He who teaches truly also suffers with the infirm; and he who loves Jesus encourages the wavering spirit to strength. He who walks with a verbose man will not escape contention; and he who delights in falsehood will never be a friend of wisdom. He who is assiduous in external things will not make progress, and boasts without cause that he is a monk. The purpose of holiness is quickly corrupted when a monk wanders outside his cell rather too often through [unclear] desire. He who abandons the secrecy of his cell without the command of an elder does not strive toward the perfection of the holy purpose. Beautiful is the company of good men and of those who fear God; and he who has chosen to live with them will not feel confusion.

    The heart of a young monk is the tablet of the world, on which the conduct of elders is now inscribed, [unclear] to be erased. The worst writer of a beautiful heart is the elder who either does or says shameful things [unclear] before a young man. He who infects a young man with reckless speech is like the impious Herod who

    Homily XII

    He killed the boys. The evil that a young man receives from a foolish and negligent old man, even when he has been made a priest, he will not amend. Every vessel that is filled with filth is corrupted; and a monk who is negligent in the novitiate, when he has grown old, is not amended. Cursed is the old man by whose evil manner of life young men perish, because he who leaves evil tracks for those who follow is like one who with his own hand has cast a blind man headlong into a pit. Before the eternal Judge each man is worthy of as many deaths as there are innocents who have perished by his wicked example.

    Young man, seek an old man as the guide of your life: not one who has completed many years in a lax and lukewarm manner of life, but one whom the fear of the Lord and knowledge of the divine Scriptures commend. Better is the company of a young monk who fears the Lord than the fellowship of an aged teacher whose life does not have the light of divine love and the integrity of regular observance. An old man disordered in morals, lacking purity of mind and without discipline, is like [unclear], lame in the leg, being led to the grave. An old and lax monk is like a foolish man who, not knowing the boundaries, is captured with robbers at a drinking banquet. An old man without maturity is like an elder-wood pipe crushed under the feet of players.

    Vainly does he boast that he has been a monk for many days, if he has not grasped the beginning of inward conduct. He who loves the purity of his heart guards himself at all times from the company of undisciplined brothers. Just as a stain of pitch clinging to the garments of dancers grieves virginity, so a good young man blushes at the filthy words of elders. Lascivious speech does not belong to a man who fears God, because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; and he who utters filthy words is not clean before the Most High. If sinners begin to hate you because of the fear of God, do not be saddened, because unless you displease the wicked you will not attain the perfection of the good. For to displease the wicked on account of justice is praiseworthy, and a manifest sign of divine love. If you love your soul, flee the counsels of the undisciplined, and do not keep company with mockers. Walk with the good, and let him who fears the Lord be your counselor.

    Concerning monks sent on the road. Homily.

    Folio XXVII

    It belongs to monks to flee the world, and, for love of solitude, to avoid the crowds of men at all times as much as they can. A monk is named from solitude, although he is called one from unity. He cannot be a monk who delights in the throng of peoples; and he who delights in cities has not yet tasted monastic sweetness. If you are a monk, you must not leave the solitude of the monastery without reasonable cause; and if you are bound to silence, do not delight in the conversations of worldly people. Whoever loves wandering excursions on the road has abandoned his conscience; and he who is often outside the monastery does not preserve the purity of his inward progress.

    He who goes about the houses of his parents and delights in the feasts of neighbors does not consider himself a monk; and he who goes to the banquets of drinkers kills his own soul. He who sleeps in the house of his kinsman seeks comforts; and he who avoids the assemblies of the religious follows a destructive freedom. A monk in the house of father and mother is like a lamb in the midst of wolves, and like a hare surrounded by the dogs of hunters. If you are a monk, if you are God’s servant and soldier, what are you doing in the house of your parents, or what are you seeking in the midst of the people? A monk remaining long outside the monastery among secular people is like a man who buries his only son beneath the depth of waters. For just as there is no life for fish on dry land, so there is no salvation of soul for monks in the world. Outside the river the fish dies; and the purity of a monk’s conscience is quickly violated outside the monastery. The life of monks is in the monastery, and the [death?] of souls is in the midst of secular people.

    It is a great virtue of the soul to flee the crowds of men, or, when it is entirely necessary to be among them, nevertheless to avoid them in mind. We are sometimes compelled by necessity to make a journey through the world; but the less the desire of the mind is drawn away from the secrecy of the cell, the less the purity of conscience is polluted by meeting men. Therefore every good monk must be admonished by us that, whenever by order of his senior he is sent on the road because of the necessity of any matter, his soul should never wander outward. He who does not guard his senses is quickly corrupted when evil is set before him; and he who casts away the fear of the Lord, [unclear] impure to the monastery

    Concerning monks sent on a journey.

    [unclear] will return. A stream flowing out, by its muddiness, stains the beauty of the meadows lying open round about; and when a monk gives attention to the tales of secular people, he defiles the purity of his conscience. Therefore, before you set your foot out of the monastery, arm yourself with holy prayers; and before you go out on the road, do not neglect to commend your way to the Lord with prayers. Then carry out what the lawgiver has commanded, and entrust yourself to be protected by the prayers both of the abbot and of all the brothers. Prescribe for yourself the canon of the severity of regular observance, and, with a stable remembrance of it, guard your mind from every outflow of vanities that meet you.

    Do not go anywhere out of the cenobium without the abbot’s blessing, because, since you ought to be dead and buried to this world, it will not be lawful for you to do anything further without the command of your elder. Recognize yourself as a soldier of King Jesus Christ: you must follow your emperor, without whom there is no salvation. He, fixed to the cross, is taken down not by his own hands but by the hands of others; and you, if you desire to be saved, must have your will governed by the abbot’s command. For the monk who goes out anywhere from the cenobium without the abbot’s permission is like a little sheep in the darkness that is burned up in the fire of the house. But the true monk of Christ, even when he is outside the cenobium in body, remains in the cloister of the mind; and he is no less alone among many than he is accustomed to be solitary in his cell.

    The lover of Christ thinks of Jesus even in the midst of a crowd; and he who is a true worker of virtues keeps his heart firm in the fear of God in every place. For even if he is not in the monastery in body, yet in heart, because of the vigor of his spirit, he has always stood firm and stable, as if alone in the cloister. The spirit is not polluted by the movement of the body, when the solitude of the mind is preserved. You must live with the same holiness on the road, O monk, with which you are commanded to conduct yourself in the cenobium, and you must walk with a certain greater caution, lest you scandalize anyone by a more lax example, where there are as many judges of monks as there seem to be onlookers present.

    The eyes of all secular people look up to monks, and they seek in their works the holiness which they hear them to have professed. A monk gives more offense by one rash word than a man given to the world does by ten thousand. For however light and buffoonish a worldly man may seem, nevertheless he has not learned to tolerate the insolence of monks with an even mind, because in his rustic simplicity he believes all cloistered men to be not such as they are, but such as they ought to be. Hence an evil word or deed among them is ascribed to the monk for damnation, whereas it is imputed to the worldly man for pardon. Nor without reason. For the monk who has professed a holy and approved canon is bound to direct his whole effort toward perfection, and in word and deed, in all purity of mind and body, far to surpass the conduct of secular people. For a light or idle word, which is granted to secular people for pardon, is judged for destruction in cloistered men.

    Gold is more precious than all metals and is more desired by mortals, and in no other is a stain or corruption of falsity more quickly charged. And the flaw which is discerned in gold with judicial severity is passed over in the other metals because of the baseness of their nature. Gold gladdens the eyes by its beauty and strengthens the innermost parts of life by its virtue. Gold, when smelted in the fire, is not diminished; and the true monk of God is not changed from the purpose of holiness in the tribulation of persecution. A small [unclear] in a golden vessel is very displeasing in the sight of a powerful man; if an earthen vessel is crooked, no one detests it. When a monk offends in small matters, a great outcry of many people rises against him, because his conduct is compared to gold. The canonical life of monks is gold, a mirror. Gold in the midst of mud receives no stain of its nature, but preserves all its beauty inviolate.

    So too the true monk, a lover of Christ, remains among men, when sent on a journey, just as he has learned to conduct himself in the secrecy of his little cell, because he walks pure in mind as well as in body before the Lord. For if he is a true monk, he is not polluted by the dust of another’s manner of life, nor does [unclear] delight him away from the rectitude of [unclear]. He who is secure in heart is not divided even in the midst of those making a tumult. Therefore, monk, you who desire to be good, gather your mind back to yourself; and before you leave your cell for the journey, dispose your heart. Let the fear of the Lord always be the companion of your journey.

    Homily XII.

    And let the guardianship of monastic discipline never depart from your side. Stop your ears with the remembrance of the last things, lest the hearing of vain speech pollute the integrity of your mind. Humbly cast your eyes down to the earth, lest they look upon what it does not befit a servant of God to desire. Do not take part in the conversations of carnal men; if you cannot avoid their presence, beware lest you lend them your mind. Even in the midst of ribald men, do not transgress your rule, and do not abandon your accustomed gravity. Do not fear the insults and reproaches of [unclear], and let your heart not be troubled by the words of men of darkness. The observance of monastic discipline is justice; and those who despise the simple pursue the innocent with laughter. Preserve your holy purpose in all things, and the Most High will avenge the injury.

    Do not say in your heart, “I suffer violence,” nor be ashamed at the words of those who mock you. The glory of a monk is to endure insult, and the crown of beauty is to rejoice in reproaches. He who is patient under injuries is stronger than Atlas, and he who is not saddened when mocked is greater than all. If you have fixed your desire in heaven, nothing on earth will disturb you; and if you are a true monk, your heart will exult at injuries. There is a judge in heaven who knows all things, and there is the Most High God who cares for all things. He is the just rewarder of merits, and he will remember his poor. The more deeply you cast down your soul now in this life, for love of God, into the depth of humiliation, the more in future glory you will be exalted above the rest.
