    For by patience heaven is ascended, and through humility one comes to the kingdom. For it was also necessary for Christ himself to suffer, and so to enter into his glory. A delicate soldier is he who seeks pleasures while his emperor patiently endures insults and mockeries, and while he hangs on the gibbet of the cross for his army, he follows after pleasures. A soldier who goes forth naked to battle without arms, and a monk who disdains to embrace patience and humility amid insults: for both there is swift destruction. The monk who is a sincere lover of Christ is not angered by injuries, does not threaten those who inflict insult, stands fixed in his holy purpose, and, however much the wicked rush upon him, is not moved. As timely rain increases the hay in the meadows, so merit grows for the monk from the humble endurance of injuries. Humility is the sinew of all virtues, and constant patience under injuries for the love of God is the mine of good works.

    Therefore, when you are about to go out from the monastery onto the road, prepare your heart for the endurance of injuries, and strengthen your mind against the insolences of mockers. When misty fellows shout after your back, repeating the name “monk,” remember Christ, mocked and spat upon before the governor, who did not answer a word, but silently preserved patience. Imitate him as your leader, O monk; always listen to him as your teacher, for he was meek and humble of heart. Do not answer a word to those who mock you; do not turn your face backward, but say with the prophet: “Those who sought evils for me spoke vanities, and meditated deceits all day long. But I, like a deaf man, did not hear; and like a mute man not opening his mouth. And I became like a man who does not hear, and has no rebukes in his mouth.” This Christ did; this Jesus taught; this the king of all commanded. If you wish to be his disciple, you must always be ready for all injuries.

    When you are set upon the road, do not neglect to say your canonical prayers with whatever devotion you can; and always turn over something good with you in your mind, either by praying or by meditating. The Lord walks with you, and his holy angels accompany you as you walk. And therefore preserve a clean heart in all things, lest you offend the majesty of so many and such companions. The Lord is all eye and ear; from his knowledge nothing is hidden. Keep constant guard over your words, and let deliberation of the heart precede every word of your mouth, so that you speak nothing at all of which you could repent. A monk will speak both few words and reasonable ones, and his lips never exceed measure in speech. All his conversation is directed to the edification of his neighbors; and he who teaches very many by his conduct, even when silent, speaks useful things. He who is a true lover of God walks most humbly on the road; and he who fears the Most High restrains his mouth from laughter. In all your life, think yourself mortal, and live dying, as one who is already sending forth his last breath. Happy the kingdom and rich before God the province in which monks rise up with Boötes, since where there is no fear of God, the theaters are filled with cloistered men. A monk on the road

    Concerning monks sent on the road.

    He who has God as his friend easily disdains familiarity with men; and he who speaks with angels takes very little delight in the conversations of mortals. Whenever on the road you see a sign of the Lord’s Passion or of the Crucified One, do not pass by unless you say: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, for the pain of your wounds, for the shedding of your most holy blood, and for your most innocent death, which you endured for us on the altar of the cross; and I beseech you, by your bitter Passion, have mercy on me now and in the dread hour of my death.” Repeat this very brief prayer often as you go, and never pass by an image of the Crucified One unless you have given thanks to the Savior.

    Do not contend with him who walks with you on the road, lest, when he has returned to the monastery, he lie about some evil thing against you. He who provokes the companion of his journey to impatience is like one who drives a mad dog with a blow to bark. A wicked man is overcome by gentleness; and he who is humble in heart calms a soul that has been stirred up. In the midst of secular men do not pour out speech, lest perhaps he take up mockery against you. We allow good things to be spoken [unclear] among young men; but let the one who is lesser in rank listen to him. The weary ploughman hastens to rest; and the monk whole in spirit, running the byways, returns with longing to his cell. Let the word be restrained in the mouth until reason brings forth a judgment of fairness; and let speech that can instruct hearers not be hidden.

    Do not put trust in the songs of flatterers, since [unclear] they have shot down the innocent; they soothe the ears with ill-composed speeches. A monk who is nourished on contentions is like [unclear], and like a [spastic?] man who, under the name of religion, stirs up quarrels. In the presence of the learned do not add to the speaking, lest perhaps, when you do not understand the parable, you be laughed at by those standing around. He who recognizes himself as a monk is [unclear] by profound speech; and he who teaches little ones makes [unclear] the question. When you go to men unlike you in purpose, do not boast in anything; but if you are questioned, answer humbly in few words. When set upon a journey, always think of God, and regard the reverence of your elder as accompanying you. Do absolutely nothing that you would not wish to be made known to him; since, as the sacred [writer] says

    On All Things, XII.

    The servant of Christ is believed to act in Christ’s stead in the monastery, and therefore he is deservedly honored by all. Therefore live as though you always had him present before your eyes; and whatever you would not presume to do or say while he was looking on, do not attempt in any way when he is absent. For it is foolish consolation, when conscience is biting with guilt, for sin to be hidden from men and to flee the judgment of the pastor, when one knows oneself to be sick unto death. The monk who does an evil which he wishes to be hidden from his prelate has violated the integrity of the monastic canon, and has gravely sinned against the fifth degree of humility. For thus it commands: The fifth degree of humility is this: if he has not concealed from his abbot, by humble confession, all evil thoughts coming into his heart and evil deeds done by him in secret. These are the admonitions of father Benedict; these are the holy teachings of monastic instruction. If you, monk, despise or neglect them, you will be convicted of forgetfulness of your own salvation.

    It is a sure sign of humility if a monk does not refuse to open his heart to his elder, and does not wish any of the evils he has committed to be hidden from his pastor. He who confesses his fault with humility will be strengthened against the adversary of his salvation; and he who hides his thoughts will make progress in evil. For there is no thought of evils so small that it does not gradually grow if neglected; and no vice so slight that it does not gain strength if it has been dissembled. Therefore evil thoughts must be repelled immediately at the beginning, because when a depraved thought is not suddenly extinguished it produces delight; delight produces consent; consent casts one headlong into action. Then an action of evil, often repeated, begets habit; habit begets necessity; necessity brings in despair; despair contempt; contempt obstinacy; and that brings forth the eternal death of the soul. For Scripture says: When the impious man has come into the depth of evils, he despises.

    Is not your abbot, O monk, the pastor and physician of your soul? Are not I, my dearest brothers, after God, the one who feeds your mortal bodies with necessary nourishment? Am I not compelled to minister the word of salvation to you? If you sheep flee the pastor, what are the pastures of the spirit which you expect from us? The sick man who flees the physician despises his own salvation and willingly kills his own soul. Therefore the monk who walks in the way of malice and turns aside from the paths of justice is near to death; and he slips so much the more deeply into the depth of vices, the less he reveres the judgment of those who correct him. But he is truly a monk who keeps his soul from every iniquity and does nothing at all which he would wish his pastor not to know. He who conceals his way is not pure; and he who flees the presence of the judge increases suspicion. Like a sheep walking in the desert, which is seized by the wolf, so the negligent and impure monk who withdraws himself from the knowledge of his pastor is devoured by demons. The sick man running to destruction, and the monk hiding every sin: there is no salvation for them unless they return to the physician.

    Monks returning from a journey should immediately on that very day, according to the monastic canon, prostrate themselves in the sight of all the brothers, so that whatever has been committed on the road through negligence may be expiated by the common prayers. For the common prayer of many avails much for washing away sins, if it has been poured out to the Lord with the fervor of devotion.

    Here ends On All Things, XII: On Monks Sent on a Journey.

    On the Daily Expiation of Sins.

    On All Things, XIV.

    As long as we are placed in this corruptible life, dearest brothers, we offend daily in many things; and however holy our conduct may seem

    On the daily expiation of sins.

    We are not without sin. For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks many things. For Scripture says: “There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin.” Likewise the holy evangelist John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Indeed, through commerce with the flesh, which is too much delighted, the soul sins, and the strength of the spirit is diminished by despair. For the mind is deceived by the presentation of sensible things, and readiness to sin is strengthened by long habit. The weakness of the flesh enfeebles the fervor of the spirit, and the frailty of the will resists the holy purpose of the mind. Hence Solomon, the most wise king, says in the book of Proverbs: “Seven times in a day the righteous man will fall and rise again; but the impious will fall into evil.” By the testimony of this saying we are admonished not to grow slack in the purpose of holiness, even if it should happen that we have fallen seven times in a day.

    As often, O monk, as you have fallen through sin from the purpose of holiness, so often rise again to your former fervor, not with sloth. It belongs to human frailty to fall, but to diabolical obstinacy to remain cast down in the mire of crime. The demons sinned once, and in their obstinacy they were made hardened and pertinacious, never thereafter to return to repentance. But men, as often as they have fallen, can always rise again to repentance, and by tears and prayers obtain the grace of God which they had lost by sinning. For the heart of man is flexible and can be moved in either direction, because no man in the flesh is to be believed able to become so evil that he cannot, if he wishes, recover from his malice and, with God granting it, reform his mind toward goodness. Conversely, no one becomes so good in this mortal life that he cannot become evil, if he misuses the grace of the Lord.

    Since these things are so, my brothers, you must be admonished by my exhortation today to walk carefully: so that he who, with conscience as witness, is already advancing on the paths of righteousness may persevere in them by progressing daily, and he who understands himself to be guilty before the Lord may amend his life as quickly as possible. If human frailty daily impels you, or, to speak more properly, casts you down and makes you sin, let the love of God and of your own salvation also incite you daily to expiate your fault humbly through true contrition. Thus also the righteous man falls seven times in a day and rises again, because although he slips through human frailty, nevertheless, always persevering in the purpose of holiness, he is strengthened more and more in spirit in the love of God. For while he keeps his conscience free from grave sins, he is unwillingly stained by daily negligences; and when he sees that he cannot live without faults, he groans the more, humbly recognizing his weakness. But if he has even been overtaken by a graver fault, he soon rises again to amendment through repentance.

    Therefore, considering the condition of human frailty, the ancient moderators of monastic discipline established various kinds of expiation, by which both monks of good will might daily advance toward better things and the wicked might be compelled to the observance of the regular life. For in the Rule the holy father Benedict commands thus, saying: “With all solicitude let the abbot take care concerning delinquent brothers, because the physician is not needed by the healthy, but by those who are ill.” For this reason the first leaders of regular observance established by prudent consideration that daily after Prime a chapter of faults should be held in the appointed place, in which, with the abbot or prior presiding [unclear], the actions of all the brothers should be brought into the open with fair examination.

    This place, my brothers, bears the type of the purgatory of souls, because here not only are past sins expiated, but we are also fortified by expiatory repentance [unclear]. For in this place, which we call the chapter room, whatever you have committed openly is corrected and expiated through salutary repentance. Here each day, with the paraphrast pronouncing it, you learn your monastic law, according to the integrity of which you promised to live; here every day you hear the exhortatory word of salvation; you listen to the briefly recited victories of Christ’s martyrs and their manifold sufferings for the orthodox faith. This is the school of monks, necessary for the consideration of regular discipline, in which all that is commanded to be observed by cloistered men is learned. There are two things, my most beloved brothers, which this place requires of you: the first, that in correction [you be] always humble

    Homily XIII. Folio XXX.

    that you maintain patience; the other, that you willingly receive our exhortation, such as it is. For the first purpose, our holy lawgivers, wishing you to be ready, command that the brave deeds of the martyrs, whose imitators you ought to become, be read; and then, so that you may be teachable in spirit, they ordered one passage from the Rule to be added. And so, that by imitation of the holy martyrs you may be strong and patient under necessary rebukes, the sequence of their passion is read here in your ears; and, in order that you may prepare your minds for saving doctrine, a reading from the Rule which you profess is recited to you together with it. The holy martyrs of Christ encourage you to patience by their example; and the blessed Benedict admonishes you by his teaching that you should also be ready for injuries.

    Therefore let none of you, most beloved brothers, in this place refuse humbly to receive penance daily for his negligences; let no one disdain it. This place is the public place for expiating sin, in which the severity of judgment is so tempered that the kindness of discretion is not violated. For I wish to be the physician of your souls, not their destroyer. Therefore come securely to the examination of our judgment, and humbly proclaim yourselves openly concerning negligences committed. I do not wish to burden you beyond the Rule, so as to transfer the most secret offenses of conscience from sacramental confession to the public examination of faults, which we know that certain men have done, to the grave [unclear] of the souls of their subjects. For thus our lawgiver Benedict says in the Rule: But if the cause of the soul’s sin has been hidden, let him make it known only to the abbot or to spiritual elders, who know how to heal their own wounds and those of others, not to disclose or publish them.

    There are two places in the monastery for the expiation of sin: one for those sins that are manifest, and the other for those that are hidden. For manifest sins must be expiated publicly before all in the daily proclamation of faults; but hidden sins, and those whose disclosure would scandalize the weak, must be referred to confession. For he whose sin is manifest must also be punished publicly; and he who has offended in secret must also be corrected in secret. There are certain rulers of cloistered men who do not fear to bring the hidden sins of their subjects to public examination; and in my judgment they do not execute the rights of prelacy prudently enough, since they close off from their subjects the way of salvation and bind their confession, most free though it is, under the bond of ill will. How dangerous this is, there is no one even moderately wise who does not understand. For the holy founder of monks rebukes this rashness of a pastor, saying: Let the abbot exercise solicitude with great care, and with all sagacity and industry take care not to lose any of the sheep entrusted to him. Let him know that he has undertaken the care of sick souls, not tyranny over healthy ones.

    We have appointed for you four spiritual confessors from among the seniors, so that if any one of you has been seized beforehand by some hidden temptation, and has found our [unclear] inexperienced or suspect, he may securely have recourse to them for his consolation. Although we have found these things hitherto known to the whole congregation [unclear], whom we have observed to have withdrawn trust from us both in confession and outside it. For all know, and you plainly see, that I seek nothing more in you, desire nothing more, than your salvation and the daily increase of spiritual progress. For you are my crown, you my honor, you my joy, because then I consider myself happy when I know that you have made progress in the love of God.

    You have obtained a great opportunity for making progress, dearest brothers, since the place in which we serve the Lord as soldiers is removed from all tumult, and we do not cease to advance you toward better things by daily admonition. But whenever any one of you has fallen into some sin through human frailty, he is not permitted to lie long in dejection of spirit, where one is daily proclaimed by another in true fraternal charity for his negligences. This is a workshop of salvation, in which the mind is fed with the nourishment of heavenly doctrine, and the soul is daily cleansed from the stains of offenses by public satisfaction. This place is an earthly purgatory, in which the monk is corrected with discretion for his negligences, and through humble patience, for the love of Christ, is daily offered to his Creator in a long martyrdom. [unclear] brothers, in this assembly, receive with discretion those proclaimed for faults; it is yours to endure all things most patiently

    On the Daily Expiation of Sins.

    to suffer. For it is necessary that we make satisfaction for our sins; but if we neglect to do this in this life, in the life to come, compelled, we shall necessarily do it. There are some among you who take corrections very hard. To them we declare what we have often said, that in the future they must endure very grievous things, they who refuse to endure small and light things here. But I, considering their weakness and ignorance, am gravely tormented within myself, because I see their minds wounded, and yet I am afraid to apply the necessary medicines. For if I apply remedies suited to the diseases, I fear lest, made fainthearted, they fall into despair, or certainly, given over to a reprobate mind, withdraw entirely from their holy purpose. Therefore I use as much discretion as I can, as all of you will bear witness for me, preferring to send the weak through patience with charity to purgatory rather than, from just severity, to have the despairing descend into hell.

    For who in this mortality could ever make satisfaction for sins who did not apply a good will to penitence? For good will alone commends the works of penitents. But although many are punished unwillingly, they are still far removed from perfect satisfaction. Believe me, my most beloved brothers, that satisfaction for sins is commended more by suffering than by acting. For even the Lord and Savior of us all, Jesus, by suffering expiated the sin of the whole world on the altar of the cross. Would that you knew how effective a medicine it is for the soul wounded by sins to receive proclamations and corrections with humble patience, and also, for the increase of perfect satisfaction, to bear injuries and insults with equanimity. I am certain that humble patience in adversity far surpasses every kind of satisfaction; and the readier the mind has been to bear insults and injuries for the love of Christ, the more easily and quickly it will obtain from the Lord pardon for all its sins and a fuller indulgence.

    For this place in which we now speak is the workshop of purgation and expiation, in which zeal for regular discipline holds primacy, discretion presides over examination, charity directs and completes all things. Hence in this very place patience is very necessary for you; without its presence no satisfaction will be consummated. The monk who is a zealous lover of his salvation loves this place as a workshop of expiation, and never goes forth from it without having been made better than himself. For this place is to be feared and dreaded by demons, but dear and greatly venerable to the holy angels of God; in it the fault of humble monks is washed away, and whatever is committed openly is also expiated publicly before all. But if any hidden fault has been committed by any of you, the secret confession of the penitent will likewise purge it away. In both cases pure confession with humility is required, and both here and there patience is judged necessary for you.

    Therefore, whoever you are, monk, who desire to be good, prepare your soul in all patience, so that you may hold the tranquility of mind most constant as much in adversities as in prosperities. When you have been proclaimed by some brother for your negligences, patiently [unclear] the rebukes from the senior, you who offend daily in many things. He endured countless injuries most patiently for your salvation, and why should you not suffer humbly for your sins? Bear patiently with all humility, faithfully bringing to mind how innocently the mighty Son of God was accused. For if he, just and innocent, who committed no sin, suffered insults, why should you not patiently bear rebuke with tolerance in satisfaction for sins? But if you did not deserve the proclamation in judgment, nevertheless endure it patiently for the love of Christ; now it will be reckoned to you not only as satisfaction for preceding sins, but much more as justification. Therefore whether a monk is proclaimed justly or unjustly, he has no ground for just defense, because if he has sinned he suffers according to his desert; but if he is innocent, he is the more bound to patience. For no one unless patient and humble will be able to imitate Christ. But since the monk is especially bound to be a disciple and imitator of Christ, it is especially fitting for him to be patient. Without

    Homily XIII.

    Fol. XXXI.

    [Without?] sword and fire a monk can be a martyr, if for love of God he has kept true [unclear] patience in his soul. For the true monk is neither puffed up by praises nor saddened by blame; he shows himself patient under injuries; at insults and reproaches he is glad and humbly keeps silent. No one is stronger than the patient man who knows how to conquer himself and humbly to endure adversities for love of God with a tranquil mind.

    But the hard, impatient man is proud and arrogant, since he does not follow Jesus, the teacher of humility; and therefore he is indignant at just rebukes and [unclear]. As the furnace tests gold, so insults and injuries test a monk, whether he truly loves Christ. Humility and patience in adversity are the true badges of monks; whoever is not clothed in their adornment glories vainly in the name. He who is not humble cannot truly be a monk; he who does not keep patience in adversities cannot be a true disciple of Christ.

    Hence king Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his own spirit than one who storms cities.” For a man’s teaching is known through patience, and his glory is to pass over wrongs. The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests men among us. The monk who follows Christ in truth and who is a meditator on the Lord’s passion is patient under all injuries, not forgetful; amid insults he exults in spirit and rejoices. For, as blessed [Christopher?] says, all who have wished to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecution, and whatever evil befalls them they overcome with the greatest constancy.

    And although patience is necessary for a monk in every place and time, nevertheless in the daily examination of faults it must be guarded with especially diligent attention: there correction of morals is carried out, and whatever has been committed against the standard of monastic purity is amended in each one by the senior. Therefore before we enter this place, all should think in the morning, and the mind should be strengthened against those things that can happen, so that if perhaps a rather harsh rebuke occurs, it may not overturn the mind from the state of tranquillity. For even if we have resolved to bring insult upon none of you, nor to do injury, nevertheless we do not deny that it can happen, so far as can be, that someone who has been corrected may think himself rebuked beyond his desert, since he weighs our paternal corrections by the words rather than by the intention.

    As God knows, we seek your salvation in all things, and nothing else: to cut away vices by the roots, according to the ordinances of our religion. We sincerely intend to injure no one. We cannot please everyone in all things, but we are especially compelled to displease those who, while sinning against the rule each day, promise themselves impunity for their crimes. Of these king Solomon said: “An evil teaching belongs to those who abandon the way of life, and he who hates rebukes shall die.” The pestilent man does not love him who corrects him, nor does he go to the wise. He who does evil deliberately flees the light and hates correction because he is foolish; but he who is sensible in spirit gives thanks to his corrector.

    Therefore in this matter I do not fear the hatred or murmuring of subjects, knowing that I have taken on the care of sick sheep, to whom, whether willing or unwilling, I am bound to apply the remedies of salvation. If it could be done, brothers, I would very much wish to disturb none of you in anything, even slightly, but to live among you with the greatest tranquillity and cheerfully to serve the Lord our God in peace of mind and body. But because not all of you truly seek the things that are God’s, I must rebuke and sometimes disturb the restless, lest impunity for smaller crimes provide boldness for graver ones. For I know what necessity I suffer through the danger of pastoral care; and therefore I neither can nor ought to be silent when you sin, lest I be judged somewhere as consenting. I gladly endure it if, for this reason, it happens that I am hated, because this cannot be done without the gravest danger to your souls.

    We ask you through our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us, that for love of God and for the remission of your sins you endure our paternal and necessary rebukes at all times patiently and with true humility. Let each one consider in himself that there is no day on which he does good and does not offend in some respect; and let him know that he will receive in this world the reward of his works: good things for good, and for evil things [unclear]. Therefore let him strive, as much as he can, in this life to make satisfaction for his offenses

    On the Daily Expiation of Sins

    [unclear], and humbly to expiate all their iniquities by the daily chastisement of the body. Know, my brothers, that there is no sin so small that the justice of almighty God lets it go unpunished. And therefore, since there is none of us who has not offended in many things, arm yourselves, I beg you, with patience and humility, so that whenever you are corrected for your sins, you may bear it with all gentleness. For in this time of free choice you can, with a small expiation, make sufficient satisfaction for many debts, for which after death in purgatory the soul will be tormented, even for small ones, for a long time and most grievously.

    Indeed voluntary satisfaction is of great value; but that which is done from necessity earns less toward grace. Altogether, brothers, it is fitting and necessary for the soul to be cleansed from fault, if it is to reign in heaven and rejoice with Christ. But the soul that has neglected the cleansing of its faults in the present life will be heavily punished in the life to come. Let none of you say, my dearest brothers, what many ignorant people have been accustomed to say: “It is enough for me if my soul has undergone the pains of purgatory.” Believe me, brothers, whoever says this word from the heart does not consider what purgatory is to be. For he does not know what he is asking for, who desires purgatory. Just as a man is foolish who, when he could pay his debt free, scorns to do so and willingly goes to prison, so he deserves to be judged the most foolish of all men who, when he can make satisfaction to God for his sins in this life, puts it off to the future.

    In this life repentance is fruitful, and voluntary satisfaction avails much by merit; but after death there will be no place for repentance, but each one will then receive according as he has done in his body, whether good or evil. Think on these things, brothers, while you live in health, lest, overtaken by the command of death, you at last grieve too late. Let the salvation of today not wait for the morrow, and let the man who can pay his debt with grace while at liberty not allow himself to be dragged to prison with torture. As much as each one can in his whole life, so much let him take care to make satisfaction for his sins, since the spirit returns securely to the Lord if, while still existing in the body, it is daily purified by the fire of divine love.

    Here you have a place in which daily expiation is made for public guilt: if you kept true and humble patience in your mind, you would without doubt obtain certain remission of all. But what you ought to do for secret and hidden sins, not only the rule admonishes you, but also daily sacramental confession instructs you in all things. At the altar we are accustomed every day, each one devoutly, to offer the Son of God’s majesty; and none of us approaches that holy washing and mystery unless he has first confessed according to custom, since the highest purity is required where, through the Mass, the salvation of the whole world is renewed.

    Who among us, dearest brothers, amid these things does not daily make progress in the love of God, unless he shamefully and wholly lays aside every desire for progress? For I dare to say that the monk who does not make progress in this holy congregation is utterly convicted of having forgotten his own salvation. Believe me, brothers: God will save no one against his will. If you neglect your own progress, nothing but yourselves will be blamed. For God is the intellectual light that enlightens every man coming into this world, as John, the eagle that soars aloft, says; but those who do not receive the light will necessarily remain in darkness. He who turns his mind away from the faith that is in the Son of God remains in darkness; and for him who does not do the works of light, nothing that he sees will profit him for salvation. Outside the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ there is no salvation, and he who thinks otherwise is not a Christian.

    Let not a foolish consideration of piety seduce you, O man, so that you believe anyone outside the faith of Christ, in any religion whatever, is to be saved, however innocently he may live or according to the law of nature; for just as outside Noah’s ark there was no life for men, so outside the Christian faith there is salvation for no one unto eternal life. For Christ, the only Son of God, is the one and only Savior of the world; whoever does not believe in him, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he will be condemned with the devil. But you, my brothers, who now believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, I beg you henceforth to live in such a way that, Christian in name and in deed, you may be able to come to his fellowship: who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, through all ages of ages.

    On True Repentance

    Homily xiv. Of monks. Homily xiii. Folio xxxii.

    Although our whole way of life, my dearest brothers, can rightly be called penance, since indeed we seem both dead to ourselves and already buried to the world, yet because we are surrounded by mortal flesh and sojourn in the midst of a sinful nation, it cannot happen that, by the impulse of our own frailty, we do not daily offend in some matter; and for the expiation of this, satisfaction must be made by doing penance not only generally but also specifically.

    For penance is necessary for all mortals, by which they may both bewail the evils they have committed, with the intention of amendment, and henceforth, so far as can be done, resolve to live without sin. It is proper to monks to do penance without interruption, and continually to pray both for their own sins and for those of others. For a monk does not have the office of teaching, as Saint Jerome says, but of lamenting: one who, if weak, should mourn himself, or, if perfect, should mourn the world, and in fear await the coming of the Lord. If you are a perfect monk, do penance for the sins of others; but if you are weak, you must much more do penance for your own.

    Therefore it is always time for a monk to do penance, since he is appointed as intercessor before God not only for his own sins but also for the offenses of others. But who among you is there, brothers, who is not burdened by his own fault? Which of you, I ask, does not need penance? I see you offending daily in many things, and I grieve; I perceive how you neglect penance for past things, and I tremble. Do you not recognize that you are mortal? And why do you not satisfy the name of monk, by doing penance, necessary in time? Remember, I ask you, the threatening Scripture which says: Do not delay to be converted to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you.

    For you will not escape death, which for you, old men, is at the door, and for the younger lies hidden in ambush; but when you least think it, the spirit, forced from the body, will depart. Therefore, if you recognize that you are sinners, if you desire to come to God's mercy, I pray you: take it up, and amend your conduct in all things according to the purity of the rule. It is enough that until now you have neglected true penance, and have continued for so long a time in a way of life too lukewarm. For God, who overlooks the sins of men because of penance, has not promised prolongation of life to those who put off repentance. Consider the long-suffering of God, who has so long mercifully borne with you as you sin daily, and do penance, so that you may find the forgiveness you desire.

    For the Lord says through the prophet: I do not want the death of the wicked man, but that he turn from his evil way and live. In the holy Gospel also he says: Do penance; for the kingdom of heaven will draw near. Penance is a great good for mortals: it cleanses filthy souls, and recalls obstinate minds from destruction. Here divine Augustine says: Penance heals illnesses, cures lepers, and raises the dead; it increases health and preserves grace. Penance restores a step to the lame, sight to the blind, abundance to the withered, and strength to the weak, as all things truly commend it: where contrition pierces the mind; where humble and pure confession brings forth hidden sin; where obedience makes satisfaction according to its powers; where the penitent so grieves over past things that he truly guards at all times against future ones. True penance is that which the love of God adorns with groans and tears, where the sinner grieves more over the offense against God than he fears the torment of hell.

    And who of us, most beloved brothers, would not grieve; who would not groan that, among the lawless monks, he has sinned against the Most High, from whom we have not only life, but also await the promise of eternal happiness? Woe to us, brothers, if we neglect to do true penance in this life, for the sake of which, that we might always do it, we were made monks. For our way of life ought to be occupied in Jesus Christ crucified alone, and from the consolations of the world, O monk, [unclear]: not pleasures, not delights with the world, nor laughter, nor any consolation of the flesh, but grief and bitterness with tears; and if you do not continually give yourself to these, you have lost the name of monk. It is not permitted you to rejoice with the age, you who are dead to the world; nor ought you to seek any consolations of the present life, you who promised the Lord to serve according to the monastic rule in solitude. Yours it is, monk,

    On the true repentance of monks.

    to despise always and everywhere the joys of this world for the love of God, and not to refuse to undergo any adversities or hardships for the honor of your Savior. For thus the canon admonishes you; thus the monastic institution commands; thus reason necessary for salvation persuades. You are ordered to be content with every baseness and extremity, and always fearful in all things. But I see very many of you perverting the rule of salvation, and living in the monastery otherwise than you ought. Monks now do not fear to seek delicacies in monasteries, though they came from the world to conversion poor and beggarly. For the things they could not have outside, if now they are lacking in the monastery, they rebel against humility as though they had suffered a most grave insult. Woe to the monks whom not the love of God but want has made cloistered; whose god is their belly, and who think of nothing less than poverty.

    It is not for you, O monks, henceforth to seek in the monastery the delicacies which the rule commands you utterly to deny. It befits us to despise all the pleasures of the present life, and to love absolutely nothing in this world except God. For your whole way of life ought always to be bound to divine services, you who promised to live according to the spirit and not according to the flesh. He who is a true monk does not live without repentance, but daily chastens his body by abstinence, whoever truly longs for the banquets of eternal happiness. For it cannot be that a monk should enjoy the delicacies of the present life and eternal ones; but if he longs for those, he must despise these. For the monk who professes the cenobitic canon is commanded to be a disciple of Christ the Savior; if he desires truly to please him, he must become his imitator. Thus he says to him in the holy Gospel: Whoever wishes to be my disciple, let him follow me. But what “let him follow me” means, Saint John the Apostle teaches in a certain epistle, saying: He who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked.

    And the Lord himself again says in the Gospel: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And he who loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. And he who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Your teacher has not spoken obscurely, O monk, nor has he wrapped his sentence in riddles, but he has put forth an evident speech, by which you can pretend no excuse. For Christ himself is the exemplar and rule of a good and perfect way of life for every Christian, and especially for the monk; the cloistered man who does not follow him with all his strength and with his whole heart boasts in vain of the profession of faith.

    For just as one is called a Christian from Christ, so a disciple is named from imitation of the master. Therefore imitate the master in your conduct, so that you may prove yourself a true disciple of Christ. For the Lord Jesus Christ, whose disciple you profess yourself to be, O monk, though he was rich, became poor for us; but you, though base and needy, seek abundance of all things in the school of poverty, and though the preceptor commands you to despise all things for love of him, you again desire to possess all things in the monastery.

    Your Lord and teacher was obedient to the Father for us even unto the death of the cross; but you, full of pride and impatience, either refuse to obey your superiors for love of him, or obey unwillingly and with indignation. He, for your salvation, not only endured with the greatest patience throughout his whole life the words and reproaches of wicked men, but also tolerated blows and livid stripes and horrid wounds for love of you. Nor did he refuse to undergo a most shameful death, in order to recall your soul from the error of death to the life of eternal light. From the day of his birth he lived poor and humble in the world, and was sated with no tribulations and oppressions, so that he might restore you, a most lost man, to the knowledge and love of God by teaching and benefits. For what would we be if the Son of God had not appeared as man, except most lost? And what are we, if we do not imitate the master according to our strength, except ungrateful? Woe to us ungrateful mortals, who scorn to follow humbly our Lord and Savior. Let us examine our way of life, brothers, and compare the disciples to the master whose name has been invoked over us, and we shall plainly understand how far we have withdrawn from the paths of our most kindly preceptor. But let us return to him with our whole heart, I pray, and let us do repentance, because we have withdrawn far from the way of salvation, serving the flesh rather than the spirit.

    Let no one deceive himself with the vanity of hope; let no one wait for the last hour of this life, when he can no longer sin, as repentance, because neither does the quantity of life have certainty

    Homily XIV.

    Fol. XXXIII.

    [unclear] — nor does the delay of repentance [bring] security.

    He who, while healthy, does not repent is a fool; and he who does not amend his vices when he can, by the just judgment of God loses the deferred power to do so. For repentance is fruitful when it has been voluntary, by the freedom of choice; but when the danger of death is already imminent, it seems rather to be necessary than undertaken by the penitent’s own choice.

    Let no one say in his heart, my brothers, let no one think that the labor of repentance is hard, and for that reason must be put off until the very last particle of this life. That thought is exceedingly dangerous, because the fixed term of life which divine providence has appointed for each person, just as it wished to be hidden from all, so it will not prolong for anyone who deliberately puts off repentance.

    If we wish to be safe and secure in conscience, let us do repentance while we are healthy, while we can sin, while as yet we are not being pressed by any necessity of imminent death. For it is a very doubtful matter to do repentance when necessity already compels, and the imminence of death makes you no longer able to sin: when, that is, you have not abandoned sins, but they, because you are powerless, have abandoned you.

    O how many, deceived by the hope of a longer life, descend to the abyss of eternal damnation, who when healthy held repentance in contempt. For the longer you put off repentance, the less disposed you will always find yourself to repent. For wickedness takes strength with time, and there is no sin so small that it does not grow when neglected.

    Therefore embrace repentance while you are healthy, and do not put it off from day to day, because you understand what you can do today, but you do not know what will happen tomorrow. Each new day brings its own small inconveniences, and he who today is not disposed to repentance will perhaps be less fit tomorrow.

    But let none of you say: What have I sinned, that repentance should seem necessary to me, since my whole life is nothing other than a certain hard and prolonged necessity of repentance? You have heard Scripture testifying that there is no man upon earth who does good and does not sin, since no one is clean before God. For even if you do not commit the great crimes of human impiety, such as homicide, theft, adultery, fornications, and things like these, nevertheless, because you have been placed in that calling in which you ought with all your strength to raise every effort to the state of perfection, sins which are small for mortals living in the world are certainly imputed to you as more serious.

    For all sins must be avoided by cloistered men, as far as they can be, not only those which hinder salvation, but also those which stain the perfection enjoined upon them. And which of you lives with such purity as monastic perfection requires? It is a great sin for a monk if he has laid aside his effort toward perfection, if he has lived negligently in the monastery, if he has transgressed even one commandment of the canon and the Gospel.

    But who among you, brothers, loves the Lord God with such sincerity, such charity, and such fervor of love, as a man is bound to love his maker and redeemer? Or whom will you give me from among all of you who does not sometimes exceed either in taking food or in drink beyond what accords with the integrity of monks? Which of you does not offend in word, or who is not sometimes troubled by evil thoughts? Whom among you has sloth not struck, and whom has gloomy laziness not disturbed? Who is there in this little congregation of yours whom pride does not touch, and whom impatience has not rather often made a murmurer?

    O, let each one of you consider the paths of his manner of life, and he will find that he fails in many things at any moment whatsoever. For what if a monk has committed no evil? What if he has kept himself clean from this wicked age? He will not be able to be perfect unless he has both turned away from evil and done the good which his perfection requires. For one without the other does not suffice, but perfection in man arises from both.

    Therefore, brothers, we must always keep watch with the greatest zeal, so that we satisfy the institution of the holy fathers, according to which by public profession we have solemnly bound ourselves to live, in order that we may direct our effort without interruption toward the perfection set before us. Let consideration of our own weakness not draw us back from the holy effort, because we are helped no less by the grace of the Creator than we run by our own desire. Just as every day in many things [unclear] more negligently in the good purpose, let us renew [unclear]. Let us join tears to holy prayers, and always [seek] the help of God with devout [unclear].

    On the true penitence of monks.

    Let us [unclear] with supplications. Let us preserve charity inviolable in all things, since it is charity that covers a multitude of sins. Each day the good soldier of Christ, who desires to be faithful to his Lord, should examine his conscience by scrutinizing it at least once, and should weigh carefully how much on that day he has advanced or fallen short in holy desire. Whenever he discovers that he has sinned in anything, let him at once do penance, and with tears ask mercy from the Lord. Let him not await the uncertainty of tomorrow: salvation is today; and one who can immediately find pardon should by no means interpose delay. Let him at once grieve in his heart that he has sinned against the Lord; let him also renew his holy purpose with fresh fervor, and let him consider that day wholly lost on which he has not, by making progress, become better. Prayer should always be on the monk’s lips; continual compunction should be in his heart; tears of devotion should flow continually from his eyes; and the exercises of inward love should never depart from his memory. Often there should be in the mind of the cloistered man the most bitter remembrance of the Lord’s Passion; and all the prayers he offers to the Father should be presented in the power of the blood and wounds of our Lord Jesus Christ. On his lips there should always be words bearing before them the mark of a contrite mind, and either prayer should be offered to God or meditation on his words should be turned over.

    Let the devout monk turn away from evil and do the good that he can, with cheerfulness and the discretion of the Spirit of God, since, as has been said, for doing penance it is not enough to change one’s habits for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also strives to adorn one’s conscience with good works. Therefore, my brothers, as you know, four things are required for true penitence. The first is true contrition for sins, which is a grief of heart voluntarily undertaken in detestation of those evils that one has committed. Of this Scripture says: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” And again: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation.” For the companion of penitence is the grief of contrition; the greater it is, the more fruitful penitence will be. For true contrition is commended by grief of mind and attested by the continual cleansing of tears. Great is the usefulness of tears, because there is no sin so grave that contrition accompanied by tears does not wipe it away. Hence the holy doctor Augustine says: “O humble tear, how powerful and virtuous you are, because yours is the kingdom, yours is the power. You do not fear the gaze of the judge; you impose silence on those who accuse of wrongs; alone you enter to the king, but you do not depart alone; you conquer the unconquerable and bind the almighty.” The same man also says: “The holier anyone is, and the fuller of holy desire, the more abundant is his weeping in prayer.” True compunction has grief; grief, however, is shown by tears, and with these penitence is adorned as with certain ornaments. True compunction makes the soul shudder at sin; and when it has begun from fear, increased by its own growth, little by little it rises up into love, whose virtue is great and whose power is truly admirable; to it every enormity of sins immediately yields. For whomever true compunction of heart has made a suppliant, the merciful Lord immediately hears him. O happy tears, O saving affliction and truly sweet bitterness, which the devil fears, through which the compunct soul rises up to the mercy of God. For, as holy Pope Gregory says, the more abundantly fault is lamented, the higher the knowledge of truth is reached; because, for seeing the inward light, a conscience long polluted is renewed when baptized with tears.

    The second thing that belongs to the truth of penitence is a firm purpose of amendment, since whoever has the word of confession in his mouth and does not have in his heart the purpose of amendment is either deceitful or empty. But whoever has it in his heart and not in his mouth is either proud or timid, and in no way fit for true penitence. For Scripture says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Although this saying, beloved of Christ, is principally to be understood of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, nevertheless it seems rightly applicable to true penitence. For without confession of the mouth, contrition of heart alone is not enough for penitence, especially from that time when the statute of the Church decreed confession necessary for salvation. Therefore the third thing necessary for the truth of penitence is confession of the mouth; without it neither contrition nor the purpose of future amendment is sufficient. What sort this saving confession ought to be, I know none of you is unaware.

    Homily XIV.

    Nevertheless I say that perhaps it will not be useless: confession ought to be personal, complete, free, humble, voluntary, and shamefaced. For the holy prelate Ambrose says that shamefaced confession avails very greatly with God for the remission of sins to human beings, and the punishment that we cannot avoid by defense we lighten by humble shame. Due confession of sins is a great thing, because it at once restores to spiritual health the soul of the one confessing, wounded by offenses; it also justifies the humbled mind and grants pardon for sins. For all our hope after the fall of sin consists in the humility of confession, because guilt is not forgiven unless it is revealed in confession, through the priest, to God, who knows all things.

    For in confession there is a place for mercy, as Solomon says in the Book of Proverbs: He who hides his crimes will not be directed; but he who has confessed them and left them behind will obtain mercy. Likewise it is written in the Psalm: I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin. The holy evangelist John also says in the first epistle: If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, so that he forgives us our sins, and he will cleanse us from all iniquity. And the holy prelate Augustine says: Confession is the salvation of souls, the scatterer of vices, the restorer of virtues, the conqueror of demons, and the heaper-up of all good things. It closes the mouth of hell and opens the gates of the heavenly paradise. Cassiodorus also, commending the virtue of true confession, speaks thus: O blessed confession, which removes eternal reproach, because whatever repentance has found as guilt it renders absolved for everlasting ages.

    Fourth: for true penitence satisfaction is necessary, by which, namely, cutting out all the causes of sins, we remove them, and for the things [which we have wrongly committed] we appease the Lord with holy works. Hence the divine pope Gregory says: We in no way make satisfaction if we cease from iniquity, unless we also pursue with contrary lamentations the pleasures that we loved. The most holy pope Leo also says in a sermon: By prayer the favor of God is sought; by fasting the desire of the flesh is extinguished; by almsgiving sins are redeemed; and at the same time through all these things the image of God is renewed in us.

    Confession, moreover, is the voluntary accusation of the offender, from shame and through the keys of the Church, making satisfaction for sins, with the obligation through penitence to chastise in himself, at the priest's command, those things that he has brought forth. Confession ought to be simple, humble, pure, faithful, frequent, bare and open; discreet, voluntary, personal, shamefaced, complete, secret, full of tears, made at the proper times, strong, and truly accusing oneself from the heart, because true penitence requires all these things; it so bewails past sins that thereafter it commits no more things to be mourned.

    On abstinence and the fasting of monks: Homily XV.

    Abstinence together with fasting, dearest brothers, is a great and necessary good for a monk, so that, namely, in mind he may not sin through desire of the flesh and evil thoughts, and in body he may abstain from foods and drinks that generate wantonness of spirit. For the desire of the mind is quickly inflamed into lust if the body is nourished too carefully. Considering the very great usefulness of this good, the most holy fathers of old, who handed down precepts of life to monks, all with one judgment established for us a fixed measure of fasts; under its moderation the body would take as much refreshment of foods as nature required, not as much as the intemperance of the will desired.

    Holy Scripture also commends fasting to us in many ways, since it so often mentions it with praise. For the Lord God says through the mouth of his prophet Joel: Turn to me with your whole heart, in fasting, mourning, and weeping. Likewise in the Book of Judith it is read thus: Know that the Lord will hear your prayers if, remaining steadfast, you continue in fasts and prayers in the sight of the Lord. Similarly we read in Tobit: Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good, more than storing up treasures of gold, because almsgiving frees from death, and it is what purges sins. Our Lord Jesus Christ also said to his disciples in the holy Gospel: Blessed are you who now hunger, because you shall be filled. But the best fast of monks is to abstain from all things that can pollute the soul, that is, not to [unclear] idle [unclear].

    On the abstinence and fasting of monks.

    ... to bear speech; to admit no vain, useless, or shameful thoughts; to commit nothing unbecoming a servant of God; and to omit nothing that belongs to the consummation of righteousness. For unless the mind has fasted from vices and sins, bodily abstinence will profit nothing for the salvation of the soul. Hence the blessed priest Jerome says: Your abstinence and fasting are pleasing insofar as they are offered with holy conduct, so that what in others are coverings for vices may in you become ornaments of virtues. For what does it profit for the body to be worn down by abstinence, if the soul grows dark with pride? Or what virtue is there in not drinking wine, and being drunk with anger, lust, hatred, and envy? Or what will it avail us for eternal salvation, brothers, that according to the Rule of our holy father Benedict we do not eat meat, if we do not subdue the vices of the flesh?

    For the thrice-holy pope Gregory says: In vain is the body worn down by abstinence, if the mind, divided by disordered impulses, is scattered among vices. Therefore Scripture says: Sanctify a fast. To sanctify a fast is, by adjoining other good works, to show abstinence of the flesh worthy of God. Indeed, if abstinence from foods alone made a man virtuous, there would have been no need to add “sanctify”; but because fasting alone is not sufficient for the sanctification of the soul, it is necessary that it be adorned with the ornament of all virtues. For those who abstain from foods and do evil imitate demons, for whom there is always fasting, and sin is never absent. A fast acceptable to God is to restrain the body through abstinence from desire for evils, and through the spirit of compunction to mortify continually the deeds of the flesh for love of Christ.

    Let the mind of the one fasting be fervent in the love of God; let the conscience always be clean from vices; and the fasts of humble servants will please the Most High. Let monks have daily fasts, as the canon of the holy preceptor Benedict has established; let their hearts be clean, as the Lord Jesus commanded in the holy Gospel; let their refection be moderate, fleeing satiety, since just as from excessive fullness the body is corrupted by diverse and various diseases, so in it the disordered movement of lust is stirred up. For moderate and measured food is both medicine for the body and a support of virtue for the soul. For Saint John, the golden-mouthed bishop, says: Nothing is so pleasant as food well digested and cooked, nothing so healthful, nothing so sharpens the keenness of the senses, nothing so drives away sickness, as moderate refection. For sufficiency, with measured nourishment, produces health and pleasure together. But abundance makes disease, brings troubles, and generates various illnesses. For what excessive hunger does, immoderate fullness of foods also customarily does. Hunger indeed in a few days takes a man away and frees him from this penal life; but excess of foods consumes the human body and makes it rot, and wastes it with long illness, and at last consumes it with a cruel death.

    Therefore, my most beloved brothers, in order that you may live sound in mind and healthy in body, hold to this rule of living which the holy fathers have prescribed for you by word and shown beforehand by living example: fleeing all luxury of foods and drinks, indulge the body only so much as is sufficient, when nature requires it, for good health. Let food [unclear] hunger, but not incite the body to lust; let drink extinguish thirst, but not overthrow the mind or the senses; let clothing ward off cold, but not cause the soul to grow soft in love of vanity. Always remember, brothers, that gluttony shamefully expelled our first parents from the kingdom of paradise and innocence. They did not devour bird, fish, calf, or pig, so that you should think the food itself at fault, but presumed against God’s command in the matter of a very common apple, so that you may know that not the food but the appetite is liable to the vice of sin.

    For it can often happen that a person takes richer foods without fault, provided he regulates his appetite, while another takes cheaper foods not without guilt of conscience, when by immoderation he exceeds the measure of temperance. Therefore let none of you think himself secure from the vice of gluttony for the reason that he eats neither rich nor delicate foods, since not the food but the appetite for food is held at fault. For it is very possible to incur the guilt of sin while eating beans and vegetables, and for another, taking the most delicate birds as food, not to sin. Hence one of the holy fathers says: A belly filled with any foods whatever brings forth nurseries of lust; nor can the mind prevail to govern the rudders of discernments when it is suffocated by the weight of foods. For not only the drunkenness of wine is accustomed to intoxicate the mind, but also excess of all foods [unclear]

    ... as food well digested and cooked, nothing so healthful, nothing so sharpens the keenness of the senses, nothing so drives away sickness, as moderate refection. For sufficiency, with measured nourishment, produces health and pleasure together. But abundance makes disease, brings troubles, and generates various illnesses. For what excessive hunger does, immoderate fullness of foods also customarily does. Hunger indeed in a few days takes a man away and frees him from this penal life; but excess of foods and drinks, fleeing luxury, indulge the body only so much as is sufficient, when nature requires it, for good health. Let food [unclear], but not incite the body to lust; let drink extinguish thirst, but not overthrow the mind or the senses; let clothing ward off cold, but not cause the soul to grow soft in love of vanity. Always remember, brothers, that gluttony [unclear] our first parents from...

    Homily XV.

    and makes it unsteady, and altogether strips it of every contemplation of integrity and purity. Therefore great discretion is needed, so that only such food as is necessary for sustaining life is supplied to the body, and no excess of indulgence occurs. Hence the holy pope Gregory says: “It is a great labor of discretion to give something to the body that demands food, and to deny it something; by not giving, to restrain gluttony, and by giving, to nourish nature.” For through abstinence vices are to be extinguished, not the flesh; and through food the body is to be nourished, not sins. Thus, therefore, it is necessary that a monk maintain the art of continence in his diet, so that he kills not the flesh but the vices.

    For often, while we pursue the enemy in the flesh, we cruelly slaughter, through immoderate abstinence, the spirit of devotion which we love. More often, too, while out of too much compassion we spare the flesh as if it were a fellow-citizen, we nourish an enemy for battle against ourselves. But when the vice of gluttony rules, men lose everything that they have done bravely, because when the belly is not restrained all virtues are at once overwhelmed. For a man does not rise up to the conflict of the spiritual contest if the enemy set within ourselves, namely the appetite of gluttony, is not first subdued by us with God’s help; for unless we overcome what is nearer to us, we hasten in vain to fight against what is set farther away. Indeed, war is waged in vain in the field against foreign enemies if within the city walls there is a citizen lying in ambush. We never overcome the assaults of demons unless we first overcome gluttony in ourselves.

    Let no one, brothers, deceive himself by empty persuasion, so as to believe that there is no sin among beans and vegetables if the mind slackens, with excessive pleasure, the appetite for receiving them. For wherever appetite, made wanton in consumption, extends beyond the norm of nature, [unclear]. See, whether in the monastery or outside it, we never eat meat; fish here in this rural district are seen very rarely; no one among us has ever seen more sumptuous foods; we neither can nor indeed ought to have delicate dishes. Our foods are barley, oats, beans, peas, and vegetables, milk also and cheese and eggs. From these we receive the daily supports of our life; each day hunger stirs appetite, lest disgust arise. Outside the season of the Lenten fast, fish are so rare for us that scarcely once in a month are they brought from our river, and then very small. In the whole Bursfelde reform there is no monastery less provided for in the necessity of fish.

    But can we therefore not fall into the vice of gluttony because we cannot obtain more sumptuous foods? Indeed, since the fault is not in the food, as has already been said, but in the appetite, one who eats peas or beans can sin no less in eating than he who is accustomed to consume the most sumptuous and choice foods. Poverty does not make us altogether secure from gluttony, though it removes occasions for sinning in more delicate things. We do indeed have a simple and rustic diet, by which nature may be sustained somehow; this, my brothers, I ask that we take care of: that in that which produces nausea in the delicate, our conscience may not be polluted by excess. Let us take with patience and thanksgiving from what the Lord has given as much as necessity itself requires; and let us not think that the snares of the devil cannot harm us, for he overthrew the first human beings in paradise not with more sumptuous food, but with a modest and cheap apple. For the fault is not in the food but in the appetite, when either we desire things forbidden to us, or, gaping after things granted [unclear], we use them otherwise than we ought.

    Abstinence befits a woman more than a monk [unclear], who, since he has been specially called to Christ’s warfare, ought not, according to his profession, to devote himself to any delicacies. Our poverty imposes upon us a certain necessity of abstinence, because we can restrain ourselves to temperance the more easily, the less we can find anything into which we may flow away in delights. Therefore, I ask, let us turn the burdens of want into weapons of salvation, so that the less we are refreshed with more sumptuous foods, the more purely we may fast in holiness of mind. For temperance is more easily preserved in poverty, though in riches it is certainly more quickly endangered.

    What the food of monks ought to be, blessed Jerome shows, saying in a certain letter to Paulinus: “Let your food be cheap and in the evening: vegetables, that is, and legumes; and sometimes regard the eating of a few little fish as the highest delicacies.” Whoever desires Christ and feeds on that heavenly bread does not greatly seek what dung he may make from costly foods. The lover of Christ loves abstinence; he cherishes fasting as one remedy for soul and body alike; he takes the greatest care that his heart not be weighed down by excess, nor does he take more food than nature, content with little, demands. But the monk who rejects fasting, who [unclear] the nurse of virtues, abstinence

    On the abstinence and fasting of monks.

    [Who] hates abstinence, who greedily gulps down foods, who drinks wine or strong drink and whatever can intoxicate, to satiety, is unworthy of the very name of monk and cannot be a disciple of Christ. Woe to our times, in which already very many clerics and monks have shamefully cast aside the virtue of abstinence; and those who ought to have shown the people the way of salvation no less by example than by word, given over to feasting and continual drinking and pleasures, immersed against all clerical decency, hasten to go before them into the perdition of eternal death.

    Scripture says: “The beginning of man’s life is bread and water.” But now our monks and cloisterers buy for themselves, at great expense, whatever is sold most dearly, whatever is found most sumptuous; they bury it by gulping it into their bellies, and through intemperance corrupt soul and body alike. Amid banquets they debate fasting, and when they have become drunk they praise temperance. There each man boasts himself conqueror of the vices, when he has already been conquered by gluttony and drunkenness.

    “Take heed,” says our Lord Jesus Christ in the holy Gospel according to Luke, “lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation.” It is not fitting for a man dedicated to God to eat or drink to satiety, nor is it lawful for a monk to eat more than nature requires. Let eating allay hunger; let it not bring on repletion. Far away be the belchings which satiety is accustomed to generate in feasters; let vomiting and indigestion never be heard among monks. By the moderation of [sound discretion?] all cloisterers must be guided, so that each nourishes the body with foods and drinks in such a way that, serving the spirit, it may be able to live, and not so that, grown fat, it begins to run riot against the command of the mind.

    Let satiety always be far away, for nothing so inflames the body and excites the generative members as undigested food and a belly hot with wine or beer. Hence blessed Jerome, admonishing Eustochium toward temperance, the preserver of all virtues, says in a certain letter: “Let the bride of Christ flee wine as poison, for wine and youth itself are weapons against youth, which is more prone to gluttony. Avarice does not so shake youth, nor pride puff it up, nor ambition delight it, as those vices of fleshly pleasure which seem to be born with us. We shall easily lack the other vices if in fear of the Lord we keep watch even moderately. But this enemy is within, always shut up inside; wherever we go, we carry this adversary with us. Wine and youth: a double fire of pleasure. Why do we add oil to the flame, or why do we supply fiery fuel to a little body already burning?”

    Gluttony has laid low many who walked chastely in the middle of the road; and those whom the devil could not overcome by his own promptings, excessive drinking of wine cast into the abyss of luxury. Therefore Benedict, the most holy founder of our life, when enumerating the instruments of good works, set among the chief ones: to chastise the body, to embrace hardships, to love fasting. For no one truly follows Christ who, delicately nourishing his flesh, lives in a monastery without daily abstinence.

    Moderate abstinence, pleasing to God, works many good things in us if it is continued with religious intention to the end of life. For first of all it increases merit and nourishes in us every kind of virtue. What was the reason why almighty God forbade our first parents the eating of the apple under threat of death, unless to show the occasion of their merits through the good of obedience? For, as Scripture bears witness, God created two intellects from the beginning, namely the angelic and the human, to which he might communicate himself through grace for the enjoyment of eternal happiness. Yet although he created each from the gift of his grace, he most rightly ordained that they should become forever happy also from their own proper merit, so that in them both mercy and conversion might obtain the merit necessary for salvation.

    The angelic intellect was at once divided in two: while some fell by pride of their own will, others, humble and subject, adhered through love to their own beginning. Those, indeed, apostatizing from their beginning, departed unhappy; but these, for the merit of their adherence, were endowed with everlasting blessedness. The human intellect, however, was sent down into flesh; and soon, at the devil’s persuasion, it transgressed the commandment of God and feasted on the food forbidden to it. Hence follows the perdition of the whole human race, which no one other than the Son of God, made man from the Virgin,

    Homily XV.

    [unclear] no one could. For what condemned our first parents except the transgression of the commandment? For God’s concern was not with food, but with obedience. For if man had abstained as almighty God had commanded him, certainly through this obedience, in his innocence, he would have merited the enjoyment of eternal happiness. For it is established by the tradition of the Scriptures that man cannot be saved without the merit of free will; for although the grace of God works all things in all, nevertheless it will save no one without the cooperation of his own will, except only infants baptized in the name of the Trinity, and those who cannot have the free use of reason.

    For just as free will accomplishes nothing toward salvation without the grace of the Savior, so the grace of God will not save an adult without the merit of a good will. But the first man, placed in paradise and having transgressed God’s commandment through intemperance, did not have the merit of obedience in a good will; therefore, wretched and unhappy, he was cast out. But the almighty mercy of God resolved from eternity to restore the one who had fallen through weakness, whom he knew to have been deceived by the envious serpent’s suggestion rather than by his own malice. He assigned this guilt to the passion and death of his only-begotten Son, to be born in time of a virgin, so that he who by his own rashness [unclear] might through the obedience of the mediator be restored to salvation.

    For it was impossible that the human race, lost through disobedience, should come to the Creator’s mercy except through the obedience of such a mediator, who is God and man, in whom there is both the strength of power and the innocence of nature. For we were blind through ignorance and mute through silence. The mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus, came, appointed to enlighten every man coming into this world; he handed on the knowledge of God to mortals, and, by dying for the lost, set the greatest cause for love of the Redeemer. He instructed the understanding through faith, by which we know God; he stirred the affection through his passion, so that we might deservedly love him above all things. Therefore, if we love our Lord and Redeemer with complete sincerity, it is plainly fitting that we chastise our body for love of him.

    For our abstinence will conduce to merit for us in two ways: namely, when by fasting through obedience we [unclear] the statutes of the fathers, and when, by abstaining through charity toward God, we show ourselves pleasing to our Redeemer, who for our sake endured death. Abstinence increases merit, commends obedience, bestows wisdom and learning, purges the affection, enlightens the understanding, grants victory against demons, perfects religion, obtains pardon for sins, subdues illicit motions of the flesh, brings effectiveness to prayers, and displays to one’s neighbor an example of virtue. Abstinence purifies the mind, adorns the soul with virtues, and heals the weak little body. He who loves abstinence is wise; and he who, by loving fasting, [unclear], is strong. [unclear] the dwelling-place of wisdom; but he who pursues banquets will die in poverty of soul. It is difficult for a man who passes his life in delights to become wise. Nature is content with few things, and the health of life is preserved in modest things. Long-continuing voracity has harmed many, and more have perished by drunken excess than by the sword. For habit seems to alter nature; and the longer it has grown strong, the more forcefully it now [unclear] in any matter.

    Among the Helvetians there is a man named Nicholas, whose abstinence has turned the people of all Germany to admiration; and today, as you have heard, he is named in everyone’s mouth with the title of holiness. He was once a farmer in a certain Helvetian village, and in the rustic manner he was accustomed, among fourteen [unclear], to administer justice to disputing villagers. It happened at a certain time that he could not revoke a judgment of his associates which he considered unjust; and, fearing danger to the salvation of his soul, he left his house, wife, children, and all the business and goods of the world, and withdrew alone into a nearby wood for the love of God, in which he leads a solitary life. And behold, today is the twentieth year since he entered the solitude, and he has taken no human food. I speak of things most well known to all, nor do I think there is any man living in Germany who has not heard the fame of this miracle. But lest perhaps anyone in the future should believe that we have been deceived by pretence, we cite Helvetia, together with the bishop of the church of Constance, as our witness; they have observed his conduct and life most carefully.

    On the abstinence and fasting of monks.

    He is a man most acute in intellect; although utterly ignorant of letters, in [unclear] another hermit, once Antonius, he understands the meaning of Scripture very well. And we saw that he disputed most eloquently with a certain master about the sacrament of the altar; this he will not be able sufficiently to admire who has scarcely tasted heavenly things through the practice of contemplation. I have set forth this about food, brothers, so that you may understand that there is nothing so difficult that custom, continued over a long time, does not make it light. That holy man, as he himself confesses, did not suddenly arrive at the height of this abstinence, but with the passage of time and by degrees, little by little, withdrawing from himself somewhat of his food, until he was able to abstain so greatly throughout. For he abstained, as we have said, from every corruptible food for almost [unclear] years.
