By the example of this man, my brothers, let each one learn to withdraw daily something else from his food and drink for the love of God, and so to minister to his body not as much as he can, but as much as is enough for the sustenance of nature. For, as Boethius bears witness, nature is content with very few and very small things; if it be made to flourish for a time with superfluous foods, what you have poured in becomes either [unclear] or harmful. Many illnesses are produced by many dishes, and gluttony of the belly dulls the mind and torments life. For the wise man says: Sweet is the sleep of the worker, whether he eats little or much; but the fullness of the rich man does not allow him to sleep. The belly must be filled without satiety, and one must rise from table without disgust, so that, namely, we may eat not as much as appetite demands, but as much as nature requires. But variety of foods must especially be avoided by monks; for he who lives on varied dishes, testing what nature demands to be put into the stomach, feasts not without the vice of gluttony. The strength of our body is to be restored with moderate and simple food, not shamefully oppressed with varied or many foods, because the body was not created for food, but food for the body. That variety of foods brings diseases upon the body we prove from the temperance of the ancients, whom the simplicity of all their foods preserved for a very long time in this life. But our most holy lawgiver, the hierophant Benedict, the most modest of all the chief monks, prescribed for us a rule adorned with the highest discretion, in which

    Homily XV.

    which so weaken the body that they do not raise the mind into pride, lest the exercise of humility become material for vices. Fasting detests idleness; it does not love verbosity; it loves seclusion; it applies itself to prayers and tears. Fasting, as Saint Ambrose bears witness, is the death of fault, the destruction of offenses, the remedy of salvation, the root of grace, the foundation of chastity. By this step Moses, the righteous man, came to God; by this gift Elijah ascended into heaven in a chariot before he died. Those who walk in the spirit love fasting, and those who profess chastity necessarily flee an abundance of delights. For hunger is the friend of virginity, the enemy of wantonness. Fullness, however, betrays chastity and nourishes wantonness. For fasting extinguishes the burning arrows of the devil; persistence in prayer restrains them; and continuance in vigils in the love of Christ repels all the snares of demons. Hence Saint Leo the Pope says in a certain sermon: What can be more effective than fasting? By its observance we draw near to God, and, resisting the devil, overcome seductive vices. For fasting has always been food for virtue, and abstinence the nourishment of holy chastity. From abstinence, indeed, chaste thoughts proceed; it begets reasonable desires and modest counsels as well; and through voluntary afflictions the flesh dies to concupiscences, while the spirit is renewed in virtues.

    Therefore, my brothers, let us fast a fasting of virtue out of love for him who did not refuse to undergo death for us, and let us abstain not only from unlawful things but also, as far as possible, from permitted things, so that we who in many matters offend against the commandments of salvation may, in recompense of satisfaction, henceforth restrain ourselves from every pleasure. Let us fast from every sin; let us take no food of malice; let us devour no banquets of pleasure; let us not become drunk with the wine of luxury. Let us fast from all depravities; let us abstain from evil works; let us not speak useless, empty, idle, scurrilous, and pernicious words; and let us always beware of harmful and perverse thoughts that separate us from God. Let us always keep watch most zealously in prayers to God, knowing that he whom we invoke with our prayers is everywhere most present to us. Let his praise always be in our mouth; and when we cannot praise his magnificence with speech, let us adore him in the heart with the desires of a most chaste love. For then our fasts are pleasing to him, when they have been adorned with holy works and continual prayers. For the prayer of the righteous man, as sacred Scripture bears witness, penetrates the heavens; it becomes the more effective, the more it is found adorned with charity and fasting. Let us join to it, as it were, two wings, fasting and charity, and it will obtain for us from the Lord whatever we have asked that is conducive to salvation.

    On the Lenten fast of monks: Homily XVI.

    Since, by the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearly beloved brothers, we have begun the Lenten fast, reason requires that we say something briefly about its observance. For although you have many writings of the holy fathers concerning this most sacred exercise of fasts, nevertheless, because I know by experience that my sermons among you are not wholly without fruit, I gladly impart to your edification what the Lord has bestowed. For, as blessed Jerome bears witness, the action of the living voice has a certain hidden inner operation, which in Greek speech he more elegantly called energia; and the speech of the teacher, delivered by his mouth, is stronger for persuading.

    But I, set apart in your midst by the name of shepherd alone, confess that I am young, unlearned, and lacking the experience, together with discretion, necessary for the governance of souls. Hence it comes about that I speak with a certain shame and embarrassment, a young man among elders, an ignorant man among the learned, a disciple among masters. Therefore I beg that none of you despise the simplicity of my speech; let no one take it ill that I speak, because even if I am not fit for speaking, nevertheless by reason of the duty of the pastoral care entrusted to me I confess before God that I am bound to admonish you. Charity gives me lively boldness for speaking, and the more ready you show yourselves to hear, the more you provoke me to speak. Nor will the labor be heavy to me, however great it may seem, by which the salvation of your souls is perfected. Help me with your prayers, that the Lord Jesus may speak in my mouth and grant strength to my little talent to bring forth into the midst whatever can produce in you an increase of holy fervor. For I am unable to profit your charity by my sermons as much as I desire, because I am compelled to be occupied too much with the care of secular business.

    On the Lenten fast of monks.

    Only by day, and in that part of the night which after the night lauds I am accustomed to spend sleepless, have I devoted myself to exhorting you, setting down on slips what occurred to me as needing to be said. And so I wished to introduce today’s discourse from the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, who speaks thus about Lenten observance: Although at every time the life of a monk ought to have the observance of Lent, nevertheless, because this virtue belongs to few, we therefore advise that in these days of Lent they guard their life in all purity, and that all alike wash away in these holy days the stains and negligences of other times. This is then done worthily if we refrain from all vices and give our effort to prayer of the heart.

    If this virtue belongs to few, namely that at every time they lead a life of Lenten observance, it is now plainly evident that few monks in religion live according to the purity of the Gospel, since all who profess the warfare of Christ are bound to direct their effort toward the summit of perfection. For a monk, according to the interpretation of his name, is solitary; and in the monastery he is then rightly believed to live according to the Gospel and the rule which he has professed, when, for love of God, he has despised the affairs and honors of the world, and conducts himself before God and men in all purity of heart: strenuous in work, clean in thought, sparing and peaceable in speech.

    This is the life of a monk, having Lenten observance at every time: to chastise the body for love of God through abstinence, and to nourish the mind through inner compunction. He lives rightly who lives justly, who loves God above all things, who with the greatest zeal and the greatest diligence observes his commandments in words and deeds. For he is the true monk of Christ who imitates Christ with all his strength.

    But if you wish to imitate Christ, O monk, observe most diligently what I am about to say. Flee the world and all consolations of the flesh, so that you may deserve truly to be solitary. Never permit vain, useless, foul, and harmful thoughts to dwell in your heart; rather, always think something good, and let the memory of the Lord’s passion never depart from your soul, so that each day with thanksgiving you may contemplate the Lord hanging on the cross. Consider God present to you everywhere: he sees, knows, and understands whatever you have either thought or done, since nothing is hidden from him.

    Keep your heart clean from every stain of sin, and always have a pure conscience fervent in the true love of Christ. Let no idle time fly away from you, but let thought always find you engaged in good works. Do not grow sluggish with much sleep, and make yourself far removed from every sloth of tepidity. Embrace moderation in food and drink, and live as sparingly as is permitted, so that the body, moderately sustained, may always serve the spirit in humility and by no means rise up against the command of reason.

    As soon as you have sensed some torpor arising in you, flee to the memory of the most bitter passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and bring back into your mind whatever can drive away sloth most swiftly. Break up, I beg you, all the hours, since torpor of mind, when ignored, suddenly increases, and sloth which is not at once extinguished by a new fervor of mind is immediately strengthened into grave destruction of the soul. For of all evils in a monk the worst is if, through torpor and sloth, he has provided a place in his heart for the seed-bed of vices.

    And you, O monks, must keep watch against this beast not only every day, but every hour and moment, since once admitted into the heart it never enters alone; rather, the whole mass and wellspring of all vices accompanies it. There is no more destructive plague for a monk than the torpor of sloth, through which every fervor of devotion is extinguished; and, faithful service having been abandoned, the mind, shaken by idleness and leisure, is hurled down into the pit of despair. Whoever permits the delay of sloth quickly falls away from the purpose of holiness.

    Against this Solomon admonishes you in the Book of Proverbs, saying: Go to the ant, O worker, and consider its ways, and learn wisdom. Though it has no guide, nor teacher, nor ruler, it prepares its food in summer and gathers at harvest what it may eat. And again he says: Desires kill the lazy man, because his hands were unwilling to labor at anything. Nothing is worse for those professing the purpose of holiness than leisure, because it not only stores up no good, but also consumes and scatters everything previously stored up. For the fervor of holy devotion rejoices and makes progress by advancement; but by cessation it grows sluggish and little by little, not to say suddenly, vanishes,

    Homily XVI. For the root of despair is sloth, and the mother and nurse of all vices. For just as a garment both produces and nourishes the moth, so the most destructive plague of acedia both begets and fosters despair. Indeed this beast is accustomed to vex monks more than others, and especially those who lead a withdrawn life in solitude. Therefore, monks, you must take the greatest care against this enemy of the salvation of souls; you must fight not by fleeing, but by resisting bravely; and you must diligently consider that no one has attained the honor of holiness by torpor and sloth, nor has anyone deserved the kingdom of eternal happiness except by great and continual labor.

    Therefore the mind must always be renewed by daily and fresh increases of virtues, and this perilous path of life is to be measured not by what has been traversed, but rather by what remains. Let no one promise himself security in this life, which is wholly called temptation, full of as many dangers as there are affections in the soul; but let each one beware that he who could become better from worse does not become worse from better. And especially on these holy days let us all take care, as far as we can, to become better, adding for ourselves, according to the counsel of our divine teacher, something to the customary burden of our service: namely special prayers, abstinence from food and drink, so that each one, beyond the measure imposed on him, may of his own will offer something to God with the joy of the Holy Spirit; that is, let him subtract from his body something from food, from drink, from sleep, from talkativeness, from security, and with the joy of spiritual desire await the holy Pasch.

    For he is proved to be a monk of little religion at other times who on these holy days is not found more religious and, in the love of God, more fervent and more devout. Hence the divine Pope Gregory says in a certain homily: Lent must be observed with the greatest observance, so that fasting in it, on account of the Lord’s days which have been subtracted from abstinence, unless illness has hindered someone, is by no means relaxed, because these days themselves are the tithes of the year which we are commanded to offer to the Lord. Saint Ambrose also says: He keeps Lent who by fasting and watching ascends to Easter. For just as at the remaining time of the year to fast is a reward, so in Lent not to fast is a sin. For those fasts are voluntary, but these are necessary; those come from choice, but these from law. To those we are invited; to these we are compelled. And therefore he who passes over the appointed number by eating on one day is not accused as the violator of one day, but is charged as a transgressor of the whole of Lent.

    On these sacred days all desires of the flesh must be restrained; the body must be chastised by abstinence, so that if perhaps at other times we have lived with too little moderation, we may in some way make recompense by this Lenten fast. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us follow the admonitions of our most holy father Benedict, and with all the diligence we can let us exercise ourselves in holy works, subtracting something each day from our body, for the love of God, from food and drink, so that we may prove ourselves true servants of God.

    Next, however, our holy founder adds, saying: Nevertheless, this very thing which each one offers, let him suggest to his abbot, and let it be done with his prayer and will, because what is done without the permission of the spiritual father will be attributed to presumption and vainglory, not to reward. Therefore everything is to be done with the will of the abbot. The words of our holy lawgiver, brothers, are clear, lest anyone be able to have recourse to the veil of ignorance. For if everything is to be done with the will of the abbot, then without his permission absolutely nothing is to be done. Indeed, the more a good work is adorned by many virtues, the greater its merit before God must without doubt be. Therefore when a monk, by the license and blessing of his abbot, subtracts something of food or drink from his body for the love of God, he is to receive from the Lord not only the promised reward of eternal fullness for that abstinence itself, but also the kingdom for humility, and for the merit of holy obedience he will attain without end the fellowship of all the saints in heaven.

    For the monk who, having once professed, has subjected his head to monastic institutions has resigned his own will to Christ in the hands of the abbot; and if thereafter he should again usurp it by his own judgment, he has already shamefully denied Christ. For what else is a monk who usurps the ownership of his will, if not an unjust professor of a thing that belongs to another? Therefore let the monk be humbly subject to his abbot for the love of Christ always in all things; let him presume nothing at all.

    On the Lenten fast of monks.

    ...to act against his command: let him omit or neglect nothing that has been enjoined upon him by him. Let him take the utmost care not to distress or disturb his pastor by restless conduct; nor let him murmur against him, nor disparage him, nor say any evil [unclear] against him. Rather let him revere him with the sincere affection of charity, as Christ's vicar, and not grieve his mind by troublesome or disorderly words or deeds. Let him, moreover, assist his labors as much as he can, and intercede for him before God with continual prayers. Monks sin greatly against God who are not afraid to grieve their abbot by troublesome detractions and wicked manners. Therefore whoever as a monk desires to be good, whoever truly wishes to be devoted in the Lord, should always and everywhere venerate his abbot with pure love as the vicar of Jesus Christ in the monastery; he should humbly obey his commands in all things, and in no way depart from his direction.

    But the abbot, for his part, should strive to show himself in all things a worthy pastor to his monks, one who feeds the sheep of Christ entrusted to him both by word and by example, in all the gentleness of charity. Let him not disturb the brothers without just and reasonable necessity; let him not be a despiser of the holy community; let him recognize himself as the steward of the things of the monastery, not their lord. Let him not be a mocker of his subjects, not turbulent, not troublesome, not a tyrant, but their sincere lover, pleasant in speech, gentle and upright in manners, holy in conduct, clean in conscience, always devoted in mind to God. Let him at all times bear solicitous care for the souls entrusted to him, and neglect none of those things that seem able to conduce to their salvation. Let him not on this account raise himself on high because he has been placed as ruler of others, but let him remember that he has so much the more to fear, insofar as he is most certainly bound to render account for all in the dread judgment of God. Let him correct the proud, rebellious, and contumacious as a lord; the humble, obedient, and governable, let him kindly cherish as a most gentle father, and wisely distribute to each one his right without acceptance of persons. Let him always consider himself the mother and nurse of the monks, and therefore those whom he can bring back to better things by gentleness he ought not to exasperate with troublesome words and harsh invectives. Let him always bear solicitous care for the sick, and provide for all in such a way that they have no just cause for murmuring. Let him learn from his own weaknesses how he ought to have compassion on his subjects. For he cannot be a good pastor of souls who disdains from the heart to suffer with the necessities of his sick subjects. But he can become a good abbot among monks who knows how to adapt himself to the persons of the sick in such a way that, as often as a brother asks something of him, taking upon himself the form of the person asking, he says in his heart: What would I wish to be done for me in this matter, according to the right judgment of reason, if I were in the position of the one asking? But if the abbot imagines himself in mind to be a subject, he will let no one go away from him distressed.

    We have now said, brothers, what sort of men it is fitting for you to be toward us for the love of God, so that, existing as good monks, you may please the Lord Jesus in truth. You have heard nevertheless what sort of pastor I ought to show myself to you; whether I do this or not, you yourselves will judge better than I. For we shall fast in vain and shall see no fruit of Lenten observance, unless we all remain in true brotherly charity, with purity of heart in the love of God. For what does it profit toward the rest of salvation to afflict the body through abstinence and fasting, and not to be concordant before God in the true charity of ecclesiastical union? Or what good will it do to abstain from richer foods, and to defile the conscience with evil works or thoughts? For in order that the fasts we have begun may be pleasing to God, it is necessary that they be not only alien and remote from vices and sins, but also adorned with the fullness of all virtues. For holy Ambrose says: What does it profit to fast in the belly and to be wanton in hunting; to abstain from foods, to wander in sins? Do you think, brothers, that he fasts who at first light does not keep watch at church, does not seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but, rising in the morning, gathers his servants, sets out the nets, brings out the dogs, ranges through groves and woods; who, I say, drags servants along with him, perhaps hastening rather to church? For his own pleasures he heaps up the sins of others, not knowing that he will be guilty both of his own fault and of the ruin of his servants. And Saint Leo the pope says: The sum of our fasting does not consist in abstinence from food alone...

    Homily XVI.

    For food is not fruitfully withheld from the body unless the mind is recalled from all iniquity. The blessed Jerome also says: What does it profit for the body to be made thin by abstinence, if the spirit swells with pride? What virtue is there in not drinking wine, and in being drunk with anger, hatred, and the other poisonous cups of the soul?

    Therefore let none of you promise himself sanctity from abstinence from foods alone, since whatever is required for true penitence is judged necessary also for fasting. For fasts profit unto salvation for those who are contrite for their sins in a true purpose of amendment, who fervently devote themselves to good and holy works. Hence those who fast from food and drink must also abstain from all vices, so that the mind, adorned with the beauty of virtues, may sweetly burn in the love of Christ, and may in no way grow lukewarm from the progress of habitual conduct. For the virtue of abstinence is nothing if it has not been adorned with the works of charity. Therefore hear my counsel, monk, if you wish to make your fast fruitful before God. First cleanse your conscience from every stain of sin, so that no desire of evil may remain within; so that the mind may become fervent in the exercise of divine love, and also be praiseworthily adorned with all virtues. Through the remedy of contrition and confession wash away past sins, and by persisting in prayers with tears, strengthen your mind thereafter against all temptations with God’s help. Toward [unclear], as much as you can, be fervent in the exercise of love; toward yourself, in a pure conscience, be rightly tranquil; toward your brother, be ordered in true charity. In humility always be foremost; firm in constancy and obedience. Diligently exercise chastity by pious action, and your mind in the Passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, so that thereafter there be no day on which you have not at least once gone over his life and death in meditation with thanksgiving and tears. For rude and too unpracticed, not to say ungrateful, is the Christian who is so immersed either in temporal affairs or occupied with the pleasures of the flesh that he does not daily remember, at least once, with thanksgiving, the most bitter Passion of his Redeemer.

    Fol. XXXIX.

    But the monk who forgets the benefits of our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not once each day call to mind his Passion with thanksgiving, who does not every day meditate on the evangelical law of the Lord, is deservedly judged the most ungrateful of all men. Nothing is more powerful than that prayer which is offered to God the Father in union with and in the power of the Lord’s Passion. Too justly is that spirit to be condemned which, redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ, is led away by the pleasures of its flesh, so that it does not remember such great benefits of God toward it. For there was no cause for the Son of God to become man except that he wished to justify us sinners: born in the world for us, suffered in the world for our sins. It is fitting, therefore, my brothers, that with all devotion we celebrate this Lenten fast, dedicated to his most sacred Passion, who first deigned to do such great things for our salvation, who, in order to rescue us from the destruction of death, did not hesitate to give himself for us unto death. Let us do, for the love of Christ, whatever good we can; let us endure, in consideration of his Passion and death, every adversity that may befall us in this world, since the Lord Jesus, who out of charity willed to suffer for us, has truly shown himself most worthy that we should love him with all our heart. For if, brother, you acknowledge yourself a sinner, Christ has saved you by his death. Contemplate him hanging on the cross as is fitting, and you will be healed from every bite of sin. For nothing is found in this world more effective for curing the wounds of conscience, nothing more powerful for purging the sight of the fearful mind, than continual meditation on the wounds of Christ. For the most precious blood of the Lord, poured out, has been made a sufficient medicine for sin. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: Brothers, that we, wounded by sin, may be healed, let us look upon Christ crucified. For just as those who looked upon the bronze serpent in the desert did not perish from the bites of serpents, so those who

    On the Lenten fast of monks.

    Those who look upon the death of Jesus Christ with [faith?] and devotion are healed from the bites of sins. But if you trust that you have been justified from sin, then all the more and more fervently must you look upon Christ hanging on the cross; without the merit of his passion no one lives justly on earth. For outside faith in Christ there is no righteousness, and however religiously a man may live, if he does not believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, he will in no way attain eternal salvation; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he will necessarily perish forever. The death of Christ opened the gate of salvation, through which no one else can enter except one who faithfully believes in Christ. For this reason Christ humbly submitted himself to the condemnation of death, so that he might free believers from the yoke of eternal damnation.

    O infinite charity, piety without measure: who among those who believe in you, eternal Majesty, would not marvel at such astonishing benefits granted to us? For your passion, Lord Jesus, is the price of our salvation, the final refuge of sinners, the singular remedy of weak minds, the fountain, origin, and end of all good things. Let us now therefore, dearest brothers, recall and diligently bring back to memory the bitterness of the Lord’s passion, so that, since we recognize that we are necessarily sinners, we may at last be justified through the merit of that same our Savior.

    For meditation on the Lord’s passion surpasses all the exercises of this world, if it is continued for a long time with the fervor of inward devotion. That mind of a monk which, kindled by zeal for divine love, has been accustomed each day, at least for a short hour, to hold the memory of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ with tears, does not easily lie open to the suggestions of demons. For that heart which the love of Jesus possesses always remains inaccessible and closed to all evil thoughts.

    Happy indeed is that monk, and never to be named except with honor, who meditates day and night with loving zeal on the teaching and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; who never forgets his Savior; who, whether he eats or drinks or does anything else, always beholds with the eyes of the mind the Lord Jesus hanging on the cross. No destructive thoughts move about in his heart; no evil or idle word proceeds from his mouth; he thinks of nothing but Jesus crucified for us, and whatever he says sounds of Jesus or of righteousness. As soon as he sees a painted image of Jesus crucified, he dissolves into tears, and, made as if senseless by the excessive desire of his mind, is filled with a most sweet bitterness. He can admit no consolations of the present life, because when he thinks that his Lord is seated in heaven, he weeps over his own exile prolonged on earth.

    He loves nothing in this world except Jesus; he seeks nothing other than the Crucified. If riches are at hand, his heart utterly disdains to set itself upon them; but if they are lacking, he by no means seeks to find them. For when he recognizes himself to be a disciple of poor Jesus, he understands very well that the riches of this world are a great impediment to Christian perfection. Having scanty food and a poor covering for the body, he is content with his Lord, who was made poor for us and foretold that those hungering for righteousness are blessed. Happy, I say, is that monk who can truly say with the holy martyr of Christ, Theophorus: “My love has been crucified, and therefore my heart receives no consolation of this world.” And that saying of the Christ-loving Paul: “For me the world has been crucified, and I to the world.”

    Now therefore, my dearest brothers, hear my counsel, and sanctify the fast you have begun by the continual memory of the Lord’s passion. For I tell you that among all the exercises of monks none can be holier, none more acceptable to God, none more salutary for you, than that which is practiced in daily diligence in meditation on the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, with compunction of inward love. For this exercise of the saving passion suddenly makes from a sinner a penitent; from one lukewarm and dry, by wondrous compunction, a devout man; from an impious man, a just one. It covers a multitude of sins; it gives strength to the spirit against demons; it sets an end to all [unclear]; and it confers strong increase upon the holy virtues of the soul. The devoutly continued memory of the Lord’s passion purifies the conscience of the one meditating; it illumines the understanding in every knowledge of truth; it sweetly inflames the affection in the love of God. Devout meditation on the passion of Christ causes one to despise all the delights of this world, and to fear nothing, however hard or adverse. It exterminates lusts; it subdues the luxury of both mind and body; it puts envy to flight; [unclear].

    [unclear]

    He loves nothing in this world except Jesus; nothing other than the Crucified, who blessedly foretold righteousness to those hungering for it. Happy, I say, is that monk who can truly say with the holy martyr of Christ, Theophorus: “My love has been crucified, and therefore my heart receives no consolation of this world.” And that saying of [the Christian?]: [unclear] the world [unclear] memory of the passion

    Homily XVII. Fol. XL.

    it restrains; it calms greed; it [unclear] sloth; it mitigates anger; it roots out pride from its very roots. Moreover, no passion for a carnal thing wearies the mind of the person whom the Passion of Christ truly occupies. O how sweetly he burns whom the memory of the Passion of Jesus has sweetly inflamed; and how blessed is the mind that embraces continual meditation on the death of Christ. O good Jesus, my crucified love, who are the salvation and savior of faithful souls: grant us to keep continual memory of your Passion; grant your servants always to commend the fasts they have begun with good works, because then our abstinence will be most pleasing to your uncircumscribed majesty, when it has been adorned with meditation on your precious blood; you who live and reign with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.

    Here ends Homily XVI.

    On the Sleep and Wakefulness of Monks. Homily XVII.

    The monk who always thinks that he is going to die allows no time to pass idly. Scripture says: “Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” On the contrary, concerning the forgetful and sluggish it is written: “They are a people without counsel and without prudence. Would that they were wise and understood, and provided for their last things.” The remembrance of death brings watchfulness into the soul and extinguishes every disordered thought of the mind. He who rightly fears death never grows sluggish in good work. For the wise man says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently, because neither work, nor reckoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge will be in the underworld to which you are hastening.” For the monk who is a true worshiper of God spends no moment of time uselessly, but night and day, in the exercise of good work, he carries out the watchfulness of the mind with the greatest devotion; and while sleeping in body he constantly says in spirit to God: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.” Sleep is an image of death and a binding of the body’s sense; but he who is a true lover [unclear].

    On the Sleep and Wakefulness of Monks.

    For they mercifully allowed monks in community a space of five hours before the night lauds, and they likewise added two or [unclear] hours after Matins for sleep. He for whom this, namely seven hours for resting, is not enough shows himself to be an excessively lazy and slothful monk. Therefore we are admonished to keep watch not only in mind but also in body, because no man can preserve himself in true purity if he disdains to keep bodily watch in God’s service. Let us therefore keep watch, dearly beloved brothers, especially in these holy days of Lent, in which we have declared war on the vices and are vigorously prepared to conquer and overcome the ancient enemy, the devil. For hear the holy prince of the apostles admonishing us with these words: “Brothers, be sober and watch.” Why did he give this admonition? “Because,” he says, “your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith.” And so, my brothers, let us keep watch as long as we are set in battle, lest, weighed down by drowsiness or idleness, we be overcome by the adversary of our salvation. For as long as we live in the flesh, we must fight bravely against the enemy by watchfulness and the chastisement of our body. Let the labor of the contest not frighten you, because, even if our adversary is troublesome, nevertheless he is so weak and feeble that he can overcome no one except one who is willing, and one who has entirely cast away all guard over himself. But the Lord Jesus Christ, our helper and protector, is strong; he gives strength to those who fight eagerly, and in heaven he will grant the victors the unfading crown with all his saints. Just as dust is scattered by the wind, so our adversary the devil, confounded and terrified by the voice of those singing psalms with humble devotion, is put to flight. Therefore let none of you, dearly beloved brothers, act negligently; let no one grow sluggish at the time of prayer through laziness of mind and drowsiness; let no one fear the devil’s contest with disordered fear. Stand manfully for the everlasting salvation of your souls against the [raging?] enemy; regard your own flesh as no less suspect than demons. For you know, with not only Scripture bearing witness, but also being taught by long experience

    Homily XVII.

    [Unclear] we believe that God is present everywhere; in prayer there is need of great reverence, so that our mind may agree with our voice in every respect. Let us consider, therefore, brothers, before whom we stand, and in whose sight, in the presence of the angels, we recite the psalms in prayer. For a monk who at the time of prayer occupies his heart with vain thoughts is like a man who, standing before a king or emperor and speaking with him about matters very necessary for the safety of his body, is called by his servant, leaves the king, and turns himself to the vain and useless conversations of the servant. Anyone who did this would truly be judged foolish by all, and would rightly seem deserving of punishment with the gravest penalties. But what does the monk deserve who, standing before the supreme king of all and speaking with him about the salvation of his soul, suddenly turns his inner eyes to useless occupations, and, neglecting the presence of the eternal king, admits vain or even pernicious thoughts into his mind? If the mocker and despiser of an earthly king is punished by the cutting off of his head, what does one deserve who despises the heavenly emperor?

    For this reason I warn you, brothers, and with all the sincerity I can I ask that you purify your hearts, especially at the time of prayer, from the stain of wicked thought, so that you turn over in your mind only what you chant with your mouth. As the angels, with fear and the greatest reverence, always stand before God, chanting the perpetual hymn of praise, so let us also take care, my brothers, to stand before him with a pure heart, a clean conscience, and most fervent devotion, so that we may chant his praises far more in spirit than in body. Therefore let us separate our minds from all earthly business; let us cleanse our consciences from all enticements of the flesh; let us put on the fervor of the Holy Spirit; and let us drive far from ourselves all sluggishness and idleness. For just as a heavy burden weighs down the back of a slothful man, so sleepiness at the time of psalmody is accustomed to oppress the minds of monks. Nothing harms monks more than acedia, which little by little enfeebles all the powers of the mind and extinguishes the whole fervor of the spirit.

    For as soon as a monk begins to fall away from the fervor of holy devotion, countless evil thoughts creep into the mind, and he is then able to repel them all the less, the farther he is found to have withdrawn from his former fervor. From this arises sleepiness in the performance of the divine services; the mind is excessively weighed down by sadness and melancholy, which the monk, growing lukewarm in soul, strives with all effort to relieve not by spiritual but by earthly and carnal little consolations. And the longer he advances in this estrangement of mind, the more he is hardened, as though insensible, against the exercise of compunction; and the more he gapes after the consolations of the flesh, the farther he wanders from the inward fervor of the spirit. For what makes you sleepy at the time of psalmody except acedia? Because the mind that falls into torpor soon makes the body drowse.

    But again I warn you, brothers, as I have often been accustomed to do, that you flee idleness and sleepiness, especially at the time of prayer; for just as drunkenness brings forgetfulness upon the soul, so also sleepiness makes the mind mad and foolish before God. Beware this vice of sleepiness, you young men, with which we grieve that some of the seniors have already been infected by long habit; for them drowsing is familiar in choir, and compunction of mind toward God is very rare. Beware, I say, this evil habit of sleeping; after it has once led a monk away captive, it rarely allows him to be free. Therefore, at the beginning of conversion, especially [unclear] delays. But make haste, and do not put yourself off to future hours: he who is not ready today will be less fit tomorrow. For it is difficult to cure an infirmity that is long-standing and has grown old through duration.

    Let us see with what diligence and attentiveness servants stand before earthly kings and princes, so that we may not be ignorant how it befits us to stand before God, who alone is the king of all and lord of the universe. The eyes of all look to the lord, and all and each wait most diligently upon his nod, lest, when he commands, anything escape the attendant through negligence. From this, therefore, let us consider with what purity we ought to stand before the Lord God in the assembly of prayer day and night, from whom we desire to obtain the kingdom of eternal happiness. Not voice, not

    On the Sleep and Wakefulness of Monks.

    [unclear]: but an intention fervent in the love of God deserves to be heard. Therefore flee drowsiness and sluggishness of mind as a deadly poison, because sleep and idleness are the fountain of all vices. The watchful eye, however, is the servant of inward devotion; and the monk who truly loves Jesus Christ keeps himself from every excess. The man who is watchful sharpens his mind with understanding; but the monk who sleeps much shamefully blinds his soul. The monk watchful in prayer and fasting is fearsome to the devil; but he who is sated with food and sleep is not permitted to rest by the spirit of fornication. For wakefulness dedicated to prayers breaks the heat of lust; it also powerfully extinguishes the fire of concupiscence; it purifies the inmost parts of the heart; it illumines the mind; it inflames the affection toward love of heavenly things. Wakefulness is the parent, nurse, and guardian of good thoughts; the certain victory over the temptations of the ancient enemy; the flight of phantasms; the death of vices, the life and fountain of all virtues. Sleep, however, is to many the companion and fomenter of lust; the robber of a man's life; the image of death; the bringer of forgetfulness; the spouse of sloth. Immoderate sleep corrupts the stomach, injures the brain, and dissolves body and soul alike. A monk frequently given over to sleep spurns wisdom, prostitutes chastity, neglects the salvation of his soul, wastes precious time, slays the mind, nourishes vices.

    Therefore whoever of you, most beloved brothers, desires to come to the rest of heavenly happiness, let him strongly repel from himself all sluggishness and laziness of mind; let him first learn to conquer himself, so that thereafter he may be able to overcome the devil, the enemy of his salvation. For unless you first [unclear] the evil that is in you, when will you overcome that which is external? Choose to rule over your passions, and, with the Lord's help, you will easily overcome all things that befall from without. Purge your mind of every disordered concupiscence, so that you may love Jesus alone in truth above all things, with whom you hope to rejoice [unclear]. No one, however, will reign with Christ in heaven who has not imitated him on earth with holy manners, as holy Scripture says: He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked. For the Lord Jesus, who by his death freed us from the destruction of eternal damnation, was himself made willingly the mediator of God and [unclear]; he himself is the way by which the path of life is to be continued for us; he himself is the mighty guide of the journey; he himself is the norm and rule of the saving conduct of Christianity. No one comes to God except through Christ; no one will see the Father except through the Son. Therefore, if you wish to come to salvation, you must pass through the Savior. For he himself said in the holy Gospel: No one comes to the Father except through me. And that other saying: I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will find the pasture of eternal life. And again: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Along this way, by living with pious and holy manners, I pray you, my brothers, always walk; this truth love fervently with a pure heart; to this life, which alone is lasting, hasten ardently. Let the teaching of Christ never depart from your hearts, but remain in memory at all times, since he refuses to become a true imitator of him who is not exercised day and night in meditation on his words. Therefore, always watchful in prayers, live with such purity of mind that, when he calls you in the hour of death, you may deserve with joy to hear Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in unity through all ages of ages. Amen.

    On Patience and Meekness. Homily, xviii.

    Among all professors of the Christian faith there is today no kind of men for whom the virtue of patience seems to be more necessary than for the company of monks. For, as charity among many grows cold in these our days, to use Paul's language, we have been made a spectacle to mortals, so that wherever a monk comes among worldly men, he is marked out by the fingers of nearly all who see him, to be mocked and laughed at. Why I have said this you know, you who are not ignorant of what recently happened in the town of Bingen. A drunken crowd of youths and boys received a monk

    Homily XVIII. Fol. XLII.

    ...someone passing along the public road, and, as though he had presented himself as a traveler because of the rain, he threw him into the mud; and by abusing the man with injury he made a pitiable spectacle of his own shamelessness. No one was present to restrain the insolent men; nevertheless the patience of the monk overcame the furious men, and, full of love for Christ, when he was being badly treated he answered nothing other than “Thanks be to God.” Hence, the more he showed himself tranquil in mind and spirit, the more the rascals dragged about the innocent man, thinking that he was heated with wine, whom the love of Christ had made joyful and glad.

    He left to all monks a great lesson of patience: although he could have avenged himself, he did not wish to do so when wronged. Would that, my brothers, for the love of God and for our sins, we were as patient in the smallest things as that good man was in the greatest. There are among you certain men, I say it unwillingly, too insolent and impatient, who are moved to anger by any word, even one not insulting; and when they are justly corrected for their negligences, they murmur unjustly, adding sin to sin through impatience.

    But to what end do I set before them the patience of that remembered man, when they do not heed Jesus Christ, the most patient of all men? For indeed, whoever does not embrace patience and humility by the example of the King of heaven, by the imitation of no [unclear] [unclear].

    On patience and meekness

    If you wish to keep the bounds of tolerance, there must first of all be someone present who inflicts insult. “If I had been,” says the lazy and unspiritual monk, “in the days of the martyrs, I would have feared no kinds of punishments to undergo for the love of Christ; I would voluntarily have exposed my body to the torturers, so that I might carry away the crown of martyrdom.” Great rashness of folly. You have never been able to endure a word patiently for the love of God, and you promise the steadfastness of the holy martyrs? You fear a slight correction, you who promise that you will give your body for Christ.

    If martyrdom delights you, hear what the most blessed Pope Gregory says: “If, with Christ helping us, we strive to preserve the virtue of patience, and live in the peace of the Church, we also hold the palm of martyrdom. For without sword and flame we can be martyrs, if we truly keep patience in the soul. To die at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in open deed; but to bear insults and to love one who hates us is martyrdom in hidden thought.” Patience, indeed, is to suffer another’s evils with equanimity, and to be gnawed by no grief against him who has inflicted the evil.

    What now will you say, lazy monk, who, unable to endure the very slight martyrdom of words, boast so insolently of steadfastness in shedding blood? Learn, wretched man, to have patience in light matters, and consider that, as Scripture says, “he who is unfaithful in a little thing, who would entrust him with what is greater?” You murmur at everything that is done in the monastery; when reproved, however gently, for your grave faults and negligences, you endure it most impatiently. No one in the monastery walks rightly for you; no one except you, in your estimation, conducts himself religiously. As it seems to you, you alone are holy in the community; you, the most learned of all, allow no one to know what you alone are ignorant of. You think yourself worthy of all honors above everyone, because you not only lack patience but retain neither true humility nor obedience.

    This is not the road by which one goes to the kingdom of heaven: when a monk is proud in the school of humility, and a Christian lives in his conduct contrary to Christ. But a monk, a minister solemnly sworn to Jesus Christ, in order that he may imitate his Lord, ought not to be proud but humble, obedient not rebellious, gentle not cruel, nor insolent but mild.

    A monk, however, who is proud, wrathful, contentious, and a lover of his own will, such as, alas, those set over temporal affairs often are, whom among us according to the Rule we call cellarers, their pride has made for many the road to destruction. Grief compels me to speak, and shame forbids me, although you all know the fall by which the devil lately put us to shame in a brother. Who in our whole congregation was prouder than he? Who went about filled with greater insolence? Because he seemed among us to have more experience of temporal affairs than all the rest, for that reason he thought himself more excellent. The Almighty permitted him to fall, so that he who [unclear] refused to recognize his own weakness might at last, confounded and not without the scandal of many, understand that God is the adversary of the proud.

    I grieve vehemently, and more than can be said. The fault of the one who fell seems to me the heavier, because when he fell we are all put to shame. May God grant him to do true penance, so that those who had been scandalized by his fall may be edified by his satisfaction before God and men.

    Pride has always been destructive to monks, and the mind of a man which it has once invaded it plunges into the pit of all vices. Beware pride, my brothers, because it is the beginning of every sin; it is what, through the envy of the devil, introduced death into the world. Pride is the death of all virtues and the source and spring of all vices. But humility, the nurse of virtues, especially befits monks, because it makes them both mild and meek. For every proud man is impatient, and every arrogant man is an enemy of meekness. He who is humble of heart has patience in adversities for the love of God; and he who is tranquil in soul before injuries merits a double crown. A patient man in adversities becomes very near to God; but he who is proud and impatient gladdens his enemies. For Scripture says: “Better is the patient man than the strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than the conqueror of cities.” Likewise the holy bishop Augustine: “A just and pious man ought to be ready to sustain patiently the malice of those whom he desires to become good, so that rather the number of the good may increase, and he may not by like malice add himself to the number of the wicked.” For patience is very necessary to us, brothers, so that, doing the will of God, we may receive [unclear] in Christ.

    Homily XVIII. Fol. XLIII.

    promise. Adversities are present to us every day, by which we may be exercised; therefore, just as the cause for endurance is never lacking, so, I pray, may necessary patience always be present. We are oppressed by want and poverty of necessary things; we are burdened by the commerce of weak flesh; moreover the world tempts us in order to entice us; the devil tempts us in order to lead us astray. Among so many adversaries of our salvation, brothers, it is necessary that we keep watch in all patience and humility, since in this pilgrimage, as long as we live, we are placed, so to speak, in the midst of evils.

    Our poverty ought to suffice us, because it is not the part of monastic religion to be exalted in temporal things, but rather to be humbled, so that monks, poor and imitating Christ, who was made poor for us, may deserve to glory with him forever in heaven. What if we see certain wicked men and sinners in the world abounding in riches? If good and just men are rich in this world, provision is made by God’s providence not for their strength but for their weakness, so that by benefits they may be summoned to better things. “I was young,” says the prophet, “and I have grown old, and I have not seen the just man forsaken, nor his seed begging.” “Cast,” he says, “your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you; he will not allow the just man to waver forever.”

    The Lord Jesus knows what is fitting for the salvation of each one of his little servants, and therefore he distributes the gifts of the present life unequally according to the capacity of individuals. For not all things are fitting for all people; therefore, among the just in this world, with respect to temporal goods, some are poor, while others are wealthy. Concerning the poor the Lord Jesus says in the holy Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And he speaks through the prophet, saying: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.” For it is not conducive to eternal salvation for all men to possess the riches of this world, but it is advantageous for certain persons, according as the Lord of all has foreseen to be more useful for each.

    Concerning just and good rich men Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: “The blessing of the Lord makes men rich; affliction shall not be joined to it.” But if the wicked and reprobate abound in riches in this age, this ought not to move the good to indignation; rather, let them fear him who leaves no good unrewarded and no evil unpunished. For the wicked, whom he cannot reward in heaven because of their iniquity, he rewards in this life for their good deeds; and for the good, whom he nourishes here in poverty for righteousness’ sake, he preserves eternal rewards in heaven. But just as not all the poor in this world are just and good, so not all who are rich in temporal things in this life are wicked. The reward of the wicked on earth must rightly be borne without indignation, since not the love of God but justice has willed it to be present.

    Therefore, just as the wicked have nothing in heaven, so you who have professed monastic poverty ought to have nothing on earth, but, in hope of that good toward which you are striving, you ought to endure most patiently whatever adversity befalls on the way. For, as Paul, the holy lover of Christ, says: “The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which shall be revealed in us.” Those who are rich in Christ should join mercy to humility; but those who are poor should take up patience, with innocence, for the love of God. The delight [unclear] of Christ is cast down neither by poverty nor raised up by riches, but, standing firm in himself, he rules his spirit calmly and cares nothing for transitory things. Thus he who is a true monk is neither lifted up by praises nor broken by reproach; he does not swell with an abundance of necessary things, nor is he contracted by poverty. He despises both joyful and sad things alike, since, as the prophet had said, “the sun shall not burn him by day, nor the moon by night.”

    But we, dearest brothers, should make a virtue and a good will out of necessity, and from the hardship of poverty which we necessarily suffer we should obtain for ourselves a good and a great advantage; and this can happen only if, for the love of God, we bear this very poverty manfully and with a tranquil spirit. The deformed way of life of our predecessors has brought upon this monastery the want that we suffer; if we keep his commandments with a perfect heart, the mercy of almighty God will in time, without doubt, relieve it. From almost two hundred years back, as a similar conjecture follows.

    On patience and meekness

    [unclear]: the purity of monastic institution in this monastery of Sponheim, as also in almost all the others, failed; and the disorder of the monks’ life utterly dissipated the whole substance of earthly goods.

    Indeed, when in the year of the Christians one thousand four hundred and sixty-one, Frederick, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, a most Christian man, who was residing at [Simmeren?], held the depraved life of monks in his principality in great hatred, he reformed three monasteries, expelling the deformed monks, and introduced men excellently trained from other monasteries. First, indeed, he brought two monasteries of regular canons of Saint Augustine back to the observance of regular discipline: Rebdorf, that is, among the [unclear], and Schwabenheim among the [Stauronesians?] in the district of the [Nagavienses?]. Finally, in the aforesaid year of the Lord, he also renewed this present monastery of ours, Sponheim, for reform of the order; and, after removing the abbot with five monks, he restored four others in their place for observance, setting over them my predecessor Johannes of Kolenhusen, now serving as abbot in Seligenstadt.

    They found the place so oppressed by poverty and burdened with debt that there was no one who believed it could be restored, since all the annual revenues had either been sold or alienated under title of redemption; indeed, nothing at all was left on which they might live. Brother Heinrich, one of the first four reformers sent from Mainz, is present as narrator and witness of the things we say; from his mouth you will know all things more fully. And behold, the seventeenth year is now underway since this place began to be restored under the chapter of the reformed union of Bursfelde, and still we are tortured by no small poverty.

    Therefore I have said these things, brothers, so that you may know that we do not bear alone the want that we suffer, since those four men who first reformed the monastery endured heavier things; beans and peas filled their bellies, and a thin pear-drink supplied them drink in measure. The mercy of God has called us to this place, in which through patience we may overcome the [antidicuus?] of our salvation, so that, according to the counsel of the divine Apostle, having scant food and clothing with which we may be covered, being content and giving thanks to the Lord in cheerfulness of mind, we may [serve?]. For we have not been called to feasts of the flesh, nor to the delights of this world, not to pleasures nor to the consolations of the present life, but to serve as soldiers for our Lord and emperor Jesus Christ in abstinence from all the delectable things of this age, in pure conscience and humility of heart.

    Attend now therefore to your calling, O monks, and do not [unclear] the purpose [unclear] you desire to attain. Woe to you, faithless monk, who, having become a despiser of your calling and a transgressor of your vow, do not live monastically in the monastery; you who were called to endure tribulation patiently for the love of God, and [unclear] concerning refreshment. For your profession commands you to go humbly content in every usefulness and extremity of garments, and you do not fear to apply zeal to the fastidiousness of clothing. You have been called to thirst, and you, not content to drink water, delight in drinking wine to satiety, contrary to the monastic canon. You were made a monk to fight strongly against the adversary of your salvation, and you, having cast away from yourself the courage of the virtues, go about sluggish, [unclear], and naked; indeed, what is graver, accompanied by a band of vices. You were invited to keep watch in holy prayers, and you are dissolved in inert sleep and shameful sloth. You were called into the subjection of humble obedience, and you, swollen with pride, scorn to obey the precepts of your elders. You have been called into charity, and you do not fear to carry hatred in your breast against your brother. You have been called into weeping and tears, and [unclear] laughter with disordered deep guffawing. The Lord called you in the monastery to repentance, and you, dissolved into wantonness, join sin to sin. You were called to meditate day and night on the law of our Lord Christ, and you, walking after vanities, devote yourself to tales and perishable things. You have been called to heaven, and you, loving the world, pursue earthly things. The Lord called you, humbled, into meekness, and you go about full of rancor and pride. You were called by the Lord to the perfection of the purest monastic manner of life, and you rot like a beast in the dung of vanity and negligence. To the observance of

    Homily XVIII.

    You have been called to the [choir?] of God, and you, given over to the pleasures of the flesh, think of Christ least of all. You have been invited to love the Lord Jesus above all things, and you walk after the evil desires of your heart; you show yourself ungrateful to your Redeemer. You who ought to live by the Spirit savor earthly things, and, sunk in pride, despise all the holy exercises of spiritual conduct. And what will you answer on that day of judgment to the Judge, who will say to you in your utter ingratitude: “I, who am Lord of all, humbled myself for your sake, taking the form of a servant, and being found in fashion as a man. I poured out my blood for you; for you I endured blows; and for you I underwent a most bitter death by my own willing choice. I loved you, O monk, with my whole heart; I redeemed you by my blood from perpetual death; I, out of love, called you to the heavenly kingdom, if you had kept my commandments. But you lived in opposition to my precepts; and, what is more serious, though you had been sworn to my words, you did not fear to show yourself against me, your Lord, as an apostate, impious traitor. Now therefore render an account of your stewardship.”

    What then will you answer, O lazy and idle monk, who now consume this acceptable time so fruitlessly, and despise living in true monastic purity according to the Rule? What, I ask, will you answer? Will you deny the works of wickedness which you have committed, and through deceit display the good works which you now scorn to perform, so that by lying you may circumvent the Judge and thus escape the penalty owed to your demerits? But you must not be unaware that all things you have done, said, or thought throughout your whole life, good and evil, are manifest in the sight of the Judge; and nothing can be hidden from him, who alone knows all things. For all things are written in the book of God, and your conscience will bear open testimony against you concerning all the evil things you have done, so that not even the smallest thought will be able to lie hidden. For the Scripture of the prophets says to God: “For the thought of man will confess to you.” You are to be judged before the tribunal of the One who knows all things; before whose terrible judgment every creature will stand with very great fear and trembling, where no excuse at all is admitted, but each person, with appeal set aside, will receive the sentence owed to his merits. Thousands upon thousands of holy spirits

    Folio xliiii.

    will stand beside him; and do you trust that you can deceive yourself by lying while he is judge? But hear my counsel, and, rising from your destructive sloth, at last awaken, and in due time flee from justice to the mercy of God through true repentance. Do not put it off from day to day, because it is very dangerous for one who remains in sins to be confident, and to refuse the remedy of salvation that is offered. Remember that you are going to die, and that when you do not expect it you will be called to judgment. Consider, I beg you, how the uncertain span of life slips away, and how quickly all mortal things decay. Nothing among human things is stable, nothing fixed, nothing firm; but all things that we see are corruptible, and change with time. Consider also where our brothers Valentinus, Martinus, and Ioannes now are, who in the present year were living with us, healthy, unharmed, and joyful; they spoke with us, ate, drank, and worked together with us, thinking least of all that they would die this year. Behold, when they did not think it, death came and snatched them away, and set their souls before the tribunal of the dread Judge, who rendered to each according to the works of his hands. Behold, now learn from the example of your brothers that you too are going to die, and perhaps you will pass from this world much sooner than you can estimate.

    Come to your senses, wretched man, while you still can; do penance in the time of your health, when the Judge promises mercy, and do not defer today’s good to the uncertain [tomorrow?]. Rise up, even now, late though it is, from the sloth of your more negligent past conduct, in which until now you have shamefully rotted, and purge your conscience of every stain of sin; wipe away with tears the evil you have committed; and henceforth live innocently, as befits a monk. Take hold of the perfect purpose of amendment, and understand that the kingdom of heaven is promised not to those who begin the good, but to those who persevere to the end. Know also that one does not arrive at heaven by sloth and torpor, but by great labor, by the very greatest effort of a will to make progress, and by unwearied zeal in spiritual exercise. Therefore, wishing to serve the Lord and to please him in truth, always remain within yourself, fearful in awe, and prepare your soul for temptation. One must resist with strength the disordered movements and desires

    On Patience and Meekness

    of the flesh: one must struggle with a most steadfast mind against all the enticements and vanities of the world; by prayers and greatness of spirit the devil, the adversary of our salvation, must be put to flight. No drowsy, lazy, and slothful man will ever have come to the kingdom of God; no one without continual labor and many sweats has obtained heaven. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent,” that is, those who have learned steadfastly to resist the evil desires of the flesh, “seize it.”

    Turn over the deeds of all the saints, and nowhere will you find anyone sanctified without great and continual labor. For even if no one becomes holy by his own powers, nevertheless the gracious mercy of the almighty Lord, which grants to those who strive both the will to do good and the strength, sanctifies no one without the works of a good and right will. Since, therefore, God wills all men to be saved and none to perish, we, my brothers, must take the greatest care not to receive his grace in vain, but rather strive with all our strength so that, like fertile ground, we may always answer the free gifts of so great a sower with fitting fruits from the works of good will.

    Let us therefore arm ourselves with the shield of faith and put on the breastplate of constancy and saving patience, so that, prepared against all things that can befall us, through humility and the fervor of the Holy Spirit, with our Lord Jesus Christ helping us, we may overcome. In all these things patience is very necessary for us; without its support there never was, nor could there be, any perseverance in good and holy works. For there was no other way to heaven for the saints than patience; nor could he ever be sanctified who cast patience aside.

    Indeed, all who pleased almighty God from the beginning of the world down to this our age triumphed over the prince of the world in no other way than through patience. Hence they could all most rightly say that saying of the psalmist: “For your sake we are put to death all the day; we are counted as sheep for slaughter.” The most holy apostle of Christ, Paul, also, recalling the patience of the saints of old, says among other things: “They went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted; the world was not worthy of them; wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves and in the caverns of the earth.” For all who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution, since, as the prophet says, many are the tribulations of the just, and from all these the Lord will deliver them.

    Patience, therefore, is necessary for all mortals, and especially befits cloistered persons, since, just as adversities are never lacking to the just in this world, so no one will be justified without patience. Now the chief degrees of patience, as the diligence of the ancients distinguished them, are three. The first and lowest is that of those men who neither seek adversities nor willingly endure them; but when they happen, they are weighed down in spirit and cast down with grief. They also sometimes complain and murmur for a time against those who inflict them; but after the inflamed agitation of the mind has passed, they return to themselves, and are seen patiently to endure the insult inflicted without revenge.

    Yet the patience of these men, not of great virtue, is always very close to a fault of the mind, and for that reason must often be reckoned of no merit, and sometimes of lesser merit. And although such persons in our times are said to be distinguished by the virtue of patience, nevertheless, compared with the ancient saints, they do not deserve this venerable name of Christian long-suffering and endurance. For that does not seem to be true patience which has been darkened by bitterness and indignation of an agitated mind.

    The second degree of patience is said to belong to those men who, although they do not seek to endure evils, nevertheless when they come, receive them willingly and kindly, and embrace them most patiently as a gift sent by God. And such persons are truly to be called patient: those who, kindled by divine love, bear with equanimity whatever adversity occurs, and preserve in tribulation the same tranquillity of mind that they previously had in prosperity. I would not doubt that that most holy Job the Idumean was of their number: he not only, struck by extreme adversity, patiently bore all things, but even, placed in a whirlpool of evils, gave thanks and blessed the Lord. “The Lord [unclear] gave; the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

    All Christians should preserve this degree of patience, and before others especially cloistered persons. For the wise man says: “The teaching of a man [unclear]

    Homily XVIII. Folio XLV.

    ...is recognized by patience. For the more each person has been instructed in the law of the Lord and in knowledge of the teaching of rational nature, the more patient he will be in adversities. What if I speak more boldly, as a lover of truth: adversities profit us more than prosperity, if we are learned and not forgetful [unclear] of our proper condition.

    But a third degree of patience remains, certainly the highest and most perfect, rightly granted to those who not only, when there is need, bear contrary things calmly for the love of God and the usefulness of the brethren, but also, more fervent and inflamed with the spirit of charity, hasten gladly to expose themselves to receive insults and injuries. And this kind of patience is divided into two parts, just as a twofold class of martyrs is found. For some, although they could have hidden when persecution of believers was raging, with Christ’s charity burning in them, and with no one compelling them, but by their own free will, presented themselves before the tribunals of the persecutors, publicly confessing Jesus, the Redeemer of the world, and received the torments inflicted on them with joy. Others, although they did not thrust themselves forward unbidden, nevertheless joyfully accepted martyrdom when it was offered, always prepared to endure for the faith of Christ whatever the cruelty of tyrants might have thought to inflict.

    To these most illustrious confessors rightly obtain a neighboring degree: if the cruelty of the impious, by persecuting them, did not remove them from this world, nevertheless they in no way lost the glory of martyrdom. For, crucifying their flesh in this world for the name of Christ, they endured both a voluntary and a daily martyrdom; they were made glorious through abstinence and humility, always steadfast in mind and most patient, and most ready to accept bodily martyrdom. You also, O monks, should take care to be [unclear] with all your powers; and although enemies who kill the body for Christ are now lacking, by resisting the desires of the flesh and patiently sustaining adversities for the love of God, you should show yourselves martyrs in mind and spirit. In the peace of the saints, the best kind of martyrdom is to afflict the flesh by abstinence for the name of God, to desire nothing in this world, to advance always in good works, and, if any evil occurs, to bear it in all things gladly and patiently with cheerfulness of mind. To this new [unclear] of patience, dearest brothers, henceforth...

    ...lives, if you desire to reign with Christ forever. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ: so that what each person desires to be done for himself, he should also cheerfully bestow upon his brother.

    On True Humility

    Homily Nineteen.

    It is the opinion of nearly all learned men, dearest brothers, that the highest and chief virtue of monks is none other than humility, because it is the mother and nurse of all virtues. Humility indeed makes the monk; pride destroys and corrupts him. The Lord says through Isaiah: “To whom shall I look, if not to the poor little one, and the contrite in spirit, and the one trembling at my words?” For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble; because the beginning of every sin is pride, and without true humility no one can attain salvation. Since this is so, I think it necessary for me, brothers, to exhort you without interruption that, fleeing pride, you should always preserve deep humility in all your works. Indeed, no good work is believed to please the Lord God when it is presented without the seasoning of humility.

    For humility is a most healthful medicine for the souls of the faithful, because it aids all: it presses down the swollen ulcers of the spirit; it restores what is wasting away; it corrects what is depraved; it removes what has grown out excessively. Humility is the mother and parent of all virtues: you strengthen patience; you arouse compunction; you illuminate charity; you adorn chastity; you make prayer fruitful; you commend fasting and abstinence. O holy humility, truly beloved of God: through penitence you justify the impious; you preserve the just in their purpose of holiness; you powerfully open heaven to your lovers; you close hell to penitents. O humility, venerable and exceedingly pleasing to God: you compelled the Son of the eternal Father to descend from heaven into the womb of most chaste Mary, the perpetual virgin; you made him appear visible to us; you caused him, wrapped in poor cloths, to be laid in a manger, so that he might adorn us in heaven with the ornaments of perpetual happiness. You [unclear] the Son of God with the circumcision of the flesh...

    On the True Humility of Monks.

    You impelled [us] to undertake it, so that, [circumcised?] in mind, we might be able to enter the promised inheritance of the saints. And great is the humility of power, which made the king of heaven and earth withdraw from the face of one most vile man, and dwell for a seven-year exile in the land of the Egyptians. You compelled Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, to assume a human body for our salvation, and made him undergo also the most bitter passion and death by his own voluntary will. And great is your dominion, O venerable humility of holiness, since the kingdom of heaven is promised to you, to whose worshippers the gift of everlasting blessedness is granted; and whoever keeps to your footprints is raised up to the height of the angels, as Christ says in the holy Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” And the king of heaven says to certain [unclear]: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” The most blessed mother also, the untouched Virgin Mary, in her sweetest canticle of praise, speaks thus of Almighty God: “He has put down the mighty from their seats, and has exalted the humble.” And the prophet says in the psalm: “The Lord has looked upon the prayers of the humble, and has not despised their petitions.” For the prayer of the humble penetrates the clouds, and until it draws near it will not be comforted, and it will not depart until the Most High looks upon it. Humility makes the monk who is pure in his conscience most pleasing to God; and the more he casts himself down by humbling himself for God’s honor, the more glorious he will appear in the kingdom. The monk who truly humbles himself becomes a son of the Most High through participation in grace, and with the king of heaven, Jesus Christ, he will rejoice forever. He who truly desires to imitate Christ should also take up true humility; clothed and fortified with it as with a breastplate of strength, he may do great things, and, thinking only lowly things of himself, may not incur the stain of vainglory. For this is the true perfection of monks: always humbly to recognize one’s own imperfection, and to consider rather what good is lacking to him than what he has in the world. For true humility always stretches forward to what lies ahead through the desire of charity, and, carefully mindful of things past lest it lose the merits it has gained, and desiring to acquire through the zeal of devotion the things not yet possessed, in the fervor of holiness

    Homily XIX. Folio XLVI.

    [unclear] is raised up; it is sustained by the rock of humility alone. For truly, if true humility is lacking, the gathering together of all the other virtues will be nothing other than a kind of collapse of a house built without a foundation on sand. For in the spiritual building humility lays the stable foundation; charity orders the breadth of that house; the wall is raised on high by the continuation of good works in fervor of spirit; the roof is placed at the summit in faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and in firm hope of the promise of eternal protection and happiness; and its length is arranged in the long-suffering of patience with most beautiful ordering.

    Therefore, my brothers, again and again I admonish, adjure, and beseech you to take care to found the building of spiritual exercise in the depth of humility, because no good work is pleasing to God if it has been offered apart from true humility. Now there are many things which have been wont to move the servants of God toward true humility. For consideration of their own worthlessness humbles some within themselves before God, because, when they consider that by experience they have already often found themselves wretched and weak, being humbled they place all their hope and confidence in God. Others, weighing carefully the multitude of God’s benefits toward them, fear the judgment of ingratitude; and therefore in the sight of God, with great fear and reverence of gratitude, they always go forward humble. And who among us is there, brothers, to whom the compassion of almighty God has not also granted many benefits, even individually? If we wish to be grateful for them, we must above all be humble.
