    Others, after a multitude of sins, converted to penitence by divine kindness, diligently recall to memory how many evils they have committed against the law of the Almighty; and for these, humbled in bitterness of spirit, they detest their impieties with horror. But we offend in many things; whence it is necessary that we humble ourselves always in mind and heart, and even in body, so that grace may abound where sin formerly abounded. Often, moreover, the providence of divine compassion permits certain persons to sin enormously for a time, so that afterward, converted to penitence, they may learn to remain inwardly humble. Better is a humble penitent than a proud man who has not sinned, because humility justifies penitents, while pride condemns the arrogant eternally, even if they have done nothing else evil than this alone, that they are proud.

    Others, carrying in their heart by daily meditation the bitter passion of Jesus Christ, humble themselves the more, the more they know that they are greatly indebted for such and so wonderful benefits of that same Redeemer of theirs. The Son of God humbled himself, having been made man for us; and, filled with many reproaches, he voluntarily underwent the most shameful death of the cross, that he might free us from the destruction of perpetual death. What Christian man, and especially what monk, will not humble his soul greatly before God, when he has recalled to memory such humility of his Creator and Redeemer? For truly, the man whom the humility of Christ does not move to meekness will profit from no admonitions of men. In vain do we say that we are monks, unless we have followed Christ humbly according to our powers. For this reason he said in the holy Gospel that he himself is the way, so that we might imitate his humility, and so that the conduct of so great a master might become the spiritual form of the disciple.

    Therefore, brothers, as much as we can, let us strive with all our strength that all that pride has made swollen in us may be leveled, renewed, and reformed by humility conceived from meditation on the most bitter passion of Jesus Christ. O how fitting it is for us to humble our souls for love of Jesus Christ, my brothers, since God himself and the Creator of all, made [unclear] of humility, cast himself down for us into such great humility. Therefore the supreme medicine for inducing true humility in a servant of God is for him daily, and often, to recall to memory the most bitter passion of Christ Jesus.

    Tribulations also, adversities, and infirmities, together with poverty or want, have made many humble, who perhaps in prosperous and favorable circumstances would have perished, puffed up. And we trust that what we often customarily say is conducive to our salvation: poverty, since we have a great cause of humility, while we find no material for exaltation and pride. Others, by continual exercise of virtues and by memory of the death which shortly they must necessarily suffer, have come to great humility. Whom would not even the attentive meditation of death humble, however proud? Or who is so fierce in spirit that he would not gradually put down his swelling pride, if he reflected more diligently that he is soon to die? Accordingly the conscience of a monk ought never to drive away from itself the memory of future death, so that he may remain both humble and sorrowful, and, standing firm in humility, not [unclear].

    h ij

    On the true humility of monks.

    But the continual [fear?] of God forbids every wantonness to the heart. The free compassion of God also forestalls some, and makes them humble by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. Everyone who is led by the Spirit of God utterly detests pride.

    He who truly knows himself is most wise, and cannot depart from the meekness of humility. But every proud and arrogant man is ignorant, even if he seems great and famous among mortals. For true wisdom will rest in the dwelling-place of holy humility, and it is itself shown more clearly through the lesson of patience. Humility is born from knowledge of God and of oneself, and this is rightly called true wisdom.

    He who has truly known himself now has nothing for which to be proud, since, knowing his own vileness, he thinks nothing lofty, but, placed in sorrow of soul, cries to the Lord: What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you account him? Man has been made like vanity; his days, as it is written, [unclear] under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation.

    For humility with chaste fear greatly pleases the Lord God in his servants, since he approves no virtue of a man unto salvation without it. Therefore, if we desire to climb to the lofty threshold of the kingdom of heaven, we must be very humble, because there is no other road to heaven except that of the deepest humility, by which both the Son of God himself and all the saints ascended. But all who have tried to enter the kingdom by another gate, their head of pride having been struck back on the threshold of humility, could by no means enter. For the gate of humility does not admit the proud, and the narrow road of meekness does not receive lovers of greed and self-exaltation.

    Therefore whoever has [unclear] to come to the height of the heavenly [unclear], let him ascend by the steps of humility; without these, whoever begins to ascend undoubtedly falls into the depth of perdition and death. For humility is the ladder of heaven, beautifully distinguished by twelve rungs; concerning its ascent our lawgiver, blessed Benedict, says in the Rule: If we wish to reach the highest summit of humility, and swiftly to arrive at that heavenly exaltation, we must set up for ourselves that ladder which appeared to Jacob in dreams, by which angels were shown to him ascending and descending. Without doubt that descent and ascent is understood by us to be nothing other than to descend by exaltation and to ascend by humility, as divine Scripture tells us: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

    The ladder itself, set upright, is our life in this world, which is raised up to heaven by the Lord when the heart has been humbled. For we say that the sides of the same ladder are our body and soul. Into these sides the divine calling has inserted the different steps of humility and discipline that are to be ascended. Thereafter, indeed, he enumerates those twelve steps in order with a sufficiently beautiful arrangement; since they are all very well known to you, it would be superfluous to spend longer on reviewing them on this occasion.

    For it is enough in this place to remember the holy canon, upon the words of which you all long ago willingly swore, so that you may know that humility is no less necessary for salvation for you than love of God and, at the same time, of neighbor. For humility is said to be the monk’s greatest virtue, and it is so necessary to his profession that without it he cannot be saved. A monk exalted in mind and proud is not the bondman of Christ, but of the devil; he will have no share with the Son of God in heaven, but will be tormented without end with the demons in hell.

    For Christ, the teacher and instructor of humility, detests all the proud, and admits into his company only the humble, the gentle, and the meek. But the devil is the head and inventor of pride, whose servants and disciples are all who follow his pride and self-exaltation. For he himself, the king of the proud, cannot bear the humble; he flees the gentle, and does not dare to stand in the sight of the meek in heart. For Christ dwells in the assembly of the humble servants of God; but in the midst of the proud the devil stirs up the contentions and quarrels of those at discord.

    Where there is humility, there is true peace and the highest tranquillity; but where pride rules, there rancor, anger, disturbance, and discord confuse everything without ceasing. Therefore, my brothers, avoid pride, since if it cast down the exalted angels from heaven, when would it not condemn poor cloistered men? It made demons from angels, and, without doubt, [unclear] companions of demons

    Homily XIX.

    At all times, with all your strength and as much as you can, flee all pride and ostentation, since unless you greatly humble your souls, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Walk always before the Lord Jesus in the simplicity of your heart, having a pure conscience in all things, lest your humility become bestial; for it contributes nothing to salvation for a sinner to acknowledge himself publicly and, by persevering in evil, not to amend his fault. For the true servant of Christ sanctifies his humility by good works, and amends all the guilt of his past life by continual penitence. Daily he recalls to memory the evil that he remembers having committed, and groans deeply that he has offended the Lord. He walks very cautiously, and so laments past offenses that he by no means commits further things to be lamented. The monk who is truly humble follows the fasting Lord in a pure conscience, and fears nothing more in this world than to offend the teacher whom he imitates. Whatever he does and wherever he goes, he always thinks of the Lord Jesus as present, and by continual meditation examines how he may please him alone. For this is truly Christian humility, and humble Christianity: to [unclear] sin in true compunction, and to preserve the conscience in all purity at all times, not only from fear of punishments but rather from love of Christ. The true humility of monks continually does whatever good it can for the honor of God, and thinks that it will do nothing that it knows displeases Christ. True humility of monks [unclear] human [unclear], and, serving the Lord in the fervor of charity, is a companion of the holy angels, a friend to the citizens of heaven, and very formidable to demons. For demons fear and flee nothing more than the humility of the servants of Jesus Christ, because, since they themselves are most proud by their vicious will, they are most violently tormented by humble devotion. For where true humility is, demons cannot remain; for as ice is dissolved by fire, so malignant spirits are scattered from the presence of a humble monk. O humility, venerable mother and preserver of all virtues: yours is the kingdom, yours the power; you confer the kingdom upon the humble; you bestow the glory of eternal happiness upon the meek; without your guidance no one comes to heaven; whoever follows you does not fear hell. Whoever gathers works of virtues without you is like one who carries dust into the wind. You are the seasoning of all good works; for just as food in the mouth of the eater is not savory without salt, so without your companionship no one will be established as a friend of God. Humility made the Son of God man; humility will make the servant of Christ equal to a holy angel. An angel, through pride by his own choice, became the devil; and a Christian man through humility becomes an angel. Humility opens heaven to the meek servants of God, and pride plunges arrogant men down to hell. Humility makes friends of God, and pride makes companions of demons. Humility enlightens the mind to true wisdom, and pride blinds the understanding of the one whom it possesses. Humility purges the man whom it possesses from all disordered affections; and pride fills its worshipper with all crimes and filthiness. Humility makes its lover a servant of God; pride, however, makes him a slave of the devil. Humility makes one wise in the law of the Lord; pride, however, renders man foolish, away from the knowledge of the Most High. Humility brings the poor man into the fellowship of God; and pride makes the rich man a member of the devil. Humility is the mother and nurse of all virtues; and pride is the [source?] of all vices. Humility, with charity as mediator, covers a multitude of sins; pride, however, by itself introduces the fullness of all vices. Humility makes a monk’s good works most pleasing to God; pride, however, renders idle the endeavors of the proud before the Creator. Humility receives from the Lord whatever it has asked; but almighty God resists the prayers of the proud. Humility always has, in the Lord’s mercies, a pious confidence with cheerfulness of mind; pride, however, with the sting of despair, begets disturbance in man. Humility always has joy of spirit in the love of Christ; pride, however, is always occupied by pernicious fear. Humility, the [support?] of good works, neglects none of the spiritual exercises; pride, however, despises all pursuits of salvation. Humility justifies sinners; pride, however, condemns its followers. Humility makes one near to God; pride, however, makes one alien from the grace of God.

    On the True Humility of Monks.

    Humility eagerly obeys the commandments of God with a willing disposition pleasing to him; pride resists the precepts of the Most High. Humility heaps up the merits of everlasting blessedness; pride, however, prepares for itself the most grievous torments of hell. Humility provides security at the point of death; pride brings horrible fear and calamity to the dying man. Humility frees the soul of its devotee from every distress in the dread judgment of God; pride, however, accuses before the judge all the haughty whom it deceived in the world. Humility will place the servants of God at the judge’s right hand; pride will set those to be damned at the left. Humility will plead the cause for its own and will prevail in judgment; pride, surely confounded, will hand the haughty over to the devil. Humility will repay the reward of eternal blessedness to its friends; pride, however, will give the torment of perpetual damnation to all the haughty. Humility will be crowned without end in heaven; pride, however, will suffer immeasurable torment with the demons forever in the lower regions.

    Humility, crowned with Christ, reigns in the heavens; and pride, despised, will be tormented with [unclear] in punishments. Humility, joyful and glorious, will sit forever at the right hand of [unclear]; pride, however, sorrowful and ignominious, will lie without end in the torments of hell. Then the humble will exult in glory, and all the proud, because of excessive pain, will cry out in punishment for all ages. There the humble will stand in the sight of God and of all the saints in great joy and everlasting exultation, receiving, for the voluntary poverty of this life, unfading riches; for meekness, a kingdom; for sorrow [unclear], and for the spontaneous mortification of the flesh, heaven. But the proud and arrogant, placed in hell, seeing such great glory of the humble whom they despised in the world, will lament in so sudden a change of [unclear], and will be troubled with horrible fear, groaning under the very great anguish of spirit and saying in the fury of pride: These are the poor and humble monks, once clothed in vile garments, separated from men, abstaining from the eating of meats and from every filthiness of the flesh, whom we held at one time in derision and as a likeness of reproach; senseless as we were, we judged their life madness, and their end without honor. Behold how they are counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints.

    Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice has not shone upon us, and the sun of understanding has not risen for us. What does pride now profit us, by which, when we were then puffed up, we despised the humble? And what does the boastfulness of riches possessed in the world bring us? All things have passed away, and through continual contumacy we have been counted among the demons; because we always had humility in hatred, we now suffer immeasurable torments. But the humble will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the care of them is with the Most High. These things, my brothers, always think upon beforehand, because without doubt they are thus to be; and therefore assume humility of mind, flee every [unclear] through it, keep a pure conscience, and may you deserve to obtain the rewards of eternal life. Amen.

    On the True Obedience of Monks: Homily XX.

    If the humility of monks has been true and perfect, it brings forth the whole fullness of the holy virtues. But if it has lacked the splendor of the virtues, true humility was never in the mind. For first it brings forth true obedience, and a profound subjection in all things for the love of God. For the monk who truly lives as a pilgrim in the flesh shows himself in all things an eager [disciple?] of our Savior Jesus Christ; for love of him, despising every vileness and extremity, he glories in being subject to his abbot, obedient in all things. Obedience is a great virtue: it opens heaven to the humble monk and by its strength closes hell. Obedience restores the way of paradise and reforms peace between God and man. This, however, is true monastic obedience: that which is rendered to the commands of superiors not from servile fear but from an inward affection of charity, which, persevering until death not through fear of punishment but through love of justice, works good in cheerfulness of mind. There are two most beautiful wings of the mind by which the monk flies from earth to heaven; one of these is called humility, the other is known as the obedience of subjection. The monk who has not been adorned with these wings has entirely lost both the name and the merit of his dignity. Nor is he to be called a monk, but a deceitful and most false apostate, who [unclear] lives in the monastery and continually observes without hu

    Homily 20. Folio XLVIII.

    the obedience of humble subjection. For a monk without obedience is a monster of the devil; and he who resists the commands of his superior will inherit the punishments of hell. The disobedience of the first man lost the life of eternal happiness from the beginning; the obedience of Jesus Christ restored it. For he was made obedient to the Father for us even unto death, and by his most innocent passion he restored to us the happiness that had been lost. Therefore the path to salvation is humble obedience, as our holy lawgiver, blessed Benedict, cries out in the Rule: “Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive and effectively fulfill the admonition of a loving father, so that by the labor of obedience you may return to him from whom you had withdrawn through the sloth of disobedience.”

    Obedience is the tree of eternal salvation, which grows in the garden of monastic humility. Obedience is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and the quiet tomb of one’s own will. Obedience is the merit of heavenly happiness and the one lesson of monastic discipline. Obedience is the extermination of all self-exaltation and pride, and the persecutor of all vices. Obedience overcomes wickedness and extinguishes every disordered pleasure of the flesh. Obedience makes the conscience pure and clean, and preserves true humility in the mind. Obedience is the remedy of the wounded soul and the foundation of the whole monastic observance. Obedience is the faithful custody of all good works and the discipline of a sincere mind. Obedience is the beginning of mortification and the glorious ornament of the monk. Obedience is the preserver of peace and concord; without it the vigor of monastic discipline perishes. Obedience always directs the keen edge of the mind toward God; and he who has truly been mortified in spirit despises all the consolations of this world. Obedience makes the monk near to God and far removed from all the filth of the soul. Obedience is the adornment of holiness and the garment of beauty; without it no one would come to the kingdom of eternal glory. Obedience is the mother of victory, and he who knows how, for the honor of God, to be humbly subject will obtain the crown of martyrdom in heaven. Obedience separates the monk from the world, and whoever follows it with his whole heart will be great before the Most High. Obedience is the consummation of Christian perfection; in its humble workshop, the more a monk advances, the holier he becomes. Obedience is sure security at the hour of death; for the more ready the monk was for obedience to commands, the more securely he will fly away when he departs from here. Obedience is the rewarder of humility and the chief mark of merits. Obedience is the rule of Christian gentleness and the strongest nourishment of inward charity. Obedience is the shelter of chastity and the purest ornament of innocence. Obedience is [unclear] voluntary mortification; its merit is of such dignity that he who is rebellious and proud wears the monastic habit without cause. Obedience is the voluntary mortification of the members; its merit is of such dignity that man has nothing greater to offer in honor of God.

    Let each one offer, for love of God, what he can: without doubt that man has offered more than all who has, because of God, killed his own will through obedience. It is indeed a great good to distribute one’s possessions, for love of Christ, to the use of the poor, and to relieve the want of the needy with alms. But as much as the whole outweighs the part, as much as the free choice of the will is nobler than necessity, as much as heaven is distant from earth, so much more has that man offered who, out of love for God, has by a spontaneous will denied himself forever. For whatever temporal substance you have offered to God is not yours but another’s, and is of less value than your own, both in estimation and in reward. You have one thing of your own which, offered above all things, is pleasing to God. What is this, unless the free will which the almighty Creator has placed in your power? A good will, however, is greater than all riches, because nothing richer is offered to God, nothing is consecrated more acceptably. This most precious gift to God, my brothers, you once offered when, denying yourselves and all worldly things for his honor, you put on the monastic habit.

    Remember, I beg you, the words of your holy profession, and let that solemn promise never depart from memory, which each one of you uttered in the sight of God before us, saying: “I, brother Johannes, promise stability, conversion of my morals, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery, which has been built in honor of blessed Martin, in the presence of lord Johannes, abbot.” Behold the bond by which we have voluntarily bound ourselves to obedience; behold [unclear] four

    ...the warfare which we have professed. For these are the vows which our lips pronounced; these are the sacrifices of pious devotion which we offered to God. Certainly, my brothers, the things we have promised are great, and the necessity laid upon us to keep what we have professed is greater. For unless we faithfully observe all that the rule of our holy father Benedict enjoins upon us, the justice of almighty God will judge us severely as perjured and impious transgressors. For it is very dangerous not to render to God what has been promised, and through forgetfulness of the holy institution to violate one’s purpose.

    Therefore, to fulfill the duty of pastoral care, I am accustomed daily to admonish you to the observance of regular discipline; nor hereafter will the necessary word of salvation ever be lacking to you, so long as my spirit perseveres in this prison-house of flesh. But you, I pray, take care that you not be unfruitful hearers, since the matter concerns the soul, which, once lost, is never recovered. Therefore, whichever of you have come together in the monastery to run in the arena of the intellectual contest, whichever of you for love of Christ have once renounced your own will and the world, take up holy obedience for the helmet of salvation, and you will bring back a certain victory over the enemy.

    For obedience is the strongest armor of monks, which no adversities will be able to harm. For Scripture says: He who keeps the commandment will experience no evil whatsoever. In Proverbs also it is said thus: An obedient man shall speak of victories. Obedience renders a monk invincible in all temptations, and he who follows in all things the counsel of his senior will never suffer harm to the salvation of his soul. For obedience is a short and rough road, by which one quickly ascends to the height of perfection. But the monk who is a true soldier of Christ never trusts in his own judgment, but in all things follows and observes the direction of his pastor. Indeed, he who is a true lover of Christ, who wholly desires to be a most faithful monk, loves his abbot as God’s vicar, and cheerfully acquiesces in all things, always obedient to his commands, counsels, and ordinances.

    In order that a monk may be able to do this with confidence, one to be ordained to the abbacy should not be a child, not unlearned, nor carnal, not lacking discretion, nor light-minded, or inexperienced in spiritual contests, but a man gray-haired in character, learned in the divine Scriptures, walking in the spirit, pious in true conversion, in the conduct of holiness, gentle, tranquil in mind, and discreet, one who knows how to show judgment to the wicked and compassion to the well-disposed. For whenever a restless, turbulent, indiscreet, and inexperienced man is set over monks as abbot, at once the integrity of regular discipline suffers shipwreck. Subjection must necessarily perish, and with it the obedience of humility, when the subjects cannot firmly have confidence in the pastor. For if the abbot is a mocker of his brothers, or an importunate despiser of the weak, who will open to him any secret of his heart?

    Therefore one must keep watch with the greatest solicitude at the beginning, so that such a prelate be ordained as pastor over sheep left destitute, who seeks nothing other than the honor of God and the salvation of souls. The monk who will have obtained such a pastor should give thanks to God, because in these our times he occurs rarely, one who knows how to show himself in all things a worthy and suitable prelate. He is rightly to be loved by all his subjects, and, as the vicar of Christ in the monastery, to be honored with continual veneration. Let the thoughts of all be opened to him securely, because he seeks nothing other than the advancement of each one. If a physician of sick bodies must be prudent, experienced, and endowed with the highest discretion, how much more fitting is it for an abbot, who is the physician of souls, to be the best of men?

    Happy are the monks to whom God’s mercy has granted a useful and suitable pastor, if nevertheless it has not denied them even the ability to understand this very fact. Otherwise a good pastor, in his uprightness, is not recognized by evil sheep; but those who corrupt the integrity of the order by their depravity rarely judge truly and rightly about pastors. Because of the ingratitude of subjects, rulers are very often changed for the worse; and monks who despise a good and useful pastor when he is present in this life receive, by the just judgment of God, a foolish and useless successor. Those who are subject in simplicity walk rightly, and those who truly imitate Christ do not pass judgment on the one set over them. For we have a pastor whom we may follow, the Lord of faithful souls, our Lord Jesus Christ; looking faithfully to him in the soul, we shall not rashly judge the visible pastor. “The scribes and Pharisees,” he says, “have sat upon the chair of Moses; what they say to you, do; but what they do, do not imitate.” Hear these things, O monk, and [unclear]

    Homily XX.

    Fol. LIX.

    O lover and devotee of your own salvation, consider the form of obedience which you are to follow. The abbot, whether he is good or bad, holds in the monastery the place of Christ's vicar; he deserves the obedience of all his subjects not by his own merit, but in Christ's name. For we understand the saying, "He who hears you hears me, and he who spurns you spurns me," not only of the apostles, but of any prelate in the Church of God who has been appointed guardian and ruler of souls.

    Therefore, if you have a good, suitable, holy abbot, hear his voice as the command of God, since he bears God's place; and whatever he commands you, be obedient in all things. Let his teaching be for you a rule of life, and his holy conduct an example of a purer discipline. For he is a friend of God and likewise Christ's vicar: in the one respect he deserves that you love him, and in the other that you obey him in all things when he commands.

    But if you have obtained a shepherd who is untrained, inexperienced, or certainly less suitable, take care, I beg you, not to wish rashly to examine his actions. Rather think that your sins deserve to have an unprofitable shepherd. Consider in him not what he is, but what he is called; and honor the shepherd for the love and reverence of Him whose vicariate he bears. Remember at all times that the obedience which you promised to God is to be rendered purely and simply to His vicar; for if the abbot is bad in his conduct, nevertheless he does not lose the vicariate of Christ unless he is [lawfully?] deposed. Nor does the reprobate life of your shepherd absolve you from the obedience promised in religion.

    The meaning of our customary proverb must be upheld: reprobate monks do not deserve to have a good abbot. Do not think, dearest brothers, that this example has been brandished against you. For I trust that I am not a bad shepherd, although I cannot deny that I am untrained and inexperienced; nor have we ever admitted any evil suspicion of you, since we seek nothing more than to nourish and enlarge brotherly charity in all things.

    Frequently monks come to us, wandering either with reason or without cause, who for the most part turn the matter of their own instability back upon their abbots. And I, who desire you to be instructed in everything holy and useful, paternally exhort and warn your Charity that henceforth you do not lend your ears to these circumcellions, who disparage the ways of their own shepherds and strive to hide their own crimes by [accusations?] against others. This is not the necessary integrity of monastic discipline: to turn the cause of the rebellion and disobedience of subjects back upon the head of the shepherd.

    He who is a true monk does not rashly judge the affairs of others; and he who is a son of humble obedience does not search out causes for rebellion. But he who gives consent to the passions of the flesh can never be at rest; and he who scrutinizes another's life is a despiser of his own salvation. A monk grounded in the love of God does not judge the command of his superior; and he who always beholds Christ as present venerates his shepherd as an angel of God.

    Audacity makes a monk degenerate, and presumption has cast many into prison. An insolent, wanton, and headstrong monk has lost the resolve of holiness, and unless he is recalled to his senses by hard chastisement of the flesh, he has already set his foot toward hell. He who weighs the command of his superior with inquisitive rashness is not obedient; and he who is grieved at an order is not a true disciple of Christ. For true obedience does not murmur, does not hesitate, does not seek a loophole, does not delay, does not excuse itself, nor show a hostile sign of reluctance. At the command of the superior, for the love of Christ it always rejoices, comes gladly, and obeys cheerfully with haste.

    For what else is a monk but an anxious contender, who, armed with the virtues of humility and obedience, always keeps watch in the arena of contest, and, victorious under the triple battle-line, fights more strongly against his own self? Blessed is that monk who, making himself nothing in his own eyes, has learned to overcome the will of the flesh, and through the continual practice of spiritual warfare climbs the steep mountain of true obedience. Truly blessed is that monk who, despising all the consolations of the world, has placed his whole self in the love of Jesus Christ, and now desires nothing more among visible things.

    It is not for monks to seek riches, honors, and pleasures in this world; nor is it fitting for a soldier of Christ to think of anything other than Christ. O monk three and four times blessed, who for the love of Christ mortifies his own will to the end of life and humbly perseveres in true obedience.

    How great a good humble obedience is before God, my brothers, no one can adequately express; divine testimony chose to prefer it to all sacrifices. It is obedience that reconciles the soul to God, and through the shedding of blood crowns martyrs.

    [Blank page in the source scan.]

    Homily XXI.

    [unclear]: for love of him you have set me, an unworthy man, over you as abbot. For I shall not be burdensome to you while you run well; but if anyone turns aside from the way of truth, I am compelled, even unwillingly, to oppose him as best I can.

    A monk should always think of his entrance into the monastery, and never forget the first purpose of his institution. In all your works also, O monk, always consider that you will not remain long upon the earth, but that shortly you will depart from this life, and perhaps will die when you do not expect it. Therefore keep inviolate the purpose of holiness, and always be vigilant in good works, so that when the Lord comes and calls you, he may find you prepared. Remember that you are a pilgrim on earth, and have here no abiding city; but just as a traveler hastens quickly toward the end of his journey, so death draws near to you daily without interruption. Therefore while you are healthy, set in order the house of your conscience, so that you may not fear death; for he rarely dies well who is not prepared as though he were to die daily.

    O how securely does the monk depart from this life who, keeping his conscience clean in all purity, lives at all times without reproach according to the integrity of the rule of our most holy lawgiver, even unto death. Let your mind continually hold in memory our Lord Jesus Christ as present, indeed as nowhere absent; and let no hour pass in which you do not think with thanksgiving of him suffering for you. Stand in humility and true obedience, and no adversities will ever prevail against you. Just as a tree, sending many great roots into the earth, is not easily torn from its place, so a monk who possesses charity and obedience in humility, together with the other virtues, is in no way overcome by demons. Obedience, brothers, is a great virtue, which brings the other virtues into the mind, and, once brought in, preserves them through the service of humility. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who was made obedient for us unto the death of the cross, illumine your hearts by his grace; who lives and reigns with God the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for all ages of ages. Amen.

    On continence and true chastity: Homily XXI.

    I would very greatly wish, my dearest brothers, that I had been endowed by God with that grace by which, as your pastor, I might be worthy and suitable in deed as well as in speech. For I know, nor does it escape me, how dangerous a thing the governance of souls is for a young and inexperienced man such as I am, when one who has not yet learned to direct and govern himself according to the rule of justice presumes to enter upon the teaching of others. I blush to open my mouth in your midst to teach, since, after only a short time as a disciple, I am compelled before maturity to be a teacher.

    But since it has so pleased you, and you have wished to have me, a young man, as master, pardon me, because necessity compels me to fulfill, as best I can, the office entrusted to me. Help me, I pray, brothers, with your prayers, so that the mercy of God may bestow the strength that the inexperience of my age denies. For I desire you to walk before God in all purity of mind and body, so that you may be pleasing to him to whom you gave yourselves from the beginning.

    Look upon our Lord Jesus Christ as the leader of the journey undertaken toward heaven: he, born of Mary, the ever most chaste virgin, preserved forever the most perfect chastity of mind and body. Follow this teacher, in whose service you have consecrated your hands, so that you may keep the continence enjoined upon you not only in body, but also perpetually guard chastity with a mind brighter than sapphire and carbuncle. For chastity, a most beautiful virtue, especially befits cloistered persons; through it every impulse of lust is restrained under the yoke of reason, and, when the fury of vices has been extinguished, the bearing of the body preserves all propriety. An incontinent and lascivious monk, who follows the filthy lust of the flesh, is counted with the demons who withdrew from the Lord.

    For there are three things without the perpetual observance of which no one is judged worthy to be named among monks. The first of them is the obedience of humble and true subjection; the second is the renunciation of property, as the rule commands; the third is the inviolate keeping of perpetual continence and chastity. Whatever one of these a monk violates, he has corrupted the purpose of his order. For chastity is sustained by companions, namely fasting and temperance; if at any time it has been deprived of these, without doubt it quickly totters. Chastity is the greatest ornament of monks; adorned with it, they are introduced into the company of angels.

    On continence and true chastity.

    Nothing is more beautiful than chastity: it makes clean what was conceived from unclean seed; from an enemy it also makes a member of the household, and from an earthly man an angel. Chastity is the fairest virtue of all virtues; when it is vowed to be kept for the love of Christ even unto death, it is rewarded with an inestimable prize. Chastity is next to the fellowship of angels, and the supreme medicine of the Christian mind. Chastity is the lovely dwelling of Jesus Christ, the eternal king, and the wondrous beginning of future incorruption. Chastity is the fullness of heavenly grace, through which every corruption of nature is restored. Chastity is the most powerful of all virtues; through it, in a fragile vessel, nature is overcome in a wondrous contest. Chastity imitates the angelic life, and in the midst of mud knows no sprinkling of stain. Blessed is the person who has truly deserved to receive from the Lord God the gift of chastity, and has guarded it inviolate in Christian humility unto death.

    Chaste is he who, for the love of Jesus Christ, pure in mind and body, keeps himself from every defilement of the flesh; who burns sweetly in the love of God with the fervor of the Holy Spirit; who desires absolutely nothing in this world; who firmly restrains [unclear] and his senses.

    Chaste is he who, mindful of the profession of spiritual warfare, suppresses the movements of the flesh by reason, and immediately from the beginning strongly extinguishes all the itching sparks of lust. Chaste is he who flees every material and occasion of lust; who has made a covenant with his eyes that he should not even think of a woman; and who sets a guard over his senses, lest any foul or immodest things be brought in. Chaste is he who avoids the company of the wanton, and always turns his eyes away lest he behold vain things. Chaste is he who detests the frequent company of all women, and who at all times regards his own frailty with fear and vigilance as suspect. Indeed, chaste is he who in mind and body imitates angelic nature, and who by holy conduct admits no corruption. Chastity is a gift of grace, not a work of nature or of human industry. Chastity makes the humble monk most pleasing to God, since one who lives in mortal flesh without corruption is a companion of the angels. Whoever has obtained true chastity is always humble; and whoever understands its nature does not arrogate possession of it to himself, but to the Lord who gave it. For no one is chaste by his own powers, since frail man is not sufficient to overcome nature unless he who created nature and all things has granted it. For whenever nature is overcome through chastity, God manifestly works together with man. But chastity itself has a difficult beginning in the young, until the movement of unlawful thought is brought into contempt. Chastity overcomes fornication by fleeing it rather than by fighting it, since lust is girded about with so many subtle weapons that it must be avoided of one’s own accord before it engages. Therefore whenever the mind is touched by movements of lust, divine help should be invoked without delay; no space for deliberation should be given to unclean thought, but as soon as it begins to be felt, it should be brought into contempt by the remedy of forgetfulness.

    With a deceitful enemy, one who always uses ambushes, no conversations at all are to be entered into; and with unclean thoughts [unclear]; and unless you immediately suppress the movements of lust from the beginning, they are strengthened. The holy apostle of Christ, Paul, warns that one must fight against any vices, but fornication alone he commands to be fled.

    We carry about against ourselves the material of [unclear]; therefore he wishes us to flee the enemy. Chastity is nourished by fasting; by gluttony it suffers shipwreck. Therefore, if you love chastity, love fasting, so that it may have necessary nourishment. He who is chaste follows the industry of the bee; and he who is truly a monk, as though adorned with all flowers, is beautified with every virtue. Not everyone who does not know lust is chaste, but he who, in pure and clean flesh, for the love of Christ, obtains [unclear] holiness of mind. Otherwise, what profit is the purity of the dwelling if its inhabitant is foul and unclean? Blind paganism once had its virgins too, sacrificing to Vesta; but because they did not offer the chastity of their bodies to the true God, nor hold right faith in mind, they descended with their demons, those whom they worshiped, into the depth of hell.

    For chaste is he who, for love of the Creator, restrains the flesh from every lust, and offers his mind to God himself, adorned in every way with holy virtues. [unclear]

    [unclear] of Jesus Christ, today there is no true chastity, nor one meritorious unto eternal salvation. Live chastely, O monk; conduct yourself pure and holy; and as long as the spirit remains in the body, do not presume, from the mire, to have confidence in chastity.

    The food of chastity is fasting and abstinence, and in every action the firm support of wholesome continence. But when you have attained all things, do not trust; for he whom we know to have eaten nothing fell from heaven. The mortification of the body is both very necessary and useful for preserving the beauty of chastity; but however much you have advanced in both, do not trust in your own self, but, always watchful and hoping in the help of the Lord, fear. For unless you continually and most urgently keep yourself in the fear of the Lord, the house of your conscience will quickly be overturned.

    He runs in vain who presumes to guard chastity by his own strength. For unless the Lord has built the chaste dwelling, he labors fruitlessly who constructs the wall of abstinence. And unless you, with all your strength, have stood forth as a co-worker of divine grace, you will in no way obtain the beauty of chastity. For God will not make you chaste without your will, nor will you obtain this great gift unless he comes to the aid of your weakness through his mercy. It will therefore be yours, O monk, with good will, to offer the desire of chastity, and in humble confidence to await sure increase from the Lord. Apply effort, and the Lord’s help will not be lacking.

    Chastity is a gift of grace, not of nature; and to live in the flesh beyond the flesh belongs to angelic strength, not human. Nevertheless it is not difficult for a man of good will to preserve chastity, especially one who is separated from the tumult of worldly people and lives solitary in the midst of monks. A monk also who, young and innocent, enters a monastery of good reformation, if he continually occupies his mind in the fear of the Lord, is less assaulted by lust. For experience of desire is pernicious, since, as someone truly said, Venus wishes to conquer souls, not to satisfy them. But a monk who is zealous for his own salvation can easily extinguish the burning of desire if, fleeing idleness and fullness, he is willing to occupy himself continually in spiritual exercise.

    Indeed, among all vices none assaults chastity more greatly and dangerously than security and idleness. If a monk has overcome these two evils, he will easily guard chastity. Hence the most holy princes of monks, wishing to cut off the causes of desire, established for us a sparing and slender diet according to a fixed measure, so that the body may be sustained for necessity and not grow fat for desire. They also decreed sparing sleep to be useful for monks, because immoderate rest stretches the flesh no less than gluttony. But idleness, as the most pernicious plague of the soul, they wished to be far from cloistered men, most wisely dividing the time so that a monk would never be found idle.

    Hear these things, brothers, and grasp them with the mind, you who carry a great treasure in a fragile little body. Flee idleness; always do something good, so that whenever the tempter, the devil, approaches, he may find you usefully occupied. For truly, the man who is idle lies open to the snares of the tempter; but he who is occupied in a good work has closed every entrance to snares. Therefore the soul must be occupied with continual exercise, so that it is never found idle.

    Blessed is that monk who occupies his mind at every time in good exercises, and never drowses in the sleep of torpor and sloth. Blessed is the spiritual soldier of Christ who always watches in the fear of the Lord and immediately restrains from the beginning all disordered movements of the flesh. For it is not enough, for guarding true chastity unharmed, if anyone dallies as though deliberating with unclean thoughts. The first movements of wicked thoughts must be resisted, since where delay begets danger, one must immediately fight with strength. One must always keep watch against the adversary of our salvation, who is never more quickly conquered than if he is at once suffocated at the beginning.

    Continual exercise is needed, brothers, because the mind always occupied in holy studies is like a very high tower of strength; stationed in it, the most watchful soldier of Jesus Christ fears no snares of hostility. Therefore I beseech you, my dearest brothers, do not consume time in idleness, lest you increase in yourselves the matter of vices, you who are not ignorant of the cunning of the malign spirit. Preserve continence in all things, and apply temperance, the directress of virtues, to all your works. Always consider how you ought to walk before the Lord in all religion and holiness.

    Of continence and true chastity.

    …to God, in whose words you have sworn; and so live that you may not fear to appear in his judgment. You are monks, segregated from the world by voluntary promise into the ministry of our Lord Jesus Christ; whence it behooves you, under the necessity of salvation, to lead a life higher and holier than the rest of your fellow Christians, and to overcome all depravity of flesh and soul. For it behooves you to be always most chaste in mind and body alike, and stained by no filth of corruptible flesh. An incontinent monk is an apostate; and he who defiles his flesh with the filth of women is like one violating an oath. Lust is the pit of hell; and despair is always next to incontinence. A monk who once slips into the fervor of the flesh is rarely kindled to true compunction of heart. For the vice of fornication, growing strong by long habit, is not easily conquered, unless it be amended by force through contrary remedies. It is of greater difficulty to rise again to true chastity after a fall of the flesh than to remain in continence [already] possessed. It is very easy, by the cunning of [feigned] uprightness, to fall into any vice whatever, [rather] than to amend a sin strengthened by habit. For, as a certain gentile truly says, "easy is the descent"; [but] to come together to true [chastity] from the flesh—"this is the work, this the labor." Let us consider those who have fallen into this most shameful pit, and afterward, compelled to penance by the authority of [their] elders, [observe] how they behave in the midst of the brothers. Truly they have no signs of [true] compunction, but in dryness of heart they lead a restless life. No devotion of mind is seen in them, but everywhere they follow the solace of the flesh. O how rarely is anyone converted to the sweetness of inner love who is once cast headlong into the pit of fornication! For unless, before he comes into this misery, he has been founded in the fear of the Lord, [once] fallen he recurs to true compunction with difficulty. Live therefore soberly, dearest brothers, and always watch in holy prayers; for unless you walk most cautiously in all things, you will by no means be able to escape the snares of the demons. Love abstinence; guard humility above all things. For no one can press down the motions of his flesh who has scorned to subdue gluttony and pride. The insolent demon of fornication is never better conquered than if true humility of heart be preserved in the fullness of all virtues. For just as the omnipotent God, resisting the proud, gives grace to the humble, so the devil, fleeing the humble, casts the proud headlong into fornication. He, therefore, who—gluttonous, eating and drinking to satiety—desires to conquer the spirit of fornication, as it were carries oil to the fire. And he who strives to extinguish the motions of lust by abstinence alone is like a man who is seen to swim in the midst of the waves with one hand. Let continual prayer to God be joined to abstinence, and one will sail securely in the ship of holy humility. Let prayer always be in the monk's mouth, and the memory of the passion and death of the Lord Jesus; let him never withdraw from the meditation of it. For nothing so strengthens the mind and soul against the demon of fornication as devout meditation on the passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. As often, therefore, as you feel an inordinate motion of the flesh, as often as [you] perceive the invisible enemy at hand to harm [you], straightway flee to the Son of God hanging on the cross; and with knees bent to the ground let such a prayer be formed by [you]: "O Jesus, my crucified love, by the pain of your wounds have mercy on me; by the shedding of your most holy blood help me in this struggle." And by the power of the Savior all petitions are made firm. Nothing more attenuates the ambushes of the ancient enemy, nothing more weakens the strength of his malice, than if a devout servant of Christ [perseveres] in the meditation of the Lord's most bitter passion. As anyone flees before the face of the pursuing judge, so the devil swiftly vanishes from the sight of a monk meditating with attention on the passion and death of the Savior; [and] his motion of wicked thought is extinguished, when the bitterness of Christ's passion is recalled to the mind. Just as snow is dissolved by the warming sun, so the devil is put to flight by meditation on the Lord's passion. The greatest defense of chastity is always to invoke the divine help. But unless straightway, from the beginning of the temptation, you run to the Lord—but [delay]—little by little, from the delay [comes] detriment. For [if] you admit delay in pernicious thoughts, the demons soon bring on an insensible blindness of mind

    Homily XXI. Folio LII.

    [unclear]. For unless the mind has first been blinded, the will does not succumb to the demon. But the spirit of fornication first grievously darkens the mind; afterward it fights until it has cast the blinded man down into sin. Then, after it has cast the monk into the mire of unspeakable crime, it interposes itself in two ways so that he may not rise again to penitence. For either it subtly strives to make the gravity of the sin seem light, so that he may not fear a great punishment; or it recalls the strictness of judgment to the fallen man’s memory, so that he may fall into the pit of despair. By these snares the sinful soul is caught, and the longer it has lain in the depth of misery, the more hardened it becomes.

    Flee idleness, O cloistered men, and shun gluttony and fullness of the belly with all your strength, since the monk who fills his belly with food and drink supplies the demon of fornication with materials for doing harm. Take up true contrition of heart, and restrain the illicit motions of the flesh through the tears of prayer. For no one is able rightly to conquer his body who has not first taken up the goad of contrition. But he cannot attain the grace of holy contrition who [unclear] perfectly deny himself. Yet whoever has perfectly denied himself for the love of Christ, already overcoming the assault of the flesh, will more easily obtain the grace of contrition. For he who is mortified in will desires nothing carnal, nothing shameful.

    But who among us, brothers, would dare to say that he has attained this grace of mortification? Who among us does not know himself to be weak? We run in the stadium of spiritual warfare, and in daily contest we fight against vices. We have received no confidence of peace, even if at times we have peace. The more familiar to us is the weakness of the flesh, the harder are the battles of chastity. Hence we must be especially watchful, since we carry about with us a familiar enemy and endure, as it were, a household instigator of evil. Therefore, as long as we live in this mortality, let us always fear the corrupter of chastity. Let us avoid everything that excites lust, and, as far as we can, let us flee sloth and idleness. For fullness of bread and idleness are the strongest enemies of true chastity; unless they are driven far away by abstinence and by the work of salutary exercise, they threaten chastity with imminent shipwreck.

    Guard your hearts with every watchfulness, O my dearest brothers, and always keep watch in spirit against your adversary, who never sleeps. Arm yourselves with the breastplate of perfect faith in Jesus Christ, so that in deed and belief you may be true Christians. Always be of one mind in brotherly charity, and be without pretense concordant in the true observance of regular discipline. Love fasting and continence; pray always without ceasing. Flee the eye as a destructive plague of the soul, and continually exercise yourselves in holy works. Love silence, and do not flee monastic solitude, if you desire to obtain true purity of mind and body. Keep continual guard over eyes, ears, and speech, lest death enter the soul through the windows. Flee conversations with women, and shun even the touch of holy women as the kindling of fire. No one safely gazes willingly upon what brings the desired sting of death. Always behold with the faithful eyes of the mind, through love, our Lord Jesus Christ dying for you on the cross; occupy yourselves wholesomely each day in his evangelical teaching; give humble thanks alike for his passion and death. If, with continual perseverance, you do these things in true simplicity of heart until death, we trust that you will be rewarded with fellowship among the saints.

    On the brotherly charity of monks. Homily XXII.

    We have heard, my dearest brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ commanding in the holy Gospel: Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do the same also to them. This is indeed a brief but solid commendation of brotherly charity, without which no one can ascend to the love of God. For no one can love God who is convicted of not loving his fellow Christian. Hence the blessed apostle John says: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him. Hence, if anyone says that I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. Therefore holy Paul, lover of Christ, exhorts us, saying: Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. And Peter, prince of the apostles, admonished us thus: Before all things, he says, having constant mutual charity among yourselves, because charity [unclear].

    On the Brotherly Charity of Monks.

    It covers a multitude of sins. How necessary brotherly charity is for salvation the Lord of all, Jesus Christ, made clear, saying: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. The second is like unto it: Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” For whatever is commanded anywhere in the whole course of the Scriptures is without doubt referred to these two commandments.

    Here by “neighbor” we understand not one joined by the necessity of blood, but every man by the fellowship of reason, and especially the Christian, whom each person is commanded to love as himself, with whom he is seen to await eternal salvation. But you, brothers, it especially befits to love one another in the true charity of the Savior Jesus, upon whom the monastic profession enjoins with all your strength to strive toward the summit of perfection. For as covetousness is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all goods. First you ought to love God above all things with a pure heart for his own sake, because he is the highest good; and then to love your neighbor with sincere charity for the Lord’s sake.

    These two precepts of charity are joined by the authority of Christ, so that one can in no way be fulfilled without the other. For he who truly loves God cannot hate his neighbor. If he hates his neighbor, he does not truly love God. For the love of God begets love of neighbor, and through love of neighbor the love of God is nourished. If one of these loves is lacking, the other by no means grows strong. For he who does not truly love his neighbor shows himself empty of the love of God. Therefore we love truly when we love our neighbor, that is, every Christian man, more diligently with sincere intention.

    For brotherly charity is the bond of peace, which alone nourishes concord in a dwelling and preserves Christian unity among brothers. Charity is the begetter of gentleness and the noble mother of catholic piety. Brotherly charity is fearful to demons, since it makes victorious all those whose inner court of the heart it surrounds. Charity extinguishes the fire of lust and covers every multitude of sins. Charity renders men most dear to God and makes them companions of the holy angels. Charity preserves the church in the unity of the saints, outside which no one attains eternal salvation. Brotherly charity orders the morals of the cloistered and makes [God?] dwell in the midst of monks. Charity does injury to no one, but ministers help to all through compassion. Charity drives out every vice, because it is the sole nurse of all virtues. The charity of brotherhood preserves the reform of the cloistered in vigor, and works great salvation of souls. Mutual charity confirms obedience and makes brotherly correction fruitful. Charity nourishes true concord among brothers and preserves the sweet-smelling chastity both of minds and of bodies. Charity makes monks in the house of God to be of one mind, and laudably concordant in every good work. Mutual charity lightens the rigor of the order; and all things that seem hard and harsh to carnal men it changes through habit into nature, as though they were certain very light things. Charity is the most beautiful beauty of monks, adorned with all virtues. Charity utterly drives hatred and envy out of the monasteries of the servants of God, and by its presence makes the remaining deadly crimes flee far away. The charity of brothers is a fitting dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and the fortress of a serene conscience. Charity keeps minds harmless from cruelty and supplies to all a gentle ease of spirit. Brotherly charity seeks the salvation of all and does not allow the one who has it to grow sluggish in idleness. Charity does not abhor want, but from love of the brothers is ready to endure every poverty. Charity is the water of heavenly sweetness; if anyone drinks it in the fervor of the Holy Spirit, he does not dread the perpetual thirst of hell. Brotherly charity does not seek the enticements of the flesh, but directs pure, holy, and unstained affections toward the neighbor. Charity has the name of chaste beauty, which cannot be shared with things or actions of most impure pleasure. Charity loves purity and cleanness, and admits no impurity. Charity, in the operation of love, considers not the flesh of the neighbor but the soul, which it does not doubt was created in the image of God. Brotherly charity raises up the delinquent neighbor by pious admonitions, and keeps all its actions pure and harmless from every malice. Charity walks in peace and tranquillity of mind, and saddens the neighbor neither by word, nor by deed, nor by sign. Charity humbles itself as much as it can in all things, and most lovingly ministers to an infirm neighbor as to the son of God. Cha-

    All, XXII.

    Charity judges no one rashly, but humbly corrects a neighbor who sins with the gentlest admonitions. Charity is terrible and fearful to the reprobate, but loving and kindly to the gentle. Charity counts others’ inconveniences as its own, and weeps for the affliction of the brethren as though it itself suffered. Charity suffers with all who are placed in necessity, and is saddened no less by others’ misfortunes than by its own. Charity reproaches the neighbor with nothing, but for the love of God always bears the weaknesses of all with equanimity. Charity is constant in good works, and as long as it remains in the heart it is never idle. Charity neglects none of those things to which it is bound, but keeps all things with the greatest diligence. Fraternal charity is the fulfillment of the law, since whatever is commanded after the worship of God is referred to love of neighbor. Hence the holy lover of Christ says: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For, You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet the property of your neighbor; and if there is any other commandment, it is renewed in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love of neighbor does no evil. Therefore love is the fullness of the law.” And so, my dearest brethren, we beseech you through our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, that you always keep fraternal charity unharmed, without which you can neither truly love God nor fulfill any commandment of his. For the keeping of fraternal charity is as necessary to you for salvation as the nourishment of food and drink is to bodies for the preservation of life. For the body dies without necessary nourishment, and all the virtues of the soul are scattered without fraternal charity. For fraternal charity preserves the multitude of monks in unity of spirit, since without the bond of mutual love none of those in the cloister perseveres without disturbance of the community. The monk who pursues his brother with hatred is removed far from the charity of God. For the holy evangelist John says: “He who hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes, because darkness has blinded his eyes.” But the chaste and prudent lover of neighbor walks secure in the light of the Holy Spirit, and he is not disturbed by anyone, nor does he disturb anyone else. [unclear] we are immortal. [unclear]

    Folio LIII.

    For true love of neighbor is mild, sweet, and most dutiful, and in all its companionship gentle, peaceable, and tranquil. Yet among those in authority the vigor of discipline guides gentleness, and the clemency of fraternal consideration beautifully tempers vigor. For each must be so tempered by the other that vigor is not rigid, nor love lax. The lover of fraternal charity does not leave the way of justice, and he who rightly loves his neighbor introduces nothing of corruption. For true love of neighbor neither covets another’s possessions nor requires the services of attendants, but, having despised all things that can overthrow the state of the soul, pursues only the soul’s increase. For it is not sincere charity to seek gifts of corruption from one’s neighbors, or, in the manner of children, to love with an affection of likeness one who comes running because little presents are being distributed. The friendship of monks among good men who are zealous for the same purpose ought to be common, and far removed from every affection of the flesh. Let it be pure, simple, right, and lasting without injury to anyone, and let it have in itself nothing of suspicious conspiracy. This is not the rule of fraternal charity: to seek private little meetings of forbidden consolation, and without the prior’s blessing to devote oneself to secret, indeed prohibited, conversations. You expend your love upon your neighbor not rightly but rather perniciously whenever, contrary to the form of regular observance, it comes together for the solace of the flesh. The love of a monk ought to be solid and very far removed from every transgression of regular discipline, since charity that either gives to a neighbor or receives consolations harmful to the spirit was never sincere. Therefore take care to direct the eye of the mind not to the beauty of the flesh but rather to the contemplation of the soul, if you wish rightly and laudably to love your neighbors. For when the flesh is loved without regard for the soul, not sincere but carnal and impure love is generated. Consider that your brother has a soul like yours, and always think that both of you await an equal happiness. Whether we understand it of the belly or of the soul, we are immortal by soul, not by body.

    On the brotherly charity of monks.

    On the brotherly charity of monks.

    [Unclear] one is commanded to love in another, and to direct the regard of charity toward the soul rather than toward the body. For just as we are distinguished from brute animals by reason and understanding, so the gaze of our love should be referred to the mind, by which we understand, not to the body, which we have in common with beasts.

    Far from holy monks be all affections of the flesh, for they know the rule of mutual and sincere charity. Let love toward one another be pure, upright, and conceived from fear of God alone, so that no advantage of any corruptible thing intervene, but the simple intention of charity remain.

    But charity, simple and pure, [unclear] does not seek the byways of evil conspiracy; nor does it [unclear]. In giving to each his due, it does injury to no one, and whatever it does not wish to be done to itself, it never transfers to the person of another. Do not think that he possesses true charity of brotherhood in his heart who [unclear]. It preserves peace in all things and raises no matter or cause of destructive dissension.

    Charity, giving to each one his due, does injury to no one, and whatever it does not wish to be done to itself, it never transfers to the person of another. Do not think that you have true brotherly charity when you love one another with a view to the flesh or to the advantage of some temporal thing; for where the Lord is not the cause of love, the affection of the one who loves is always faulty, either in part or in whole. But he rightly loves his brother who loves him with the love of God and on account of the common participation in the kingdom which we await.

    Therefore, as Saint John the bishop says, we have been baptized into one body of the Church, so that we may not be dissolved, but in that concord and friendship which belong to one body we may preserve forever charity and mutual harmony with one another. Just as no one outside the unity of the Catholic Church can obtain salvation, so no one without brotherly charity is believed able to be saved.

    Charity, then, is necessary for you before all things for salvation; without it, the remaining works of the virtues are utterly fruitless. For there can be nothing good, nothing of saving merit for life, which has not drawn its origin from it. Charity is a kind of short road to the virtues; if anyone enters upon it by the straight path of the journey, he will need no guidance of a leader.

    Pure, simple, and upright charity is not accustomed to injure one’s neighbor, nor to inflict evil on anyone. Charity is accustomed to expend its affection [unclear] for all, and whatever it hopes will conduce to its own salvation, it desires this to be common to all people in Christ Jesus. Charity performs the office of love without any disturbance; and though it loves all people exceedingly, yet for no one is it provoked to bitter zeal. It is always solid, always constant, always stable and firm, because it is touched neither by passions nor agitated by movements of unrest.

    It offers itself as common to all, and bestows its love on individuals in such a way that nevertheless it seems nearest to all. Charity, in those things which pertain to the reason of the mind and soul, does not neglect itself; but in those things which concern the advantage of the body, it often sets the causes of others before its own benefits. Great is the command of true charity, which compels a person to make another’s inconvenience his own.

    Therefore you, my brothers, who have solemnly girded yourselves for Christ’s warfare, who through the arduous road of obedience long for eternal life: if you do not wish to run in vain in the arena of so laborious a contest, take care, we exhort you, above all things always to preserve brotherly charity inviolable within you. For unless you have sincere and perfect charity toward one another, you labor without fruit in regular observance.

    Abstinence from eating meat will contribute nothing to you toward the salvation of souls; the renunciation of all private property will profit nothing toward the attainment of eternal happiness, if in your hearts [unclear] does not hold a place.

    Therefore, desiring to be saved with Christ in truth, love one another; and as Christ loved you, so, we pray, love one another. Whatever each one of you desires to be done to himself, let him bestow that very thing upon his brother without envy, for the love of God, at all times.

    Let divine love conquer in you all quarrels of the flesh and any contentions whatsoever; and let no destructive dissension of the flesh find a place where the fullness of brotherly charity ought continually to dwell. For if all of you in the monastery live according to the law of Christian instruction, you necessarily always abstain from injuring one another. But if through contentions and wrongs you wound one another mutually, you are certainly neither monks nor true Christians. For it befits all cloistered persons and monks to be outstanding in the observance of charity and to be far removed from the rancor of envy and hatred.

    If therefore the monk, stable in the purpose of holiness until death, is faithful in the ministry of God, so that also in love

    Homily XXIII. Fol. LIII.

    ... of the Creator may sweetly burn, and never withdraw from purity of conscience. For whoever perfectly loves the Lord God with his whole heart, and keeps his conscience clean from every pollution of sin, always shows charity to his neighbor pure and sincere. But he whom either envy burns, or hatred stirs up against a brother, is manifestly neither truly loving God nor having a pure and upright conscience. Therefore everyone who persecutes his brother with hatred and indignation is neither a true monk nor worthy of the name Christian, but in merit and conduct a minister and companion of demons. Therefore let hatreds depart far from this holy congregation of yours; let there be among you no destructive contests of contention; let no zeal of bitterness be found there; let no speech of [unclear] pride be heard. Let the concord of brotherly unity flourish here continually; let the innocence of Christian purity adorn the consciences of each one, so that we may live in this brief time in such a way that after death we may glory with Christ in eternity.

    On Man’s Love toward God.

    Homily XXIII.

    Nothing is so just, nothing so holy; nothing in human actions can be so honorable as always to love God with the whole heart and with all one’s strength above all things, and for love of him to fear neither death nor any kinds of punishments. There is in us no greater cause for any action than divine love, because, since God is the author of all things, nothing is loved more justly than he; and since he is the greatest of all goods, nothing is loved more fruitfully than he. God first loved us: the highest loved the lowest, the greatest the little ones, the omnipotent the weak. Therefore, my brothers, let us love the Lord God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, by whom we are most sweetly loved; he not only created us in his own image and likeness, but, which is the greatest proof of love, mercifully called us through the teaching and death of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, to the kingdom of eternal blessedness. Never did any fleshly mother love her only-begotten son so tenderly, sincerely, and strongly as almighty God loved us; for our instruction he not only willed to become man, but also deigned to undergo death in the flesh he had assumed for our salvation. No greater love has ever existed, if we rightly consider who it was who endured such things for us. For out of love for us, he who was free from the debt of death voluntarily dies; and he who had always remained immune from every sin, innocent and righteous, is condemned [unclear] for our sins. Therefore it is commanded us by the most just reasoning that we love the Lord our God with our whole heart, who, when we did not exist, created us out of his goodness alone, and when we had perished, mercifully freed us.

    Love of God is the greatest of all virtues, since whatever good, whatever virtue, is done in this world, if it is not done from charity toward God, is void of reward. Charity toward God purifies the conscience from every fault, because he who truly loves the Lord his God with his whole soul and in his whole heart and with all his strength undoubtedly grants no place in his conscience to vices. For it is certain that into the heart which the love of God occupies, no uncleanness of vices enters. The love of God is an unfailing treasure: he who possesses it is richer than all the wealthy of the world; he who lacks it is more wretched than all the poor. Hence the holy apostle of Christ says: “For those who love God, all things work together for good,” since nothing is lacking to those who fear him. Happy is the man in whose heart no attachment of earthly love dwells besides the love of Christ; who sighs for the memory of no human being; in whose conscience purity resides, and divine love always burns most ardently. Love him, O my brothers, who for love of you descended into the Virgin’s womb; always carry him in your hearts, who by his death opened heaven to you. Let the love of Christ be in you at all times, brothers, strong as death, so that your life may be conformed to Christ’s teaching; and when it is necessary to die for his love, you may not then fear, just as he himself first deigned calmly and kindly to undergo death for us. For the love of Christ makes a monk near to God, and he who is always fervent in the charity of the Lord will attain the fellowship of angels. The love of Christ makes a man most strong against all the assaults of demons, and no less in adversities than

    On Man’s Love toward God.

    [unclear] in prosperity, patience together with [unclear]. The love of Christ teaches one truly to despise the world, to account all its delights and all the comforts of the flesh as nothing. The love of Christ quickly weakens the illicit movements of the flesh; it brings into the mind a most pure chastity. The love of Christ sweetly raises the mind to heavenly things by desire for him; separated from earthly things, it preserves it in spiritual exercise. The love of God makes all hard and rough things smooth; for where Christ is loved in truth, tribulations and any adversities are counted as delights. The love of God is always assiduous in good works, and is never [unclear]. The love of God despises present things, and powerfully raises the mind to eternal things. The love of God neither seeks honors nor seeks riches, but, [crucified together?] with Christ through desire, covets absolutely nothing except that. The love of God remits to the penitent the multitude of sins, of deed, and the faults of all. The love of God suddenly justifies the impious man; and the more love has grown, the more perfection [unclear], and the more strongly it is cultivated. The love of God is a tower of strength, to which none of all the ministers of diabolical depravity can approach. The love of God is the consummation of all justice and the end of monastic discipline. The love of God [unclear] the monk and makes him complete in all good works. The love of God is [unclear] of inward sweetness, by which all filth of earthly corruption is driven out from the mind. The love of God honors souls and makes them pure and immaculate from all stains. The love of God perfectly illumines the mind in all knowledge of heavenly goods, and by pious affection purges it from all unclean vanities. The love of God makes the one who truly has it most learned, and wonderfully instructed in every scripture. The love of God makes the monk formidable to all enemies, and confers angelic power on those who persevere. The love of God defends a man in dangers, since whoever truly loves God fears no opposing things. The love of God makes the one who has it secure in the hour of death and safe from demons, and joins the soul to the heavenly companies. The love of God leads its possessor back to the heavenly homeland, and confers on souls the everlasting glory of God. The love of God is the greatest of all good works, and, in the faith of the one Christ, the foundation of all virtues. The love of God is the best thing in the universe, in which all things are [unclear].

    Homily 23.

    Fol. LV.

    ... while we walk innocently in spirit. He truly loves God who, always intent on good works, keeps himself pure and unstained from this world. But he loves the Lord God rightly who desires absolutely nothing in this world. He truly loves God with all his heart who, for love of him, bravely despises the world’s honors, riches, pleasures, and all comforts of the flesh.
