He loves God with all his soul who, always solicitous in the observance of his commandments, does not neglect to do any of the things that are pleasing to him. For the love of God neglects [nothing], but is accustomed to preserve and fulfill most diligently everything that he has commanded. Whoever loves God in true charity has fulfilled the law, the prophets, and the Gospel. Therefore by your works you will bear witness whether you truly love God.

    For everyone who has deserved to receive the root of divine love always shows great and manifest signs of love. Indeed, the fire of divine love makes the one who possesses it pious in all things, chaste, gentle, and most humble, and, both in adversity and in prosperity, always tranquil in the same constancy of mind, without disturbance. The monk who truly loves the Lord God will, according to the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, always obey the commands of his seniors cheerfully in all things; in hardships and adversities he embraces patience and everywhere preserves true humility. The love of God makes its possessor very rich in all good works, and renders him far removed from every kind of vice. The lover of God does not murmur at the command of obedience; in accusations he does not rashly excuse himself; he does not touch his neighbor with the gall of bitterness, nor is he disturbed even when injured. Whoever is a true lover of God preserves his life irreproachable in all purity of mind and body, and demonstrates in himself a fervent charity not only in word but also in deed and truth.

    Whatever beautiful, whatever pleasant or delightful thing is seen in the world, whatever flatters the wantonness of lascivious flesh, the true lover of God despises it all with the utmost constancy, and desires nothing other than to please Christ and to live with him as soon as possible. Great and incredible to those who do not know it is the power of divine love, which always impels a man to work well and never allows him to live idle. For what else is the inward love of God than a sweet drunkenness of the soul, by which a man is snatched away from all the consolations of the world and, as if he felt nothing of what mortals do, is enriched in the fellowship of the Holy Spirit alone? Whoever is a true lover of God, being a monk, has put away for Christ’s sake every curiosity of the world and every solicitude for worldly things; and, as if he did not feel them, he transcends in his soul all the stings of cares. Hence with the Apostle he cries: The world has been crucified, and I to the world.

    O wine of divine love, how sweetly you make drunk, how innocently you satisfy, how wisely you make foolish, how chastely you inflame. For everyone who has been made drunk by your savor, separated from every tumult of carnal pleasures, rests sweetly in the shadow of the Holy Spirit. Because of the exceeding drunkenness of the spirit, he speaks things alien to carnal and worldly people, and nothing contrary to God is heard from his mouth. This is the unstained satiety of spiritual wine, which is extended so much the more through desire, the longer it is continued. O holy and venerable simplicity of the lover of Christ: even if to many who savor earthly things it seems to be folly, nevertheless before God and all his saints it is the greatest and truly the highest wisdom. Let the world have its prudence; let it have honors, dignities, and riches. But I would choose the merit of one simple monk truly loving God rather than the sovereignty of the whole world.

    The love of God is the soul’s highest and always most chaste pleasure; its burning enlightens the mind and sweetly inflames the affection. The love of God is the fountain of heavenly grace, because the grace of the Holy Spirit makes fruitful with the fruits of all virtues the mind which Christ’s charity purifies by ploughing. The love of Christ reconciles human beings to the friendship of almighty God and reveals to mortals the will of the highest majesty. The love of God makes the monk acceptable to God, because he requires from us not knowledge, not learning, not eloquence, but charity. Therefore the monk who has publicly offered himself to the Lord God ought to care for nothing except God, lest he seem to have a divided heart; for just as God is one, so love toward God cannot be divided. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: He loves you less, Lord, who loves anything together with you which he does not love for your sake. Just as God is perfect, so also he must be loved by us with that strength [unclear], because he does not withdraw...

    On the love of man toward God.

    [unclear]: whenever, besides him, something is loved together with him. The love of God then advances rightly when nothing is mixed into it that could weaken it. Let each one of you, as much as he can, strive with the whole strength of his mind to love the Lord his God above all things, because love for God alone is what will open for you the gate of paradise. For the more ardently you now love God, the greater glory you will receive in the heavenly homeland. Happy is that monk in whose conscience, besides the love of Christ, no imagining of any occupation remains; who, waking, thinks of nothing other than Christ; sleeping, dreams of Christ; living and dying, sighs most steadfastly for Christ. O how well and securely he dies who has always been solicitous in the exercise of divine love, and at all times zealous in the observance of God's commandments. For only the love of God is admitted into the kingdom of heaven; and the more fervent the mind has been in loving, the greater will be the reward in the kingdom of heaven. He who loves much, even then, is to receive less in glory. Therefore let each person love as much as he can, from his whole heart and from his whole soul and from his whole strength, because our God is not to be loved lukewarmly or sluggishly, but fervently, wisely, and sweetly. The love of God grows and is increased by spiritual exercises, just as a blazing fire spreads when wood is supplied. For indeed, if the wood is withdrawn, the fire is extinguished; and if spiritual exercises are interrupted, charity is soon shipwrecked. But true love of God is never idle, but at all times is delightfully occupied in those things that nourish and preserve charity. For the lover of his God never forgets his beloved, but always meditates on his presence and beauty; and now in most devout prayers he speaks to Jesus, now in the holy Scriptures he marvels at him speaking to himself. The true lover of Christ meditates day and night on the law of the Lord, and with the greatest diligence does everything that he understands to be pleasing to God. O how sweetly he burns whom the love of God has truly inflamed; how pleasantly he glows whose mind the flame of the Holy Spirit has set alight. Blessed is that monk who, full of divine love, wholly withdraws himself from earthly vanities and rests in the shade of heavenly desire. O if we had love for God so strong, so whole—

    On serenity of conscience.

    Homily 23.

    With great solicitude we must keep watch, dearly beloved brothers, and with continual meditation take care that we always keep our conscience, whose testimony we cannot evade, clean and unstained from every contagion. Nothing is more beautiful, nothing more pleasant, nothing, finally, more precious than a good conscience; when a mind, having in itself the manifest testimony of its own rectitude, suffers no remorse of destructive unease. An upright and good conscience is an incredible exultation of the mind and a sure consolation in every adversity. The monk who has obtained the testimony of a good conscience neither refuses even to live nor fears the coming of future death. A good conscience is always joyful, always pleasant, always fearless, and truly tranquil in the peace of Jesus Christ. In a good conscience there is always peace, piety, goodness, light, virtue, honor, joy, gladness, sweetness, and pleasantness without dissolution. Conscience is the treasury of the soul, because whatever is placed in it is preserved for the provision of the future life. A good conscience is the best treasure; if anyone neglects to have it, he must be judged the most wretched and most unhappy of all men. A good conscience is the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit and an earthly paradise of all graces. A good conscience does not fear the detractions of the wicked, and a mind conscious of rightness despises the lies of rumor. A good conscience is always cheerful, and he who—

    Homily 23. Fol. LVI.

    He who works the righteousness of God is not sorrowful to no purpose. A good conscience always advances in the love of the Lord; and he who lives innocently will not fear danger. A good conscience has peace and concord with all in God, and cares for its own salvation in humble simplicity. A good conscience strengthens the soul; but he who is constant in evils will fall into despair. A good conscience confidently reproves the foolish man; but he who is evil keeps a bitter silence. A good conscience gladdens the soul; but he who is conscious of his own evils suffers continual desolation of mind. A good conscience rebukes the impious man; but he who has lost the testimony of uprightness always fears reproof. A good conscience is the most beautiful adornment of the soul; and he who does not care for wisdom in this life will die in want. A good conscience is the dwelling-place of virtues and the true mansion of heavenly mysteries. A good conscience is the consummation of all philosophy and the fullness of all sciences. A good conscience is the best teacher of virtues, and the completed discipline of all studies. A good conscience bears the best fruit of holiness; and, standing founded in the fear of the Lord, admits no sin. A good conscience is more precious than all the wealth of the world, and much sweeter than all desirable things that can be had in this life. A good conscience is the merit of Christian perfection, and the beginning from which future blessedness may humbly be presumed. A good conscience is a fertile field of virtues, and the sweet and pleasant fragrance of the paradise of God. A good conscience is the sweetest companion of this life, and a glorious mediator between God and man. A good conscience is very fearful to demons, but a pleasing friend to the holy angels. A good conscience makes the dying man secure against the snares of demons, and deserves to have the escort of angels. A good conscience does not fear to appear in the sight of the judge, nor does it fear the judgment of accusing synderesis. A good conscience has hope in God, and, without hesitation, in quietness, the best confidence; for he who remembers that he has committed no evil comes confidently to the examination of judgment. A good conscience will be richly rewarded by the Lord God, and is changed into everlasting joy. A good conscience is not one that commits no evil, but one that, for love of God, preserving purity from every sin, also most becomingly adorns itself by the exercise of all good works. For a good conscience, according to the admonition of the prophet, wholly turns away from evil, and with the most zealous intention always and continually does good. A good conscience especially adorns a monk, and makes him far removed from secular actions. A good conscience follows the Lord Jesus in simple purity, and is stained by no spots of errors. For a conscience that is good, and as long as it is good, cannot be erroneous, but always remains founded in the truth of the Holy Spirit. But a conscience that has become erroneous is not good. For error both opposes truth and in no way shares in goodness. When conscience is erring, danger is near, and the descent to hell is very steep.

    There are many among cloistered persons who are weak and too feeble in spirit, who, preoccupied by various causes, are not always guided by the right judgment of their consciences. And often, indeed, a small or great error of conscience arises from ignorance: namely, whenever someone less experienced in spiritual exercise doubts whether the way he is considering in his mind is good or bad. For who, walking rightly in his simplicity, understands all things? In doubtful matters the counsels of elders are to be sought; and what they have decreed, the monk should not hesitate to embrace as a judgment of truth. Sometimes conscience errs from negligence, when a monk neglects to examine himself by the scrutiny of reason and does not labor to seek out truth in doubtful matters. From this a pernicious error arises in the conscience, through which reason is gradually darkened. Frequently also pride makes conscience erroneous and far removed from the knowledge of truth. For the proud man, although he understands that he does not know, nevertheless desires to appear wise and learned to all; therefore he is ashamed to confess his ignorance. Sometimes, moreover, error of conscience arises from singularity, with which presumption is always [said to be] mingled. But this plague is often troublesome to monks and to those who profess holiness without the necessary foundation of humility. For the sheep that walks singular paths is more quickly caught and strangled by wolves. Sometimes also an excessively disordered affection hurls conscience into error: namely, when a man loves his own will more than is fitting. For whoever is led by the affection of his own sensuality is often blinded in the judgment of truth.

    On serenity.

    From this it undoubtedly comes about that many have errors in their consciences, because they love too much the pleasures of their own flesh. Every proud, lustful, unclean man, entangled in great or public crimes, darkens his conscience by deliberate perversity; and how wrongly he thinks about the future recompense of deserts, he often makes manifest both by words and by deeds. A malicious affection perverts the judgment of rectitude, and the disordered concupiscence of the flesh clouds the understanding. Sometimes, moreover, excessive and immoderate faintheartedness makes the conscience err; this evil is born partly from ignorance, and partly is generated from one’s own sensuality. In this scrupulosity, however, let the monk follow the counsel either of the abbot or of some elder more experienced, and let him not rashly defend the opinion of his own head. Excessive scrupulosity is dangerous, because it hurls the conscience into error and unhappily trips up many. For everything that is done against conscience is said to build toward hell. Excessive perplexity of mind has also harmed many, and has cast them headlong into various errors. But he who is truly a humble monk brings himself to the examination of his ruler. For whoever, in doubts that arise, makes use of the counsel of his superior is not easily tripped up by the snares of demons. For the more the consciences of monks have been exposed to the examination of a wise prelate, the more secure and more brightly shining they will be.

    Therefore, dearest brothers, care must first be taken that you have consciences free from every error; then pure from all vice; and finally adorned with the holy works of all virtues. Therefore let the monk who desires to make progress in truth guard his heart with every custody, and, so far as can be done, apply a closure to his senses, nor permit anything deadly to enter. But if, by any occasion, he recognizes that he has fallen into some sin, let him at once strive to blot it out by true penitence, and let him not grant time to the wicked seed to grow stronger for the worse. While the wound is small, let a remedy be applied, because if it is neglected it grows beyond measure. Therefore, my brothers, resist bravely the first movements of demonic suggestion, and overcome the enemy when he is small and weak. But if the sensuality of the body has become altogether wanton, let it be brought back to obedience by harsh mortification, just as we know our holy father Benedict did, when he rooted out the slippery wantonness of the flesh by the stings of nettles and briars. Finally, if you diligently recall to memory the dreadful future punishments of the impious, you will easily repress the illicit movements of the flesh. For there is no one who does not fear pain more than he loves pleasure. Bring back more often to your mind also the joys of heavenly felicity, to which you desire to come; for if you consider them faithfully, you will strongly mitigate the fire of the flesh. Whatever delights in the world is corruptible and momentary; but the joys of eternal pleasures remain without end forever. It is therefore foolish and of extreme madness to choose a transitory advantage and to despise that good which remains forever. He is judged foolish among men who prefers a basket to gold; but he is held most senseless before God who sets temporal pleasure before eternal goods.

    He who loves a serene conscience should flee idleness, since, as Scripture says, every idle man is in desire, and idleness has taught much wickedness. The soul must be occupied with good exercises, and the fire of holy conversation, which burns with charity, must be nourished by continual use. For the idle man lives neither for himself nor for his neighbor, but is always given over to his belly or to sleep; he opens his mind to vice, and keeps it closed and empty of virtues. Idleness, the kindler of lust, quickly extinguishes the fervor of spiritual devotion. Abstinence also is very necessary for a monk above all, so that his conscience may remain clean. For, as Saint Jerome says, a full belly easily foams into lust, and he who nourishes his servant delicately will find him insolent. The lover of serenity of conscience is constant in holy prayers, since, as dogs flee a stone, so demons flee devout and continual prayer. Let him also diligently beware of acedia and, at the same time, sadness of mind; and as soon as he feels some temptation creeping in, let him have recourse to the consolation of the Scriptures. For [unclear] the mind which the word of God has filled, a foul thought will enter. Whatever we do, whatever we think, whatever we perform, let us know that the presence of God is always at hand, and we shall easily overcome disordered delight. A good conscience never forgets the presence of God, but always meditates that its judge is present.

    Homily XXV. Fol. LVII.

    Come now, my brothers, so that you may have consciences pure from every crime; and if anyone feels himself burdened in some offense, let him return without delay, through true penitence, to the necessary purity. For unless at all times you have clean and good consciences, you live as apostates, not monks.

    On Continual Preparation for Death. Homily XXV.

    The highest philosophy of cloistered men, my dearest brothers, is continual meditation on death. Hence a certain wise man, considering the usefulness of this philosophy, admonished every mortal, saying: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.

    Meditation on death draws a man back from the pleasures of the flesh and brings on contempt for all corruptible things. Meditation on death despises present things through voluntary poverty and drives the mind toward desire for things to come. Meditation on death drives pride far away and plants true humility in the heart of the one meditating. Meditation on death makes the monk solicitous about the observance of regular discipline and never permits him to be idle. Meditation on death cuts off all the vanities of the world and preserves the mind in the highest temperance. Meditation on death makes one despise the vain and transitory honors of the world and think of nothing but the future judgment of God. Meditation on death does not fear the poverty of this life, because it desires eternal riches with its whole longing. Meditation on death endures all adversities of this world most patiently for the love of Christ, because it hopes for nothing but the heavenly reward.

    Meditation on death makes the monk humble and obedient in all commands of rectitude. Meditation on death makes the monk quiet and stable in the congregation, and well in concord with all in Christ. Meditation on death makes the monk quiet and peaceful, and tranquil without any disturbance of mind. Meditation on death exterminates all dissolutions and levities, and preserves the monk mature and salutarily sorrowful in all things. Meditation on death makes the monk solitary and continually devoted to holy prayers. Meditation on death hastens penitence and brings in true compunction. Meditation on death withdraws desire from every vanity and keeps the conscience serene and most pure. Meditation on death makes a man despise all the comforts of this world and prepare daily for departure. Meditation on death teaches one to flee idleness and makes a man watch continually in the fear of the Lord.

    Meditation on death does injury to no one, because it always fears the strict account of judgment. Meditation on death mitigates anger and all disordered movements, because when a man thinks that he will soon die, nothing external disturbs the mind. Meditation on death makes the heart contrite and humble, because attentive memory of future things permits no one to be proud. Continual meditation on death makes one’s departure safe at the last, because it has made the one meditating over a long time prepared.

    Meditation on death is especially fitting for cloistered men and monks, whom renunciation of all earthly things and the very profession of the rule have already made dead and buried to the world. Meditation on death [unclear] to run prudently in the warfare and to renew daily the purpose of holy fervor. Continual meditation on death is very useful to cloistered men, because it both powerfully represses the vices of the flesh and grants no entrance to perverse thoughts of the mind.

    For the holy bishop Augustine says: Fear concerning future death necessarily [concutit?] the mind, and, like a nail of the flesh, fastens all movements of pride to the wood of the cross. And the holy champion of the Church Jerome says: Nothing will profit you so much for temperance in all things as frequent thought of the shortness of life, whose end is certain, but nothing is more uncertain than its hour. Therefore meditation on death corrects all intemperance and orders the conduct of the one meditating, stable in beautiful variety. Meditation on death grants true wisdom to a man and perfects the highest philosophy among cloistered men. For it was also Plato’s opinion that the whole life of the wise is meditation on death, because we are all born under this condition: that from here we depart again through death. For Scripture says: We all die, and like waters we slip away into the earth, which do not return again. And the holy apostle of Christ, Paul, says: It is appointed, he says, for men to die once and

    On continual preparation for death.

    Continual meditation on necessary death makes a person never trust in earthly things, but await his departure in every place and time with foresight. Meditation on death always expects the end of life in every place, because it is wholly ignorant of the point of dying. Whoever daily meditates on the coming of future death disposes himself for dying at every time with all the diligence he can. For nothing is more certain to us than death, although we all do not know the hour of dying. Therefore, brothers, with all the urgency we can, we admonish your charity that you always think that you are going to die, and that with such foresight you diligently prepare yourselves for dying that, when the hour of departure comes, you may not fear.

    Let no one promise himself a long life in this world, because nothing so deceives mortals as the hope of a longer age. For what does a more prolonged age accomplish in human beings except that it makes them liable to more offenses and always less disposed for dying? The longer we live in this world, the more we fear death. A longer age accumulates greater debts of spiritual obligation; and the old man fears all the more to come before the sight of the strict judge, the more he recognizes before the Lord that he is bound to render account in many things. For the soul leaves its body unwillingly when it is driven by the heavier goads of its conscience. But he who is pure from all wickedness of iniquity and adorned for salvation with the necessary comeliness of virtues does not fear to die, because through death he goes to everlasting life. Therefore, O monk, as you wish to die, so live now, because death cannot be evil when the integrity of a good life has preceded it.

    For anyone dies securely who loves the Lord Jesus above all things and, despising all the goods of this world for love of him, truly keeps his words. He departs securely from this life who always lives in the love of God without stain of conscience. He dies securely whose life is defiled by no pleasures of this world. But the death of sinners is worst, whose life was evil and contrary to divine ordinances. For him who lives in sins, contrary to God, death becomes a dreadful entrance into hell. He does not die by death who has lived well; and rarely does he die well who is shown always to have lived badly. He dies securely who loves God above all things with a pure mind and at every time keeps himself unstained from this wicked world. Death is desirable to the good and upright in heart because it sets an end to exile and restores life in heaven. Death is the abandonment of the body, the overturning of a dark prison, and the laying down of a heavy burden. Death is the end of present evils, the finish of sorrow, and the grave of every earthly pleasure. A good life in the faith and charity of Jesus Christ makes death precious and especially desirable to the servant of God.

    Now therefore, brothers, strive to anticipate death with holy works, and by zeal for virtues make pleasant for yourselves what nature has willed to be necessary for all. Remember that we all are necessarily mortal, and that when we do not think it, we shall pass from this world. For, as a certain venerable prelate said: we are all taken from the midst as the fates decline, and we are drawn where life, when completed, calls us. Therefore, my brothers, let us do whatever good we can while we have time, lest, overtaken by the command of death, we grieve too late that we were very negligent. Time alone is ours; all other things are another’s. The labor of our spiritual warfare, even if it seems somewhat hard to lukewarm minds, is nevertheless very brief and will quickly be ended with life; but the reward of good works that will be given to us remains forever.

    Let meditation on death soon to come never leave you, but by consideration of the strict judgment, which no one can escape, let it continually pierce your minds in the love of God. Behold how many monks have gone before us in this monastery of Sponheim, by living and dying, through almost four hundred years from its first foundation; of them there is today among us no memory at all left. As many as we are, they were; what they are, after a short time we shall be. They all were mortal, as we are; they died and returned into the dust of the earth, as we shall be. I am the twenty-fifth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim; unless twenty-four had gone before me to death, I certainly would not have come as the twenty-fifth to this abbacy. I too shall shortly give place to another, so that the twenty-sixth number of abbots may be filled. After him another in turn will be ordained, and the death of one becomes the installation of another; and while one succeeds another, all are subjected to the command of death. Where then are

    Homily. XXV.

    Fol. LVIII.

    the brothers who preceded us in this monastery: Just as there is no memory among us of those who preceded us, so also we shall be in everlasting oblivion among those who follow. Let us think on these things beforehand, dearest brothers, while we are alive, [unclear] fall into death. Just as daily we hasten toward death, so daily, according to our powers, let us prepare ourselves; for he dies secure who in life is adorned with good and holy works. Do not let the hope of a longer life deceive you, for the longer you live in this world, the shorter you are going to live. Behold, daily tending toward death, we die; daily one part of life is cut away from us; and the longer our life is prolonged, the more the remaining time of living is shortened. All that we have lived through in time we have wholly lost, because it has passed away; what we live today we share moment by moment with death; how much time for living remains to us in the future we do not know. Why, then, do we trust in the vanity of this life, since we are soon to die? Therefore, brothers, let us continually think that we shall soon arrive there whither [unclear] of all our elders [unclear]. We, placing our hope in the sacrament of my Lord, the Savior of all, and despising the pleasures of the world for love of him, shall be able to drive away the indiscreet fear of dying in this way: if each day we prepare ourselves as though about to die immediately. Yet it is one thing to have dread of death, another to have trembling. For the Lord Jesus too felt dread of death, not trembling, in order to show the properties of the two natures. Continual meditation on death, therefore, is altogether necessary for us who are weak, so that the mind, not yet perfect in the charity of Christ, may be roused to the grace of compunction as if by a certain violent impulse. For the memory of future death, like a nail driven into wood, pierces the mind with useful dread. The memory of death brings in arduous penitence and true sobriety of mind. The memory of death is necessary for beginners, whose conversion begins from servile fear, so that it may successively be lifted through filial fear into charity. The memory of death and of the strict examination of the future judgment of God is especially necessary for those who by evil habit and by [unclear] are drawn to sin. And there are certain among you too lukewarm and negligent in spiritual warfare; admonishing them, we exhort them paternally to remember that they are mortal, and thereafter to live in such a way that they do not fear to die. For it is very dangerous to live in that state in which one would fear to die. We must live so that we await death secure; and this can at last happen if, fervent in all purity of mind and body, we continually burn in the exercises of divine charity. Let us live as innocently as can be done, according to the Rule of the divine father Benedict, which we have professed, and we shall have good hope, because almighty God will have mercy on us, who does not permit a man of good will to perish. Let us always think of God as present to us everywhere, who sees all things, knows all things, understands all things, rewards all things; and let us live with that purity with which we have promised to serve his most holy majesty.

    End of the twenty-fifth homily of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to the monks.

    Here is the end of the first book of exhortations to the monks, in my own hand. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, writer. On the [unclear] day of the month of June, in the Christian year one thousand four hundred eighty-six, in the fourth indiction. My age: twenty-four. He dedicated this work to my predecessor, now abbot of Belgenstadt, most dear to [unclear].

    Letter.

    John Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Sponheim, though unworthy, to the reverend father lord Johannes de Colenhausen, abbot of Seligenstadt, formerly of Sponheim, my dearest predecessor: with prayers, a mind prompt and ready to give pleasure.

    Venerable teacher, I recently sent you my first book of exhortations to monks, containing twenty-five homilies; after I learned that it had been approved by your examination, I judged that this second one also, which I now send, should confidently be inscribed to your name. In that one, for the instruction of the brothers, I collected twenty-five homilies which I had delivered before them; in this one I have arranged the sermons by number, according to the order in which they were spoken in their presence.

    I do not fear to undergo the examination of your paternity, since I have always had you as a gentle teacher, and long ago found you to be a sincere lover of truth. For you are strong in talent, both mild and profound, directed toward progress. The management of household affairs and the poverty of the place often draw me back from salutary study, and turn my mind away, against the purpose of my will, to the concerns of others. Only on feast days and Sundays is leisure granted me for writing; on these, out of reverence for God, I am not accustomed to admit any business of the peasants. Sometimes also, after the customary matins have been sung, I am accustomed to devote what remains of the night to the study of letters, and, as far as I can, to work by lamplight at something for the instruction of my brothers.

    For I desire in all things to follow in your footsteps, and, if I can, perpetually to [unclear] the praiseworthy custom of teaching one’s subjects which you introduced. I know that I am bound to this by my office; and although I am rude and unlearned, nevertheless I willingly wish, according to my powers, to be diligent both in learning and in teaching. I submit these sermons to your examination, and with humble supplication I ask that the file of your mastery correct them.

    I have collected a few out of many into order, since I neither committed them all to writing, nor did an excessive extension of the book seem to me either necessary or useful. For on feast days, when we are free from the tumult of worldly business, we devote ourselves to reading according to the rule of the Scriptures. And lest I seem to occupy the place of pastor in vain, what I have worked out by lamplight at night I am accustomed to speak after None, in place of the regular study, and to recite from a small sheet before the brothers in chapter. For I find by experience that this diligence of mine not only profits the brothers for edification, but also helps me toward skill in composition.

    Farewell, venerable teacher, and pray for us. From Sponheim, on the twelfth day of the month of September, in the year of the Christians 1486.

    Sermon I. Fol. LIX.

    In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the second book of exhortations to monks, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim and afterwards [of Würzburg?]. How cautiously monks must live: sermon one.

    Many things indeed, most beloved brothers, are necessary for you to consider in this life, if you desire [to attain?] the glory of eternal salvation. For you know that Scripture testifies that your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; and we know that he must be resisted with great vigilance in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ and in works of charity. Therefore let no one trust presumptuously in his own powers in vanity; for unless you keep yourselves humbly in the fear of the Lord, you will quickly fall into the snares of the devil. “The greater you are,” Scripture commands, “humble yourself in all things,” for God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. For it is fitting that a monk be humble, and a true contemner of this world. A monk must always be solicitous in the observance of regular discipline, and continually zealous in the fear of the Lord. A monk must be chaste and modest in mind and body alike, and serve God, as he promised, in all purity. A monk ought not live according to his own will, but according to the rule and according to the direction of his pastor, conformably to the norm of cenobitic institution. A monk ought to love [unclear] and holy [unclear], and occupy his mind usefully in the reading of the Scriptures. A monk, at every time even unto death, ought to be solicitous that he may be perfect in the observance of the commandments of God and of the rule. But so that you may know what things are necessary for you, who live together in holy religion, for perfection, I shall describe for you a certain path of the virtues, by which one must direct the way to the kingdom of heaven. Now all the virtues cohere mutually by the bond of relationship, so that he who perfectly possesses one seems to have them all; but he who lacks even one may be said to possess none at all. The first of all virtues necessary for salvation is the most holy catholic faith, separated from every error and pollution of heresies, and originally rooted in the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as Scripture testifies, without faith it is impossible to please [unclear]

    That monks must live cautiously.

    and justice and truth; and in action, justice and sincerity; and no iniquity will have dominion. For faith without works is dead, and merits nothing toward the salvation of eternal happiness. To have faith without works of charity is to imitate the demons, who, though they are far removed and alien from all charity, nevertheless both believe that God is just and tremble. Hence concerning believers who do not show works of charity, the Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah and afterwards through himself in the holy Gospel, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” He who praises Christ with his mouth without works is like a man who doubts in faith. For if he truly believed, he would fear God as [unclear]. Faith without works is like a body dead without spirit, which, once removed by a man, is hidden from sight in a tomb. If you believe rightly and live badly, you destroy your own [unclear] with a sword, because for one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin to him. Beware, my brothers, lest you admit any error in faith, and take the greatest care that there be no wickedness in action. Follow the faith that holy Church commends to us; live your life as the Gospel commands, and the cenobitic norm. Then have hope in God’s mercy at all times most certain, but not alien from the fear of the Lord. Hope is a certain expectation of future good through the grace of the merciful God, and a solicitude for meriting the crown of justice through the exercise of charity. Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, which the grace of God works in us, accompanied by the rectitude of a good will. Hope is that by which one hopes to come to the happiness of eternal life, which he desires; and, by the mediation of God’s grace, he composes and fits himself and his will to meet it. Hope is a good, difficult, future, one and possible thing; for no one hopes for the contrary. For no one hopes for evil, nor for what is trivial, nor for what is present or past; nor are we ignorant that hope is not of the impossible. Hope is the moderator of all labors, and the sole consoler in the midst of tribulations. Hope in future good gives rest in this life to those laboring for Christ; just as, for those contending in combat, the expectation of the crown through continual victory lessens the pain of wounds. Hope strengthened the martyrs in torments, and made them, in the virtue of charity, stronger than all their persecutors. Hope of eternal blessedness preserves the Church, and gave to holy confessors and to virgins charity in Christ

    Sermon I.

    ...so that I might move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. And if I should distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I should deliver my body so that I might burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.

    Consider yourselves carefully now, my brothers, and question your consciences, whether you have true charity of God; without it all other things avail nothing for salvation. For you have heard the apostle’s clear declaration, in which he says that charity is necessary for salvation. Let no one trust in the wisdom of this world; let no one vainly exalt himself over natural gifts received; let no one presume upon bodily continence, since if charity is lacking, the observance of the rest contributes nothing to salvation.

    But lest anyone presume a false estimation of himself, the holy apostle set forth certain signs and operations of charity, saying: Charity is patient, is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.

    Have the charity of God in you, my brothers; unless you keep it, you labor in vain by striving. We have often told you that humility is altogether necessary for you; it is not only a great virtue, but also the nurse of the other virtues and the chief guardian of them all. For Pope Gregory says: He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.

    For humility is the greatest virtue of monks, since they are bound to be humbler than the others who live their life in the world, inasmuch as by profession they are constrained to strive and tend toward greater perfection. Humility is the stable foundation of the virtues; whatever has been built upon it will be overturned by no whirlwind of storm. Through pride the devil fell from heaven; through humility man ascends.

    We are called monks in vain if we have not been humble; for just as fire is extinguished if it lacks the fuel of wood, so a monk without humility is judged very unworthy of his name. By Christian humility the devil is conquered and, as if struck by a nail, [unclear]. No jewel is seen more splendid in monastic adornment than humility; if a monk despises it, he has denied both his profession and the humble Christ.

    Prudence succeeds humility; it always directs all things according to the rule of reason and does nothing except what is right, honorable, and praiseworthy. Prudence knows what it ought virtuously to seek, and it knows well what, according to the right judgment of reason, it ought to avoid. True and perfect prudence is that by which we seek that highest, unchangeable good and order all things to their due and right end.

    Prudence preserves the observance of regular discipline stable in its vigor, and brings wandering monks back to the complete reform of the purpose they have lost. Prudence directs the monk on the right way of salvation and lets him turn aside to neither side. Prudence preserves peace and concord among the brothers, and orders right action in each case.

    Prudence is very necessary for you, my brothers, so that by it you may know in every action what things you should undertake and what, in turn, should be avoided. True prudence, not of the flesh but of the spirit, teaches you to despise the world and to desire only those things that are future and eternal. Prudence teaches a man to stand firm in himself, and to turn aside from the purpose of holiness neither in prosperity nor in adversity.

    Prudence teaches one to order present things beautifully; it brings past things back to memory for instruction, and foresees future things lest anything happen unexpectedly. Prudence corrects offenders vigorously and fruitfully, and orders everything that it either does, says, or thinks, according to the judgment of reason, to its due end.

    Be therefore prudent as serpents and simple as doves, because prudence [without?] goodness is wickedness, and simplicity without rational prudence is called foolishness. For the most holy Paul, apostle of Christ, says: Be prudent, lest you be deceived by the fraud of others, but simple, lest you deceive anyone. For this is the office of a prudent man: neither to be able to be deceived, nor to wish to deceive anyone.

    A prudent man does not abandon the judgment of reason, and does nothing of which one must repent; for he is called prudent from foreseeing. Justice accompanies prudence; it is the most splendid of all the virtues. For without justice, all the remaining virtues are nothing. Justice is the preserver of religion, the mother of grace, the nurse of observance, the nourisher of life, the begetter of peace, and the source of piety

    That monks must live carefully.

    Justice is the virtue that distributes and preserves to each person what is his own; it neglects private advantage in order to preserve common advantage and equity, without which no commonwealth can long subsist in peace. For the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “A kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, and injuries, and insults, and diverse deceits.” The order of justice first has regard to God, then to the fatherland, thereafter to parents, and afterward to all in common according to distinctions of rank and the merits of dignities. To God, first of all, at the command of justice, we owe religion, faith, worship, devotion and acts of thanksgiving, and true love from the whole heart under obedience. To ourselves, next, we owe purity of mind and body, continence with zeal for perfection, so that through obedience we may be permitted to return to him by whom we were created. In the third place we owe to the fatherland its advantage, honor, and defense, and we must procure its usefulness as much as we can, together with justice itself. Fourth, we are bound to parents by honor and obedience, and, in their necessity, by care and every kind of support. Fifth, we owe obedience to our prelates and superiors, and humble subjection for the love of Christ. Sixth, as prelates, we owe doctrine and example to subjects, and correction to those who offend. In the seventh place, moreover, we are bound to elders and princes by honor, and by subjection without crime for the love of God. Eighth, we owe reverence to venerable persons, and honor to priests. Consequently, to equals we are bound by friendship; to inferiors by consideration; to benefactors by return of service; to friends by fellowship; to enemies by patience; to the poor by mercy; to the wretched by consolation; to all by charity. This, moreover, is true justice: that we love God with our whole heart for his own sake, and our neighbor in God as ourselves, and our enemies for God’s sake, distributing to each what is owed to him by right and providing for the advantage of all.

    But since excessive justice easily falls into sin, temperance is necessary for you in all things; it alone makes men perfect. Temperance is the virtue that, by reason, discerns and overcomes the movements of the soul and every lust, so that impulse in acting may not exceed the equity of the law. Temperance is an excellent virtue: it rules pleasures and preserves all things in due order. Apply temperance to all your actions, words, and also your thoughts, and apply the discretion necessary to the virtues. Whatever good you do with discretion receives the name by the merit of virtue; but what is done without discretion must be called vice. Discretion is the moderator of all virtues, and the greatest ornament of prudence and justice. Discretion is necessary not only for prelates but also for subjects, since it gives to virtue its fairest and most honorable beauty. Hence a certain wise man said: “There is a measure in things; there are, finally, fixed limits, beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.”

    For this, brothers, strength of soul is necessary for you; through it you may become not only steadfast in adversities, but also ready and cheerful in difficult matters. For who, without the greatest strength of soul, could despise this world with its pleasures, and persevere in holy monastic religion under the laws of obedience even unto death? Strength of soul sees the powers of pride, fearfully to be dreaded, from the charity of Christ. Strength belongs to the little ones: to despise peaceful pleasures. Strength lies hidden in prosperity, is shown in adversity, and is manifestly declared through patience. A strong soul is not one that avenges injuries inflicted on it, but one that patiently endures them; and if it has taken an adversary into its power, it thinks that it could have taken vengeance. The strength of monks is to despise the world, conquer the flesh, spurn all the honors and pleasures of the world, and place all hope and confidence in God alone. The measure of strength is to be neither fearful nor rash, because one walking on the right road turns neither to the right nor to the left. That monk is to be judged strong who is temperate in all things, moderate, and just. Hence the most holy [unclear] says: to despise the flatteries of prosperity; to overcome in the heart the fear of adversity. The saints were made strong in battle, because they tame the flesh, shine with virtues, are strengthened in spirit, fail in earthly things, seek heavenly things, can be killed, cannot be bent, nor can they endure false things. Through weakness they fear, and, though harmed, they never depart from conquering truth.

    Justice is the virtue that distributes and preserves to each person what is his own; it neglects private advantage in order to preserve common advantage and equity, without which no commonwealth can subsist in [unclear] peace. For the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “A kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, and injuries, and insults, and diverse deceits.” The order of justice first has regard to God, then to the fatherland, thereafter to parents, and afterward to all in common according to distinctions of ranks and the merits of dignities. To God, first of all, at the command of justice, we owe religion, faith, worship, devotion and acts of thanksgiving, and true [unclear] from the whole heart under obedience. To ourselves, next, we owe purity of mind and body, continence with zeal for perfection, so that through obedience we may be permitted to return to him by whom we were created. In the third place we owe to the fatherland its advantage, honor, and defense, and we must procure its usefulness as much as we can, together with justice itself. Fourth, we are bound to parents by honor and obedience. Sixth, as prelates, we owe doctrine and example to subjects, and correction to those who offend. In the seventh place, moreover,

    Sermon I.

    The monk, therefore, who is strong with true virtue neither dares rashly nor fears without counsel. For courage and constancy together are the royal road, from which the rash and stubborn man turns aside to the right, but the fearful, faint-hearted, and timid man to the left. The monk, constant and strong in spirit, never withdraws from the purpose of holiness, but is neither cast down by adversities nor lifted up by prosperities. Hence also the most holy bishop Ambrose says: “The fool changes like the moon. But the wise man is not broken by fear, is not changed by power, is not exalted by prosperities, is not sunk by sorrows.” For where wisdom and virtue are, there is constancy and strength of spirit. Therefore the wise man is always the same in spirit; he is neither diminished nor increased by changes of circumstances, nor does he, like a little child, waver so as to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but remains perfect in Christ, founded in charity and rooted in the perfection of faith.

    Finally, my dearest brothers, perseverance is necessary for you in every good and virtuous work; without it no one ever comes to the crown of glory. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.” Take away perseverance, and neither will virtue have a reward, nor service a recompense, nor a benefit merit grace. For perseverance alone in good works deserves to receive the crown of praise; without it, it profits nothing to have begun a good thing. No virtue has merit if perseverance is not brought to its increase. The kingdom of eternal happiness is promised not to those who begin the good, but to those who persevere in the good until death, because the denarius will be paid to the laborers in the vineyard not in the morning or at midday, but when evening has come.

    For he who began well is not to be praised, but he who continued well to the end is to be honored. Therefore, my brothers, I am accustomed diligently to admonish you, and I ought never to cease, that you carefully attend to your calling and walk cautiously in all religion and holiness, as you know you have sworn. Seek the Lord while he can be found.

    Let the life of Christ the Savior be your imitation; by the foundation of your institution you are bound to follow him according to your strength, not by steps of the feet but by likeness of affections. But in all things walk [unclear]; always place the fear of God, in true humility, before the gaze of the mind. For you have need of great purity, you who in mind and body have consented to the holy warfare of Christ. It now belongs to you, O brothers, to despise the world and all things that are in the world for God’s sake with perpetual courage; to overcome all motions of carnal pleasures; to flee sin; to occupy yourselves constantly in good and holy works. Your life also, so far as human weakness allows, ought to imitate angelic purity and to flee and detest all depravity. The holy angels are never idle, but are always, without weariness or [unclear], diligent in the praises of God. The holy angels love God above all things, and do not withdraw even for a moment from his charity. In imitation of them the monk ought to be assiduous in the service of Christ, and always occupied in good works according to the Gospel and the Rule.

    The monk ought to have the charity of God most fervently, and true [charity] of neighbor [unclear]. The monk ought to have the charity of God most fervently: he who does not wish to become idle should love; how much more strongly does the most chaste love of God impel the mind it possesses toward arduous things. For fervent love toward God perfects the monk and does not allow him to be idle. For the most holy Pope Gregory says: “The love of God is never idle. For it works great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it was never true love of God.” For if the mad poet spoke truly of carnal love, “he who does not wish to become idle loves,” how much more strongly does the most chaste love of God impel the mind it possesses toward arduous things. Love God, brothers, with your whole heart, as far as the strength of desire can extend itself, and you will be able most easily to observe all the things that have been commanded you.

    For nothing is difficult to one who loves; but all hard things, all heavy and arduous things, burning love makes easy.

    What Is the Good Ordering of the Monastic Life: Sermon Two.

    We have read that the institution of our most holy father Benedict, which in common usage we call religion or order, shone forth as most holy at the beginning of its foundation, and that throughout the whole church of the Latins it was very widely extended in many ways. Hence for very many years in this very order there flourished many men who were wise, learned, and most holy, and

    What constitutes the good ordering of monastic life.

    who splendidly illuminated the whole Church. For there are those who write that from this our monastic religion fifteen thousand six hundred, both men and nuns, have been entered in the catalogue of the saints. This multitude of saints in the order, brothers, is set before us for imitation, not for vain boasting. How can their multitude conduce to our salvation, if we do not imitate the manner of life in which they went before us? Whenever we desire usefully to praise the most holy men of our order, let us hasten by holy conduct to come into their company. For then we shall glory fruitfully in the multitude of saints of our order, if, by living rightly, we diligently strive to increase their number. For this reason we set before you so great a multitude of saints: so that, when you see that many before you in this very order conquered the world and the flesh, you may at last rise up from your lukewarm manner of life. The virtue which God’s compassion bestowed on them he will not deny to you if you ask in true charity. They conquered the world because they loved Christ with total devotion, despising all things for love of him. They despised all things, and the Lord Jesus provided for them whatever seemed necessary for the sustenance of life.

    This fervor of the monks’ devotion endured for many years after the first foundation of the order in great constancy, and converted the souls of many thousands of men to the Lord. But nothing is stable among human things, and nothing lasting among perishable things. Holy religion bestowed riches on the monks, until in time the daughter suffocated the mother. For, as Scripture says, all who wish to become rich fall into the temptations of the devil. The beloved grew fat and kicked back; made corpulent and enlarged by earthly possessions, he abandoned the holy pursuits of the first institution; he went after vanities and false follies, and abundance of temporal things made him poor and wretched in spiritual riches. This lamentable deformity of our order began about two hundred years after the passing of the divine father Benedict, and grew more and more with time, until at last the harmful poison spread itself through the whole order. Yet this deformity did not occupy the order suddenly, but at last, through the succession of many years, almost the whole of it; although almighty God never wholly deprived it of good men, but always left for himself some who had by no means bent their knees before Baal. For men of mercy arose, whose righteous deeds will never be handed over to oblivion; taking pity on the ruin of the order, they put their shoulder beneath the labor, and, with the Lord generously granting aid, restored it in many places.

    To be sure, many varied particular reforms flourished in the order many times and at different periods, but there was never any general reform that brought the whole order back to the integrity of regular observance. Finally, however, we see that the particular restorations, which we have said were numerous, have almost all collapsed again. Most recently, namely in the year of the Christians 1420, when the general council was being celebrated at Constance, a certain new and hitherto latest particular reform took its beginning in Germany; from a certain monastery in the parts of Saxony, then indeed the poorest of all, called Bursfelde, it [unclear] the [unclear] of its name.

    The first author and leader of this most holy reform was Johannes Rode, abbot of the distinguished monastery of Saint Matthias at Trier, who, being appointed general visitor of the order by the aforesaid Council of Constance, first exhibited reform in himself, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should be judged reprobate. For he first reformed both himself and the monks of the mentioned monastery; he issued a confirmation in conformity with the Rule; he obtained from the Apostolic See confirmation of the holy work. Among all the monasteries of the order, however, Bursfelde, a humble and poor little monastery, first received this reform, which afterward spread to Reinhausen and to a few monasteries of Saxony neighboring it.

    At length, when Johannes Rode, abbot of Saint Matthias and leader of our reform, had died, since no suitable successor for the enlargement of the enterprise begun could be found in that same place, Johannes de Hagen, abbot of Bursfelde, who had already reformed certain monasteries, a holy man and very zealous for the order, was elected at the urging of Jakob, archbishop of Trier. Content with his poverty, he did not consent to leave Bursfelde, lest he seem to have preferred riches to poverty. Therefore he remained in his own monastery, and another was appointed in the place of the first reformer. Since this man seemed comparable to his predecessor neither in learning nor in zeal, he could accomplish little for the continuation of the enterprise begun, nor expand the reform among many. Meanwhile it happened that Nicholas of Cusa, priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church

    Sermon II. Fol. LXII.

    ...the legate of the apostolic see to come into Germany; and since he burned with great zeal for our order, he established and introduced many things for its reform. Hearing, moreover, of the good reputation and most fervent purpose for regular discipline of the aforesaid abbot in Bursfeld, he summoned him to himself and appointed him general reformer of the order, and through his diligence reformed several monasteries. On this occasion at last he instituted an annual chapter for the preservation of the reform; he transferred the presidency from St. Matthias to Bursfeld; he obtained from the apostolic see the confirmation of all the things that he had instituted for the good of the reform.

    The first abbot of Bursfeld in the reform was John, a monk from Reinhausen, duly appointed; the second was John called of Hagen; the third was Theodoric, whom we have seen; and the fourth is John, who is now newly appointed in governance. Therefore, dearest brothers, we have briefly touched upon the origin of our reform so that you may know with how much labor it began, and so that you may persevere constant in holy regular observance even unto death. For among all the reforms of our order that have preceded, none was ever more conformable and consonant to the Rule of the divine father Benedict, and more alien from foreign inventions. We have read the statutes of nearly all the other reforms, but we judge none more consonant than ours to the Rule and to the purity of Benedict's intention.

    This is the Bursfeld reform, most holy in the order, which both teaches true obedience and preserves subjection in humility. In this holy religious life monks live poor and without private property; they live humble; they live obedient. O venerable union of monks, in which twin charity commands, obedience serves, humility complies, prayer keeps watch, perseverance fights, holy chastity triumphs. This is the school of regular discipline, the instructress of Christian humility, which directs conduct toward rectitude and restrains the vices of the flesh. In this arena of virtues no one is permitted to follow his own will against the Rule; no one is forbidden to do good. In this holy union life is lived according to the purity of the Rule, and if anyone begins to stray from the path of rectitude, he is at once recalled to the observance of justice by the diligence of the seniors. The Rule of the most holy father Benedict is read publicly three times a year, so that no one may attempt to excuse himself from observance under the pretext of ignorance.

    There are two things that promise me great hope for the perseverance of this holy reform: namely, the annual chapter and the diligent biennial visitation of the monks. If either of these is interrupted in any way, the reform is at once endangered. Consider now, therefore, dearest brothers, and take the most diligent care you can, lest you occupy this monastery of the divine bishop Martin uselessly under the title of so venerable a reform; for unless you live purely, holily, and blamelessly according to the Rule and the statutes of the order, you trust in the name in vain.

    We shall speak to you a few admonitions for your salvation; by zealous observance of them you will deservedly have both the name and the dignity of our Bursfeld reform. First of all, before all else, direct your effort with all desires toward monastic perfection; whenever you sense it growing lukewarm, renew it at once by attentive remembrance of the Lord's passion and most innocent death. For even if we are not bound by necessity of salvation to be perfect, nevertheless we are bound to strive toward perfection with all our desires. For as soon as a monk casts away the effort to advance, he falls into the pit of falling away.

    The second thing that the holy custom of our reform has established for you to keep strongly preserves the effort of advancing in the desire once conceived. Therefore, when you rise, having been awakened for Prime, do these things in secret. Examine and discuss the future course of the coming day, and prudently consider what useful thing must be undertaken. Set before your hearts how cautiously you wish to live throughout the whole day, and arm your spirits with patience against all things that could come upon you as adversities. Whatever you do, complete it in the fervor of charity, and always order all words and deeds to the praise of God.

    A third thing we judge useful and necessary for you: that through most devout prayers you should always strive to implore divine assistance in all things. And it seems very fitting to us, as we have often said and always admonish, that each one of you should at least once a day keep remembrance of the Lord's passion, and for the many benefits received from God should at least once offer thanksgiving. In order that this may be done uniformly by each of you, listen to this brief form that we have arranged, and if you wish, write it down for yourselves: I adore, praise, bless, and glorify you, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, savior and giver of life to the souls of all the faithful, and I give you thanks from the depths of my heart

    What Constitutes a Good Ordering of the Monastic Life

    for your [return?] afterward into the land of your temporal birth. I give thanks to you, sweetest Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for all your labors, journeys, and wearinesses; for hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, poverty, and want; and for the necessities, injuries, insults, mockeries, and slanders which you sustained throughout your whole life for us, voluntarily and not under compulsion. And as often as you moved your hand to work, your foot to walk, or as often as you opened your mouth to speak, so often do I bless, praise, glorify, and humbly adore you, and with all the powers of my heart I always give thanks to you, mediator of God and human beings, sweetest Jesus Christ. I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, most merciful king of the heavens, for your most holy teaching, for the establishment of your faith and of the evangelical sacraments, for the calling of the nations, for the justification of sinners, and for all your wonders and powers, and for all your benefits, which you have bestowed either on me in particular or on all others together with me in general. I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, most kindly savior, for your charity which you had toward the human race, and for your whole most bitter Passion and all the pains which you sustained for us wretched ones. I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for the sorrow and sadness of your most innocent heart, which, when the time of the Passion was at hand, you sustained for us, when you said to your disciples following you:

    “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” I beseech you, through this sadness of your heart, O Lord God, have mercy on me now and at the hour of my death, and take from me all melancholy and disordered sorrow, granting me at all times a salutary sadness for my sins. I give thanks to you for the sorrow of your most holy heart when, placed in agony, you prayed to the Father as many as three times that he would transfer from you the chalice of the Passion, and, with sweat poured forth in wondrous anguish, you wholly resigned yourself to his will for us. I give thanks to you, O king of heaven and earth, for your captivity, for the insults, injuries, and mockeries which you sustained throughout the whole time of the Passion for our salvation and that of all. I give thanks to you

    with immeasurable grief. I adore you, Lord Jesus Christ, crowned with thorns, and I give thanks to you for the piercings and pains of your most holy head, for the blows, spittings, and all the mockeries cruelly inflicted by the impious upon your majesty. I adore you, Christ Jesus, Son of the living God, bearing the very heavy weight of your cross; I adore you, stripped before the multitude looking on; I adore you, stretched out by hands and feet and very cruelly fastened to the cross with iron nails. I adore you, Jesus Christ, eternal king, hanging and dying on the cross for me; and I give thanks for the pains of your wounds, I give thanks for the pouring forth of your most precious blood, I give thanks for your most innocent death, which you voluntarily sustained for our sins and for those of the whole world. I give thanks for your immeasurable goodness, because you called me from fear to faith, because you caused me to be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, and because you deigned to call me away from the vanity of the world to serve you in true tranquility of mind, into this holy congregation. I beseech you through your most holy

    name, O sweetest Jesus, mediator of God and human beings; I beseech you through the pain of your wounds and through the merit of your most bitter Passion; I beseech you through the pouring forth of your most holy blood and through the power of your most innocent death: grant me pardon for all my sins; pour into my heart the sweetness of your most fervent love; give me

    Sermon II. Folio LXIII.

    thanksgiving after Matins, which is the most suitable time for prayer, because the silence of the night’s quiet is wont to increase devotion. For I say what experienced men attest to be true: no prayers are more effective for obtaining what is sought than those which they offer to God the Father with remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and with gratitude.

    The fourth thing which we have indicated to you as necessary for regular observance is this: that you keep watch in guarding the outer senses, because no one can adequately guard the city of his own heart who neglects to close the gates. Love silence, and flee all the tumult of this world. Apply holy prudence in all things that you do, and love retirement wherever you are. For a monk who loves publicity and wandering excursions was never a true lover of observance.

    Fifth, we admonish you to flee the pernicious idleness of the soul; for this pestiferous [unclear] nourishes grave vices and always gives birth to unclean thoughts. Therefore whoever is a lover of virtues and loves his own salvation, whoever desires to come to eternal happiness, let him flee idleness as from the face of the devil, if he desires to avoid sin.

    Sixth, for the purity of regular observance, by necessity of salvation, it is required that the renunciation of private property be kept inviolate by all until death. For a monk who has private property prepares for himself a road to hell. But the one who receives and spends money in the monastery should be a public minister; let no private person dare presume to do this. Possession of riches does not befit monks, since they are commanded to imitate Jesus in poverty of spirit. Let us hear the holy Apostle of Christ saying: Having food and clothing, with these let us be content. By God’s mercy we provide you with necessary things: not as much as the disordered desire of pleasure demands, but what nature, content with few things, requires. And so, just as it is not lawful for you to have anything without the abbot’s consent, so, since we supply everything, it is not necessary either.

    The seventh thing that makes a monk is humble obedience to preceptors. No one can be a true monk who scorns obedience and denies to his superiors the humble subjection which he promised. This disease of disobedience arises from elation and pride of mind, just as pus is generated from a bad ulcer. But, as Scripture says: pride is hateful before God and men, and the beginning of every transgression. The delight of monks is the imitation of Christ, who obeyed the Father even unto death.

    The most beautiful virtue, chastity, adorns the eighth place; when it is scorned, all the integrity of regular life is necessarily shipwrecked. For a monk, by necessity of his salvation, is commanded to live chastely until death and perpetually to abstain from every venereal pollution. There are three principal vows of monastic life; for monks to live contrary to their observance is certain damnation. For the profession of monks, under sentence of eternal damnation, commands them to live without property, under obedience to the pastor, and in perpetual chastity. When one of these three is taken away, monastic integrity is violated, and transgression condemns the contemner.

    In the ninth place, therefore, we admonish every person dedicated to God always to beware of so great a venomous serpent: his own will. Unless he holds it suspect at every time, he easily falls into the pit of damnation. Attend to the Rule: for monks are not permitted to have either their bodies or their wills in their own power. No one sins unwillingly. If you have perfectly submitted your will to God and to your abbot in all things, you will easily avoid sin.

    The tenth thing which can preserve in you the integrity of regular observance, my dearest brothers, is that in all adversities and contradictions you have most steadfast patience for the love of God. For patience is a great virtue, which by another name we call endurance; without it no one will come away victor over his temptations. Therefore the Lord says in the holy Gospel: In your patience you shall possess your souls. What is patience, if not to bear calmly one’s own injuries and those of one’s people, and all other adversities whatsoever, for reverence and love of God? Believe me, brothers, [and] the saying of the Apostle when he says: Patience is very necessary for you, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive [the promise].

    What are the signs of true humility.

    [unclear] overcome. An abundance of foods [brings with it?] useless courteous talk; your belly, filled with wine, stirs up unclean promptings of the flesh and of lust. If you wish to be chaste, be abstemious. It is most shameful for a monk to serve the belly and gluttony, since for love of God he has renounced all his pleasures of the world.

    The tenth thing which a monk in regular observance does as useful and strenuous is that he be most diligent concerning the service of God. For indeed he who is a true servant of God, as all monks ought to be, is always fervent in the work of his Creator, both that he may love, and because, where he truly knows fullness to be, he prepares himself to be dutiful to Him in ministry with devotion. For it is in the Scriptures: Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently. Therefore, dearest brothers, you will approach the future [unclear] of the supreme and unchangeable God; sweetly, wisely, fervently, and cheerfully sing psalms, and with all the devotion and purity of mind that you can, diligently praise your Creator and Savior. Far, far from the hearts of those singing psalms be all sloth; let no drowsiness be admitted in life among those praising [Him], since God is present in the midst of those singing psalms. It is fitting for souls of devotion to be present with fervor. Because there are many [unclear] in the divine services, all pure, [unclear], and most full of charity, in which simple thoughts speak and all things are done duly.

    On the other hand, when Compline has been sung by day and in due manner, let the monk come to the secret place and to his cell; let him examine his conscience as to what business has occupied him. This is the excellent and praiseworthy practice of the brothers of the Bursfeld reform: that after Compline no one should lay himself down upon the coverlet of his bed unless he has first diligently and earnestly examined his conscience concerning faults or negligences committed during the day. If, after this examination, you find that you have offended in anything during the day, you know from learned custom what must be done. Hidden things are to be carried over to the morrow with contrition and humble confession; manifest things, however, are to be reported daily at chapter for blame, as is observed. For this is the practice of the reformed order, this the gladness of the reform: that they do not now allow the faults of offending brothers to grow, if once they have begun to cut them away with care. How is the soul purified day by day? [unclear] as in that state [unclear] without change; thus it is almost necessary, and charity must first be stirred up often by fervent exercise toward [unclear].

    What are the signs of true humility: third sermon.

    Most beloved, let no one deceive himself by his own estimation; let no one lead his heart astray by foolish and empty presumption. Not all who wish to appear humble before God are humble, nor are those who keep silence under injuries always patient. For the roots of true virtue are hidden in the secret of the heart, and not in the display of outward show alone. For often one who wishes rather to be considered humble than truly to be so appears among you, and shows many signs of pride, but either no signs of humility or certainly very few. If he suffers vehemently and excessively from those who err, as by right we ought [unclear], who desire to have not virtue but the appearance of virtue. Why, I ask, do you deceive yourselves, [unclear] mercy, and shamefully destroy yourselves by misleading yourselves, you who, despising truth, love falsehood?

    So that you may know how proudly you live, we shall say plainly the signs and true marks of true humility, because some of them remain hidden in the heart alone, while others must also break forth and become manifest to all who behold them. Let this be for the true monk a mirror of perfect humility, in which, looking each day, he may examine himself. Therefore the first sign of true humility, I say, is one that each person can recognize in himself: that he is able to regard himself as lower and more vile than all people, not with painted speech, but by the humble judgment of the heart. This is the greatest sign of profound humility: that the true monk, always advancing toward a better manner of life, believes himself a useless and unworthy servant of God. True humility belongs to the heart, not to speech; it is the pursuit of the mind, not of bodily display alone. That monk is truly humble who loves God above all things; who always keeps himself pure in all things from every transgression of the command of God and of the rule; who does great works of piety and justice and, by a true estimation of himself within himself, feels humble.

    The second sign of true and profound humility is attained by the man who, running well in the fear of the Lord and persevering, would confess his negligences at all times before God and human beings. For the more he has advanced in good works, the more he sets his sins and negligences before the eyes of his mind. Contrition for his delights in

    Sermon III. Folio LXIII.

    ...he bears continual [unclear] in his heart; and, always contrite in spirit, praying and groaning to the Lord with tears, he asks pardon and mercy.
