Nor does he pray only for his own sins, but also for the sins of the whole world. The greatest remedy against elation of mind is the remembrance of one’s own faults.

    The third test of humility is that he desires to keep in secret with himself all the good works that he does, and conceals his own progress out of zeal for humility. For he who is humble does not boast vainly, nor does he seek praise from men, since he hopes for the glory of eternal happiness. Whoever among you considers himself humble and a true monk should not, for God’s sake, despise this sign of profound submission and abasement.

    The fourth mark of true humility is this: descending voluntarily into the abyss of contempt for himself, he regards all his brethren, even those openly sinning, as better than himself before God. Forgetful of his own good deeds, he wisely considers his own evils; but passing over the evils of others in silence, he makes known at the proper time the good things they have done. This is the condition of true humility: always to [unclear] and proclaim the good works of others, but prudently to disparage and conceal one’s own for the avoidance of pride.

    Having attained the fifth sign of pious humility, he is quiet in his simplicity and does not speak of others’ defects, unless, when reason cannot do otherwise, he strives to admonish gently and meekly. At times he also wisely dissimulates rebukes, and waits for and observes a more opportune time.

    The sixth sign of humility is shown when a monk, out of love of humility, is found slow and not ready to accuse and reprehend the sins of others. For one who is truly humble always considers his own weakness, and silently ponders in secret how many evils he himself has committed against God’s justice. Hence he is greatly afraid to reprehend the deeds of others, because he recognizes himself as a sinner and therefore unworthy to judge others. We except the prelates and rectors of monks from this rule of humility to the extent that they know themselves to be obliged to the correction of subjects.

    The seventh sign of true humility is that he gladly receives corrections and amendments for his faults and negligences, and is not embittered by any pain against the one who reprehends him. Whenever the humble man is corrected by someone, he rejoices in spirit with the prophet, saying: Let the just man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head. Of the proud, however, Scripture says: They have hated the one who rebukes in the gate. He who is truly humble loves the one who corrects him, but flees the flatterer.

    The eighth mark of true humility is plainly shown when, after being corrected, he does not defend, deny, cloak, or excuse his fault, but confesses it with simple shamefastness. A truly humble monk, when he is corrected, does not murmur; he does not protest that he has exceeded the measure of equity, but immediately, falling to the ground before the judge, cries out most meekly: I have sinned; I confess my fault; I ask pardon; I promise amendment.

    The ninth mark of monastic humility makes those who possess it mute in speech: sweet, modest, and not clamorous in voice. A monk whom you see clamorous and headlong in speaking you will judge not humble, but proud and rash. The humble man, however, speaks modestly and as if under silence, and is always found readier to hear than to speak before others. It is shameful for a monk to raise his voice too much while he speaks, since, crucified to the world, he is commanded to love silence.

    The tenth mark of perfect humility is possessed by the one who is accustomed to interpret everything whatsoever he hears about his neighbor in the better part. For our Savior says in the holy Gospel: Do not judge, and you will not be judged. And again: With whatever measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you. The apostle also says: Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness and manifest the counsels of hearts. Who are you, who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls, not to you.

    The eleventh mark of holy humility is that he despises no man in his heart on account of any excesses whatsoever, but sets all before himself by merit of sanctity. He also considers all who publicly offend to be better than himself, and therefore condemns no one. He always considers in his heart with himself what evil he himself has done; but he humbly weighs the good deeds of others as outweighing his own. Therefore he spurns no one, disparages no one, contemns no one, since he desires all to be saved in the Lord.

    The twelfth perfect sign of true humility is that he does not desire to be praised by men, but whenever he is commended by someone, he blushes, groaning with sorrow of mind. But when the praises of others are recited in the con...

    What are the signs of true humility.

    has placed [it] in Jesus: he despises all the glory of this life. The thirteenth sign of true humility is not only to despise praises and favors in the truth of the mind, but also prudently to avoid those by whom he sees that he is praised. Those who are truly humble flee their praisers, and whenever they are praised, making no reply, they fall silent. The esteem of a great reputation is burdensome to the humble man, and the more he is proclaimed by men, the more he is confounded within himself. For true humility advances when it is reviled; when praised, it incurs danger.

    The fourteenth perfect sign of monastic humility: in rebukes and disparagements, if he suffers any, he conceives spiritual joy, and a great increase of divine love. When wronged he is pierced with compunction, and is all the more strongly stirred to contempt of the world. Whenever he is reproved insultingly by someone, if he is humble, he judges himself justly corrected. For he does not consider his own innocence in the charge, but humbly and compunctiously weighs that he has gravely offended God in other things.

    The fifteenth sign of perfect humility: he never kicks back against one who corrects him, but preserves silence in all tranquility of soul. He is not accustomed to rebuke to his face, nor word for word, even the faults very well known in his reprover, but, as if mute, to keep silence about everything.

    The sixteenth sign of profound humility: he despises all the consolations of the world and seeks no friendships of mortals. For true humility, which is taken up for love of Christ, delights nowhere except in Christ alone. But he cannot abide in the love of Christ unless he has learned to deny both his own will and the world with all its disordered pleasures. Thus the Lord says in the holy Gospel: If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple.

    The seventeenth sign of humility: he does not divide himself among many things; he does not greatly seek the assistance and benefits of men, but remains humbly in his own moderation or even extremity. For benefits received from men he is not accustomed to applaud much, but to show himself grateful in few and simple words. The little gifts of the weak loosen minds, and often render the unwary useless and superfluous in speech. But the mind that is truly humble does not delight in the conversations of worldly men, because they often impede the purpose of purity. The love of Christ does not love publicity.

    The eighteenth sign of humility: from the heart he has compassion for all who suffer for the love of Christ, and he most patiently tolerates the defects and weaknesses of others, and prays for the amendment of sinners. For true humility shows to the weak who sin the inward feelings of piety and compassion; but false and simulated humility, because it is truly pride, swells against the frail with hard and undiscerning severity, and becomes the cause of danger to many when, in correcting, it exceeds the norm of the charity of God. But he who is truly humble always fears to exceed the due measure of correction, and therefore is inclined more to mercy than to excessive severity.

    The nineteenth sign of true humility: the mind perseveres free from all envy, and favors all men and prays for them. By divine judgment, [unclear] of God favors all, and rejoices together in the perfections of others. He judges no one unworthy of God's benefits; he thinks all better than himself. He regards all as his foremost ones, because he loves all as himself.

    The twentieth sign of perfect humility: with bitterness of heart he recalls to memory the multitude of his sins, and therefore considers himself unworthy of every benefit and grace of God. Hence, seeking the depth of humility, he imitates the publican of the Gospel, who, having the memory of his offenses, did not wish even to lift his eyes to heaven. For the monk who is truly humble for the love of Christ always bears in his heart the holy sadness of compunction and repentance for the evils that he has done.

    The twenty-first sign of cenobitic humility: he trusts the judgment of others more than his own, and for Christ's sake totally subjects his own will to another's command. When we attend to the signs of monastic humility, we perceive today few observers of it, though we see many monks professing it. O times, O morals, in which we all promise humility, and very few of us truly take care to keep inviolate what has been promised.

    The twenty-second sign of cenobitic humility: he will abominate and despise beautiful, new, costly garments, and all garments cast off by others to have and

    Sermon VI. Fol. LXV.

    He longs to put on [unclear]: he gladly uses cheaper garments, and takes very great delight in those things which others despise. Fine garments, beautifully arranged, do not befit a monk, but the very cheapest, with which the body may be protected only from the injury of harsh weather. For all fastidiousness is forbidden to cloistered men, since by reason of their profession made before God they are bound to contempt of the world. Humility flees lofty things; it seeks the things that are humble.

    The twenty-third sign of the humility of the monastery shows a monk servile toward the brethren and voluntarily devoted to acts of service, and ready for everything whatsoever he may be ordered to do. For true humility obeys even inferiors with a most ready will, and is never indignant against the one who commands. As much as he can, he desires to serve all for love of Christ, since he faithfully loves God with his whole heart. For whatever service he has bestowed upon the brethren, he firmly believes that it has all been shown to Christ.

    The twenty-fourth sign of humility a monk then attains in truth, when, for love of God, he delights to take care of the meaner offices in the monastery, which the rest despise. We have read that many have ascended this degree of true humility, and we do not doubt that they are of great merit before God. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted; for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. The humble monk imitates Christ; the proud one, the devil.

    The twenty-fifth sign of monastic humility is, in an assembly of any people whatsoever, always to seek the lower place for sitting, and to prefer oneself neither to an equal nor to an inferior. It is not for monks proudly to contend over preeminence of place, nor does it befit a soldier of Christ to wish to surpass others in honor. For the true monk who loves humility, content with every lowest position, desires to excel no one.

    The twenty-sixth indication of humility most especially suits him who, though he is learned and educated, because of the lowly humbling of himself, hides all learning and knowledge. For the monk who is truly humble is always found readier to listen than to speak. For the divine priest Jerome says: A monk has the office not of teaching but of lamenting, that he may either mourn himself or the world, and await the Lord's coming in fear. The arrogance of monks is hateful both to God and to men, and is always liable to sin.

    The twenty-seventh sign of humility is perfectly attained by him who, for love of regular discipline, delights more in being silent than in speaking. The humble lover of Christ loves silence, and, lest he offend in speech, is accustomed to say very little. Humility is rarely found among the talkative; and he who is swift to speak casts down his own soul. A talkative and garrulous monk is not without pride, and he who is foolish multiplies words. Whoever desires in spiritual combat to overcome his adversary through humility must not refuse to restrain his tongue from much speaking and from every idle word. It is written in the book of Proverbs that in much speaking sin will not be lacking.

    Whoever has attained the twenty-eighth sign of perfect humility will avoid laughter and all [unclear] gestures of those guffawing. Weeping, not laughter, most befits a monk, since he is dead to all the frivolities of the world. For the wise man says: The fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely laugh silently.

    The twenty-ninth indication of perfect humility takes its beginning from the fear of the Lord; for whose honor, as much as he can, it flees and detests every sin. For a monk who does not fear to sin has not truly been humble. But the monk who follows Christ according to his powers in true humility is accustomed to flee every sin, and, as much as he can, to exercise himself in the pursuit of virtues. Humility confesses its sin; and as often as it has offended even in the smallest matters, it does not rest until it has amended all things through true penitence. He who is truly humble is also always found zealous for preserving purity of conscience. For the nourishment of humility is charity, which does not permit the one who has it to be idle.

    The thirtieth sign of true humility shows a monk confirmed in the purpose of holiness, and makes him subject to all the brethren, even the younger. Whatever the shepherd commands, he obeys simply; he never debates the precepts of the elder; he does not ask the reason why he commands so. If impossible things are commanded, he is ready in spirit; for whatever is hard and arduous, he is prepared without contradiction. He is directed by the counsel of his shepherd; he believes him, trusts him, obeys him; he willingly is governed by his command. You have now heard, my dearest brothers, the thirty indications of true humility. O good God, where are the works? Which of us will boast that he has true humility, so that in these signs he suffers no defect? [unclear] shame are they

    On the arduous way that leads to life.

    our times, in which the charity of many has grown cold; the integrity of holy religion has perished; the devotion of almost all has breathed its last. Our monks seek holiness without the merit of virtues; they wish to have merit without the exercise of labor; for that reason a saint is not found today in the monastery. The fervor of holy compunction in very many is either rare or lukewarm, because where one lives for flesh and blood, the fervor of inward charity is not possessed. It is not enough for you, O monk who glory in observance, to have nothing of your own, not to touch a woman, to reside in the monastery under obedience to the shepherd, not to eat meat, and in the other things that are external matters of regular discipline, for the acquisition of which all other things have chiefly been instituted. Therefore without the charity of God all things profit you nothing, because it alone and uniquely is what distinguishes between good and evil works. O monk, monk, whoever you are who live lukewarmly in the monastery without the fervor of charity, do you think that the outward apparatus of discipline can make you safe? Charity is what sanctifies the one who has it; charity commends the other virtues and all good works to God. Have charity, and all the works of piety that you do will be pleasing to God.

    On the arduous way that leads to life.

    Sermon IV.

    You have heard, most dear brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ saying in today’s reading in the holy Gospel: “How narrow is the gate and strait the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.” Is not Christ himself the way, who had said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”? But how does he now call it strait in the Gospel, when he himself is the one who had said: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light”? What else is the yoke of Christ but the strait and narrow way to the kingdom of God? How then is it also narrow? Let your charity hear. The yoke of the Lord Jesus is sweet to the good, hard and unbearable to the reprobate. The way of Christ to life is broad and pleasant to those trained in humble charity, but narrow and bitter to the proud. Nothing is so hard, nothing so terrible, nothing so arduous, that it is not easy and pleasant to one who loves God. Again, nothing is so light, nothing so easy, nothing so small, that it is not heavy and burdensome to an evil will. Therefore the Lord said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.” If you wish to carry my yoke upon you, first learn the meekness and humility of my heart, because unless you are meek and humble, you will by no means be able to carry my burden, as though it were a heavy weight and an unbearable load. I am a humble way; I do not contain the proud. I am a narrow gate; I do not admit the swollen with pride. Unless you despise in spirit all things that are worldly, unless [unclear] the pleasures of the flesh with necessary diligence, as [unclear] burdened with sins, you cannot enter the kingdom through me. I am a humble and meek way, and I receive the humble; I am a strait door, and I admit the poor in spirit and the clean of heart.

    Brothers, we are hastening to eternal life by the narrow way of truth; it is necessary that we procure in time all things that are necessary for so arduous a journey. There are, moreover, four things especially necessary for travelers; without them the journey is dangerous, and the goal is rarely reached.

    The first thing that we say is necessary for travelers we believe to be knowledge of the roads. For one who strives to walk far through trackless places without knowledge of the roads is sometimes entangled in dangerous errors. Therefore let the prudent traveler either first learn the road, or take to himself a skilled companion for the journey, lest he either fall into the hands of robbers or depart from the straight path of the journey. Therefore, since we desire to return to the fatherland of the heavenly kingdom by a very narrow way known to few, it is necessary that we have as guide and companion of the journey Jesus Christ himself, who named himself the way and the truth. Outside Christ there is no true knowledge; he who neglects to have Christ as the companion of his journey runs in vain and without fruit. Therefore let us learn the way of life, most dear brothers, without knowledge of which no one reaches the fatherland, no one will come to eternal life. Let us firmly believe our Lord Jesus Christ, the one mediator of God and human beings, true God and human being, outside faith in whom no one will be saved, however innocently he may seem to live. For he himself says in the holy Gospel: “He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life in

    Sermon III. fol. LXVI

    abiding in himself. But he who does not believe in the Son: the wrath of God remains upon him. What does it mean that wrath remains upon him, except that the first, original sin is not removed from him? For after the institution of the New Testament, original sin is removed from those who believe in him through faith in Christ alone. Circumcision was given to the fathers as a sign of future salvation; nevertheless none of them could enter the kingdom of heaven before Christ the Savior rose from the dead. Therefore outside faith in Christ there is no salvation, since, as he himself said, he who has not believed has already been judged and will be condemned. Let us remain in Christ through faith and love, because he himself is the way of salvation; he is truth without error; he is life without death. If we have the Lord Jesus as the guide of our journey, we walk confidently.

    Secondly, it is necessary for travelers to pass through the lands of their journey without injury to anyone, because if they commit either theft or robbery, or any other similar sin against the commonwealth, in the end they would come to be punished by penalty and would not reach the intended destination of their journey. But we, brothers, placed on the road by which we are making our way to the homeland of the heavenly kingdom, must take the greatest care that we commit nothing, in word, deed, or thought, contrary to the justice of God, but that we render to each one his own right and due: to God first of all piety, worship, and charity; to our neighbor love; to ourselves the holiness of perfect purity. For indeed, if we live otherwise than Christ taught, we do not remain on the straight road of salvation that leads to the kingdom. We shall remain on the road if we keep the commandments of God; we shall walk in truth if we love the Lord our God himself with the whole strength of the mind; we shall come to life if, turning away from evil, we continually persevere in the practice of good.

    Thirdly, it is necessary to have provision for the journey, because if one reckons the journey within himself, he prepares travel-money and expenses according as necessity requires. A journey both great and arduous remains for us; we must prepare expenses for many years, lest we fail on this road by which we are going. The provision for this journey of ours to the supercelestial homeland is not gold, not silver, not the deceitful riches of the world, but faith in Christ and love of God. Holy virtues are unfailing provision for the soul toward the kingdom of heaven; strengthened by them, it walks the road of God in cheerfulness. The soul faithful to Christ and accompanied by holy virtues cheerfully completes the arduous road of this long pilgrimage. To love God above all things, to exercise oneself constantly in good works, to keep conscience in all purity, to do injury to no one: this provides true provision for the soul toward the everlasting homeland in heaven.

    Fourthly, it is considered necessary for travelers that, before they arrive at the end of the journey they have begun, they not forget their purpose. For he must be called a foolish traveler who is called back from his journey by the games of children and forgets where he was tending to go. And we, dearest brothers, who have taken up the road of monastic religion, must always think of our end, because every day death hastens on, even when we do not notice, and presents both the unprepared and the prepared alike for judgment. Meanwhile let us do good while we may, as much as we can, and let us not delay to be converted to the Lord with our whole heart. Christ is the way through which we go to the kingdom of God; Christ is the truth in which, remaining, we do not err; Christ is the life for which we hope. Hear, brothers, what he himself says in the holy Gospel: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. This is the way that you have entered from the beginning of your monastic profession; if you wish to proceed along it rightly and laudably, you will have to love Christ above all things, living purely in observance of the Rule. It is yours, brothers, to love nothing in this world and to chastise the flesh for love of God. It belongs to monks to despise all delights and pleasures of the present life and to desire nothing except the everlasting feasts. The faithful minister of Christ follows his Lord, and where Christ is, there also his minister will be. Therefore whoever among you, as a lover of his own salvation, desires to come after Christ to the kingdom of heaven, whoever wishes to guard and preserve to the end those things that he promised on entering religion, let him keep these things also.

    First of all, as far as he is able, let the monk learn through faith and devotion, while in sincerity of

    On the arduous way that leads to life.

    [unclear] to know, and at all times to occupy himself piously and soberly in the holy Scriptures. And whatever holy Church, the mother of the faithful, has decreed either to be believed or to be observed, let him believe and keep faithfully and firmly, and let him in no way depart from her determination. For all who once remained outside the ark the flood destroyed; Noah alone, with those who were in the ark, escaped safe. The ark furnished a figure of the Church, and the thing done prefigured a mystery. Hence there is no salvation for human beings outside the Church, which our Lord Jesus Christ built upon the firmest rock. Every unbeliever is not in the Church, and therefore will necessarily perish, just as those once did who were not in the ark. For all who do not believe in the Lord and Savior of the world, Jesus Christ, Jews, pagans, Gentiles, Saracens, and heretics and schismatics who have withdrawn themselves from the unity of the Catholic Church, are placed outside the ark of salvation; and if they persevere in error, without doubt they are to be damned forever with the demons.

    Since, therefore, faith is the foundation of salvation, without which it is impossible to please God, the monk must know what he ought to believe, and [unclear]. It is most shameful for a monk not to know the rules of the Christian faith, and to be utterly ignorant of what he is bound to believe for salvation. We do not say that by curious argumentation you ought to examine the things proposed to you for belief, since, as holy Pope Gregory says, faith has no merit where human reason provides proof. But this we advise: that the monk ought to be diligent in the divine Scriptures, so that he may know what holy mother Church commands to be believed, and may be able to guard against all errors contrary to the faith. Therefore let every monk, a soldier of Jesus Christ, be firm and steadfast in the Catholic faith; let him be sober and diligent in the Scriptures and constant in good works.

    The second thing which we believe necessary for a monk walking on the way of eternal salvation is that he should strive to know himself. For knowledge of oneself is the best of all forms of knowledge, and therefore rightly to be preferred to all the studies of mortals. Yet the beginning of this salutary knowledge is exceedingly difficult, because there are very few who do not love the world. For everyone who follows the world and loves the vanities that pass away cannot be a knower of himself. And nothing impedes a human being more from knowledge of himself than that human being himself. He who is fed on the pleasures of his flesh, who is lifted up into pride by the vain knowledge of this world, or by riches or honors, is not permitted to come to knowledge of himself. But to know many things and neglect oneself is not wisdom but rather madness. It belongs to the heap of a heavier damnation to learn many things and shamefully to be ignorant of oneself.

    Let each of you therefore consider what he is, whence he is, and what he is going to be. A human being, certainly, is nothing through himself; whatever he is, he is from God and for God. What is a human being except a wayfarer and pilgrim of, as it were, one day upon the earth, who today is seen alive in the world, but in the morning, snatched away by death, is seen no more? All our life, every action, every day, every hour shows how nothing we are: we who by living die, by acting are corrupted, with time are extinguished and changed. O tearful race of human beings, unstable, wretched, and weak, how airy, blind, and vain I perceive you to be, when I make comparison from those who have preceded us to death to us who are present.

    He spoke truly who compared you to the leaf of a tree. The wind, snatching it from the tree, casts it to the ground; in its place another new one afterward grows up, subject to a like fall. But what has fallen to the ground is dissolved in the ground, and thereafter never returns to the tree. Hence a certain sage of the Greeks says: “As is the race of leaves, so too is the race of men.” The race of man is very like the race of leaves, because it grows green for a time and is dissolved in the earth; neither does the leaf return to the tree nor the human being to life.

    There now follows the third thing which I think very necessary for a monk walking in the way of God: [unclear] the human being who [unclear] himself a wayfarer of this [unclear], not of exaltation and pride, but of much and continual humility, since we are earth and a certain compacting of dust, and after a few days are to return again into dust. But because true humility belongs to few, for that reason the way of salvation is called narrow and is found by few. By humility one comes to the kingdom, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel: everyone who humbles himself for God’s sake will be exalted, and he who exalts himself will be humbled.

    Sermon III.

    F. LXVII

    [unclear]. Fourth, for the monk journeying to heaven it is necessary [unclear]: that he make himself a stranger to every sin, because no one is admitted into the kingdom of God unless the highest purity of conscience commends him.

    A conscience adorned with holy virtues and good works is [unclear]: it opens heaven for those [unclear]; therefore it despises the world out of love.

    Hence Peter, Christ’s [unclear] and crucified [unclear], chief apostle, says in his second epistle: “But you, bringing all care to bear, supply virtue in your faith; and in virtue, knowledge; and in knowledge, abstinence; and in abstinence, patience; and in patience, piety; and in piety, love of brotherhood; and in love of brotherhood, charity. For if these things are known to be present in you and abound, they will not leave you empty or without fruit in the knowledge of our God Jesus Christ.”

    One virtue stands as a foundation, as witness [unclear], and as the way of good things; and, having shaken off other things from the flesh, it says [unclear], and carries us not into the fabulous Elysian fields of the poets, but into the angelic choirs: namely Christian faith, truly adorned with charity, which flees every sin.

    Fifth, the journey of the traveler to the heavenly kingdom is arduous: he undertakes it so that, by keeping the will of God, he may follow it in all things. Whatever is said or done, he examines the few things carefully, whether it accords with anyone [unclear] and with the ordinances of the Church. But if it is found to be contrary either to God or to the Church, let him flee it at once, lest he fall into sin.

    It belongs to a wise man [unclear] to examine all things [unclear] by the counsels of prudence, and to think carefully before he acts. But he who wishes to be [unclear] and secure on this road should imitate, in life and conduct, according to virtue, our God Jesus Christ, who is for all things in eternal life.

    Sixth, what we judge necessary for our traveler is that he diligently love the saving study of the Scriptures. Let him not be curious in reading, nor given over to vain studies, but simple, pure, and upright in mind.

    It does not befit a monk to cling to the writings of the Gentiles, nor to apply himself to the fables and foul studies of the poets. He who pursues vain things now, what will belong to wisdom? [unclear], because curious [unclear] quickly [unclear] and into sin. A monk must always flee every reading of vain superstitions; because it does not yield nor conduce to the divine knowledge of the Scriptures. Our traveler must abstain from it at all times.

    Seventh, we judge it very necessary for our traveler that he prudently direct his senses and thoughts, and guard them from every disordered desire.

    Our stubborn little ass must be restrained by the bridle of discipline [unclear]; the thorn of sin [unclear] into weakness. Whoever always thinks that he is walking in the sight of him who sees all things preserves his conscience pure and [unclear] with the greatest diligence.

    He is always watchful in the fear of God; always, out of love for the heavenly homeland, he chastises his little body with fasting and abstinence. The monk who recognizes that he is a pilgrim and stranger in this world never forgets the heavenly homeland, since he sees nothing on the way of the present life in which the soul should take delight.

    The eternal traveler [unclear] considers no spectacles of the road; nothing among passing things delights him in his pilgrimage, but at every time he sighs for the end of the journey. He always thinks sweetly of the homeland; he bears heavily that his pilgrimage is prolonged or delayed, and therefore he desires to have nothing in this world except the Lord Jesus, into whose sight he hastens diligently to appear.

    Eighth, necessary for our traveler is the tireless exercise of the love of God.

    For no one will be able to come to the heavenly homeland who departs, he says, from the path of charity. The charity of God is the way to God; if anyone has neglected it, burning within himself even briefly, he has strayed miserably from the true road of the heavenly homeland.

    For in Scripture charity is this: that he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. But he who is not in charity is already [unclear], because he has withdrawn from the way of salvation; and walking in the darkness of sins, he will never [unclear] to the kingdom.

    How sin is to be fled.

    Sermon V.

    You have heard, my dearest brothers, all that Saint John the Apostle says about sins. Whoever commits sin is of the devil, because from the beginning the devil sins.

    [unclear] and a judgment by no means to be feared [unclear]. If all who commit sin are of the devil, because in many things we all offend, then [unclear] we shall find all [unclear] from sin in many [unclear]. He says nonetheless, consequently: “Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.”

    Yet he had said beforehand: [unclear] “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” What, then, does this very contradiction mean? That no one is a son of God without sin, doing what is born of God? There is no [unclear] statement here. For [unclear] we believe that no one is without sin, because no one is without the law of sin; but he who is born of God does not commit sin, because in the law of the mind, that is, in charity, he definitely does not commit sin. For charity

    How Sin Is to Be Fled

    the multitude of sins; without it there is no good work, and it alone is able to blot out every sin. [Unclear], Saint Augustine says: “No holy and just man is without sin; nor for this reason does he cease to be just or holy, if he holds fast to holiness with affection. But those sins of the just are not to be considered mortal or enormous, but small and venial, without which a man scarcely lives this present life. For every sin is mortal when committed by a just man, if he must retain the name of justice. For mortal sin separates a man from God, kills the soul, and condemns it eternally with the demons.”

    By God’s grace we can beware of this deadly kind of mortal sin, and by uprightness of free will we ought carefully to do so. For this reason we have become monks: so that, living most cautiously under the rule of salutary obedience, we may not fall into the pit of mortal sin. Therefore the monk must always keep watch in good works, so that he may live free from mortal crime. Whoever feels his flesh troublesome and contrary to him in the way of God must, by remembrance of punishments, make it subject to the spirit, and, as it were, obedient through fear.

    Therefore, first of all, let the monk who is a lover of his own salvation always attentively consider the deceptive condition and deception of this world, and ponder how quickly every delight of the flesh passes away. Who will be able to draw his soul back from sins? He who has also diligently considered the very brief pleasure of the flesh and the punishment due to sinners. For the world passes away, and its concupiscence together with it. All who live pass away by dying, and no one is permitted to remain long in this life.

    For what is the world except a great, deep, and vast sea, in which there are as many creeping things of evils as there are evil desires of men ordered toward the good? O world, deceitful deceiver and unclean one, who foully deceives those who cling to you; all who follow you, you plunge into the depth of hell. How happy are those who despise you for love of Christ, and, making a useful separation from your vanities, depart from you in time. Whatever we discern in the world is vain, and every lover of the world is made vain and will shortly decay.

    Think that you will soon die, for nothing draws men back from sin as frequent and intent meditation on death does. For Scripture says: “Dwell upon your last things, and forever you will not sin.” The necessity of dying, when pondered, shakes the mind with fear and restrains it from vice.

    The second thing that persuades one to flee sin is fear of the future judgment, in which all men must be presented. No one can escape this dreadful judgment, and it is necessary

    Sermon V. Folio LXVIII.

    What shall we wretches say on that day, or where shall we stand before the stern judge, if, as the blessed apostle Peter says, the righteous man will scarcely be saved? If Jerome, a righteous and most holy man, feared the judgment to come, O good God, where will Trithemius, an unhappy sinner, appear? If the righteous man fears, where will the sinner stand? For what shall we say? Or what shall we answer, when we are gravely accused on every side? All the elements will stand against us as testimony; earth together with heaven will accuse us; and even if all things were silent, each person’s own conscience will be weighty. He who knows all things is ignorant of nothing, since there all things will be manifest to the one judging. There will be present the evils we have done, gravely accusing us; around and about us will be present, as testimony against us, countless demons; we shall see a dreadful chaos open beneath us; above us we shall behold the judge enraged; and from every side the utmost danger will threaten us.

    These dangers of the future examination, my brothers, always turn over in the memory of your heart, and consider diligently how dreadful it is to fall under the future sentence of the judge. In that terrible hour pure hearts will be worth more than the clever words of rhetoricians; a clean conscience will profit a man more than all the money in the world, since he who is to judge all things is not deceived, nor indeed changed by payment or prayers. O what incredible horror will invade all the impious when they are to hear the fearsome sentence: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” O the deepest sorrow of all evils, the most profound sadness of all sorrows: to be divided from the company of the saints and to be tormented with demons forever.

    Truly the day of judgment is dreadful and to be feared by all, because it is exceedingly bitter, where the gnawing worm of conscience does not die, where one once condemned to punishment is never freed. Therefore the monk who desires to obtain everlasting salvation should always keep himself, as far as he can, clean from every sin; and that voice, “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire,” should never depart from his memory. Hence the third thing which we judge greatly conducive to declining from sin is diligently to ponder the bitterness of the penalties of eternal damnation. For no temptation of carnal pleasure is so [unclear] that it will not at once fail, conquered, if the tempted person reflects with careful meditation on what the damned suffer in hell. What do the riches once possessed now profit the damned? What do past pleasures confer on the lustful placed in hell? What do the emptiest honors confer on the swollen with pride? What does power once widely held confer on the proud? Consider, brothers, what the damned now suffer in the lower regions, and, lest similar things befall you, persevere continually in good and holy works. If you fear hell, flee sin. For hell will harm nothing if a man remains in the faith of Christ, free from sins; nor will he burn in punishment who has not first burned here in guilt.

    The place of hell is to be feared, in which there is no redemption; but whoever once enters there condemned will not afterward go out to salvation. The wretched cry out in torments, in anguish, placed in everlasting horror, saying: What now does our pride profit us? Riches, honors, dignities, lust, gluttony, and all past carnal pleasures: what do they now profit us, damned forever? Behold, all things have passed away like a shadow, and all have vanished like the brief dream of one night. But we have been assigned to eternal torments, in which we know most certainly that there is no redemption. In hell, as Augustine testifies, even if there will be the sting of repentance, there will nevertheless be no correction of will in the damned; iniquity will be blamed by them in such a way that the equity of justice can by no means be loved or desired by them.

    There then the devouring flame of hell burns those whom carnal delight now defiles; and each person is burned so much the more in torments as here in the flesh he takes greater delight against God. In the lower regions, as Gregory bears witness, there will be intolerable cold, inextinguishable fire, the immortal worm of conscience, intolerable stench, palpable darkness, inestimable pains, scourges striking without interruption, the dreadful sight of demons, the confusion of crimes committed, and despair of all good things. But of all the punishments in hell, this is to be judged by far the gravest: that there the damned are deprived forever of the vision of eternal light. Here the most blessed bishop John Chrysostom says: Gehenna is more intolerable, and all men shrink from it. For who does not know that that punishment of hell is very horrible? Yet if anyone should posit a thousand, indeed ten thousand Gehennas, all that he says is nothing compared with this: the soul hated by Christ, driven away from the glory of the saints, and hearing that terrible voice from the mouth of the judge of all: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I do not know you,” and “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for you and the devil,”

    How sin is to be fled.

    [Unclear], a voice by far the most terrible of all terrible things: O sentence to be feared, and exceedingly horrible to all mortals, to be hated by Christ for one’s deserts, reproached by the judge, separated from the fellowship of glory, and no longer to retain any hope of recovery.

    Consider now, brothers, the punishments of the wicked that will most certainly come, and compare whatever pains of this life, whatever torments of the passing age, and all imaginable tortures of this world, with those eternal punishments of the damned, and they will be as nothing compared with something, imagination compared with truth, sleep compared with waking. You will easily overcome the temptations of the flesh and the law of sin, if you continually keep the thought of these things in your memory.

    O eternity, what an inconceivable time; an age without end; a world without time. Blessed is he who now foresees in time how, after this very brief life, he may fare well in eternity.

    The fourth thing that can draw a person back from sin is to keep continually in the heart the memory of future and everlasting happiness. Truly the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which shall be revealed in the saints, where there will be no discord, no dissonance at all, but the highest peace of all and the everlasting concord of rejoicing saints.

    In the blessedness of the holy ones in heaven there is true joy without sadness, peace without discord, goodness without malice, gladness without end, light without darkness, everlasting life without pain. There is sweetness without bitterness, rest without labor, praise without blame, love without vice, brightness without rust, satisfaction without disgust. Eternity remains without weariness; goodness abounds without defect; happiness continues without misery. For where God is all in all, perfect and full joy will be present for all. There the soul, or holy mind, is joined through love to its beginning; the intellect is perfectly illumined for contemplation of the highest good; from these two the enjoyment of eternal happiness is poured into those who exult. To know and love God in the kingdom of eternity is to possess, by enjoying it, the very glory of happiness. For to this end was man created: that he should understand that God his creator is the highest good; by understanding, love him above all things; and by loving, enjoy and possess him forever. This is the end of monastic institution; this is the destination of the Christian faith: that God, whom we now know through faith and love with our whole heart through works of charity, we may then in life perfectly understand and have as the perpetual object of our enjoyment.

    For the attainment of this everlasting happiness, dearest brothers, all good things must be done, even with the greatest labor; all adversities must be endured most patiently, because the very brief exercise of virtue brings us an eternal reward. Hear what on this matter the most holy bishop John says: “If every day,” he says, “we had to endure torments, if indeed we had to suffer Gehenna itself for a short time, so that we might see Christ reigning in eternal glory and be joined forever to the number of his saints, there would not be equal reason for all the sadness that can befall us, in order that we might deserve to possess the glory of so great a good.” But one does not arrive at the highest good except through the greatest labors, because, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence and the violent seize it.

    The fifth thing that ought to draw a person back from sin is to consider the honorableness of the human condition, which, by the natural guidance of reason, detests vice and loves the good of virtue. Every person who lives according to the rule of reason is a lover of virtue; but he who, defiled in the dung of vices, chooses to wallow there lives like a beast, not like a man. But by you, my brothers, vices must especially be detested and virtues loved, since for this reason you have despised the world, that in the monastery you might lead a life alien to sins and adorned with holy virtues. Therefore virtues must be cultivated by you, not the images of virtues. I say cultivated not with incense, not with sacrifice, but with love and the purpose of a most upright will. For to cultivate virtues is nothing other than to understand them attentively and to keep them inviolate, for the love of God, even unto death. For as Lactantius says, this is the office of virtue: not to sin. And therefore there is no true virtue except that which, through faith in Christ, tends toward that end where there is the highest good of man, than which there can be no better. But he who does not love God is not virtuous, since charity is the sum of all virtues. Therefore if you love God with your whole heart above all things, you are truly virtuous. Virtue is the way of good things, which through faith and love of Jesus Christ arrives at the kingdom. He who truly loves God does not sin, out of love of virtue.

    Consider your dignity, my brothers, and flee sin, because everyone whom pride puffs up, whom lust defiles, whom the other plagues of the soul infect, does not live as a man, but is confounded in himself and proceeds into the perdition of eternal death. For the more each person falls into sin, the farther he withdraws from God and the more he is brought near to hell. But since all people naturally desire the good, it is most shameful to love sin, because every sinner abandons the good and turns himself to evil.

    Sermon V.

    Sixth, it strongly draws the mind back from sin if, by habit, it continues always occupied in meditation on the Lord’s Passion. For who will be able to devote his effort to the pleasures of the flesh, if he has considered Jesus Christ, the ruler of the world, hanging for him on the cross? The death of Christ freed the world from eternal death; whoever carries this benefit with him in memory will easily abstain from every crime of vices. Finally, if anyone has considered God, present to him in every place and knowing and understanding all things, with the whole attention of his mind, he will without doubt always abhor every sin. For God is everywhere for us, not only present, but truly inward and most present; no secret escapes him, nothing remains hidden from him, but everything lies open and manifest to him. He searches the hearts of all; he knows the most secret things of thoughts, since he alone has true knowledge of all things. For who among mortals would dare, without the greatest shame, in the presence of so great a majesty, which he believes sees all things, if he weighs who and how great is the one who sees?

    Therefore, whenever the disordered motions of the flesh disturb the soul, think of the Lord God, who is the avenger of evils, as present; recall to memory the bitterness of the Passion of Jesus Christ; devoutly implore the aid of heavenly grace. Harder than stone is the man whom these things, considered rather diligently, have not been able to recall from the intention of sinning.

    The seventh thing that recalls the mind of a studious monk from the desire of sinning is that by continual reading he run through the passions of the holy martyrs. For indeed whoever rather often recalls to memory the invincible constancy of the holy martyrs of Christ cannot fail to become stronger and more robust in resisting sins. For this reason the brave deeds of the saints have been committed to writing: so that whenever we, weak as we are, read such things, we may rise up to imitation of those who have gone before. Do not look to those brothers who, with proud rashness, deny faith to the histories of the saints and think that the glorious things narrated about the most blessed friends of Christ are fables. For the virtues and good things that they do not find in themselves, they disdain to believe that the saints of God possessed. For there are many, and among them especially those who think themselves great because of their learning, who too rashly reject the histories of the holy fathers; and, since they themselves cannot enter upon the arduous path of virtue, they invent with windy talk that no one, or only rare persons, could have done so. Whatever arduous or great thing is read before them concerning the ways of life of the saints, they cry out that it is invented and fabulous; and, such as they themselves live, placed in the darkness of vices, they think that those whose histories they deride likewise passed their lives.

    But [unclear] a prudent and devout monk is not moved by the sloth of the proud, since he understands well that a certain effective power of exhortation is present in the histories of the saints. For, to confess meanwhile what is true, I am moved more toward devotion of inward fervor by the way of life of one saint than by many elaborate sermons, because, as the most holy pope Leo says, examples are more powerful than words, and it is more to teach by deed than by voice. But just as not all things please all people, so not all things suit all people. We advise each person to read more frequently and more zealously that by the reading of which the mind is stirred to greater perfection.

    The eighth thing that most strongly draws a man back from sin is charity, of which the holy apostle says: Charity is patient, is kind; it does not act perversely; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek what is its own; it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never falls away. He who loves God flees sin; but he who is the servant of crime certainly does not love God. The lover of God does not commit sin; and he who truly loves his Lord and always beholds him as present does not work iniquity. This is the highest and unchangeable good, for love of which sin is both to be fled and detested, since he who has deserved to sin only from fear of punishments does not ascend to the rewards of charity. For a servant does not sin from fear of blows, but a son withdraws from evil out of love for his parent, lest he offend his father’s mind.

    Let us avoid sin, my brothers, and with as much purity of mind as we can let us live in the sight of the Lord, because just as deadly poison, when taken, kills the body, so sin kills the soul of the offender. Therefore the wise man admonishes us in Ecclesiasticus, saying: Flee sins as from the face of a serpent, because if you approach them, they will receive you. The teeth of a lion are the teeth of sin, killing the souls of men. Like a two-edged sword is the iniquity of man; for its wound there is no healing. In Ezekiel also it is said: The soul that has sinned

    How sin is to be fled.

    [Whoever does this] imitates not God but the [unclear] of sin, the devil. Let us love God, and sin will not have dominion in us; let us love Christ, and we shall do nothing contrary to our salvation. Nothing is better, nothing stronger against sin, nothing safer than to love God, who first loved us and washed us from all sins in the blood of his only-begotten Son. For we are bound to God, and are obliged to love him with all the powers of the heart [unclear].

    First, indeed, God is to be loved by us supremely for no other reason than for his own sake, who is the highest and only good; in him alone are rest and the soul’s salvation; without him there is no salvation, no rest, no blessedness, no happiness, either in heaven or on earth. For since God is the cause, maker, and beginning of all things, he alone is the object of the soul’s blessedness; to the everlasting enjoyment of him one attains by charity alone, and one comes to love of him by purity of mind alone. Therefore, since God is the one and highest good of the soul, he is to be loved by us for his own sake with all our powers. Outside God there is nothing good, nothing holy, nothing by which the soul can be gladdened forever. For God alone is the center of the soul’s blessedness.

    Second, we are commanded to love the Lord our God, because he deigns to show himself to us as a most loving father. For thus he taught us to pray: “Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.” Truly God is the father of us all: he created us all, nourishes, feeds, and preserves us in being, lest we perish. There has never been any father on earth so indulgent, who loved his only-begotten son with so great a charity as that with which God almighty, our father, loves, cherishes, directs, and follows us with loving-kindness. Therefore we are obliged to love him with a pure heart above all things, who gives us both being and living. For he himself is our father; and Adam, who was created first of all men, did not know us.

    Third, we ought to love God above all things because of the likeness according to which man was made in the image of God, following his creator in his intellect by a certain likeness. But God is perfect intellect, infinite and everlasting; by participating in his goodness, our intellect is made blessed through grace in him who created all things. For although there is no comparison between God and man, nevertheless there is, in the rational soul itself, by the nobility of its created condition, a likeness to its beginning, of dignity not to be despised. For the prophet says: “I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” The Lord God also said in the beginning: “Let us make man to our image and likeness.” Great toward our race is the gracious condescension of divine mercy; it is fitting that we remember it at all times with a pure mind, in the observance of charity.

    Fourth, we ought to love our God above all things on account of his inestimable munificence, whom we acknowledge to have bestowed so many benefits on us though we did not deserve them. When we did not exist, he first established us in being by his goodness, and ordained us for a share in his glory, which will never end. Thus Scripture says concerning the nobility of man: “Thou hast made him a little less than the angels; with glory and honor thou hast crowned him, and hast set him over the works of thy hands.” Do you wish to know, brothers, in what respect man is less than an angel? Attend carefully to what we say here. Two intellects were created from the beginning, the angelic and the human. The angelic intellect, immediately from the beginning of its creation, was made full and perfect in the actuality of all knowable things, and by nature knew and comprehended everything that it ought to know; but the human intellect at first exists in potency with respect to all knowable things, ignorant of everything, while at the end, through many actions, it will at last acquire knowledge of all things, as the angelic intellect has it. For the perfect consummation of nature, which is in the angelic intellect from the beginning, will be given to the human at the end. Hence it is clear that between these two created intellects there is only this difference: the angelic is what it can be, while the human is to receive the likeness of angelic perfection at the end, that is, after the death of the flesh. For when the angelic intellect was first created, without any action of its own, immovably, substantially, and by nature, it was made full and perfect in the knowledge of all things; and those of them who adhered by love to their beginning, namely God, were confirmed in eternal happiness, while those who, glorying in themselves, withdrew in affection from God, are perpetually wretched and unhappy. But the human intellect, because it was created in the beginning in ignorance and deprivation of all things, must necessarily, by action, motion, and art, at last come to the knowledge of things set before it. So long as we are in the body and are pilgrims away from the Lord, our intellect, because of its excessive commerce with the body, is as it were placed in the darkness of ignorance and is confounded, and is by no means illumined unto perfect knowledge of future things. But afterward, when the soul has been separated from the body, then the intellect will rejoice in angelic perfection. Therefore we differ from the angels as much as we participate in bodily impurity.

    Fifth, God is especially to be loved by us, because he first loved us and washed us

    Sermon VI.

    from our sins in the blood of his only-begotten Son. The Creator supremely loves his creature, which he made from nothing; it is fitting that that creature itself should most greatly love its Creator, by whose goodness it was brought into being. God loves us with the greatest charity, than which no greater can be spoken or thought; and he loves us so much that he neither ought nor could love more, since in God all things are perfect, and in the immutable one there is no capacity for change.

    Consider now, my brothers, with how much fervor of mind and how much desire of heart a man ought to love his God, by whom, even without merits, he is [loved?] with the highest degree of love. Let us stretch out our soul in love of him above all things as much as we can; he is worthy that we should love him with all our strength. However eminently we may have loved God, who loves us, nevertheless we shall by no means reach that measure by which he loves us. For he himself, as we have said, loves us supremely, and his love toward us cannot grow further, since it is agreed that he loves his creature most perfectly. But however much we have loved him, we can always become more perfect in loving, and love more ardently until death.

    O we weak ones, we lukewarm ones, we consigned to a muddy prison: what shall we render to our lover [unclear]. After the death of Christ I reckon this to be [unclear] among the things set forth, since there is no comparison between the thing made and the maker.

    The sixth thing which can [bring?] us into the love of God is this: that no one outside the Christian faith will be saved, whether Christ is announced to him or he is wholly ignorant of him. How many kingdoms there are today in Asia and Africa, how many peoples, how many islands of the sea, among whom there is no knowledge at all of Christ and no faith, but every religion is in error and without the merit of salvation, even if outside Christianity they seem to adore and worship one God. For Christ is the savior of faithful souls; whoever has not believed in him is already judged, and without doubt will be condemned.

    [Unclear] what thanksgivings we shall be able to render to God, because he established us in the Catholic faith, so to speak, as [native-born?], and freed us from the destruction of death in the blood of his only-begotten Son. Let us therefore be mindful of so great a benefit, and let us take care to live in such a way that we may not be judged for ingratitude. Let us bless God the Father at all times, because he poured out the gifts of the Holy Spirit upon us, and did not permit us to be born far from the [bosom?] of the Church’s Catholic unity.

    The seventh thing which is believed able to produce love of him in our hearts is considered in the promise of everlasting happiness. For if we consider how great good things he has promised he will give in heaven, love of him will deservedly burn sweetly in our hearts. He promised his whole self to us as a reward, he who alone is the highest and utterly immutable good. Since he is indivisible, he will grant himself to be enjoyed by all in such a way that nevertheless he is possessed whole by each. He loves all by whom he is loved, and he loves each by whom he is possessed. The more we now love God with a pure mind, the greater reward we shall receive there.

    On the Knowledge of Spiritual Grace: Sermon Six.

    Saint Paul has taught us that not every spirit is always to be believed, but that impulses must be examined carefully, whether they are from God, who is the true light, lest perhaps something rise up against us from the side of darkness. For our adversary, since he is cunning, never sleeps, but devises a thousand ways by which he may catch us unawares. Yet he attacks those already advancing in one way, and acts differently with those who still dwell in the torpor of negligence. The more we have advanced in God’s commandments, the more necessary it is for us [unclear], since he knows that he cannot overcome by [unclear]. With many [devices?] envy rages against those who desire to please God out of love. In secret, under the appearance of good, [unclear]; under the appearance of good he tries to overthrow [unclear].

    Against him the best remedy is this: that a monk should submit all the thoughts of his heart to the examination of the elders. For demons hate the public light, and they are ashamed for the thoughts of the young which they suggest to come into the knowledge of spiritual elders. Let each one of you who thinks he stands in good always be anxious lest, with the devil overthrowing him, he fall. There are among you some who, both in years and in conversion, [unclear].

    On the Knowledge of Spiritual Grace.

    [unclear], who consent to their sensual appetites more than is expedient; demons mock them in various ways, as if under the appearance of good. They seek holiness without merit, and desire to have merit without the exercise of the necessary virtues. They seem to themselves great before God in devotion and pre-eminent, and in their animal passions they are not mortified.

    You err, O wretched men, and shamefully deceive yourselves, because without the foundation of most humble subjection and obedience you think to build the tower of holiness. First the disordered desires of sensuality must be mortified; the animal passions must be restrained: anger, murmuring, the rancor of indignation, and all impatience. For as long as vices rule over you, whatever offerings of private singularity you offer are not pleasing to God. All things are vain where there is not a pure conscience. The conduct of a young monk is suspect to us, however devout it may appear, when the humility of voluntary subjection does not commend it. For a monk without humility and obedience cannot be good, although by fasting and prayer he daily seeks holiness.

    The devil deceives many in the hiddenness of elation and pride, whom he permits continually to keep vigil, fast, and pray. For just as no works without humility and charity are pleasing to God, so fasting, vigils, prayers, and the studies of monks without these are not to be feared by the devil. The devil is not moved by this, by which he is not tormented. He does not much esteem the vigils of the proud man; then certainly he is moved against you, because he is tormented with envy at your virtues; he turns against you all the weapons of his cunning that he can, and strives with all his strength to overthrow your purpose of holiness. For nothing in a monk displeases demons more, nothing torments them more vehemently, than if for the love of God he has truly humbled himself in all things, and has always kept, with a cheerful mind, the service of the monastic institution under the guardianship of obedience.

    You must beware the impulses of demons, you who think yourselves something great without the merit of true virtues. I see that you are unwilling toward the commands of your elders, impatient and murmuring under correction, rather quick to rebuke another's life, but very slow in considering your own faults. These are the surest signs of the impulse of demons, and manifest indications that the necessary mortification of one's own will has been despised. You believe yourselves to be perfect and holy cultivators of great religion and inward devotion, and you have neither brotherly charity nor true humility, necessary for you as monks. You seek sensible devotion in prayers, and with eyes full of tears you now consider yourselves friends of God. For what? Do tears in prayers make one [holy?], when prayer is made with a certain elation of mind and without true humility? God gives tears; the soul struck by adversities gives them; the devil too, the deceiver of the proud, gives them. God makes fruitful with sweet tears the mind humbled in true charity, as though it were a meadow; nature stirs the weeping person in adversities; the devil pours little streams of waters into the proud under the likeness of devotion.

    Humility is the one virtue that, in the breadth of charity, makes human hearts truly devout. Nothing benefits you, O monk, whatever you may have done in your singularity, if you do not have true humility with the fervor of twofold charity. For to rise before others for the night praises; to say long prayers in private beyond the custom of the order; to continue a fast beyond the statute of the rule while others lawfully eat; to remain in secret while the rest go out to common labor: two things make these meritorious, and if they are absent all will be entirely fruitless. Indeed, whatever of a monk's works charity and humble obedience have not commended will be judged empty of merit before God and will lack reward. But you who with a swollen brow despise the precepts of the elders, doing by your own rashness not what they command but what pleases you; you who set your own inventions before the common holy exercises of the order, are still far removed from the way of life of the saints. It is not permitted you by your own rashness to abandon those things that belong to the monastic institution, and to prefer to necessary things the new and vain things that please you.

    Whatever work you do is unpleasing to God when the thing to which you are bound has been despised. The inspiration of divine grace teaches humility, persuades obedience, and follows true charity in all things; it keeps the commandment, admits no pride, despises no one, but pursues the perpetual integrity of regular discipline. But the impulse of the devil, under the appearance of good, cunningly trips up the unwary monk, and makes him subject in all things to his own judgment. It falsely tells him that all the things that pertain to preserving monastic integrity are badly instituted and contrary to him, and therefore are to be postponed to his own pursuits.

    Sermon VI. Folio LXXI.

    But in order that he may learn wisely to distinguish the Spirit of God from the impulses of the ancient enemy, mark what we say. First, then, let him judge that he has been inspired by the grace of God if he becomes daily purer in conscience and perceives [unclear] of the world to be decreasing. For wherever the Spirit of God has poured forth the gift of heavenly grace, every inclination to sin soon withdraws. But if a horror of sinning has not entered the mind, it is certainly manifest that the impulse of the devil has taken possession of the person. For when the Holy Spirit has penetrated a person’s mind, it either softens every fire of vice or wholly extinguishes it.

    Hence let each one of you examine himself diligently, and weigh by whose impulse he is moved. For the impulse of God diminishes a wicked habit, but that of the enemy increases it. Those whom the Spirit of God moves have sin diminished in them daily; but those who follow the impulse of the devil are rarely truly amended. The second sign of divine impulse is recognized from the increase of virtues, because the grace of the Holy Spirit always works great virtues in a person. Therefore, when you feel yourself advancing daily in the love of God and in good works, when you experience in yourself that the habit of sinning and every vice has less power from day to day, you ought humbly to acknowledge that the grace of God is present. For the love of God, which grace brings with it, is not idle, but is always usefully occupied in good works; it covers a multitude of sins, and does not permit the mind, exercised in useful things, to sin. The grace of the Spirit of God cannot stand together with sins, nor is it at all accustomed to be in a person without the fruit of action. The third sign of the Spirit of God in [unclear] is [unclear].

    On the Knowledge of Spiritual Grace.

    [They] despise all things of the present life. The soul which has God present within itself through love despises all comforts of the flesh; it longs to pass through hardships and to come to its God. It does not love the riches of this world; it spurns transitory honors and dignities; it strongly contemns the pleasures of the flesh. It meditates always on the law of the Lord, and never forgets the most bitter passion of Jesus Christ. Whoever among you is [unclear], brothers, let him do these things: let him [unclear] all the deceptive little consolations of this age, so that he thinks of nothing else, seeks nothing, desires nothing except the love of God. Whoever shall have obtained this sign of the present Holy Spirit, if he perseveres to the end of life, will be saved.

    The indication of the eighth good course. And then we receive the true sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit, when we humbly conform our wills in all things to the divine ordinances. This spiritual degree, when perfected, separates the monk from all the concerns of the world and calls him wholly to inward things. For the will, pleasingly subjected by affection to the divine will, separates him far from all desires that war against the spirit. Whoever has received this gift of grace of the Holy Spirit should first give thanks with humility, and should not vainly exalt himself on account of the gift; but rather, the more he has advanced, the more he should learn to humble himself in all things. Often the lofty man deserves to lose the grace of God, because he neglects to preserve it in the [unclear] of true humility. Therefore almighty God sometimes withdraws from those making progress the grace of sensible devotion for a short time, so that humility may increase in the mind, and the fervor of desire may burn more ardently to seek more. But since there are many causes among men for which God withdraws his grace from anyone, it will be worthwhile for them to be set out in order. First, then, God withdraws grace from a man because of sin, which stains the conscience with the foulness of vice. For our God, as Scripture says, is jealous and wishes to be loved alone; he does not love with any partner. Therefore whenever the mind, by desiring inordinately, turns back either upon itself or upon something else, alienated from its own beginning, which is God, it removes itself; whence it deserves to lose the grace which it had, because, when present, it would not guard the conscience inviolate. Hence the holy apostle of Christ, Paul, exhorts us not to receive the grace of God in vain, which indeed is then received fruitlessly and in vain when the mind of the recipient is made empty by the filth of vices. The little vessel into which we receive the grace of God is our conscience; when it is purified from vices and adorned with holy virtues, it is made worthy of the dwelling of the Holy Spirit.

    Sermon VII.

    Our temptation is wholly upon the earth; in it, if we do not advance in good, we fail; and there, as the holy Pope Leo says, we fall into the danger of failing when we withdraw our desire for making progress. Therefore flee sloth, and always keep watch in good works. Consider what happened to the lazy servant, who hid in a napkin the money of his lord which he had received for trading. Trade, men, I beg you, while there is time, and as long as you live be always occupied in good pursuits.

    Fourth, the grace of devotion is very often withdrawn from those who, placed under obedience, follow their own will. The monk who loves his own will most justly loses the grace of God. But he who for God’s sake humbly subjects himself in all things to the obedience of the shepherd, who spurns the will of his own heart, is filled with the various gifts of spiritual grace and illuminated by the light of inward fervor. We can offer nothing more precious and acceptable to God than if for love of him we deny our own will. Indeed, the very profession of monastic institution enjoins upon us, by necessity of salvation, to despise our own will and humbly to submit to him who has been set over us. Therefore the monk who follows the impulse of his own will is judged as an unclean vessel and unworthy of spiritual grace. Deservedly, then, the grace of God is withdrawn from the monk of his own will, who, living otherwise than he promised, lies to the Lord.

    Fifth, the grace of devotion is withdrawn from a monk when he thinks he has it by his own merits. He does not understand that sin dwells in him, unless because he ascribes to his own merits whatever good he has received. Against this ignorance of mind the holy prophet said to the Lord: Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty, because it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy. You turned your face away from me, and I was made troubled. No one [has] his devotion by his own merits, no holy man by his own powers.

    But let us recognize that all the causes of the withdrawal of the grace of God which we have mentioned pertain to our infirmity. Yet as for those who walk in perfection, another account is given, so long as they persevere. For from them the grace of God is never withdrawn, although the sensible fervor of compunction is sometimes taken away for a time. But we shall state in order the causes of this removal. First, almighty God sometimes withdraws the grace of sensible devotion from his lovers for a time, so that, while he seems not to be present when invoked, the desire of inward love may grow. All who feel the fire of divine love know this alternation of holy ardor, who are true emulators of the holy fathers. For whenever the bridegroom withdraws himself, the desire of the lover increases. She who seeks the Lord, burning with heat, whom she loves, groans for the desire of love.

    Secondly, this grace is withdrawn from the devout for an hour, lest frailty be lifted up into pride. For when, even unwillingly, we lose the grace of compunction, by humble examination we judge our infirmity, which can do nothing of itself. Therefore, so that devout worshipers of God may remain humble in their exaltation, it is necessary that they recognize their frailty.

    The third cause, indeed, merit requires, because to seek inward consolations belongs not to the strong but to the weak. The Lord must be served freely because he is good; but those who seek sensible sweetness in their devotion are delicate in the least things and seek the Lord Jesus for little consolations. The Lord must be loved usefully, and all womanish and soft affections are to be driven from the soul. Therefore, so that the Lord may increase merit for his worshipers in holy compunction, he sometimes denies the grace of sensible devotion to those who ask for it. But lest, affected by the bitterness of weariness, they grow wholly sluggish from the purpose of holiness, the consoler of the deserving does not withdraw far, but remains nearby. He swiftly returns to his friend, and the one whom he had pretended for an hour to be sad he consoles with the sweetness of spiritual presence.

    A fourth cause we join to these: that we are warned to walk more cautiously. For if we fear to lose the grace of compunction, let us learn to guard more diligently what we have. For a rare and precious treasure, the more it is loved, the more diligently it is guarded by its possessor. Therefore the monk who has deserved to receive from the Lord the grace of devotion must watch with the greatest care lest he lose it through his own negligence. But so that you may know how you ought to preserve the granted grace of compunction, lest it perish, the order of what is to be said will show you clearly. First, he who does not wish to lose the grace of inward compunction granted to him should strive, as far as he is able, to keep himself clean and pure from every sin.
