Let him beware not only of mortal and horrible crimes, but also of small ones, which are called venial, for he who despises the least things gradually falls, and he who does not beware of many small things often by habit makes one great thing.

    Second

    On the knowledge of spiritual grace.

    Third, if you do not wish to lose the grace of inward compunction, you should strive to love the quiet of solitude. For divine Scripture says: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet?” And again it says in another place: “In silence and in hope shall be your strength.” For the grace of inward compunction is quickly lost when the secrecy of solitude is not loved. Therefore let the monk who wishes to possess the grace of God learn gladly to remain with himself in his cell.

    Fourth, one must take the greatest care that you do not despise in your heart any person, however evil; for by the just judgment of God the grace of compunction is withdrawn whenever rash judgment concerning one’s neighbor is not avoided. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned.”

    Fifth, the monk who does not wish to lose the grace of inward devotion should strive to exercise himself in the cultivation of all virtues. Let him always keep watch in the fear of the Lord, always occupy himself in the exercise of divine love; let him be constantly assiduous in good works, and, as far as he is able, devout at all times in the remembrance of the Lord’s passion. For attentive meditation on the passion of Christ strengthens a person against all vices and preserves the grace of compunction.

    Sixth, be constant in holy prayers, because he who interrupts the practice of prayer is not able to preserve the grace of compunction. For the Savior says in the holy Gospel: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation.” The help of the Lord is close at hand for those who call upon him; but he who neglects to pray loses grace. But if you lose the grace of devotion in any way, you will quickly recover it by the following same six remedies.

    First, consider that without the grace of God you cannot make progress toward salvation, but that in all the good things you are going to do you are in the greatest need of his mercy. Recognize, therefore, that you are unworthy of the grace of God for doing good, although, because of the multitude of your sins, you know yourself to be unworthy. Call upon him, for he is near; and make every time that is granted you as free from the common exercises of the brothers be spent usefully and fruitfully. The grace of God is necessary for you for doing good; it is acquired by breadth of charity, guarded by humility, and recovered by the practice of saving penance. The Lord is with you so long as you have been with him in good will. But in order that you may be able to recover the lost grace of devotion, you must submit yourself to God in true humility.

    Second, for the recovery of the lost grace of compunction it seems necessary that you never lift yourself up against the Lord, but conform your will in all things to the divine ordering. We say in the Lord’s Prayer, “May his will be done”; it is fitting that we always voluntarily agree with that very prayer in mind and affection.

    Third, he who desires to recover the lost grace of devotion must strongly despise every pleasure of this world for the love of God. For it cannot happen that he recovers the spirit of inward compunction who opens the dwelling-place of his heart to earthly joys and pleasures. Therefore you must cast away every consolation of the present life, if you wish to have the divine spirit of love with its gifts.

    Fourth, you are commanded to withdraw yourself from the vain cares and occupations of this world for your own sake, and at every time to occupy your mind delightfully in the service of God. For, as the Lord says, no one can serve God and mammon; but whoever desires to serve the Lord in truth of heart must despise all the occupations of the world.

    Fifth, we advise that you remember always to occupy your heart in meditation on the passion of Christ, because there is no other way more expedient for recovering the delay [unclear] of compunction, nor any manner of prayer more effective for obtaining from the Lord whatever we have asked.

    Sixth, you should strive daily to cleanse your conscience by true penance; and whenever you have fallen into some fault, at once come to your senses through contrition. If you have taken care to keep these things with good will, by the mercy of God you will recover the lost grace of compunction.

    On the nine degrees of ascent.

    Sermon VII.

    With the pen we describe for you, dearly beloved brothers, the nine degrees by which the ascent of the human spirit into heaven is made. And although one is higher than another, nevertheless all and each direct one to the kingdom of God, and they are distinguished according to the merits of those ascending. Therefore attend diligently to what we are going to say, and consider how much you have made progress in spiritual advancement. All, as many as reach the kingdom of God, have ascended by the degrees of this ladder. The more anyone has made progress in the love of God, the higher he has already ascended.

    The first degree is nearest to hell, and

    Sermon VII.

    ... did not guard against them. No sin is so small that it is not made greater by neglect. For although we cannot wholly guard against venial sins, nevertheless we ought to take care with all our strength that they do not multiply in us. But those who, by the Lord’s mercy, make daily progress toward better things in this degree fall into sin more rarely. Yet as often as they have fallen, so often they rise again through penitence. Still, their state is close to danger, because, just as a garment torn too often is at last rendered useless, so a man who slips by sinning too often is frequently choked by evil habit. Yet if any depart from this life in this degree, by the Lord’s mercies, they will be saved not without the very grave pains of purgatory. Therefore one must hasten to higher things, so that not only mortal sins but also venial sins may be guarded against as far as one has strength.

    The second degree is believed to be ascended by those who strive, as far as they can, to avoid both venial and mortal crimes. But through excessive commerce with bodily weakness they do not persevere in their purpose, but frequently fall into the various negligences of this life, although they do not commit mortal sins. We who are lukewarm trust that we have somehow ascended to this degree: we who, placed under the observance of regular discipline, guard our minds from the graver sins with the Lord’s help. For because we are excessively lukewarm, we live very negligently and are slow to practise the exercises of holy virtues. But there are many established in the region of this second degree whom servile fear occupies; if it alone is present, it approaches the kingdom of God very little. For obtaining the glory of heavenly felicity, servile fear without charity will not suffice, because he is a slave who does not sin from fear of punishment, but a son does not do evil from the fear of God. Yet it is good to begin from servile fear, so that a man may gradually be able to arrive at filial fear, which is called chaste. For although to withdraw from evil from fear of punishments is quite insufficient for obtaining the kingdom of God, nevertheless it prepares the worker for filial fear. Hence it is the lowest degree of those making progress not to offend from fear of punishment, and not to sin lest they be condemned forever. For charity alone, discerning the merits of all, is admitted as fit to enter into the kingdom of God, and whatever has been done outside it is judged unworthy of the kingdom of God. Therefore whoever you are who have deserved to ascend according to this second degree, whoever you are who have learned not to sin from fear of punishments, if you wish to attain the joy of eternal felicity, take care to hasten as quickly as possible to higher things. For because, as Scripture testifies, no one suddenly becomes highest, we rightly permit you to begin from the lower things; but we judge it dangerous to stand long in the valley of shadows. Ascend, therefore, as much as you can each day, and do not wish to remain with beasts in the dung of foul-smelling actions, because if you do not make progress, you have failed; if you do not ascend, you descend.

    The third degree is comprised by those who, persevering in a good purpose, guard themselves from every mortal sin and also withdraw from venial sins as far as they can. They love purity of conscience and in no way commit anything that could stain it. Yet in one thing they are lower than those who follow, because, not withdrawing from evil and doing good simply for the love of God, they still remain with the weak far below the summit of holiness, in the lower places. He who truly loves God with a pure mind serves and ministers to him neither from fear of punishments nor in view of reward, but only for love of him. And for this reason all the aforesaid degrees are set before beginners; ascending gradually through them, they will at last be joined to the perfect. It is good to withdraw from evil from fear of punishments; it is good to do good for love of reward; and although it in no way suffices for perfection, nevertheless it provides the beginning and the path for those who desire to make progress. For servile fear, continued, begets filial and chaste fear; from its [unclear] spring perfect charity flows. But afterward, once charity has entered the mind, it casts out all servile fear and dread thereafter.

    The fourth degree, with all their zeal, guards them not only from mortal sins but also from venial ones, as far as is possible for them; they apply themselves most diligently to good and holy works and desire above all things to please God. In one thing they surpass the preceding, because they neither turn aside from evil from fear of punishments nor do good in hope of reward, but do all things for love of God alone and seek nothing other than the honor of God. This is the way set before those striving toward perfection; this is the true rule of holy justice: that we love God with a pure mind above all things and do all our works for his honor. For the true imitator of God neither fears punishment nor thinks of reward, but, walking in breadth of heart, commends his will to the divine ordinance. For God, because he is supremely good, must be loved not for the reward of the heavenly kingdom, nor for anything else, but for his own sake; and in every good work principally to be held in intention...

    On the nine steps of ascent.

    [Hasten?], my dearest brothers, to ascend this step of the spiritual ladder as quickly as possible, so that you may at some time be able to reach the summit of perfection. For if you, who have been placed under the obedience of monastic perfection, have advanced to this fourth step, you will now ascend the fifth without labor. For those who are placed on the fourth step do the good works of righteousness by their own will, since they have not submitted themselves, by vow or profession, to monastic constitutions. And in this one respect they are inferior to those who follow, because a good work is the more acceptable to God, the more it is commended by the merit of obedience.

    Therefore those ascend the fifth step who guard themselves from sins with all their strength and, being placed under obedience, always remain strong and constant in their resolve of holiness. Loving God above all things with a pure mind, they do good works chiefly for love of him; and in their intention they neither fear punishments nor seek rewards. They humbly obey their prelates for the love of God, and in no way wholly depart from the purity of regular observance.

    Among these are some whom the weakness of the flesh at times makes unstable in mind, and somewhat obstinate in their opinions against obedience. At times they try to defend their exercises and private little observances against the determination of their prelates, and to think themselves wiser than their rulers in the examination of spiritual matters. Flee this, O monks, because the devil lies hidden in ambush; and those whom he cannot conquer by open attack he strives to overcome by hidden contrivance. For the holier and more perfect a monk has been before God, the more readily he obeys his prelate without dispute. But if a perfect monk disdains to obey his abbot, though imperfect, in lawful and honorable matters, then surely he has lost the name of perfection. Therefore let each one be careful to apply himself to the pursuit of progress, so that he may presume to violate obedience in nothing. For Scripture says: Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to hearken is better than to offer the fat of rams. Whatever you have offered is another’s; but the truly obedient man offers himself.

    Therefore the sixth step is especially fitting for those who, living in all purity of mind and body, love the Lord above all things; who do every good they can for the honor of God alone; who do not depart from the commands of their prelates. Great is the virtue of obedience, which doubles a good work done and, increasing the merit of the one who performs it, presents him to God like a tree with its fruit. Let not the words of men who despise obedience move you, my dearest brothers: those who prefer freedom of will to the subjection of monks, and set a good work done from liberty before the merit of obedience. For even if a monk obeys from the necessity of his profession, nevertheless the good will by which, for love of God, he bound himself to obedience commends this necessity in many ways. There is a necessity by which a man is compelled to do something, where the will does not consent but always resists. This necessity diminishes the praise of virtue, because the good work was never in the will. There is also another necessity, arising from the inward inclination of the mind, which increases and does not diminish the praise of a good work, because it kindles the will more intensely toward the work itself. There is a third necessity, which has regard to the end and does not compel the will. For if you wish to cross the Rhine by boat, a fitting necessity requires an instrument. It is therefore necessary for a monk, on account of the end, to do what the abbot commands, so that he may be able to fulfill the vow which he made for the love of God. Therefore, since that end is very praiseworthy, by which the creature subjects itself out of love to its Creator, the necessity of obeying in a monk does not diminish the praise of a good work, but makes it greater. O happy necessity of monks, which took its beginning from the treasury of a good will, and is ordered to the end which is God, the unchangeable good. It is of greater praise, of more excellent merit, and of more abundant reward to do a good work from obedience by reason of a vow than if it is done without a vow from the liberty of one’s own will. But the monk once offered himself entirely, and all his will, to God, and reserved absolutely nothing for himself. Whatever good he does under obedience is brought back to the end of the religious life he has undertaken, to be preserved for the love of Christ; to this no work after martyrdom is compared. He who is continent without a vow from the venereal act performs one virtue, which is called chastity; but he who observes the same by reason of a vow steps higher, since toward the perfection of the whole religious life which he profess

    Sermon VII.

    To God and the power of acting. For no one has offered more to God than the monk who has given himself. But some who climb this sixth degree have hidden within themselves a certain defect of pride, because, while they look incautiously to themselves, they do not entrust themselves in all things to the divine will as they ought. This defect takes its beginning from a certain very subtle vanity, when the soul, trusting in its own purity, asks that some secret be revealed to it by the Lord. And in this one thing those who climb the sixth ladder differ from those of the seventh, who, being bound over to God, flee signs of vanity. For signs were given not to the faithful but to unbelievers; hence the monk who asks a sign from the Lord shows that he has not yet submitted himself perfectly to the divine will.

    Those ascend the seventh degree who keep all the things prescribed above most zealously, and, subject to God in all things, live without the stain of vanity. They flee every sin, both venial and mortal, as far as they can; they perform works of virtue for the love of God alone; [unclear] they seek no miracles of vanity. Whatever almighty God has ordained concerning them they receive gladly; they in no way at all depart from the observance of monastic purity. Yet in one respect they are inferior to those who follow, because they perhaps suffer some defect of which they are unaware, by whose impulse they sometimes commit something of their own sensuality.

    Whoever has deserved to ascend the eighth degree grants nothing further to sensuality. Here is the sweetest rest of the soul; here is perfect tranquillity of mind. Nothing vicious is left in this degree of beauty; nothing is found here that can sadden the soul. Here all things are clean, all things pure, all things holy, all things most sweetly burning with the fervor of charity. If only we may strive to ascend this degree; oh, if only we may sometime deserve to come into this harbor of tranquillity. The more one, standing in this holy ladder, has begun to taste the sweetness of inward delight, the more, hastening toward what lies ahead, he longs for it. Ever to be proclaimed are the desires of holy love, the exercises of venerable perfection, where the clean conscience of one who loves God shines without sins, where the wicked contests of vices have ceased and great tranquillity has succeeded.

    Those ascend the ninth degree who, already consummated in the eighth, keep all the things prescribed above purely and simply for the love of God, and desire nothing other than to praise, bless, and glorify God. Whoever has ascended this degree of perfection, as if forgetful of himself, resigns himself wholly to God and submits humbly. He counts himself unworthy of all God’s benefits; he cares nothing at all for himself, because he has already learned to commit himself wholly to God and humbly to be subject in all things to his ordering. Hence he neither asks for miracles nor seeks any consolations in this life, but with the holy apostle of Christ truly cries: To me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. For the world is crucified to me, and I to the world. For the true monk, lover of Christ, has offered himself wholly to God out of charity, and has despised the world with all its riches, honors, and vanities. Hence the world is said to be crucified to him, in which there is nothing that seems able to penetrate his mind. Happy are those monks who serve the Lord God with a pure conscience in true charity, who run without offense under the command of humility and obedience, who ascend this last degree of perfection. These are true monks, who seek nothing other than the honor of God. Indeed, my brothers, although monks are not bound by necessity of salvation to be perfect, for otherwise very few would be saved, nevertheless we are all bound with good will to strive toward perfection, and with whatever strength we can to long for this ninth degree. For it is very contrary to the monastic purpose to be unwilling to advance, and a kind of apostasy, after the vow of perfection, to wish to remain in imperfection. For the enemies of our salvation are the vices that attack us, and until they either conquer or are conquered, they do not cease to pursue us. Let us imitate the history of the ancient battle, when the sons of promise destroyed their enemies not in one day but successively. For it is difficult to conquer all things at once, unless the charity of God suddenly overshadows the mind. Against all the vices that attack us in whatever way, let us wage war: let us conquer gluttony today; when it has been rightly laid low, let us overcome sloth; and let us act so with the rest, that at last we may emerge victors over them all. The Lord will be present with us as we fight, and God will give victory to those who love him. Amen.

    The end of the second book of exhortations to monks by Johannes Trithemius, abbot, on the first day of September, 1486.

    These two books were printed at Strasbourg by Johann Knobloch, printer, at the expense of Johann Haselberger of Augia, in the diocese of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1516, on the twenty-fifth day of the month of August.
